There is no breast development or axillary hair. The abdomen is soft, nontender, and nondistended. Pelvic examination reveals normal external female genitalia and no pubic hair. Ultrasound confirms the presence of a uterus. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. FSH Ievel

In primary amenorrhea with absent secondary sexual characteristics, the first investigation is measurement of serum FSH to determine whether the cause is gonadal failure (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) or hypothalamic–pituitary dysfunction (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism).

Interpretation:

• High FSH → Primary ovarian failure/gonadal dysgenesis (e.g., Turner syndrome).
• Low or normal FSH → Hypothalamic or pituitary cause (e.g., delayed puberty, GnRH deficiency).

Key points in this patient:

Primary amenorrhea

• No breast development or pubic hair
• Uterus present on ultrasound
• This suggests lack of oestrogen production, so the next step is FSH measurement.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the OPD for a routine physical examination. The patient has not yet attained menarche. Height and weight are at the 85th percentile for age. Physical examination shows sexual maturity rating (Tanner stage) IV breast development with absent pubic hair. The abdomen is soft, nontender, and nondistended. A small, nonreducible mass is palpated in the left inguinal area. On pelvic examination, the external genitalia appear normal, and the vagina ends in a blind pouch. Ultrasonography confirms the absence of the uterus, cervix, and ovaries. Karyotype analysis reveals 46,XY. Which of the following is the best next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Elective gonadectomy procedure

This patient has Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS), characterized by:

• 46, XY karyotype
• Female external genitalia
• Absent uterus and cervix (due to anti-Müllerian hormone from testes)
• Blind-ending vagina
• Absent pubic/axillary hair (androgen resistance)
• Testes located in inguinal canal or abdomen

Management:

• Elective gonadectomy (removal of testes) after puberty to prevent malignant transformation (e.g., gonadoblastoma).
• Gonadectomy is delayed until after puberty because testicular androgens are aromatized to estrogen, allowing normal breast development.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 14-year-old girl presents to a government adolescent clinic with severe progressive dysmenorrhea since menarche, deep dyspareunia is not applicable, and a tender adnexal mass is felt on bimanual examination. Ultrasound suggests an ovarian cyst with internal echoes. There is no history of sexual activity. What is the most important associated condition to suspect in her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mullerian malformation

The clinical pattern suggests endometriosis presenting in adolescence, most likely an ovarian endometrioma.

• Progressive dysmenorrhea since menarche is a key red flag for secondary dysmenorrhea in an adolescent.
• Tender adnexal mass plus ultrasound showing an ovarian cyst with internal echoes is typical of an endometrioma, often described as a “ground-glass” appearance on ultrasound.

• In adolescents, a very important association to actively suspect is a Müllerian/outflow tract obstruction, which increases risk of endometriosis due to retrograde menstruation.

Other Options:

Option B. Cervical carcinoma: Unikely at 14 years and does not explain progressive dysmenorrhea with an adnexal cyst containing internal echoes.

Option C. Premature ovarian insufficiency: Would more typically present with oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea, low estrogen symptoms, and elevated gonadotropins, not a tender adnexal mass with internal echoes.

Option D. Polycystic ovarian syndrome: PCOS presents with oligo-anovulation, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology.

It does not typically cause progressive severe dysmenorrhea or a tender endometrioma-like cyst.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 14-year-old girl presents with irregular menstrual bleeding since menarche 10 months ago. Her cycles occur every 40–70 days and are occasionally heavy but painless. She has normal growth and development and is otherwise healthy. Physical examination shows Tanner stage IV breasts and pubic hair. Pregnancy test is negative, and laboratory evaluation reveals normal thyroid-stimulating hormone and prolactin levels. Which of the following hormonal patterns is most likely responsible for this patient’s menstrual irregularity?
options: Estrogen exposure without regular progesterone opposition
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Estrogen exposure without regular progesterone opposition

Irregular menstrual cycles during the first 1–2 years after menarche are commonly due to anovulatory cycles caused by immaturity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis.

Pathophysiology:

• Ovulation does not occur regularly
• No corpus luteum forms
• Progesterone is not produced cyclically
• Endometrium is exposed to unopposed estrogen
• Results in irregular, heavy, painless bleeding

Typical features:

• Adolescents soon after menarche
• Irregular cycle intervals
• Menorrhagia or prolonged bleeding
• Normal secondary sexual characteristics

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 14-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea. Examination reveals normal breast development with absent axillary and pubic hair. Pelvic examination shows a normally developed vagina with clitoromegaly and a microphallus. Ultrasound reveals masses in the inguinal region. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Partial androgen insensitivity syndrome

Partial androgen insensitivity syndrome (PAIS) is a disorder of sex development (DSD) caused by partial resistance of tissues to androgens due to mutations in the androgen receptor.

• 46, XY karyotype
• Testes present (often located in inguinal canal or abdomen)
• Variable virilization due to partial androgen action
• Ambiguous genitalia (e.g., clitoromegaly or microphallus)
• Primary amenorrhea
• Breast development may be present due to aromatisation of testosterone to estrogen
• Reduced or absent pubic/axillary hair due to impaired androgen effect

Why other options are incorrect:

• Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS): normal female external genitalia ; without clitoromegaly.
• MRKH syndrome: 46,XX with normal pubic/axillary hair and absent uterus/vagina, normal ovaries.
• Gonadal dysgenesis: streak gonads and poor breast development.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 15-year-old girl comes to the OPD due to pelvic and crampy lower abdominal pain that seems to recur at the beginning of each month and resolves after a day or two. The pain began approximately 6 months ago and has significantly worsened each month. The patient has never had a menstrual period. Breast and pubic hair development are at sexual maturity rating (Tanner stage) 5. Digital rectal examination reveals a palpable mass anterior to the rectum. A pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Imperforate hymen

Imperforate hymen is a congenital outflow tract obstruction that presents at puberty with primary amenorrhea and cyclic pelvic pain due to accumulation of menstrual blood.

• Normal secondary sexual characteristics (normal estrogen production)
• Primary amenorrhea
• Cyclic lower abdominal pain each month
• Pelvic/rectal mass due to hematocolpos or hematometra
• Negative pregnancy test

Menstrual blood cannot exit due to the imperforate hymenal membrane, leading to blood accumulation in the vagina and uterus.

Management: Cruciate incision of the hymen (hymenotomy)--> to drain the retained blood.

Why not the other options:

A) Androgen insensitivity syndrome:

• Patients have 46,XY, absent uterus, primary amenorrhea, and scant/absent pubic hair.
• Cyclic pain does not occur because there is no uterus or menstruation.

B) Asherman syndrome:

• Caused by intrauterine adhesions after procedures like D&C.
• Leads to secondary amenorrhea, not primary amenorrhea.

C) Endometriosis:

• Causes dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain--> but menstrual periods are present, not absent.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the OPD due to primary amenorrhea. Her height and weight are at the 60th percentile. Vital signs are normal. Physical examination shows Tanner stage IV breast development and pubic hair, normal external female genitalia, and axillary hair. Pelvic ultrasonography shows absence of the uterus. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
options: Complete defect in androgen receptor function
Congenital absence of an X chromosome
Defective conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone
Developmental failure of Müllerian duct formation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Developmental failure of Müllerian duct formation

Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser (MRKH) syndrome results from failure of Müllerian duct development, leading to --> congenital absence of the uterus and upper vagina.

• Primary amenorrhea
• Normal breast and pubic hair development
• Normal external female genitalia
• Normal ovarian function (46,XX karyotype)
• Absent uterus on ultrasound

Pathophysiology:

• Müllerian ducts normally form the uterus, fallopian tubes, cervix, and upper two-thirds of the vagina.
• Failure of their development causes uterine agenesis, while ovaries remain normal because they arise from gonadal ridges.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 15-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea, short stature, webbed neck, shield-shaped chest, and widely spaced nipples. Regarding this condition, all of the following statements are correct except:
options: Karyotyping is the investigation of choice and should be done in all suspected cases
Dysgenetic testes or undescended testes in mosaic Turner syndrome have increased malignant potential and require gonadectomy
Streak ovaries have high chances of malignancy and should be removed prophylactically
Associated abnormalities include bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of aorta, horseshoe kidney, SNHL, Hashimoto thyroiditis, diabetes, and celiac disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Streak ovaries have high chances of malignancy and should be removed prophylactically

This patient has Turner syndrome, characterized by:

• Primary amenorrhea
• Short stature
• Webbed neck
• Shield chest with widely spaced nipples
• Gonadal dysgenesis (streak ovaries)

Diagnosis

• Karyotyping is the investigation of choice
• Most common karyotype: 45,X
• Mosaic forms may also occur (e.g., 45,X/46,XY)

Streak ovaries themselves have a very low risk of malignancy and do not require routine prophylactic removal. However, patients with Y chromosome material (mosaic Turner syndrome) have an increased risk of gonadoblastoma, and therefore dysgenetic gonads should be removed prophylactically.

Turner syndrome is associated with:

• Cardiac: Bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of aorta
• Renal: Horseshoe kidney
• Endocrine/Autoimmune: Hashimoto thyroiditis, diabetes mellitus, celiac disease
• ENT: Sensorineural hearing loss

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl presents to the OPD for evaluation of painful menstrual periods. She attained menarche at age 13 and initially had irregular menses. Her cycles are now regular, occurring every 30 days with 4 days of moderate bleeding. Her menses have become increasingly painful; lower abdominal pain begins a few hours before menstruation and lasts 1-2 days, accompanied by fatigue, dizziness, and diarrhea. She misses school at least one day per month due to pain but maintains her grades and has no symptoms outside of menses. She has a history of depression, managed with therapy, with no recent mood changes. Vital signs are normal. Pelvic examination reveals normal external genitalia and clear cervical discharge. On bimanual examination, the uterus is mobile, nontender, and normal in size and contour. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Primary dysmenorrhea

Primary dysmenorrhea is caused by excess prostaglandin (PGF₂α) production from the endometrium during menstruation, leading to uterine hypercontractility, reduced uterine blood flow, and ischemic pain.

• Occurs in adolescents soon after ovulatory cycles begin
• Crampy lower abdominal pain starting just before or at onset of menses
• Pain lasts 24–48 hours
• Associated symptoms: nausea, diarrhea, fatigue, dizziness
• Normal pelvic examination with no structural pathology

Why not the other options:

• Adenomyosis: Usually in multiparous women >35 years with heavy menstrual bleeding and enlarged tender uterus.
• Endometriosis: Causes chronic pelvic pain, dyspareunia, infertility, and pain not limited only to menses.
• Somatic symptom disorder: Pain not cyclic with menstruation and no clear physiologic pattern.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl presents with a 3-week history of nausea, increased urinary frequency, and breast tenderness. She has never had a menstrual period. She is actively involved in her school’s volleyball team. She is 173 cm tall and weighs 54 kg (BMI 18 kg/m²). Breast and pubic hair development are Tanner stage V. Which of the following serum assays is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Human chorionic gonadotropin

In the evaluation of primary amenorrhea, the first step is always to rule out pregnancy, regardless of the patient’s age or reported menstrual history.

This patient has:

• Primary amenorrhea (no menarche)

• Normal secondary sexual characteristics (Tanner stage V)

Symptoms suggestive of pregnancy:

• Nausea
• Breast tenderness
• Urinary frequency

These symptoms strongly suggest pregnancy, so the most appropriate initial test is measurement of serum or urine β-hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin).

Why other options are incorrect

• TSH → evaluated after pregnancy is excluded if endocrine causes are suspected.

• LH → used to assess ovarian failure or hypothalamic causes later in the workup.

• Estriol → mainly used in fetal/placental assessment during pregnancy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old phenotypic female presents with primary amenorrhea, normal breast development, scanty pubic/axillary hair, bilateral inguinal masses, and absent uterus on USG. Choose the incorrect statement for the clinical condition:
options: Testosterone levels are decreased due to dysgenetic Leydig cells
Uterus is absent due to Mullerian duct regression
Breast development occurs due to aromatization of testosterone to estrogen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Testosterone levels are decreased due to dysgenetic Leydig cells

Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS) should be suspected in a phenotypic female presenting with:

• Primary amenorrhea
• Normal breast development
• Sparse or absent pubic/axillary hair
• Absent uterus
• 46,XY karyotype
• Normal testes are present
• Testosterone production is normal or increased
• Mutation of the androgen receptor causes target tissues to be unresponsive to androgens

Explanation of Findings

• Sertoli cells produce Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) → Müllerian duct regression → absent uterus, cervix, and fallopian tubes.
• Leydig cells produce testosterone normally.
• Testosterone is converted peripherally to estrogen → normal breast development.
• Lack of androgen action results in scant pubic and axillary hair.

The defect is not dysgenetic Leydig cells. In CAIS:

• Leydig cells are functional.
• Testosterone levels are usually normal or elevated male-range levels.
• The problem is androgen receptor resistance, not decreased androgen production.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 17-year-old adolescent assigned male at birth presents with concerns of inadequate masculinization during puberty. His parents report that his voice failed to deepen and he has sparse facial and axillary hair. Physical examination reveals well-developed gynecomastia, perineoscrotal hypospadias, and small inguinally descended testes with reduced testicular volume. Pubic hair is Tanner stage III and his height is normal. Laboratory evaluation shows: • Serum testosterone: normal to high • Serum LH: elevated • Serum FSH: normal • Serum DHT: normal Karyotype is 46,XY. Pelvic ultrasound demonstrates absence of Müllerian structures, and testicular tissue is present. There is no evidence of gonadal malignancy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Reifenstein syndrome

Decoding the Clinical Clues

| Finding | Interpretation

| ------- | --------------

| 46,XY karyotype | Genetic male — DSD category

| Perineoscrotal hypospadias | Incomplete virilization of external genitalia

| Gynecomastia | Peripheral estrogen effect unopposed

| Small descended testes | Testicular tissue present but dysfunctional

| No Müllerian structures | AMH secretion intact → normal

| Testosterone: normal/high | Hormone produced — receptor problem

| LH: elevated | Pituitary compensation for androgen resistance

| DHT: normal | 5α-reductase pathway intact

| Sparse facial/axillary hair | Partial androgen insensitivity

Why NOT the Other Options?

| Diagnosis | Key Differentiating Feature | Why Excluded Here

| --------- | --------------------------- | -----------------

| A. 5α-Reductase Deficiency | ↓↓ DHT with normal testosterone | DHT is normal here — rules this out

| B. Complete AIS (CAIS) | Female external genitalia, no pubic/axillary hair, primary amenorrhea | Patient has partial virilization — not complete insensitivity

| C. Klinefelter Syndrome | 47,XXY; azoospermia; tall stature | Karyotype is 46,XY — excluded immediately

| D. Reifenstein Syndrome | Partial AR mutation; incomplete virilization in 46,XY | ✅ Fits ALL findings perfectly

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 17-year-old adolescent presents to the gynecology clinic with a history of severe menstrual pain and recurrent pelvic infections since the onset of menstruation. She reports cyclical pain coinciding with menstruation and has experienced recurrent urinary tract infections. On physical examination, there is a palpable pelvic mass. Ultrasound imaging reveals a duplicated uterine cavity with one side showing an hematometra and absence of the left kidney. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Herlyn-Werner-Wunderlich syndrome

Herlyn–Werner–Wunderlich syndrome (HWW syndrome) is a rare Müllerian duct anomaly characterised by :

1. Uterus didelphys (double uterus)
2. Obstructed hemivagina leading to hematometra/hematocolpos
3. Ipsilateral renal agenesis

This is the classical triad of HWW syndrome.

Clinical Features:

• Cyclical pelvic pain after menarche
• Pelvic mass due to hematometra
• Recurrent pelvic infections or urinary symptoms
• Associated renal anomalies

Why not other options:

A) MRKH syndrome:

• Absent uterus, primary amenorrhea.
• Here duplicated uterus + hematometra present.

B) Asherman syndrome:

• Intrauterine adhesions after curettage.
• Causes secondary amenorrhea, not congenital anomaly with renal agenesis.

D) Endometriosis:

• Causes cyclical pain, but no uterine duplication or renal anomaly.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 21-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, at 36 weeks’ gestation presents to the hospital after being found to have a blood pressure of 190/110 mm Hg in the office. Initial laboratory studies show elevated serum creatinine and transaminases. She is treated with nifedipine and magnesium sulfate, and labor is induced with oxytocin. Six hours later, her blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. She now complaints of nausea, headache, generalized muscle weakness, and respiratory distress. On examination, deep tendon reflexes are absent. What is the most likely cause of the findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Renal insufficiency

This patient with severe preeclampsia was treated with magnesium sulfate, which is used to prevent eclamptic seizures.

Magnesium sulfate is excreted by the kidneys, so renal impairment can lead to magnesium accumulation and toxicity.

Features of magnesium toxicity:

• Loss of deep tendon reflexes (early sign)
• Muscle weakness
• Nausea and headache
• Respiratory depression/distress
• Severe cases → cardiac arrest

In this patient, elevated serum creatinine indicates renal insufficiency, which reduces magnesium excretion, leading to magnesium toxicity.

Management of magnesium toxicity:

• Stop magnesium sulfate
• Administer IV calcium gluconate as an antidote
• Provide respiratory support if needed

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22-year-old newly married woman presents with 8 weeks amenorrhea, nausea, breast fullness, and increased urinary frequency. On examination, the cervix is soft, bluish discoloration of vaginal mucosa is present, and painless rhythmic uterine contractions are felt on bimanual examination. Ultrasound has not yet been performed. All of the following statements regarding signs of pregnancy are correct, except:
options: Goodell sign refers to softening of the cervix and is one of the earliest probable signs of pregnancy
Hegar sign refers to softening of the uterine isthmus, allowing abdominal and vaginal fingers to approximate on bimanual examination
Chadwick sign denotes bluish-violet discoloration of vagina and vulva due to increased vascularity
Quickening is considered a positive sign of pregnancy because fetal movements are perceived by the mother
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Quickening is considered a positive sign of pregnancy because fetal movements are perceived by the mother

The diagnosis of pregnancy is traditionally divided into presumptive, probable, and positive signs.

• Goodell sign – Softening of the cervix
• Hegar sign – Softening and compressibility of the uterine isthmus
• Chadwick sign – Bluish-violet discoloration of the vagina and cervix due to increased vascularity
• Braxton Hicks contractions – Irregular, painless uterine contractions

These signs strongly suggest pregnancy but are not definitive.

Positive Signs of Pregnancy

• Fetal cardiac activity detected by Doppler/ultrasound
• Visualization of fetus on ultrasound
• Fetal movements palpated by the examiner

Quickening (maternal perception of fetal movements):

• Occurs around 18–20 weeks in primigravida and 16–18 weeks in multigravida
• Is a presumptive sign, not a positive sign
• Maternal perception can be mistaken for bowel movements or other abdominal sensations

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22-year-old nulligravid woman presents to the OPD with worsening acne on her face and body for the past 6 months. She initially attributed the acne to her diet and has been eating healthier to improve her acne and lose weight. She has lost 6.8 kg over the last 3 months; however, her acne has not improved. Her BMI is 42 kg/m². Coarse hair is noted on the chin and upper lip. Pelvic examination reveals clitoromegaly, with otherwise normal external genitalia. Laboratory evaluation shows elevated total testosterone levels with normal dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate levels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor

Sertoli–Leydig cell tumors are rare androgen-secreting ovarian tumors that cause rapid virilization in women.

• Marked hyperandrogenism → severe acne, hirsutism
• Virilization signs → clitoromegaly, deep voice, male-pattern hair
• Elevated testosterone with normal DHEA-S → indicates ovarian (not adrenal) source

Testosterone ↑ + DHEA-S normal → ovarian androgen-secreting tumor (e.g., Sertoli–Leydig cell tumor).

Why not other options:

• A. 21-hydroxylase deficiency: ↑ adrenal androgens → ↑ DHEA-S (not seen here).
• B. Adrenocortical carcinoma: Adrenal source → very high DHEA-S.
• C. PCOS: Mild hyperandrogenism; virilization (clitoromegaly) uncommon.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman comes to the clinic for a routine examination. She is a gymnast. Three months ago, she sustained a vulvar contusion during a competition but otherwise she has been healthy. The patient is sexually active with a male partner and uses an intrauterine device for contraception. She does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Examination shows a mobile, soft, nontender, flesh-coloured, 2-cm cystic mass at the 4 o'clock position at the base of the left labium majus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bartholin duct cyst

A Bartholin duct cyst occurs due to obstruction of the Bartholin gland duct, leading to accumulation of mucus and formation of a cystic swelling in the posterolateral vaginal introitus.

• Located at 4 o’clock or 8 o’clock position of the vaginal opening

• Soft, cystic, mobile, and usually painless if not infected

• Size may vary from 1–4 cm

• Occurs in sexually active women of reproductive age

When infected, it becomes a Bartholin abscess, presenting with:

• Severe pain

• Tender swelling

• Erythema and difficulty walking/sitting

Why other options are incorrect:

• Condylomata acuminata → multiple cauliflower-like warts caused by HPV (types 6,11)

• Gartner duct cyst → arises from mesonephric duct remnants, located on the lateral vaginal wall, not the vulva

• Hematoma → painful, bluish swelling following trauma

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman presents with an abdominal mass and raised AFP. AFP is never produced by which germ cell tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dysgerminoma

The patient has an ovarian germ cell tumor with elevated AFP, making yolk sac tumor the most likely diagnosis. Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is produced by yolk sac tumors and may also be elevated in embryonal carcinoma because of yolk sac differentiation. Choriocarcinoma secretes β-hCG, not AFP. Dysgerminoma, the ovarian counterpart of seminoma, never produces AFP; its characteristic tumor marker is LDH, and occasionally β-hCG may be mildly elevated if syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells are present. Therefore, an elevated AFP essentially excludes pure dysgerminoma.

Germ Cell Tumor Markers

| Tumor | Tumor Marker

| ----- | ------------

| Dysgerminoma | LDH (± mild β-hCG), AFP negative

| Yolk sac tumor | AFP ↑↑

| Choriocarcinoma | β-hCG ↑↑

| Embryonal carcinoma | AFP ± β-hCG

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 23-year-old female is being evaluated for infertility. Hormone studies reveal a normal rise in the blood estradiol level during the first phase of the menstrual cycle. Androgens synthesized in this patient's ovaries are converted to estradiol in which of the following cell types?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Granulosa

Estrogen synthesis in the ovary follows the two-cell, two-gonadotropin theory.

Key steps:

·         Theca interna cells (stimulated by LH) convert cholesterol → androgens (androstenedione/testosterone).

·         These androgens diffuse into granulosa cells.

·         Granulosa cells (stimulated by FSH) contain the enzyme aromatase, which converts androgens → estradiol.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 23-year-old primigravida at 35 weeks’ gestation presents to the emergency department with pedal edema. Her blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg, and urine dipstick testing shows 2+ protein. Laboratory investigations reveal the following: Hemoglobin: 9.2 g/dL Random blood sugar (RBS): 123 mg/dL SGOT: 250 IU/L SGPT: 300 IU/L Platelet count: 50,000/µL Serum creatinine: 0.7 mg/dL What is the next best step?
options: Corticosteroids followed by induction of labor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Induction of labor

This patient has preeclampsia with severe features consistent with HELLP syndrome, characterized by:

• H – Hemolysis
• EL – Elevated Liver enzymes
• LP – Low Platelet count

The definitive treatment of HELLP syndrome is delivery, regardless of gestational age once the diagnosis is made, especially after 34 weeks. Since this patient is 35 weeks pregnant, the next best step is immediate induction of labor (if there are no obstetric contraindications).

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

• Corticosteroids followed by induction: Steroids are used before 34 weeks for fetal lung maturity.
• Start labetalol and immediate LSCS: Cesarean is not required unless there is an obstetric indication.
• Induction at 37 weeks: Delay is dangerous because HELLP can rapidly progress to DIC, liver rupture, renal failure, and maternal death.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old primigravid woman at 10 weeks’ gestation is brought to the emergency department with vaginal bleeding and colicky suprapubic pain radiating to the back. Her temperature is 37°C (98.7°F), blood pressure is 110/76 mm Hg, pulse is 94/min, and respirations are 18/min. Physical examination reveals a dilated cervix with visible products of conception. Suction curettage is performed, and all products of conception are evacuated. Maternal serum laboratory results are as follows: Hematocrit: 32% Leukocyte count: 8,000/µL Blood type: AB negative Anti-Rh antibody titer: Negative Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?
options: Administer anti-D immune globulin to the woman.
No further workup or therapy for the woman or fetus
Order materal blood and endometrial cultures
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Administer anti-D immune globulin to the woman.

Rh-negative pregnant women exposed to Rh-positive fetal blood can develop Rh alloimmunization, leading to hemolytic disease of the fetus/newborn in future pregnancies.

Indication in This Case:

•

Rh-negative mother (AB negative)

•

Abortion with evacuation of products of conception

•

Negative anti-Rh antibody titer → not yet sensitized

Management:

Administer anti-D immunoglobulin (RhIg) to prevent maternal formation of anti-D antibodies.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old primigravida at 14 weeks gestation presents for routine antenatal visit. She has already been taking only folic acid supplementation since preconception. Hemoglobin is normal. What is the next best step in management?
options: Continue only folic acid till delivery
Give albendazole 400 mg immediately in first trimester
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Start IFA tablet — 1 pill daily

According to current antenatal care recommendations, all pregnant women should receive Iron and Folic Acid (IFA) supplementation to prevent maternal anemia and replenish iron stores.

• Folic acid is ideally started preconceptionally and continued during early pregnancy.
• From the second trimester (14–16 weeks onward), IFA supplementation should be initiated.

For a woman with:

• Normal hemoglobin
• No anemia
• Already taking folic acid

The recommendation is IFA tablet: 1 tablet daily (prophylactic dose)

Why Other Options Are Incorrect?

• Continue only folic acid till delivery: Does not meet increased iron requirements of pregnancy.
• Start IFA tablet — 2 pills daily: Reserved for treatment of anemia, not prophylaxis.
• Give albendazole 400 mg immediately in first trimester: Contraindicated; deworming is recommended after the first trimester in endemic areas.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks gestation presents to emergency with severe headache, vomiting, and blurring of vision for 6 hours. She also complains of epigastric pain. BP is 176/116 mmHg measured twice 15 minutes apart. Urine dipstick shows 3+ proteinuria. Reflexes are brisk and bilateral pedal edema is present. Fetal heart rate is 150/min. Platelet count is 95,000/mm³ and AST/ALT are mildly elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Start oral nifedipine and repeat BP after 24 hours
Immediate induction of labor without stabilization
Magnesium sulfate with antihypertensive therapy followed by delivery planning
Conservative management till 37 weeks with weekly monitoring
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Magnesium sulfate with antihypertensive therapy followed by delivery planning

Severe preeclampsia with impending eclampsia features present

Management priorities:

1. Prevent seizures → Magnesium sulfate
2. Control BP → Labetalol/Hydralazine/Nifedipine
3. Stabilize mother
4. Plan delivery

Definitive treatment: Delivery

| Condition | Gestational age | When to terminate pregnancy

| --------- | --------------- | ---------------------------

| Mild preeclampsia | ≥37 weeks | Deliver

| Mild preeclampsia | <37 weeks | Expectant management with close monitoring

| Severe preeclampsia | ≥34 weeks | Deliver after maternal stabilization

| Severe preeclampsia | <34 weeks | Expectant only if mother/fetus stable; give steroids, monitor closely

| Severe preeclampsia with danger signs | Any gestation | Immediate delivery after stabilization

| Eclampsia | Any gestation | Stabilize first, then deliver irrespective of gestational age

Danger signs requiring delivery

| Maternal | Fetal

| -------- | -----

| Uncontrolled BP | Fetal distress

| Eclampsia | IUFD

| Pulmonary edema | Severe FGR with abnormal Doppler

| HELLP syndrome | Abruption

| Renal failure/oliguria |

| Persistent headache/visual symptoms |

| Epigastric/RUQ pain |

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks is in the second stage of labor with full cervical dilatation. She has been pushing for 3 hours with good contractions. Fetal heart rate tracing is reassuring. On vaginal examination, the fetal head is at +2 station occipitoanterior, and a large caput is noted but no molding is present. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Forceps-assisted vaginal delivery

The absence of molding is the critical clue. Molding indicates the fetal skull bones are overlapping due to resistance from the pelvis — a sign of CPD. Its absence here means the arrest is likely due to inadequate expulsive effort, not a mechanical obstruction.

Forceps provide traction + rotation and are preferred over vacuum at +2 station OA in an arrested second stage with a reassuring FHR.

Eliminating the Other Options

A. Emergency C-Section ❌

• No fetal compromise, no CPD
• Head is deeply engaged at +2
• C-section at this station carries significant maternal risk (reverse traction, uterine extensions)

B. Vacuum Extraction ❌

• Vacuum is relatively less preferred here because:

• Large caput can cause cup displacement and failed vacuum
• Caput artificially inflates the apparent station
• Higher failure rate compared to forceps at this station

D. Expectant Management ❌

• 3 hours of pushing = arrested second stage by definition
• Continued pushing risks fetal acidosis, maternal exhaustion, and uterine rupture risk (prolonged second stage)

Forceps vs. Vacuum — Quick Comparison

| Feature | Forceps | Vacuum

| ------- | ------- | ------

| Caput present | ✅ Better choice | ❌ Cup displacement risk

| Rotation needed | Limited (Vacuum preferred)

| Gestation < 34 wks | ❌ Avoid | ❌ Avoid

| Maternal effort needed | Less | More

| Fetal risk | Facial nerve palsy (rare) | Cephalohematoma, subgaleal hemorrhage

Classification of Forceps Delivery

| Type | Station | Rotation

| ---- | ------- | --------

| Outlet | Visible at introitus / +5 | < 45°

| Low | ≥ +2 | < 45° or ≥ 45°

| Mid | 0 to +2 | Any

| High | Above 0 | ❌ Not performed

This case = Low forceps delivery — the safest operative category

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old primigravida is in labor. The baseline FHR is 110bpm. All of the following are possible causes of fetal bradycardia, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Maternal fever

Fetal bradycardia is defined as baseline fetal heart rate (FHR) <110 bpm for ≥10 minutes. It usually occurs due to reduced fetal oxygenation, fetal cardiac suppression, or maternal factors affecting fetal circulation.

Common causes of fetal bradycardia include:

• Maternal β-blocker therapy → crosses placenta and suppresses fetal heart rate

• Maternal hypothermia → decreases fetal metabolic rate and FHR

• Maternal hypoglycemia → reduces fetal energy supply leading to decreased FHR

• Fetal hypoxia/acidosis

• Cord compression

• Congenital heart block

Maternal fever, however, typically causes fetal tachycardia (>160 bpm) due to increased fetal metabolic rate and sympathetic stimulation (often seen in chorioamnionitis or maternal infection).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old primigravida presents with 6 weeks amenorrhea and mild spotting per vaginum. Transvaginal sonography reveals an intrauterine gestational sac with yolk sac, but no visible cardiac activity. Crown-rump length (CRL) measures 5 mm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Diagnose missed abortion as cardiac activity is absent at 6 weeks
Repeat TVS after 1 week before labeling nonviable pregnancy
Start medical termination because fetal pole is already visible
Diagnose anembryonic pregnancy because CRL is < 7 mm
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Repeat TVS after 1 week before labeling nonviable pregnancy

In early pregnancy, absence of fetal cardiac activity does not always indicate pregnancy failure. Diagnosis of nonviable pregnancy should be made only when strict ultrasound criteria are met.

Definitive diagnosis of pregnancy loss:

• CRL ≥7 mm with no cardiac activity
• Mean sac diameter (MSD) ≥25 mm with no embryo

Findings in This Case

• Gestational sac present
• Yolk sac present
• Fetal pole present
• CRL = 5 mm (<7 mm)
• No cardiac activity

These findings are suspicious but not diagnostic of pregnancy failure.

Appropriate Management: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound after 7–10 days

This allows confirmation of viability before diagnosing a missed abortion and avoids terminating a potentially viable pregnancy.

Key USG viability cutoffs

| Structure / finding | Earliest seen on TVS

| ------------------- | --------------------

| Gestational sac | 4.5–5 weeks

| Yolk sac | 5–5.5 weeks

| Embryo / fetal pole | 5.5 weeks

| Cardiac activity | \~6 weeks

Important diagnostic cutoffs

| Parameter | Important cutoff

| --------- | ----------------

| MSD cutoff to visualize fetal pole | 25 mm

| CRL cutoff for cardiac activity | 7 mm

| β-hCG discriminatory zone for gestational sac on TVS | \~2000 IU

Why Other Options Are Incorrect?

• Diagnose missed abortion as cardiac activity is absent at 6 weeks: Cannot be diagnosed when CRL is <7 mm without cardiac activity.
• Start medical termination because fetal pole is already visible: Not indicated until nonviability is confirmed.
• Diagnose anembryonic pregnancy because CRL is < 7 mm: By definition, there is no embryo/fetal pole present.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old primigravida with known Sickle cell disease at 30 weeks of gestation presents for antenatal evaluation. The obstetrician discusses indications and principles of blood transfusion during pregnancy in women with sickle cell disease. Which of the following statements regarding blood transfusion in pregnancy with sickle cell disease is true?
options: Routine prophylactic blood transfusion is recommended in all pregnant women with sickle cell disease
Goal of transfusion therapy is to maintain HbS concentration below 5%
Exchange transfusion is indicated in acute chest syndrome or severe sickle crisis
Prophylactic transfusion is contraindicated in twin pregnancy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Exchange transfusion is indicated in acute chest syndrome or severe sickle crisis

Pregnancy in women with sickle cell disease (SCD) is associated with increased maternal and fetal complications, including vaso-occlusive crises, acute chest syndrome, severe anemia, fetal growth restriction, and preterm birth.

Transfusion is not routinely recommended for all pregnant women with SCD. It is reserved for specific indications such as:

• Acute chest syndrome
• Stroke
• Severe vaso-occlusive crisis
• Symptomatic severe anemia
• Multiorgan failure
• Preparation for major surgery

Exchange transfusion is indicated in severe complications such as:

• Acute chest syndrome
• Severe sickle crisis
• Stroke

Why other options are incorrect

• A. Routine prophylactic blood transfusion is recommended in all pregnant women with sickle cell disease: Routine prophylactic transfusion is not recommended in all pregnant women with SCD due to risks of alloimmunization, iron overload, and transfusion reactions.
• B. Goal of transfusion therapy is to maintain HbS concentration below 5%: Goal is not to maintain HbS >20%; transfusion aims to reduce HbS levels (often <30–40% in severe situations).
• D. Prophylactic transfusion is contraindicated in twin pregnancy: Twin pregnancy is not a contraindication to prophylactic transfusion; management is individualized based on clinical risk.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with lower abdominal pain and an incidental adnexal cyst detected on ultrasonography. TVS shows a 5 cm simple ovarian cyst with no solid components, septations, or papillary projections. She has regular menstrual cycles and no family history of ovarian malignancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Measure AFP, hCG, and LDH levels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Start OCPs with follow-up ultrasonography

| Clinical Situation | Recommended Approach

| ------------------ | --------------------

| Reproductive-age female with benign-looking adnexal mass | Assess size of mass

| Simple cyst < 7 cm | OCP + follow-up USG

| Mass ≥ 7 cm | Surgery due to increased torsion risk

| CA-125 in reproductive-age women | Generally not routinely done because it can be elevated in benign conditions

| CA-125 > 200 IU in reproductive-age female | Suspicious for malignancy

| Adolescent female with adnexal mass | Evaluate germ cell markers: AFP, hCG, LDH

| Postmenopausal adnexal mass | CA-125 ≥ 35 IU suggests malignancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with oligomenorrhea, hirsutism, and obesity. Her LH:FSH ratio is 3:1. Which of the following lab findings is unchanged in PCOS?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. FSH

The patient has classical features of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), including oligomenorrhea, hyperandrogenism (hirsutism), obesity, and an elevated LH:FSH ratio (3:1). In PCOS, there is increased pulsatile GnRH secretion, leading to preferential LH secretion, which stimulates ovarian theca cells to produce excess androgens. FSH levels usually remain normal or are relatively low-normal, resulting in impaired follicular maturation and chronic anovulation. Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) is elevated because of an increased number of small antral follicles, while testosterone and DHEAS are commonly increased due to hyperandrogenism.

PCOS Hormonal Profile

| Increased | Normal/Usually Unchanged

| --------- | ------------------------

| LH | FSH

| Testosterone | Prolactin*

| DHEAS | TSH*

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with recurrent lower abdominal painthat occurs predictably each month. The pain is sharp, unilateral, lasts several hours, and resolves spontaneously without treatment. She notes that it consistently occurs about 14 days before the onset of her next menstrual period. She denies fever, vaginal discharge, dysuria, nausea, or vomiting. Physical examination between episodes is normal. Pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this patient’s symptoms?
options: Ischemia of the ovary due to intermittent torsion
Rupture of a dominant ovarian follicle with peritoneal irritation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rupture of a dominant ovarian follicle with peritoneal irritation

Mittelschmerz syndrome refers to midcycle ovulatory pain caused by rupture of the dominant ovarian follicle during ovulation. Release of follicular fluid and a small amount of blood leads to localized peritoneal irritation, producing unilateral, short-lived pelvic pain that occurs around day 14 of a 28-day cycle.

Key clues:

·       Cyclic, midcycle pain

·       Unilateral and self-limited

·       No systemic signs (fever, leukocytosis)

·       Benign condition requiring reassurance or ovulation suppression if severe

High-yield distinction:

o   Mittelschmerz → midcycle, brief

o   Endometriosis → cyclic but progressive, chronic

o   Ovarian torsion → acute, severe, persistent pain

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old female presented with hirsutism. Diagnosis of HAIR-AN syndrome was made. Which of the following statements is false regarding this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mild hyperandrogenism is seen

HAIR-AN Syndrome

Hyperandrogenism + Insulin Resistance + Acanthosis Nigricans

Why B is FALSE

HAIR-AN syndrome is characterized by SEVERE hyperandrogenism — not mild.

• Testosterone levels are markedly elevated
• Presents with virilization features (clitoromegaly, temporal balding, deepening of voice)
• Mild hyperandrogenism → just hirsutism/acne (seen in simple PCOS)
• HAIR-AN = extreme end of hyperandrogenism spectrum
•

| Statement | True/False | Explanation
| --------- | ---------- | -----------
| A. Severe insulin resistance | ✅ TRUE | Hallmark — type B insulin resistance (receptor/post-receptor defect)
| **B. Mild hyperandrogenism** | ❌ **FALSE** | It is **SEVERE** hyperandrogenism
| C. Temporal balding | ✅ TRUE | Sign of virilization due to severe androgen excess
| D. Clitoromegaly | ✅ TRUE | Virilization feature — seen due to marked hyperandrogenism

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old primigravida at 37 weeks’ gestation presents to the emergency department with constant, excruciating abdominal pain and sudden vaginal bleeding for the past 3 hours. She is Rh negative and received Rh(D) immunoglobulin at 28 weeks. Vital signs: - BP: 160/100 mm Hg - Pulse: 118/min Physical examination shows a firm and tender uterus. Speculum exam reveals moderate bleeding from an open cervical os. Fetal heart tracing shows a baseline of 105/min with no variability. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her bleeding?
options: Attachment of the placenta onto the myometrium
Injury to the fetal placental vessels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Premature placental separation

Painful vaginal bleeding in the third trimester with a tender, rigid (“board-like”) uterus is characteristic of placental abruption (premature placental separation).

Placental abruption refers to premature separation of a normally implanted placenta before delivery of the fetus, which leads to maternal hemorrhage and fetal compromise.

Key Clinical Features of Placental Abruption:

• Sudden onset vaginal bleeding
• Severe abdominal pain
• Tender, hypertonic uterus
• Maternal hypertension (a major risk factor)
• Fetal distress on CTG (bradycardia, decreased variability)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Attachment of placenta onto myometrium: Refers to placenta accreta spectrum, which presents with postpartum hemorrhage, not painful antepartum bleeding.
• Injury to fetal placental vessels: Seen in vasa previa, which causes painless bleeding after membrane rupture with rapid fetal distress.
• Placental implantation over cervix: Placenta previa, which classically causes painless vaginal bleeding with a soft, non-tender uterus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old primigravida presents with a history of a dog bite. Her neighbour’s pet dog has bitten her on the leg. She is currently 10 weeks pregnant. What is the next best step in management?
options: Clean the wound, administer tetanus and rabies vaccine
Clean the wound, administer only tetanus vaccine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Clean the wound, administer tetanus and rabies vaccine

Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is safe and indicated during pregnancy. Pregnancy is not a contraindication to rabies vaccination.

Management of dog bite in pregnancy:

1. Immediate wound cleaning with soap and water.
2. Tetanus prophylaxis (if immunization status uncertain).
3. Rabies vaccination ± rabies immunoglobulin depending on exposure category.

Important point:

Because rabies is almost universally fatal once symptoms develop, post-exposure vaccination must be given even in pregnant women.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman develops severe postpartum hemorrhage immediately after delivery of the placenta. On examination, a mass is felt protruding through the cervix into the vagina, and the uterine fundus is not palpable abdominally. She is hypotensive. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Johnson’s maneuver

Uterine inversion is a rare but life-threatening obstetric emergency in which the uterine fundus collapses and descends through the cervix, often causing massive postpartum hemorrhage and shock.

Clinical Features

• Severe postpartum hemorrhage
• Shock disproportionate to blood loss
• Fundus not palpable abdominally
• Smooth red mass protruding through the cervix or vagina

Immediate Management

The first step is manual replacement of the uterus (Johnson’s maneuver):

• The inverted fundus is pushed upward through the cervix toward its normal anatomical position.
• Reposition should be attempted immediately before edema develops.

Uterotonics should be withheld until after successful reposition, as they can cause cervical constriction and make replacement difficult. After reposition:

• Administer uterotonics
• Treat hemorrhage and shock
• Give antibiotics if indicated

Why Other Options Are Incorrect?

• Immediate hysterectomy: Reserved for irreducible inversion or uncontrolled hemorrhage.
• Administration of uterotonics before reposition: Worsen entrapment of the inverted uterus.
• Curettage of uterine cavity: Has no role in the management of uterine inversion.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman presents with primary amenorrhea, progressive virilization, and infertility. She was born with ambiguous genitalia. Physical examination reveals clitoromegaly, nodulocystic acne, and complete absence of breast development despite normal pubic and axillary hair. Her mother reports having developed severe virilization, acne, and a deepened voice during pregnancy with this patient, which resolved after delivery. Laboratory workup reveals: • Karyotype: 46, XX • FSH: elevated • LH: elevated • Testosterone: markedly elevated • Estradiol: undetectable • Androstenedione: markedly elevated Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal uterus with multicystic ovaries. Bone age radiograph reveals delayed bone age with unfused epiphyses. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of this patient's condition?
options: Failure of conversion of androgens to estrogens due to deficient CYP19A1 enzyme activity
End-organ resistance to estrogen due to mutated estrogen receptor
Deficiency of 21-hydroxylase leading to shunting of precursors toward androgens
Loss of GnRH pulsatility leading to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Failure of conversion of androgens to estrogens due to deficient CYP19A1 enzyme activity

This patient has aromatase (CYP19A1) deficiency, causing failure of androgen-to-estrogen conversion.

• 46,XX with ambiguous genitalia and virilization
• Primary amenorrhea and absent breast development
• Elevated testosterone and androstenedione
• Undetectable estradiol with ↑FSH and ↑LH
• Maternal virilization during pregnancy (classic clue)

Aromatase normally converts:

• Testosterone → Estradiol
• Androstenedione → Estrone

Deficiency leads to:

• ↓ Estrogen
• ↑ Androgens
• Virilization of both fetus and mother

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman with a history of peripartum cardiomyopathy following a previous pregnancy presents for preconception counselling. Her current echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 45%. What is the best advice regarding a future pregnancy?
options: Pregnancy is safe with lifestyle modifications
Pregnancy is safe with close monitoring and medical management
Pregnancy is safe as in the general population
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pregnancy is contraindicated

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a form of dilated cardiomyopathy occurring toward the end of pregnancy or in the postpartum period, characterized by left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) with a persistent LVEF < 50% is classified as a WHO Class IV cardiac condition in pregnancy — the highest risk category, for which pregnancy is contraindicated.

Key Principles

| LVEF at Assessment | Risk Category | Recommendation

| ------------------ | ------------- | --------------

| ≥ 50% (full recovery) | WHO II–III | Pregnancy may be considered with close monitoring

| < 50% (incomplete recovery) | WHO IV | Pregnancy contraindicated

This patient's LVEF of 45% represents incomplete myocardial recovery, which carries:

• High risk of further LVEF deterioration during pregnancy (due to the haemodynamic demands of increased cardiac output, blood volume, and heart rate)

Even with full recovery, recurrence risk of PPCM in a subsequent pregnancy remains \~20–30%

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman with a submucosal fibroid is undergoing hysteroscopic myomectomy using 1.5% glycine as the distension medium. During surgery, a 500 mL fluid deficit is noted. What is the next best step?
options: Change the fluid to normal saline
Continue the surgery with careful monitoring of fluid status
Give furosemide to the patient and continue surgery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Continue the surgery with careful monitoring of fluid status

During hysteroscopic procedures, distension media (eg, 1.5% glycine) are used to expand the uterine cavity for visualisation.

These hypotonic, electrolyte-free fluids can be absorbed into the systemic circulation, potentially causing fluid overload and hyponatremia.

Therefore, fluid deficit (difference between infused and recovered fluid) must be carefully monitored.

Recommended limits for fluid deficit:

• Hypotonic fluids (eg, 1.5% glycine, sorbitol, mannitol): ---> ≤1000 mL in healthy women
• Isotonic fluids (eg, normal saline, Ringer lactate): ≤2500 mL

In this case, the fluid deficit is 500 mL, which is below the safety threshold, so the procedure can be continued with close monitoring.

When to stop the procedure:

• Fluid deficit ≥1000 mL with hypotonic media.

• Signs of hyponatremia, pulmonary edema, or fluid overload.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old man presents with infertility and azoospermia. He has small firm testes and gynecomastia. Hormonal profile shows ↑FSH, ↑LH, and ↓testosterone. Which type of azoospermia is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Testicular azoospermia

| Type | Hormonal Pattern | Organ Affected | Example

| ---- | ---------------- | -------------- | -------

| Pretesticular | ↓FSH, ↓LH, ↓Testosterone | Hypothalamus/Pituitary | Kallmann syndrome

| Testicular | ↑FSH, ↑LH, ↓Testosterone | Testes | Klinefelter syndrome

| Obstructive | Normal FSH/LH/Testosterone | Ductal pathway | Vas deferens obstruction

Important Points

| ------------------

| Most important semen parameter = Morphology

| Most common reversible male infertility cause = Varicocele

| CF can cause congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman presents with 6 weeks amenorrhea and lower abdominal pain. Transvaginal sonography shows no intrauterine gestational sac but reveals suspicious adnexal findings. Serum β-hCG is 1800 IU/L. Repeat β-hCG after 48 hours rises to 2200 IU/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ectopic pregnancy

Serial β-hCG measurements are an essential tool in the evaluation of early pregnancy when ultrasound findings are inconclusive.

Expected β-hCG Changes

• Viable intrauterine pregnancy: β-hCG typically rises by at least 35–66% in 48 hours
• Complete abortion/failing pregnancy: β-hCG declines
• Ectopic pregnancy: β-hCG often shows a suboptimal rise or plateau

Findings in This Case

• Amenorrhea with abdominal pain
• No intrauterine gestational sac on TVS
• Suspicious adnexal findings
• β-hCG: 1800 → 2200 IU/L in 48 hours

This rise is inadequate for a viable intrauterine pregnancy, making ectopic pregnancy the most likely diagnosis.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

• Viable intrauterine pregnancy: Expected β-hCG rise is significantly greater.
• Complete abortion: β-hCG should be falling.
• Molar pregnancy: Usually presents with markedly elevated β-hCG levels and characteristic ultrasound findings.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman presents with amenorrhea of 7 weeks, lower abdominal pain, and spotting per vaginum. Pulse is 92/min and BP is 110/70 mmHg. Urine pregnancy test is positive. Transvaginal ultrasound reveals empty uterine cavity with a 2.5 cm right adnexal mass and minimal free fluid in pouch of Douglas. Serum β-hCG is 2400 mIU/mL. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
options: Expectant management with serial ultrasound after 6 weeks
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Single-dose methotrexate therapy

Methotrexate is the preferred treatment for a hemodynamically stable, unruptured ectopic pregnancy in appropriately selected patients.

Criteria Favoring Medical Management

• Hemodynamically stable
• No evidence of tubal rupture
• Adnexal mass typically <3.5–4 cm
• No fetal cardiac activity
• Serum β-hCG generally <5000 mIU/mL
• Patient willing for close follow-up

These findings are consistent with an unruptured ectopic pregnancy suitable for methotrexate therapy.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect?

• A. Emergency laparotomy: Reserved for ruptured ectopic pregnancy, shock, or hemodynamic instability.
• B. Expectant management with serial ultrasound after 6 weeks: Appropriate only when β-hCG is low and declining spontaneously.
• D. Dilatation and curettage: Does not treat ectopic pregnancy and may delay definitive management.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding and excessive nausea at 9 weeks of gestation. Pelvic examination reveals a uterus larger than expected for gestational age. Serum β-hCG is markedly elevated. Transvaginal ultrasound shows diffuse echogenic material filling the uterine cavity without evidence of an embryo. Suction curettage is performed. Histopathology reveals diffusely enlarged, edematous chorionic villi with circumferential trophoblastic proliferation. Immunohistochemical staining for p57 is negative. Which of the following best explains the absence of p57 expression in this patient’s lesion?
options: Inactivation of paternal genes by imprinting
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Loss of maternal chromosome contribution

This patient has a complete hydatidiform mole, characterized by:

• Markedly elevated β-hCG
• Uterus larger than dates
• Hyperemesis gravidarum
• “Snowstorm” appearance on ultrasound
• Diffuse hydropic villi with circumferential trophoblastic proliferation

Genetic basis:

• Complete mole contains only paternal genetic material
• Usually formed by:

• Fertilization of an empty ovum by one sperm followed by duplication, or
• Two sperm fertilizing an empty ovum

Why p57 is negative:

• p57 is a maternally expressed, paternally imprinted gene
• Complete moles lack maternal chromosomes
• Therefore, p57 expression is absent

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman undergoes medical management for incomplete abortion with misoprostol. A few hours later, she develops high-grade fever with chills, but there is no uterine tenderness or vaginal discharge on examination. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Drug-induced fever due to misoprostol

Misoprostol, a prostaglandin E₁ analogue used for medical management of abortion, commonly causes transient fever and chills as a pharmacologic side effect.

• Fever typically develops within a few hours of administration
• Often accompanied by chills, shivering, nausea, or diarrhea
• Usually self-limiting and resolves spontaneously
• Does not necessarily indicate infection

Misoprostol-induced fever:

• Occurs soon after drug administration
• No uterine tenderness
• No foul-smelling vaginal discharge
• No persistent fever or signs of sepsis

Septic abortion/endometritis:

• Persistent high fever
• Uterine tenderness
• Foul vaginal discharge
• Tachycardia and systemic toxicity
• Elevated inflammatory markers

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman, P2L2, is in the postpartum unit after an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery with involuntary dribbling of small amounts of urine. It has been 6 hours since the delivery and the patient has been unable to empty her bladder. During labor, she received epidural anesthesia for severe pain with contractions and her bladder was intermittently catheterized. The patient has no chronic medical conditions, takes no medications, and has no known allergies. Vital signs are normal. Examination shows a firm uterine fundus palpable at the umbilicus and fullness and tenderness above the pubic symphysis. The perineum and vagina are edematous but without lacerations. Sensation is intact in the lower extremities, but the patient is unable to void a measurable amount. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Urethral catheterization

This patient has postpartum urinary retention, characterized by inability to void with suprapubic fullness and overflow dribbling after vaginal delivery. Risk factors include:

• Epidural anesthesia
• Prolonged labor
• Perineal edema or trauma
• Intermittent intrapartum catheterization

Bladder overdistension can impair detrusor muscle function and increase the risk of urinary tract injury or infection. The most appropriate next step is Immediate urethral catheterization to decompress the bladder and measure retained urine volume.

Key distinctions:

• Oxybutynin is used for urge incontinence/overactive bladder
• Pessary placement is used for pelvic organ prolapse or stress incontinence
• Suprapubic catheterization is reserved when urethral catheterization is contraindicated or unsuccessful.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old pregnant woman presents in labor at 38 weeks of gestation. Her antenatal records show a positive GBS culture at 36 weeks. Membranes are intact, and she is afebrile. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: No antibiotic prophylaxis is required as membranes are intact
Delay antibiotics until rupture of membranes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Start intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis

Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is an important cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis. Universal screening is typically performed at 35–37 weeks gestation.

Women with:

• Positive vaginal/rectal GBS culture during the current pregnancy
• Previous infant with invasive GBS disease
• GBS bacteriuria during the current pregnancy

should receive intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, regardless of whether membranes are intact.

• IV Penicillin G (drug of choice)
• Ampicillin is an acceptable alternative
• Clindamycin or vancomycin for selected penicillin-allergic patients

Why Other Options Are Incorrect?

• No antibiotic prophylaxis is required as membranes are intact: Incorrect; a positive antenatal GBS culture itself is an indication.
• Delay antibiotics until rupture of membranes: Delays effective prophylaxis and increases neonatal risk.
• Give antibiotics only after delivery: Do not prevent neonatal early-onset GBS disease.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old primigravida undergoes first trimester screening at 12 weeks gestation. Ultrasound shows increased nuchal translucency measuring 3.8 mm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure because NT < 5 mm is physiological
Perform NIPT and quadruple test immediately
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Proceed with karyotyping

Nuchal translucency (NT) is measured between 11–13+6 weeks of gestation and serves as an important screening marker for chromosomal abnormalities and major fetal structural defects.

Significance of Increased NT

• NT ≥3.5 mm is considered significantly increased.
• Associated with:

• Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
• Trisomy 18 and 13
• Turner syndrome
• Congenital heart disease
• Genetic syndromes

Management: Offer invasive diagnostic testing (karyotyping)

• Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) in the first trimester
• Amniocentesis in the second trimester

An increased NT is an indication for diagnostic evaluation, not merely further screening.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect?

• Perform anomaly scan at 20 weeks: Important, but should not replace genetic evaluation.
• Reassure because NT < 5 mm is physiological: NT of 3.8 mm is abnormal and warrants further assessment.
• Perform NIPT and quadruple test immediately: These are screening tests; an increased NT already justifies diagnostic testing.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman is diagnosed with CIN 1 on cervical biopsy. On colposcopy, the entire dysplastic lesion is visible over the ectocervix and occupies less than 75% of the ectocervical surface. She undergoes cryoablation. Which of the following statements regarding this procedure is correct?
options: It destroys cervical epithelium up to 10 mm depth
Tissue is obtained for histopathological diagnosis during the procedure
Persistent watery discharge is the most common complication
General anesthesia is mandatory because the procedure is painful
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Persistent watery discharge is the most common complication

Cryoablation uses cold gases such as CO₂ or N₂O at very low temperatures to destroy dysplastic cervical epithelium up to a depth of about 5 mm. No anesthesia is required, bleeding is minimal, and the most common complication is persistent watery discharge. It is suitable only when the entire lesion is visible on the ectocervix and occupies less than 75% of the ectocervical area. Unlike LEEP/LLETZ, tissue is not obtained for diagnosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman presents for evaluation of infertility. She has been unable to conceive for the past 2 years. Her menses occur at 45–80 day intervals. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 77 kg (170 lb); BMI is 27.4 kg/m². Physical examination reveals facial acne and pigmented hair on the upper lip. Serum studies show elevated testosterone levels and an LH:FSH ratio of 4:1. Treatment with the appropriate drug for this patient’s infertility is initiated. Which of the following is the primary mechanism of action of this drug?
options: Activation of ovarian luteinizing hormone receptors
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inhibition of hypothalamic estrogen receptors

This patient has polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), suggested by:

• Oligomenorrhea (cycles every 45–80 days)

• Hyperandrogenism (acne, hirsutism, ↑ testosterone)

• Elevated LH:FSH ratio (\~4:1)

• Infertility due to anovulation

A common first-line ovulation induction drug is Clomiphene citrate.

Clomiphene is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that blocks estrogen receptors in the hypothalamus.

Resulting sequence:

1. Inhibits hypothalamic estrogen receptors → removes negative feedback of estrogen
2. ↑ GnRH release from hypothalamus
3. ↑ FSH and LH secretion from anterior pituitary
4. Stimulates follicular development and ovulation

Why other options are incorrect:

• Activation of pituitary dopamine receptors → mechanism of Bromocriptine, used for hyperprolactinemia.

• Inhibition of endometrial progesterone receptors → mechanism of Mifepristone.

• Activation of ovarian LH receptors → action of hCG, not used as first-line ovulation induction in PCOS.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman presents to the clinic for cervical cancer screening. HPV testing is positive for HPV type 18. What is the next best step in management?
options: Acyclovir and review after 6 weeks with repeat testing
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Colposcopy and biopsy

Detection of high-risk HPV types (especially HPV 16 or 18) during cervical cancer screening requires immediate colposcopic evaluation, even if cytology is normal.

• HPV 16 and HPV 18 are the highest-risk oncogenic HPV types associated with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and cervical cancer.
• A positive result for these types warrants colposcopy with directed biopsy to identify any precancerous lesions or early malignancy.

Why other options are incorrect:

• LLETZ: performed only after biopsy confirms high-grade lesions (CIN 2/3).
• Acyclovir: ineffective because HPV is not treated with antivirals.
• HPV vaccination: preventive, not used as treatment for existing infection.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman presents to the gynecology outpatient clinic with a 5-month history of complete absence of menstruation. She reports that her last menstrual period occurred immediately before an incomplete abortion for which she underwent uterine evacuation (suction curettage) 6 months ago. The procedure was reportedly complicated by excessive bleeding requiring a repeat curettage. Prior to this event, her menstrual cycles were regular, occurring every 28–30 days with normal flow. She and her husband have been attempting conception for the past 3 months without success. She denies hot flushes, night sweats, galactorrhea, headaches, or visual disturbances. Vital signs are within normal limits. BMI is 22 kg/m². Thyroid examination is normal. No galactorrhea on breast examination. Laboratory results: • Urine pregnancy test: Negative • FSH: 5.8 mIU/mL (normal) • LH: 4.2 mIU/mL (normal) • Prolactin: 14 ng/mL (normal) • TSH: 2.1 mIU/mL (normal) • Estradiol: 110 pg/mL (normal) Which of the following is the most likely cause of her amenorrhea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Intrauterine adhesions following uterine instrumentation

Asherman syndrome (intrauterine adhesions) is a common cause of secondary amenorrhea and infertility following uterine instrumentation, especially after postpartum curettage or evacuation of retained products of conception.

• Previously normal menstrual cycles
• Amenorrhea or hypomenorrhea after D&C/suction curettage
• Infertility
• Normal secondary sexual characteristics
• Normal hormonal profile (FSH, LH, prolactin, TSH, estradiol)

Pathophysiology

• Trauma to the basal layer of the endometrium
• Formation of intrauterine adhesions/synechiae
• Partial or complete obliteration of the uterine cavity

Diagnosis

• Hysteroscopy (gold standard)
• Hysterosalpingography or saline infusion sonography may show uterine cavity defects

Management

• Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis
• Postoperative estrogen therapy to promote endometrial regeneration
• Measures to prevent re-adhesion formation

Why Other Options Are Incorrect?

• Premature ovarian insufficiency: Elevated FSH with low estrogen
• Hyperprolactinemia due to pituitary microadenoma: Elevated prolactin, galactorrhea, menstrual disturbances
• Hypothalamic amenorrhea due to stress: Low/normal gonadotropins with low estrogen, often associated with stress, weight loss, or excessive exercise

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman presents with irregular menstrual cycles and difficulty losing weight. Her menses occur every 2–3 months. She reports acne and increased hair growth on her chin and lower abdomen. BMI is 31 kg/m². Physical examination reveals acanthosis nigricans. Laboratory studies show elevated free testosterone, decreased sex hormone–binding globulin (SHBG), normal prolactin, and normal TSH. Which of the following findings is most likely also present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased risk of endometrial hyperplasia

This patient has polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), characterized by:

• Oligo/anovulation
• Hyperandrogenism (acne, hirsutism)
• Obesity and insulin resistance
• Acanthosis nigricans

Pathophysiology:

• Chronic anovulation leads to prolonged estrogen exposure without progesterone opposition
• This causes continuous endometrial proliferation

As a result, patients with PCOS are at increased risk of:

• Endometrial hyperplasia
• Endometrial carcinoma

Why other options are incorrect:

• LH:FSH ratio is usually increased, not decreased
• Insulin levels are elevated, not low
• Primary ovarian failure presents with high FSH and estrogen deficiency

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman with PCOD has failed 3 cycles of clomiphene citrate and is reluctant to proceed with gonadotropin therapy. Laparoscopic ovarian drilling (LOD) is being considered. Which of the following regarding LOD is incorrect?
options: It is indicated in clomiphene-resistant PCOD
It reduces LH and androgen levels post-procedure
It carries a risk of premature ovarian failure if excessive drilling is done
It is the treatment of choice in obese PCOD patients
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It is the treatment of choice in obese PCOD patients

| Factor | Detail

| ------ | ------

| Obese PCOD | Treatment of choice = weight loss + lifestyle modification first

| LOD in obese | Poor response — obesity blunts the benefit of LOD

| LOD works best in | Lean PCOD with high LH, clomiphene-resistant

| Obese patients | Better served by gonadotropins + insulin sensitizers after weight loss

Why Others are Correct

| Option | Explanation

| ------ | -----------

| A | LOD indicated in clomiphene-resistant PCOD (failed ≥3 cycles CC) ✓

| B | LOD destroys androgen-producing stroma → ↓LH, ↓testosterone, ↓androstenedione → restores FSH:LH ratio ✓

| C | >4 punctures per ovary or excessive energy → premature ovarian failure risk ✓

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, at 40 weeks’ gestation presents to the hospital with painful contractions for the past few hours. She has no leakage of fluid or vaginal bleeding, and fetal movements have been normal. On admission, the cervix is 5 cm dilated and 90% effaced with the fetal head at -1 station. She received epidural analgesia. On repeat cervical examination, the cervix is 6 cm dilated and 100% effaced, with the fetal head still at -1 station. Two hours later, the cervix examination is unchanged. Fetal heart rate monitoring shows a baseline of 130/min, moderate variability, accelerations, and occasional early decelerations. The tocodynamometer shows contractions occurring every 5-7 minutes. Which of the best next step is management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oxytocin infusion

This patient is in the active phase of labor (≥6 cm cervical dilation) but shows no cervical change for 2 hours, indicating protracted or arrested labor due to inadequate uterine contractions.

• Cervix: 6 cm dilated, 100% effaced
• No progress for 2 hours
• Contractions every 5–7 minutes → inadequate frequency
• Reassuring fetal heart tracing (baseline 130, moderate variability, accelerations)

Management:

• Augment labor with oxytocin infusion to increase uterine contraction frequency and strength.

Why not other options:

• A. Cesarean delivery: reserved for failed augmentation or non-reassuring fetal status.
• B. Expectant management: inappropriate because contractions are inadequate and labor is not progressing.
• D. Vaginal misoprostol: used for cervical ripening/induction, not augmentation in active labor.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 28 weeks’ gestation presents for follow-up of an abnormal Pap test. The Pap smear shows a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL). Which of the following is the best next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immediate colposcopy

In pregnant women with HSIL (High-grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion) on Pap smear, the next step is immediate colposcopic evaluation to assess for possible invasive cervical cancer.

• Immediate colposcopy is recommended for HSIL cytology.
• Biopsy can be safely performed if suspicious lesions are seen.
• Excisional procedures (e.g., LEEP) are generally avoided during pregnancy unless invasive cancer is suspected.
• Definitive treatment of CIN 2/3 is usually deferred until postpartum.

Why other options are incorrect:

• HPV co-testing: not useful when HSIL is already detected.
• LEEP: avoided during pregnancy due to risk of bleeding and pregnancy complications unless malignancy suspected.
• Repeat Pap postpartum: delays evaluation and risks missing invasive disease.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old multigravida is taught fetal movement counting. She asks what “Cardiff count of 10” practically means. Which instruction is most accurate?
options: 10 movements in 10 minutes after a meal is reassuring
At rest, 10 fetal movements within 2 hours is reassuring
10 movements in 12 hours is required in all women
Maximum fetal movements occur at term, so counting is most useful after 40 weeks
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. At rest, 10 fetal movements within 2 hours is reassuring

The Cardiff “count-to-10” method instructs that fetal movements are counted daily, usually starting in the late 2nd to early 3rd trimester. The practical reassuring threshold is that 10 distinct fetal movements are perceived within 12 hours, and most fetuses achieve this much sooner. In day-to-day counselling and many exam stems, this is operationalized as “10 movements within 2 hours is reassuring,” and if 10 movements are not felt within the chosen counting window, reassessment and evaluation are advised.
