Among the given options, the most accurate practical instruction is that 10 movements within 2 hours at rest is reassuring.

Other options:

A. 10 movements in 10 minutes after a meal is reassuring

Incorrect. Ten movements in 10 minutes is not the Cardiff instruction and is too stringent and variable.

C. 10 movements in 12 hours is required in all women

This is closer to the original Cardiff framework, but the wording “required in all women” is not practical counselling. The method is to count until 10 are felt, usually within 12 hours, and the commonly used practical instruction is the 2-hour reassurance threshold.

D. Maximum fetal movements occur at term, so counting is most useful after 40 weeks

Incorrect. Counting is useful in the third trimester well before 40 weeks, and movements do not peak at 40 weeks in a way that makes counting uniquely useful only then.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old nulliparous woman being evaluated for infertility comes to the office due to clear vaginal discharge for the past 2 days. The patient and her partner have been trying to conceive for several months. Menstrual cycles occur every 29 days with 4 days of flow. Last week, she took penicillin for a sore throat. The patient has no medical issues and has had no surgeries. She takes a daily prenatal vitamin. Pelvic examination shows clear mucus at the cervical os. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's discharge?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ovulation

Around ovulation, rising estrogen levels stimulate the cervix to produce thin, clear, stretchy cervical mucus (often described as “egg-white” mucus).

·         Facilitates sperm transport through the cervix

·         Increases sperm survival and motility

·         Indicates the fertile window of the menstrual cycle.

Typical features of ovulatory cervical mucus:

·         Clear, watery, and elastic

·         Appears mid-cycle

·         Non-irritating and odorless

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester presents for routine antenatal evaluation. She complains of mild exertional breathlessness and pedal edema. On examination, vital signs are stable. Which of the following findings is not seen in normal pregnancy but suggests underlying cardiac disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Distended neck veins

Pregnancy produces several physiological cardiovascular changes that may mimic heart disease, including:

• Mild exertional dyspnea
• Pedal edema
• Physiological systolic flow murmur
• Tachycardia
• Supine hypotension syndrome (due to compression of the inferior vena cava by the gravid uterus)

However, certain findings are never considered normal in pregnancy and should prompt evaluation for underlying cardiac disease.

Raised jugular venous pressure (JVP) or distended neck veins suggests:

• Congestive cardiac failure
• Significant valvular heart disease
• Pulmonary hypertension
• Cardiomyopathy

Therefore, it is considered a pathological sign rather than a physiological change of pregnancy.

Why Other Options Are Normal?

• Exertional dyspnea: Common due to increased oxygen demand and progesterone-induced hyperventilation.
• Pedal edema: Common due to venous stasis and plasma volume expansion.
• Supine hypotension: Results from uterine compression of the inferior vena cava in late pregnancy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old primigravida at 30 weeks gestation is being evaluated for suspected fetal growth restriction (FGR). Based on different clinical scenarios, the obstetrician plans timing of delivery. Match the following conditions with the most appropriate timing of termination of pregnancy: Conditions: 1. Umbilical artery Doppler showing reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF) 2. FGR with EFW between 3rd–9th percentile with normal umbilical artery Doppler 3. FGR with abnormal Doppler with associated oligohydramnios 4. FGR with biophysical profile (BPP) < 4/10 Timing of delivery: a. Immediate termination b. 37 weeks c. 31–32 weeks d. 34 weeks
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1c, 2b, 3d, 4a

The timing of delivery in fetal growth restriction (FGR) depends on gestational age, fetal growth parameters, Doppler findings, and fetal surveillance tests

| Condition | Timing of Delivery

| --------- | ------------------

| Umbilical artery REDF | 31–32 weeks

| EFW 3rd–9th percentile with normal UA Doppler | 37 weeks

| Abnormal Doppler with oligohydramnios | 34 weeks

| BPP <4/10 | Immediate delivery

• REDF indicates severe placental insufficiency and high perinatal mortality risk.
• Normal Doppler with mild FGR can be safely monitored until 37 weeks.
• Oligohydramnios with abnormal Doppler suggests worsening placental function, warranting delivery at 34 weeks.
• BPP <4/10 indicates significant fetal compromise and requires urgent delivery regardless of gestational age.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old primigravida at 33+5 weeks presents with severe headache, blurring of vision, BP 170/116 mmHg, and epigastric pain. Urine albumin is 3+. Fetal NST is non-reassuring. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Start aspirin and strict bed rest
Immediate termination of pregnancy after stabilization
Wait for completion of full corticosteroid course before intervention
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Immediate termination of pregnancy after stabilization

Severe preeclampsia with impending eclampsia is an indication for immediate delivery

Features suggesting impending eclampsia:

• Severe headache
• Visual symptoms
• Severe hypertension
• Epigastric pain

Management priorities

1. MgSO₄ — drug of choice to prevent seizures
2. IV antihypertensives
3. Stabilize mother
4. Give first dose of corticosteroids
5. Immediate TOP (termination of pregnancy)

Do not wait for the second dose of corticosteroids before delivery in:

• Impending eclampsia
• Eclampsia
• HELLP syndrome
• Abruptio placentae
• Fetal distress
• DIC

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old primigravida with 33 weeks of gestation suddenly complains of headache, oliguria, and blurred vision. Her blood pressure is 180/110 mm Hg, and urine albumin is 3+. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Magnesium sulfate

Severe preeclampsia (BP ≥160/110 mmHg with symptoms such as headache, visual disturbance, oliguria) requires immediate seizure prophylaxis with magnesium sulfate.

• Symptoms like headache, blurred vision, and oliguria indicate severe features of preeclampsia.
• Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice to prevent eclamptic seizures.
• After stabilization, blood pressure control and planning delivery are considered depending on gestational age and maternal–fetal status.

Mechanism:

Magnesium sulfate acts as a central nervous system depressant and NMDA receptor antagonist, reducing the risk of seizures (eclampsia).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old primigravida with gestational diabetes is started on insulin at 26 weeks. As pregnancy progresses, her insulin requirement is expected to:
options: Decrease progressively due to improved insulin sensitivity
Increase due to placental hormone–induced insulin resistance
Drop sharply during the third trimester
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increase due to placental hormone–induced insulin resistance

Placental Diabetogenic Hormones

| Hormone | Effect

| ------- | ------

| Human Placental Lactogen (hPL) | Most important — potent insulin antagonist

| Progesterone | Peripheral insulin resistance

| Cortisol | Gluconeogenesis ↑, insulin resistance

| Prolactin | Anti-insulin effect

| Oestrogen | Mild insulin resistance

All increase progressively with placental growth → peak in 3rd trimester

| Trimester | Insulin Requirement | Reason

| --------- | ------------------- | ------

| 1st trimester | ↓ Decreases | Nausea, hCG effect, ↓ food intake

| 2nd trimester | ↑ Increases | Rising placental hormones

| 3rd trimester | ↑↑ Peaks | Maximum insulin resistance

| Delivery | ↓↓ Drops sharply | Placenta expelled

| Postpartum | Returns to pre-pregnancy | Hormones normalise

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old term pregnant woman is in labor. On PV examination, the umbilical cord is found prolapsed outside the vulva. What is the immediate step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Assess fetal viability

Umbilical cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency because cord compression can rapidly compromise fetal oxygenation and lead to fetal death. Once a prolapsed cord is identified, the first and most critical step is to assess fetal viability by confirming the presence of fetal heart activity.

Management depends on whether the fetus is alive:

• Viable fetus: Immediate measures to relieve cord compression (manual elevation of the presenting part, maternal positioning, bladder filling/Vago’s method) followed by expedited delivery, usually by emergency cesarean section.
• Nonviable fetus: Management is individualized, and emergency operative delivery may not be indicated.

Why the Other Options Are Incorrect

• Put the cord back

• Replacing the cord into the uterus is generally avoided because it may cause vasospasm and further compromise blood flow.

• Perform Vago’s method

• Useful after confirming fetal viability, but not the very first step.

• Start oxytocin infusion

• Contraindicated, as stronger contractions can worsen cord compression.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old with gestational diabetes mellitus ( GDM ) is being counselled. Consider the following statements. 1. DIPSI requires fasting. 2. Significant insulin resistance typically increases as pregnancy advances, with prominent rise in mid-second to early third trimester. 3. GDM does not increase congenital malformation risk 4. In pregestational diabetes, fetal echocardiography is indicated at 22 to 24 weeks. Choose the correct option.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4 only

Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) is characterized by progressive insulin resistance during pregnancy due to placental hormones (human placental lactogen, cortisol, progesterone).

• Insulin resistance increases as pregnancy advances, especially in the mid-second to early third trimester.
• GDM does not increase congenital malformations because hyperglycemia develops after organogenesis.
• Pregestational diabetes carries a higher risk of fetal cardiac anomalies, so fetal echocardiography at 22–24 weeks is recommended.
• DIPSI test does not require fasting (75 g glucose given irrespective of last meal).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman at 35 weeks and 3 days of gestation is found to have an amniotic fluid index (AFI) of 5 cm and absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF) in the umbilical artery on Doppler ultrasound. What is the most appropriate next step in her management?
options: Perform daily Doppler assessments and wait for improvement
Administer corticosteroids and delay delivery until 36 weeks
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Immediate delivery

Absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF) in the umbilical artery Doppler indicates severe placental insufficiency and fetal compromise, commonly seen in severe intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). This finding is associated with a high risk of fetal hypoxia, acidosis, and intrauterine fetal demise.

| Doppler Finding | Significance | Management

| --------------- | ------------ | ----------

| Increased S/D ratio | Early placental insufficiency | Close monitoring

| Absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF) | Severe placental resistance | Prompt delivery if ≥34 weeks

| Reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF) | Critical fetal compromise | Immediate delivery

Why other options are incorrect:

• Daily Doppler monitoring: Unsafe because AEDF signifies advanced compromise.
• Delay with corticosteroids: Steroids are mainly useful before 34 weeks.
• Wait until 37 weeks: Risk of fetal demise is high with AEDF.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman in labor presents with a brow presentation. What is the characteristic attitude of the fetal head in a brow presentation, and what is the most appropriate mode of delivery for this presentation?
options: The fetal head is partially extended; vaginal delivery with chin posterior
The fetal head is partially extended; cesarean section
The fetal head is fully extended; assisted vaginal delivery
The fetal head is flexed; spontaneous vaginal delivery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The fetal head is partially extended; cesarean section

In brow presentation, the fetal head is in a partially extended attitude, with the brow (forehead) presenting first. The presenting diameter is the mentovertical diameter (≈13.5 cm), which is the largest cephalic diameter and usually cannot pass through the maternal pelvis.

Therefore, persistent brow presentation is typically associated with:

• Obstructed labor
• Failure of vaginal delivery

Hence, the preferred mode of delivery is cesarean section.

Key distinctions:

• Vertex presentation → head flexed
• Brow presentation → head partially extended
• Face presentation → head fully extended

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents for evaluation of secondary amenorrhea. Menarche occurred at age 13, and her menstrual cycles were regular until she began combined oral contraceptive pills at age 20. She discontinued oral contraceptives 7 months ago in order to conceive but has not resumed spontaneous menses. She has no history of galactorrhea, visual disturbances, excessive exercise, or weight loss. BMI is 23 kg/m². Physical examination is unremarkable. Laboratory studies show normal TSH, prolactin, FSH, and LH levels. A urine pregnancy test is negative. She is prescribed oral medroxyprogesterone acetate for 10 days. Four days after completing the course, she experiences vaginal bleeding associated with mild cramping. Which of the following endometrial processes is most directly responsible for this patient’s bleeding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Apoptosis of endometrial cells

The progesterone withdrawal test is used to evaluate secondary amenorrhea.

Withdrawal bleeding after stopping medroxyprogesterone indicates:

• Adequate endogenous estrogen production
• An intact endometrium and outflow tract
• Chronic anovulation as the likely cause

Mechanism of withdrawal bleeding:

• Progesterone withdrawal causes breakdown of the functional layer of the endometrium
• This occurs through prostaglandin release, vasoconstriction of spiral arteries, and apoptosis of endometrial cells

Thus, endometrial shedding is primarily due to Apoptosis of endometrial cells

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman sustains a perineal tear during vaginal delivery. The obstetrician notes that the central fibromuscular node between the vaginal orifice and anal canal has been disrupted. Which of the following muscles does not attach to the perineal body?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Obturator internus

The perineal body is a central fibromuscular structure located between the lower vagina and anal canal. It is a crucial support structure for the pelvic floor and helps maintain pelvic organ support.

Muscles Attached to the Perineal Body:

• Bulbospongiosus
• Superficial transverse perineal muscle
• Deep transverse perineal muscle
• External anal sphincter
• Fibers of the levator ani (especially puborectalis)

Obturator internus does not attach to the perineal body.

• It arises from the obturator membrane and surrounding pelvic bones.
• It forms the lateral wall of the pelvis and exits through the lesser sciatic foramen to insert on the greater trochanter of the femur.
• It has no attachment to the central tendon of the perineum.

Clinical Importance:

• Perineal body injury can occur during childbirth.
• Damage weakens pelvic floor support and may contribute to:

• Pelvic organ prolapse
• Fecal incontinence
• Perineal pain

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1 living 1, at 34 weeks of gestation is brought to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding for the past 4 hours. She appears pale, anxious, and restless. On examination, her pulse rate is 120/min and blood pressure is 80/60 mmHg. Abdominal examination reveals a tense, board-like uterus with absent fetal heart sounds. Per vaginal examination shows the cervix to be 2 cm dilated and 70% effaced, with the fetal head at station –2. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Artificial rupture of membranes followed by oxytocin infusion
Administer corticosteroids and plan cesarean delivery later
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Immediate emergency cesarean section

This patient has abruptio placentae with concealed hemorrhage, evidenced by:

• Painful vaginal bleeding
• Severe abdominal pain
• Tense, board-like uterus
• Maternal shock (BP 80/60 mmHg, pulse 120/min)
• Absent fetal heart sounds
• Preterm gestation (34 weeks)

In severe placental abruption with maternal hemodynamic instability, the priority is saving the mother’s life through:

• Immediate resuscitation (IV fluids, blood products)
• Rapid delivery
• Correction of coagulopathy if present

Although the fetus is already dead, this patient has:

• Ongoing hemorrhage
• Maternal shock
• Unfavorable cervix (2 cm dilated, head at –2 station)

Vaginal delivery would be prolonged and delay control of the obstetric emergency. Therefore, immediate cesarean section is indicated to expedite delivery and improve maternal outcome.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect?

• Artificial rupture of membranes followed by oxytocin infusion: Appropriate only when maternal condition is stable and vaginal delivery is imminent.
• Administer corticosteroids and plan cesarean delivery later: No role in a maternal emergency with fetal demise.
• Perform urgent ultrasonography before intervention: Should not delay definitive management in a clinically obvious severe abruption.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2, at 31 weeks gestation comes for a prenatal visit. She reports increasing shortness of breath while climbing stairs and during long walks for the past few weeks. She has no cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, orthopnea, or sick contacts. Vital signs: BP: 110/80 mm Hg Pulse: 70/min RR: 18/min Fetal heart tones are normal and lungs are clear. Which of the following arterial blood gas findings is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. pH 7.45, PaCO2 29, PaO2 101

• Normal pregnancy causes a physiologic respiratory alkalosis due to the effect of progesterone on the respiratory center.
• Progesterone stimulates the medullary respiratory center, leading to increased tidal volume and mild hyperventilation. This results in increased CO₂ elimination.

Typical Arterial Blood Gas Changes in Pregnancy

| Parameter | Change | Reason

| --------- | ------ | ------

| pH | Slightly ↑ (\~7.44–7.46) | Respiratory alkalosis

| PaCO₂ | ↓ (\~28–32 mm Hg) | Increased ventilation

| PaO₂ | Slightly ↑ (\~100–105 mm Hg) | Improved oxygenation

| HCO₃⁻ | Slightly ↓ | Renal compensation

Thus, the typical ABG in pregnancy is:

• pH ≈ 7.45, PaCO₂ ≈ 29 mm Hg, PaO₂ ≈ 100 mm Hg → mild respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2, at 39 weeks gestation is brought to the labor room with active uterine contractions. On admission, per vaginal examination reveals cervical dilation of 6 cm, 70% effacement, and fetal vertex at -2 station. During examination, a loop of umbilical cord is felt prolapsing through the cervical os. Urgent bedside Doppler assessment and repeat auscultation fail to detect any fetal heart activity. A bedside ultrasound confirms absence of fetal cardiac motion. The patient is hemodynamically stable. Vitals: BP 118/76 mmHg, HR 88/min, Temperature 37°C. There is no evidence of uterine rupture or antepartum hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Initiate LMWH anticoagulation and proceed with cesarean section
Vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery for rapid fetal extraction
Allow labor to progress and await spontaneous vaginal delivery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Allow labor to progress and await spontaneous vaginal delivery

Umbilical cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency when the fetus is alive because cord compression can rapidly cause fetal hypoxia and death.

However, in this case:

• Cord prolapse is present
• No fetal heart activity is detected
• Ultrasound confirms intrauterine fetal demise (IUFD)
• Mother is hemodynamically stable
• No uterine rupture or major hemorrhage

Once fetal death has occurred, management should prioritize maternal safety rather than fetal salvage. Therefore:

• Cesarean section is not indicated solely for cord prolapse in a dead fetus
• Labor should be allowed to continue and vaginal delivery is preferred
• Operative interventions are reserved only for maternal indications

Why other options are incorrect?

• Immediate emergency cesarean delivery: Indicated only when the fetus is alive and salvageable
• Initiate LMWH anticoagulation and proceed with cesarean section: No role in management of cord prolapse
• Vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery for rapid fetal extraction: Requires a low, engaged head and is unnecessary at 6 cm dilatation

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old G2P1 woman at 34 weeks’ gestation presents with bright red vaginal bleeding that started suddenly while she was resting. She denies abdominal pain, uterine tenderness, trauma, or contractions. Her prior pregnancy was delivered by cesarean section. Vital signs are stable, and fetal heart rate tracing is reassuring. The uterus is soft and nontender on examination. Which of the following findings would most strongly support the suspected diagnosis in this patient?
options: Painful vaginal bleeding with uterine hypertonicity
Placental implantation over or near the internal cervical os
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Placental implantation over or near the internal cervical os

Placenta previa is characterized by placental implantation in the lower uterine segment, partially or completely covering the internal cervical os. It presents with painless, bright red vaginal bleeding in the third trimester and a soft, nontender uterus with reassuring fetal status.

Key  contrast:

• Placenta previa → painless bleeding, normal tone
• Placental abruption → painful bleeding, uterine tenderness, hypertonicity, fetal distress

A history of prior cesarean delivery is a major risk factor for placenta previa, making this distinction high yield.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old G2P1L1, Rh negative, spouse Rh positive, had no anti-D after previous delivery. At 18 weeks, ICT titer is 1:32. Ultrasound shows no hydrops. The most appropriate next step is:
options: Give anti-D 300 µg now and repeat at 28 weeks
Repeat ICT after 4 weeks and deliver at term if titer stays stable
Fetal surveillance with MCA-PSV Doppler from 20 weeks
Proceed to cordocentesis immediately at 18 weeks in all cases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fetal surveillance with MCA-PSV Doppler from 20 weeks

This is an alloimmunized Rh-negative pregnancy (no anti-D given previously, spouse Rh positive) with an indirect Coombs test (ICT) titer of 1:32 at 18 weeks. Once maternal antibody titers reach or exceed the critical titer (commonly 1:16, and in some labs 1:32), the risk of fetal anemia rises and management shifts from repeating titers to fetal anemia surveillance. The best noninvasive surveillance is middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) Doppler, typically starting around 18–20 weeks and repeating at intervals. Absence of hydrops does not exclude anemia, especially early.

Anti-D prophylaxis is not useful once sensitization has occurred. Cordocentesis is reserved when Doppler suggests moderate–severe anemia or when definitive fetal hematocrit is needed to guide intrauterine transfusion.

Other options:

A. Give anti-D 300 µg now and repeat at 28 weeks

Incorrect. Anti-D is prophylactic for unsensitized Rh-negative patients. This patient is already sensitized with a significant ICT titer, so giving anti-D will not prevent hemolytic disease in the current pregnancy.

B. Repeat ICT after 4 weeks and deliver at term if titer stays stable

Incorrect at this titer. Repeating titers is appropriate when the titer is below the critical threshold. At 1:32, fetal anemia surveillance is required even if the titer later appears stable.

D. Proceed to cordocentesis immediately at 18 weeks in all cases

Incorrect. Cordocentesis is not the next step for all cases. It is used when MCA-PSV suggests anemia or when there is a strong clinical indication for direct fetal hematocrit measurement and planning intrauterine transfusion.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old nulligravid woman presents for evaluation of infertility. She has been unable to conceive for 14 months. One year ago, she stopped taking oral contraceptive pills, which she had used since age 17. Her husband’s semen analysis is normal. Four years ago, she had an episode of pelvic tenderness and vaginal discharge that resolved without treatment. Her menses occur at regular 28-day intervals. Prior to marriage, she was sexually active with three male partners and used condoms inconsistently. She is 169 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 86 kg (190 lb); BMI is 31.6 kg/m². Physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s infertility?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Loss of ciliary action

Tubal factor infertility commonly results from prior pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) due to sexually transmitted infections such as Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

PID causes inflammation and scarring of the fallopian tubes, which leads to:

• Damage to the ciliated epithelial cells of the tube

• Loss of normal ciliary movement required to transport the ovum toward the uterus

• Tubal obstruction or impaired ovum transport, resulting in infertility or ectopic pregnancy

Why other options are less likely:

• Insulin resistance → associated with PCOS, usually with irregular cycles

• Ectopic endometrial tissue → endometriosis, typically causes pelvic pain/dysmenorrhea

• Primary ovarian insufficiency → amenorrhea with elevated FSH

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old pregnant woman is diagnosed with fetal growth restriction on ultrasound during routine evaluation. The diagnosis of early-onset FGR is considered based on gestational age and biometric parameters. Which of the following best defines early-onset fetal growth restriction?
options: Diagnosis before 32 weeks with estimated fetal weight (EFW) or abdominal circumference (AC) <10th percentile
Diagnosis before 32 weeks with EFW or AC <3rd percentile
Diagnosis before 34 weeks with EFW or AC <3rd percentile
Diagnosis after 34 weeks with EFW or AC <10th percentile
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diagnosis before 32 weeks with EFW or AC <3rd percentile

Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR) refers to a fetus that has failed to achieve its genetically determined growth potential and is associated with increased perinatal morbidity and mortality.

Early-Onset FGR

• Diagnosed before 32 weeks gestation
• Defined by:

• EFW or AC <3rd percentile, or
• Associated severe Doppler abnormalities

Late-Onset FGR

• Diagnosed at or after 32 weeks
• More commonly associated with milder placental insufficiency
• Often defined using EFW/AC <10th percentile with supportive Doppler findings

Clinical Significance of Early-Onset FGR

• Usually due to severe placental insufficiency
• Strongly associated with:

• Preeclampsia
• Abnormal umbilical artery Doppler
• Preterm delivery
• Increased perinatal mortality

Early-onset FGR requires:

• Serial growth scans
• Umbilical artery Doppler studies
• MCA and ductus venosus Doppler assessment
• Timely delivery based on fetal condition

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old primipara undergoes vaginal delivery. Active management of the third stage is planned, Oxytocin is available. The staff nurse prepares oxytocin in a dextrose 5% bottle because normal saline is out of stock. After starting the infusion, the patient develops headache, nausea, confusion, and a generalized tonic clonic seizure. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Water intoxication due to hypotonic free water load
Pulmonary edema due to oxytocin-induced myocardial depression
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Water intoxication due to hypotonic free water load

Oxytocin has an ADH-like effect because it is structurally similar to vasopressin and can promote water retention. When oxytocin is infused in 5% dextrose, the dextrose is rapidly metabolized, leaving free water, creating a hypotonic water load. This can precipitate acute hyponatremia, leading to headache, nausea, confusion, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. The mechanism is therefore water intoxication from hypotonic free water plus oxytocin-related antidiuretic effect.

Other options:

A. Acute hyperglycemia triggering ketoacidosis:

Unlikely. Dextrose infusion could raise glucose, but acute ketoacidosis requires insulin deficiency and typically presents with dehydration, Kussmaul breathing, and metabolic acidosis rather than acute seizures from neurologic symptoms soon after infusion.

C. Pulmonary edema due to oxytocin-induced myocardial depression:

Oxytocin can cause hypotension and fluid-related pulmonary edema in some contexts, but the dominant picture here is acute neurotoxicity and seizure, which is classic for acute hyponatremia.

D. Anaphylaxis to oxytocin preservative:

Anaphylaxis would present with hypotension, bronchospasm, urticaria, angioedema, and respiratory compromise rather than a hyponatremic encephalopathy pattern.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old with symptomatic uterine prolapse wants uterine preservation. A fertility-preserving sling cervicopexy is planned. Match the procedure to its anchoring structure. 1. Shirodkar 2. Purandare 3. Khanna A) Anterior superior iliac spine B) Rectus sheath C) Sacrum via lumbosacral fascia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1-C, 2-B, 3-A

Fertility-preserving sling cervicopexy procedures are differentiated by the structure to which the sling is anchored.

•

Shirodkar sling is anchored posteriorly to the sacrum via the lumbo-sacral fascia.

•

Purandare sling is anchored to the rectus sheath.

•

Khanna sling is anchored laterally to the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS).

Therefore, the correct matching is 1-C, 2-B, 3-A.

•

Sling cervicopexy is a uterine-preserving procedure used in women desiring future fertility.

•

Posterior anchoring to sacrum provides strong apical support but needs careful dissection to avoid pre sacral bleeding.

•

Anterior anchoring to rectus sheath and lateral anchoring to ASIS are alternative designs with different vectors of support.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a syncopal episode while getting out of bed. Yesterday, she developed right-sided abdominal pain, which has spread across the lower abdomen over the past few hours. She also noticed blood staining on her underwear after the syncopal episode. Her last menstrual period was 8 weeks ago. On Examination: - Temperature: 37°C (98.6°F) - Blood pressure: 90/60 mm Hg - Pulse: 125/min She has diffuse lower abdominal pain with rebound tenderness and voluntary guarding. Pelvic examination reveals cervical motion tenderness and right-sided adnexal tenderness, with no palpated masses. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ruptured ectopic pregnancy

Ruptured ectopic pregnancy should be suspected in a reproductive-age woman with amenorrhea, abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and hemodynamic instability.

• Amenorrhea (\~6–8 weeks)
• Sudden abdominal pain
• Vaginal bleeding
• Syncope or shock (hypotension, tachycardia)
• Cervical motion and adnexal tenderness
• Signs of hemoperitoneum (rebound tenderness, guarding)

Most ectopic pregnancies occur in the fallopian tube. Tubal rupture causes intra-abdominal bleeding, leading to hypovolemic shock.

Clinical takeaway:

In suspected ruptured ectopic pregnancy with hemodynamic instability, the next step is immediate surgical management (emergency laparoscopy/laparotomy) rather than further diagnostic testing.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old woman presents with chronic pelvic pain and severe dysmenorrhea that has progressively worsened over the past 3 years. The pain often begins 1–2 days before menstruation and improves afterward. She also reports deep dyspareunia. She has no history of sexually transmitted infections. Pelvic examination reveals nodularity and tenderness of the uterosacral ligaments. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of infertility associated with this patient’s condition?
options: Pelvic adhesions impairing oocyte release and tubal transport
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pelvic adhesions impairing oocyte release and tubal transport

This patient has endometriosis, characterized by ectopic endometrial tissue causing cyclic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia, and infertility.

Mechanism of infertility in endometriosis: Recurrent inflammation and bleeding lead to:

• Fibrosis and pelvic adhesions
• Distortion of tubo-ovarian anatomy
• Impaired oocyte release and ovum pickup
• Impaired tubal transport and fertilization

Classic examination finding is Tender nodularity of uterosacral ligaments

Common sites:

• Ovaries (“chocolate cysts”)
• Uterosacral ligaments
• Pouch of Douglas
• Pelvic peritoneum

Definitive diagnosis: laparoscopy with biopsy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 38 weeks’ gestation comes to the emergency department due to severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. The patient had an ultrasound at 8 weeks gestation for vaginal spotting but has not otherwise received prenatal care this pregnancy. Her prior pregnancy two and a half years ago ended in a classical cesarean delivery at 24 weeks gestation for placental abruption. The patient smokes a pack of cigarettes daily and uses cocaine multiple times a week. Blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg and pulse is 130/min. The abdomen is tender and has an irregular mass; no contractions are palpated. Bright red blood is noted on the perineal pad. Fetal heart tracing shows multiple prolonged decelerations to 100/min. Which of the following risk factors most likely contributed to this patient's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Prior uterine surgery

Uterine rupture is a life-threatening obstetric emergency that most commonly occurs in women with a prior uterine scar, especially after a classical cesarean section (vertical incision in the upper uterine segment).

• Sudden severe abdominal pain

• Vaginal bleeding

• Maternal hypotension and tachycardia (hemorrhagic shock)

• Loss of uterine contractions

• Abnormal fetal heart rate tracing (prolonged decelerations or bradycardia)

• Irregular abdominal contour or palpable fetal parts due to disruption of the uterine wall

A classical cesarean scar has the highest risk of rupture in subsequent pregnancies because the upper uterine segment contracts strongly during labor, placing significant stress on the scar.

Why other options are less likely:

• First-trimester bleeding → associated with miscarriage or placental problems, not rupture

• Illicit substance use (e.g., cocaine) → increases risk of placental abruption

• Short interpregnancy interval → minor contributor but much less significant than a prior classical scar

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, with gestational diabetes mellitus ( GDM ) is being treated with insulin. Which of the following statement is not true regarding the management of this patient?
options: Fasting blood glucose for controlled GDM should be <95mg/dL
Insulin is initiated when the 1-hour postprandial blood glucose is > 140 mg/dL
Insulin must be continued after delivery
Insulin does not cross the placenta
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Insulin must be continued after delivery

In gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), insulin therapy is used during pregnancy when glycemic targets are not achieved with diet and lifestyle modification. However, insulin is usually discontinued after delivery because placental hormones causing insulin resistance rapidly fall. Key management targets in GDM:

• Fasting glucose: < 95 mg/dL
• 1-hour postprandial: < 140 mg/dL
• 2-hour postprandial: < 120 mg/dL

Important facts:

• Insulin is the preferred pharmacologic treatment because it does not cross the placenta.
• Insulin therapy is started if glucose targets are exceeded despite diet control.
• After delivery, insulin resistance decreases, so insulin is generally stopped unless overt diabetes is present.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 0, presents at 13 weeks gestation. She has a history of two prior second-trimester losses at 16 and 19 weeks gestation, both characterized by painless cervical dilation. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a live intrauterine pregnancy with cervical length of 26 mm. On speculum examination, the cervix appears grossly normal with well-defined ectocervix and a visible external os. No prior cerclage has been attempted. Which of the following cerclage techniques is most appropriate as the first-line procedure for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. McDonald cerclage

This patient has cervical insufficiency, suggested by recurrent painless second-trimester pregnancy losses.

History-indicated cerclage is recommended in women with:

• ≥2 painless second-trimester losses, or
• Previous cerclage for cervical insufficiency

McDonald cerclage is the preferred first-line technique because it is:

• Simple and easy to perform
• Most commonly used
• Associated with good outcomes

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

• Shirodkar cerclage: More technically difficult; reserved for selected cases.
• Transabdominal cerclage (open/laparoscopic): Used when vaginal cerclage has failed or is anatomically impossible.
• Emergency (rescue) cerclage: Performed when the cervix is already dilated with bulging membranes.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the pediatric endocrinology OPD for evaluation of premature breast development and vaginal bleeding. She has no neurological deficits. MRI of the brain reveals a small, pedunculated non-enhancing lesion located in the hypothalamic region. Laboratory tests show elevated basal LH and advanced bone age. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Plan for neurosurgical resection of the lesion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Begin depot GnRH agonist therapy

This child has central precocious puberty (CPP) due to a hypothalamic hamartoma, a benign congenital lesion that causes pulsatile premature GnRH secretion.

• Early breast development and vaginal bleeding
• Elevated basal LH levels
• Advanced bone age
• Hypothalamic pedunculated non-enhancing lesion on MRI

Treatment of choice:

• Long-acting GnRH agonists (eg, leuprolide)
• Continuous stimulation desensitizes pituitary GnRH receptors
• Decreases LH/FSH secretion and suppresses pubertal progression

Why surgery is not first-line:

• Hypothalamic hamartomas causing CPP are usually managed medically
• Neurosurgical resection is reserved mainly for refractory gelastic seizures or mass effect

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old at 30 weeks is diagnosed with GDM. After 1 week of medical nutrition therapy, her 2-hour postprandial values remain 132 to 146 mg/dL. What is the next step?
options: Continue MNT alone because 2-hour PP target is <140 mg/dL
Start metformin as first-line in all GDM
Begin NST weekly immediately and ignore glycemic escalation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Add insulin plus continue MNT

Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is initially managed with medical nutrition therapy (MNT), exercise, and glucose monitoring.

Target Glucose Levels in GDM:

• Fasting: <95 mg/dL
• 1-hour postprandial: <140 mg/dL
• 2-hour postprandial: <120 mg/dL

If glycemic targets are not achieved within about 1–2 weeks of MNT, pharmacologic therapy should be started.

Since the postprandial glucose remains elevated, the next step is to initiate insulin therapy while continuing dietary management.

• Insulin is the preferred and safest treatment in pregnancy
• It does not cross the placenta
• Provides better control of maternal hyperglycemia

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

• Continue MNT alone: glucose levels exceed target.
• Metformin first-line in all GDM: may be used in some cases but insulin remains the preferred treatment when diet fails.
• Start NST and ignore glycemic control: fetal surveillance does not replace glycemic management.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old G3P1 presents at 18 weeks’ gestation for counseling regarding an increased risk for trisomy 21 on quadruple marker maternal serum screen. A targeted fetal anatomical survey shows no abnormalities. She understands the fetus may still have trisomy 21. What should she do next?
options: Nothing – It is likely a false-positive result
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Amniocentesis

A positive maternal serum screening test (eg, quadruple marker screen) for trisomy 21 requires confirmatory diagnostic testing, not reassurance alone. At 15–20 weeks gestation, the definitive diagnostic test is Amniocentesis with fetal karyotyping or chromosomal analysis

Key concept:

• Quadruple marker screening is a screening test, not diagnostic
• Even with a normal targeted ultrasound, aneuploidy cannot be excluded

Why amniocentesis is preferred here:

• Performed after 15 weeks gestation
• Provides definitive fetal chromosomal diagnosis
• Detects trisomy 21 with high accuracy

Why other options are incorrect:

• Cell-free DNA (NIPT) → highly sensitive screening test but still not diagnostic
• Repeat anatomy scan → cannot reliably exclude chromosomal abnormalities
• Reassurance only → inappropriate after positive screening result

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old married woman presents for infertility evaluation. Investigations reveal intramural fibroids measuring 7 × 5 cm and 5 × 3 cm at the right and left cornual ends of the uterus. Her husband’s semen analysis is normal. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Laparoscopic Myomectomy

Intramural fibroids, especially those large or located near the cornual region --> can impair fertility by distorting uterine architecture, affecting tubal patency, and interfering with implantation.

• In women with infertility and significant intramural fibroids (>4–5 cm), the preferred treatment is myomectomy to restore normal uterine anatomy and improve fertility.

Why not other options:

A) Uterine artery embolization: Used for symptomatic fibroids, but not preferred in women desiring fertility (may impair uterine blood supply).

C) Assisted reproductive techniques: Structural uterine pathology should be corrected first before ART.

D) GnRH analogues: Cause temporary fibroid shrinkage only; fibroids recur after stopping and do not improve fertility long-term.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old multigravida at 34 weeks gestation presents with intense generalized itching, predominantly over the palms and soles, which worsens at night. There is no history of skin rash or fever. On examination, scratch marks are present over the limbs, and mild icterus is noted. Obstetric evaluation is otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most sensitive and preferred investigation for confirming this diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serum bile acid levels

Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy (ICP) typically presents in the third trimester with:

• Intense pruritus, especially involving the palms and soles
• Symptoms worse at night
• Absence of primary skin lesions
• Excoriation marks due to scratching
• Mild jaundice in some patients

Most Sensitive Investigation: Serum bile acid levels are the most sensitive and preferred test for diagnosis.

• Elevated total bile acids may be present even before liver function tests become abnormal
• Bile acid levels correlate with fetal risk
• Levels ≥10 μmol/L support the diagnosis

Other Investigations

• ALT and AST: Frequently elevated but less sensitive than bile acids
• Serum bilirubin: Elevated in only a minority of patients
• Ammonia levels: No role in diagnosis

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old nulliparous woman comes to the OPD for evaluation of infertility. The patient has been attempting to conceive for the past 2 years. Menarche was at age 11, and her menstrual cycles occur 2-3 times per year and last 7-10 days. BMI is 35 kg/m². Physical examination shows mild acne and hair growth on the upper lip and chin. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following complications?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Endometrial carcinoma

This patient has features of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS):

• Oligomenorrhea (cycles 2–3 times/year)
• Infertility
• Obesity (BMI 35)
• Hyperandrogenism (acne, hirsutism)

Pathophysiology:

• Chronic anovulation → no corpus luteum formation
• Low progesterone levels
• Unopposed estrogen stimulation of the endometrium

Consequence:

• Continuous endometrial proliferation → endometrial hyperplasia → increased risk of endometrial carcinoma.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old P1 woman whose last menstrual period was 10 days ago presents to the emergency department with worsening right-sided pelvic pain. The pain began suddenly after bending over to pick up her child, did not respond to acetaminophen, and has worsened intermittently over several hours. She has had two episodes of vomiting. Examination shows abdominal guarding. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates an 8-cm enlarged right ovary with high-impedance arterial flow on color Doppler. These findings are most consistent with which diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ovarian torsion

Ovarian torsion occurs when the ovary twists around its supporting ligaments (infundibulopelvic and utero-ovarian ligaments), leading to compromise of venous and arterial blood flow.

• Sudden onset severe unilateral pelvic pain
• Pain may begin after sudden movement or physical activity
• Nausea and vomiting
• Abdominal guarding or tenderness

Transvaginal ultrasound with Doppler typically shows:

• Enlarged ovary (>5 cm)
• Peripheral follicles
• Abnormal or high-impedance blood flow on Doppler

Management

• Emergency laparoscopy
• Detorsion of the ovary and preservation if viable.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

• Appendicitis: typically begins with periumbilical pain migrating to right lower quadrant, often with fever and leukocytosis.
• Hemorrhagic cyst: causes pelvic pain but does not produce an enlarged ovary with Doppler flow abnormalities typical of torsion.
• Red degeneration of uterus: occurs with fibroids during pregnancy, not in this scenario.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old pregnant woman in the second half of pregnancy presents with acute abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She is known to have a fibroid uterus. Investigations show raised WBC count and ESR, but there is no evidence of infection. Regarding fibroid degeneration, which of the following statements is correct?
options: Red degeneration is septic and requires antibiotics with urgent myomectomy
Calcareous degeneration begins from the periphery and is most common in subserosal fibroids
Hyaline degeneration is the second most common degeneration of fibroid
Malignant transformation is the most common degeneration of fibroid
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Calcareous degeneration begins from the periphery and is most common in subserosal fibroids

Degenerative changes in uterine fibroids occur when the tumor outgrows its blood supply. Different types of degeneration are seen depending on age, pregnancy status, and vascular compromise.

1. Hyaline degeneration

• Most common degeneration (\~60%)
• Due to protein deposition within the fibroid
• Often asymptomatic

2. Red (carneous) degeneration

• Classically occurs during pregnancy
• Presents with:

• Acute abdominal pain
• Tender fibroid
• Nausea and vomiting
• Mild fever
• Raised WBC count and ESR

• It is aseptic (sterile) degeneration and is managed conservatively

3. Calcareous degeneration

• Common in postmenopausal women
• Calcification begins at the periphery
• Most commonly seen in subserosal fibroids

Why other options are incorrect?

• Red degeneration is septic and requires antibiotics with urgent myomectomy: Red degeneration is not septic and usually does not require antibiotics or myomectomy
• Hyaline degeneration is the second most common degeneration of fibroid: Hyaline degeneration is the most common, not the second most common degeneration
• Malignant transformation is the most common degeneration of fibroid: Malignant transformation (leiomyosarcoma) is extremely rare and is not considered a common degeneration

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old primigravida at 35 weeks gestation has gestational diabetes mellitus controlled with insulin (Type A2 GDM). Her glucose values are within target range and there are no maternal or fetal complications. What is the recommended timing of delivery?
options: Wait till 41 weeks for spontaneous labor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Delivery at ≥39 weeks

Timing of delivery in diabetes during pregnancy depends on glycemic control and complications:

• Well-controlled GDM on diet (Type A1) → Deliver at ≥39 weeks
• Well-controlled Type A2 GDM on insulin/oral drugs → Deliver at ≥39 weeks
• Poorly controlled Type A2 GDM → Deliver at 37–38 weeks + 6 days
• Well-controlled pregestational diabetes → Deliver at ≥39 weeks

Metabolic targets in pregnancy

• FBS: ≤95 mg/dL
• 1-hour PP: ≤140 mg/dL
• 2-hour PP: ≤120 mg/dL
• HbA1c: <6% (maximum acceptable 6.5%)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old sex worker presents with irregular menses, postcoital bleeding, and occasional foul-smelling discharge. She is advised a Pap smear. What is the best time for the test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Around ovulation

At ovulation (mid-cycle, Day 14):

• Estrogen is at peak
• Cervical mucus is thin, watery, abundant → least interference with cell collection
• Transformation zone is most everted → better access to SCJ
• Cells are well-preserved and easily interpretable
• Optimal hormonal milieu for cell maturation → clearest cytology

Hormonal Effect on Cervical Mucus

| Phase | Hormone | Mucus | Pap Quality

| ----- | ------- | ----- | -----------

| Post-menstrual | Rising estrogen | Thinning | Acceptable

| Ovulation | Peak estrogen | Thinnest/clearest | Best ✅

| Secretory | Progesterone | Thick, viscid | Poor

| Menstruation | Both low | Blood-mixed | Worst ❌

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents to the OPD with a twin pregnancy at 10 weeks’ gestation. She has 3-year-old female twins who were born at beginning of the 9th months of gestation. She also has a history of two first- trimester abortions. Which of the following correctly represents her obstetric score (formula)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. G4 P1 A2 L2

Obstetric score summarizes a woman’s reproductive history using:

• G (Gravida): total number of pregnancies including the current one
• P (Para): number of pregnancies reaching viability (≥28 weeks), regardless of number of babies
• A (Abortions): pregnancy losses before viability
• L (Living): number of living children

In this case:

• Current pregnancy (twin, 10 weeks) → counts in gravida
• Previous twin delivery at beginning of 9th month → 1 para (counts as one delivery though twins were born)
• Two first-trimester abortions → A2
• Two living children → L2

Calculation:

• G = 1 (current) + 1 (previous twin pregnancy) + 2 abortions = 4
• P = 1
• A = 2
• L = 2

Therefore: G4 P1 A2 L2

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman, G1P0, at 20 weeks’ gestation is referred for evaluation of discordant amniotic fluid volumes in a twin pregnancy. Ultrasound shows monochorionic diamniotic twins. One fetus is surrounded by severe oligohydramnios and is “stuck” to the uterine wall with an empty bladder. The co-twin has marked polyhydramnios, a distended bladder, and signs of cardiac strain. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive management for this condition?
options: Laser ablation of placental vascular anastomoses
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Laser ablation of placental vascular anastomoses

• Unbalanced blood flow between twins through placental AV connections
• Donor twin:

• Hypovolemia
• Oligohydramnios
• Empty bladder
• “Stuck twin” appearance

• Recipient twin:

• Hypervolemia
• Polyhydramnios
• Distended bladder
• Cardiac overload/heart failure

Definitive treatment: Fetoscopic laser ablation of placental vascular anastomoses. Interrupts abnormal intertwin blood flow

Why other options are less appropriate:

• Serial amnioreduction → temporary symptomatic relief only
• Corticosteroids → for fetal lung maturity, not definitive therapy
• Immediate delivery at 20 weeks → not viable

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 39 weeks gestation presents to labor and delivery with regular painful uterine contractions for the past 5 hours. She denies any rupture of membranes or vaginal bleeding. Fetal movements have been perceived normally. On initial examination, the cervix is 4 cm dilated, 80% effaced, with the fetal vertex at 0 station. She requests pain relief and receives epidural analgesia. Two hours after epidural placement, repeat examination shows the cervix to be 5 cm dilated and 100% effaced with the vertex at 0 station. A subsequent examination 2 hours later reveals no change in cervical dilation or fetal descent. Fetal heart rate tracing demonstrates: • Baseline: 138/min • Variability: moderate • Accelerations: present • Decelerations: sporadic early decelerations only Uterine activity on tocometry shows contractions occurring every 6–8 minutes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Proceed with cesarean delivery for arrest of active labor
Continue expectant management for another 2 hours
Begin oxytocin infusion for augmentation of labor
Administer intravaginal misoprostol for cervical ripening
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Begin oxytocin infusion for augmentation of labor

This patient is in the active phase of labor and has demonstrated inadequate labor progress after epidural analgesia.

Active Labor Arrest Criteria

• No cervical change despite:

• ≥6 cm dilatation and
• Adequate uterine contractions for ≥4 hours, or
• Inadequate contractions despite oxytocin for ≥6 hours

This patient does not yet meet criteria for active-phase arrest because contractions are inadequate.

Interpretation:

• Labor progress is inadequate due to hypotonic uterine contractions (power dysfunction)
• There is no evidence of fetal distress or cephalopelvic disproportion

Management:

• Oxytocin augmentation should be initiated to increase contraction frequency and strength
• Continuous fetal and uterine monitoring should be maintained

Why other options are incorrect?

• Proceed with cesarean delivery for arrest of active labor: Cesarean delivery is not indicated because active-phase arrest requires adequate contractions before diagnosing labor arrest
• Continue expectant management for another 2 hours: Expectant management may unnecessarily prolong labor when contractions are inadequate
• Administer intravaginal misoprostol for cervical ripening: Misoprostol is used for cervical ripening and labor induction, not for augmentation of established labor

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman, gravida 4 aborta 3, has a history of a miscarriage at 8 weeks, a second miscarriage at 11 weeks with absent cardiac activity, and a third pregnancy loss at 24 weeks due to preterm delivery associated with early-onset preeclampsia. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome

Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome is an autoimmune hypercoagulable disorder that leads to thrombosis in placental vessels, causing recurrent pregnancy loss and placental insufficiency.

It should be suspected in women with the following obstetric history:

•

≥3 consecutive miscarriages before 10 weeks

•

Unexplained fetal death after 10 weeks

•

Preterm birth (<34 weeks) due to severe preeclampsia, placental insufficiency, or fetal growth restriction

Antiphospholipid antibodies cause:

•

Hypercoagulability

•

Placental vascular thrombosis

•

Placental infarction → fetal loss or severe preeclampsia

Important antibodies

•

Lupus anticoagulant

•

Anticardiolipin antibody

•

Anti-β2 glycoprotein I

Management during pregnancy

• Low-dose aspirin + heparin (usually LMWH) to prevent placental thrombosis and improve fetal survival.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman's Pap smear shows AGCUS (Atypical Glandular Cells of Undetermined Significance). What is the next most appropriate step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Colposcopy + Biopsy + ECC + Endometrial biopsy

Atypical Glandular Cells (AGC/previously AGCUS) on a Pap smear carry a significantly higher risk of premalignant or malignant lesions than atypical squamous cells and may originate from the endocervix or endometrium. Therefore, evaluation must include colposcopy with directed biopsy, endocervical sampling (ECC), and endometrial biopsy (particularly in women ≥35 years or younger women with abnormal uterine bleeding or risk factors for endometrial cancer). Merely repeating the Pap smear is inadequate because AGC may represent cervical adenocarcinoma in situ, invasive adenocarcinoma, or endometrial carcinoma.

High-Yield

• ASC-US → HPV testing or repeat cytology.
• AGC (AGCUS) → Colposcopy + Cervical biopsy + ECC ± Endometrial biopsy.
• Endometrial biopsy is mandatory in women ≥35 years or those with abnormal uterine bleeding/risk factors.
• AGC has a much higher malignant potential than ASC-US, warranting comprehensive evaluation rather than surveillance alone.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 31-year-old G3P2 woman at 32 weeks gestation, a known case of placenta previa, presents with painless vaginal bleeding. On examination, she is hemodynamically stable, there is no active bleeding, CTG is reassuring, and fetus is appropriate for gestational age. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Expectant management with Johnson–Macafee regimen

Placenta previa classically presents with painless vaginal bleeding in the third trimester. Management depends on gestational age, severity of bleeding, maternal condition, and fetal status.

When:

• Gestational age is <37 weeks
• Mother is hemodynamically stable
• Bleeding has stopped or is minimal
• Fetal status is reassuring
• No labor or fetal compromise

→ Johnson–Macafee (expectant) regimen is recommended.

Components of Johnson–Macafee Regimen:

• Hospitalization and observation
• Maternal and fetal monitoring
• Blood grouping and cross-matching
• Corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity (if indicated)
• Avoid digital vaginal examination
• Plan delivery at fetal maturity or if bleeding recurs/severe

Why Other Options Are Incorrect?

• Immediate cesarean section after resuscitation: Reserved for uncontrolled bleeding, maternal instability, labor, or fetal distress.
• Induction with oxytocin: Contraindicated in major placenta previa.
• Cervical cerclage: Used for cervical insufficiency, not placenta previa.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 31-year-old G3P2 woman at 35 weeks gestation presents with sudden onset vaginal bleeding for 2 hours. Bleeding is bright red and painless. There is no history of trauma. Uterus is soft and non-tender. Fetal parts are easily palpable and fetal heart sounds are normal. Previous obstetric history reveals one prior lower segment cesarean section. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Placenta previa

| Feature | Abruptio placentae | Placenta previa | Vasa previa | Uterine rupture

| ------- | ------------------ | --------------- | ----------- | ---------------

| Bleeding | Painful, often dark | Painless, bright red, recurrent | Bleeding after membrane rupture | Bleeding ± shock

| Uterus | Tender/tense | Soft, relaxed, non-tender | Usually soft | Tender; contractions may stop

| FHS | Often distressed/absent | Easily heard initially | Severe fetal distress out of proportion to blood loss | Bradycardia/absent FHS

| Fetal parts | Difficult to feel | Easily palpable | Palpable | Superficially felt after rupture

| Key risk/clue | HTN, retroplacental clot | Previous CS, malpresentation | Velamentous cord insertion | Previous CS/TOLAC

| Investigation | TAS/USG may show clot | TVS = IOC | USG Doppler = IOC | Clinical diagnosis

| Management clue | Resuscitate ± delivery | Avoid P/V/P/S; CS if active bleed | Emergency CS | Emergency laparotomy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 1, is evaluated on postoperative day 2 for lower abdominal pain, chills, and pain with sitting. She presented to the hospital one day after spontaneous rupture of membranes without the onset of contractions. After a 26-hour induction of labor, she underwent a primary cesarean delivery for arrest of descent. Breast examination shows fullness without erythema or fluctuance. The uterine fundus is firm and tender to palpation. There is scant serosanguineous drainage from the inferior aspect of the incision. Pelvic examination reveals a small amount of blood on the perineal pad with mildly foul-smelling discharge.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Clindamycin plus gentamicin

Postpartum endometritis is the most common cause of postpartum fever after cesarean delivery, especially in women with prolonged rupture of membranes and prolonged labor.

Risk factors:

• Cesarean delivery (most important risk factor)

• Prolonged rupture of membranes (>18 hours)

• Prolonged labor or multiple vaginal examinations

• Internal fetal monitoring

Clinical features:

• Fever, chills

• Lower abdominal pain

• Uterine fundal tenderness

• Foul-smelling lochia

• Tachycardia or malaise

The infection is polymicrobial, involving anaerobes, gram-negative rods, and streptococci from vaginal flora.

Treatment (first-line): IV clindamycin + gentamicin

This combination provides broad coverage against anaerobes and gram-negative organisms, which are the most common pathogens.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2, at 28 weeks gestation presents to the labor and delivery unit with a 8-hour history of watery vaginal discharge. She denies any uterine contractions or vaginal bleeding. On examination, pooling of fluid is noted in the posterior fornix, and ferning is observed on microscopy. Nitrazine test is positive. Vital signs: • Temperature: 38.8°C (101.8°F) • Blood pressure: 96/68 mmHg • Heart rate: 118/min • Respiratory rate: 20/min Fetal heart rate: 178/min with minimal variability Laboratory results: • Cervical dilation: 3 cm, 50% effaced Uterine tenderness is noted on palpation. Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics have been initiated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Perform amniocentesis for Gram stain and culture to confirm diagnosis
Proceed with delivery regardless of gestational age
Administer betamethasone and delay delivery for 48 hours to ensure fetal lung maturity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Proceed with delivery regardless of gestational age

Chorioamnionitis (intra-amniotic infection) is a serious maternal and fetal complication of PPROM and is diagnosed clinically by the presence of maternal fever along with features such as uterine tenderness, maternal tachycardia, fetal tachycardia, leukocytosis, and foul-smelling or turbid amniotic fluid.

Management consists of:

• Immediate initiation of broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
• Prompt delivery irrespective of gestational age
• Continuous maternal and fetal monitoring

Once chorioamnionitis is established, prolonging pregnancy offers little fetal benefit and substantially increases the risk of:

• Maternal sepsis
• Septic shock
• Endometritis
• Neonatal sepsis
• Intrauterine fetal demise

Therefore:

• Tocolytics are contraindicated
• Amniocentesis is unnecessary because the diagnosis is already clinical
• Delivery should not be delayed for corticosteroid completion

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old married woman presents to an NCD clinic screening camp. She is asymptomatic. Cytology (Pap) returns ASC-US. She is not pregnant and is immunocompetent. On speculum exam, cervix looks normal. What is the best next step?
options: Start VIA and treat if VIA positive
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reflex HPV DNA testing

ASC-US (Atypical Squamous Cells of Undetermined Significance) on Pap smear is the most common abnormal cervical cytology finding. The recommended next step in women ≥30 years who are non-pregnant and immunocompetent is reflex high-risk HPV DNA testing.

• High-risk HPV infection (especially types 16 and 18) is the main cause of Cervical cancer.
• Reflex HPV testing helps triage ASC-US into low-risk vs high-risk groups.

Management based on HPV result:

• HPV positive → Colposcopy
• HPV negative → Routine screening (repeat cytology in \~3 years)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Repeat Pap in 1 year: Used mainly when HPV testing is not available or in younger women.
• Immediate colposcopy: Not required for all ASC-US because many cases are transient HPV infections.
• VIA and treat: Used mainly in low-resource “screen-and-treat” programs, not when cytology and HPV testing are available.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old nulliparous woman presents with progressive dysmenorrhea and infertility. Imaging reveals ovarian endometriotic cysts. She has no history of retrograde menstruation or prior pelvic surgery. The pathogenesis is suspected to involve transformation of peritoneal lining into endometrial tissue. Which of the following best explains this mechanism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Coelomic metaplasia

Coelomic metaplasia is a proposed mechanism for the development of endometriosis in which peritoneal mesothelial (coelomic) cells transform into ectopic endometrial tissue under hormonal or inflammatory influences. This theory helps explain cases of endometriosis in women without clear retrograde menstruation and in unusual locations.

Other mechanisms include:

• Retrograde menstruation → reflux of menstrual tissue through fallopian tubes into the pelvis (most common theory)
• Lymphatic or hematogenous spread → dissemination to distant sites such as lungs or brain
• Iatrogenic implantation → seeding after pelvic surgery (eg, cesarean scar endometriosis)

Endometriosis commonly presents with:

• Progressive dysmenorrhea
• Chronic pelvic pain
• Dyspareunia
• Infertility
• Ovarian endometriomas (“chocolate cysts”).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old pregnant woman undergoes a biophysical profile (BPP) to assess fetal well-being. Identify the normal parameter for BPP?
options: At least one episode of FHR acceleration >15bpm
Three or more discrete body or limb movements
Two or more episode of limb extension and flexion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Three or more discrete body or limb movements

The biophysical profile (BPP) is used to assess fetal well-being and includes five parameters, each scored as 0 or 2. Normal BPP parameters:

1. Fetal breathing movements

• ≥1 episode lasting ≥30 seconds in 30 minutes

2. Gross body movements

• ≥3 discrete body or limb movements in 30 minutes

3. Fetal tone

• ≥1 episode of active extension with return to flexion

4. Amniotic fluid volume

• Single deepest vertical pocket ≥2 cm

(AFI is not part of classic BPP scoring)

5. Nonstress test (NST)

• Reactive NST with fetal heart rate accelerations

Why others are incorrect:

• AFI 5–25 → not the standard BPP criterion
• FHR acceleration >15 bpm → criterion for NST in term fetus but incomplete description
• Two episodes of limb extension/flexion → only one episode is required for normal fetal tone

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old pregnant woman undergoes non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) at 11 weeks gestation. The report comes positive for Trisomy 21. What is the best next step?
options: Diagnostic karyotyping by chorionic villus sampling
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diagnostic karyotyping by chorionic villus sampling

Important facts about NIPT

| Feature | Fact

| ------- | ----

| Sample | Maternal blood

| Source | Cell-free fetal DNA from placental apoptosis

| Earliest timing | ≥10 weeks

| Sensitivity | \~99%

| Nature | Screening test, not diagnostic

| Screening result | Next step

| ---------------- | ---------

| Negative NIPT | Reassure

| Positive NIPT | Diagnostic karyotyping

Tissue for karyotyping

| Trimester | Procedure

| --------- | ---------

| First trimester | Chorionic villus sampling

| Second trimester | Amniocentesis

Timing

| Procedure | Best timing

| --------- | -----------

| CVS | Up to 13 weeks + 6 days

| Amniocentesis | 16–18 weeks

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old primigravida presents at 28 weeks’ gestation with painful uterine contractions for the past 2 hours, occurring every 5 minutes. She reports frequent fetal movements and denies leakage of fluid or vaginal bleeding. Her temperature is 37°C (98.7°F), blood pressure 125/60 mm Hg, and pulse 80/min. On digital examination, the cervix is 3 cm dilated and 90% effaced with a bulging bag of membranes. Ultrasound confirms vertex presentation. Fetal heart rate tracing is normal, and the tocometer shows contractions every 5 minutes. Betamethasone and indomethacin are administered. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Observe and reexamine the cervix in 2 hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Administer magnesium sulfate

This patient has preterm labor (regular uterine contractions with cervical dilation and effacement before 37 weeks).

At 28 weeks gestation, the management aims to improve neonatal outcomes and delay delivery briefly.

Standard management of preterm labor (24–34 weeks):

• Antenatal corticosteroids (eg, betamethasone) → accelerate fetal lung maturity

• Tocolytics (eg, indomethacin, nifedipine) → delay labor for \~48 hours to allow steroids to act

• Magnesium sulfate → given for fetal neuroprotection, particularly before 32 weeks, to reduce the risk of cerebral palsy

Since this patient is 28 weeks pregnant, the next important step after steroids and tocolysis is magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Nifedipine → another tocolytic, but tocolysis has already been initiated with indomethacin

• Progesterone → used for prevention of preterm birth, not treatment of active labor

• Observation alone → inappropriate because active preterm labor is present

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman (G1P0) at 18 weeks gestation presents for discussion of abnormal prenatal screening results. She has no medical problems and takes no medications. The results of the quadruple screen are: - AFP: High - Unconjugated estriol: Low - β-hCG: Low - lnhibin A: Low Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gastroschisis

The quadruple screening test (performed at 15–20 weeks of gestation) measures four maternal serum markers to screen for fetal chromosomal abnormalities and neural tube defects.

Markers in Quadruple Test:

• AFP (Alpha-fetoprotein)
• β-hCG
• Unconjugated estriol (uE3)
• Inhibin A

| Condition | AFP | β-hCG | Estriol | Inhibin A

| --------- | --- | ----- | ------- | ---------

| Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) | ↓ | ↑ | ↓ | ↑

| Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) | ↓ | ↓ | ↓ | Normal/↓

| Open neural tube defects / abdominal wall defects | ↑ | Normal | Normal | Normal

| Multifetal pregnancy | ↑ | ↑ | ↑ | ↑

The markedly elevated AFP suggests a fetal open abdominal wall defect, most commonly gastroschisis, due to leakage of fetal proteins into the amniotic fluid and maternal circulation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman is evaluated at 32 weeks’ gestation. Laboratory results are as follows: Arterial pH: 7.45 PaO2: 110 mm Hg PaCO2: 30 mm Hg Bicarbonate: 20 mEq/L Hemoglobin: 11 g/dL Blood urea nitrogen:5 mg/dL Creatinine: 0.6 mg/dL Which of the following best explains this patient's status?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Normal pregnancy

In normal pregnancy, progesterone stimulates the respiratory center leading to chronic hyperventilation. This causes physiologic respiratory alkalosis characterized by:

• ↓ PaCO₂ (\~28–32 mm Hg) due to hyperventilation

• Slight ↓ bicarbonate (\~18–21 mEq/L) due to renal compensation

• pH slightly alkalemic (\~7.44–7.46)

• ↑ PaO₂ (\~100–110 mm Hg)

• ↓ BUN and creatinine because GFR increases by \~50% in pregnancy

Thus, the given values (pH 7.45, PaCO₂ 30, HCO₃⁻ 20, PaO₂ 110, low BUN/creatinine) represent normal physiologic changes of pregnancy, not pathology.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman presents to the emergency department 5 days after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with severe right-sided lower abdominal pain, fever, and nausea. Her pregnancy was complicated by prolonged labor but no infection. Temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg, and pulse is 110/min. Abdominal examination reveals right lower quadrant tenderness without rebound. Laboratory studies show leukocytosis. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast demonstrates an enlarged, thrombosed right ovarian vein extending toward the inferior vena cava. Blood cultures are pending. Which of the following factors most strongly predisposed this patient to the development of her condition?
options: Direct spread of infection from the endometrium
Compression of the ovarian vein by an adnexal mass
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypercoagulable state associated with pregnancy

This patient has postpartum ovarian vein thrombosis (OVT), a rare but important postpartum complication that most commonly affects the right ovarian vein.

Clinical features:

• Fever
• Lower abdominal or flank pain
• Leukocytosis
• Occurs within days after delivery

Imaging: CT scan shows a thrombosed enlarged ovarian vein extending toward the IVC

Major predisposing factor:

• Pregnancy and postpartum state create a physiologic hypercoagulable state
• Increased clotting factors and venous stasis predispose to thrombosis

Why the right ovarian vein is more commonly affected:

• Longer vein
• Retrograde flow
• Compression by dextrorotated uterus
• Direct drainage into the IVC

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. She has a positive pregnancy test, but transvaginal ultrasound does not show an intrauterine pregnancy. Endometrial biopsy reveals hypersecretory glands with nuclear atypia and poor decidualization. This histological finding is consistent with which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arias-Stella reaction

• The Arias-Stella reaction is a histological finding characterized by hypersecretory endometrial glands with nuclear atypia, often associated with ectopic pregnancy.
• This reaction occurs due to exposure of the endometrium to abnormal hormonal levels, particularly low progesterone, which leads to poor decidualization.
• The presence of these atypical hypersecretory changes is a key diagnostic clue when evaluating for ectopic pregnancy in a patient with a positive pregnancy test and no evidence of an intrauterine pregnancy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding and infertility. Hysteroscopy shows a submucous fibroid projecting predominantly into the uterine cavity, with less than 50% of the fibroid within the myometrium. Based on FIGO classification, which type of fibroid is this and what is the preferred management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. FIGO type 1 - hysteroscopic myomectomy

The FIGO classification of fibroids is based on the relationship of the fibroid to the endometrial cavity and myometrium.

Submucous Fibroid Classification

• Type 0: Pedunculated intracavitary fibroid
• Type 1: <50% intramural extension (majority projects into uterine cavity)
• Type 2: ≥50% intramural extension

Hysteroscopic myomectomy is the treatment of choice for:

• Type 0
• Type 1
• Selected Type 2 submucous fibroids

Benefits:

• Controls heavy menstrual bleeding
• Improves fertility outcomes
• Preserves the uterus

Why Other Options Are Incorrect?

• Type 2 fibroid: Has ≥50% intramural component.
• Laparoscopic myomectomy: Preferred for intramural or subserosal fibroids, not predominantly intracavitary submucous fibroids.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman presents with secondary amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and headaches. Hormone levels show reduced LH, FSH, E, and elevated prolactin. What is the drug of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cabergoline
