This patient has hyperprolactinemia due to a prolactinoma, suggested by the triad of secondary amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and headaches, along with elevated prolactin causing suppression of GnRH, resulting in low LH, FSH, and estradiol. The drug of choice is cabergoline, a long-acting dopamine (D2) agonist that suppresses prolactin secretion, restores ovulation, and reduces tumor size. Bromocriptine is an alternative but is less effective and less well tolerated. During pregnancy, dopamine agonists are usually discontinued once pregnancy is confirmed, unless the patient has a macroadenoma with visual symptoms or evidence of tumor enlargement, in which case bromocriptine is preferred because of its extensive safety data in pregnancy.

High-Yield

• DOC for prolactinoma: Cabergoline
• Mechanism: Dopamine (D2) agonist → ↓ Prolactin secretion → ↓ Tumor size
• Hormonal profile: ↑ Prolactin, ↓ GnRH, ↓ LH/FSH, ↓ Estradiol
• Pregnancy: Stop dopamine agonist after conception unless symptomatic macroadenoma (visual defects/headache), when bromocriptine is preferred.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman, G2P1, presents with 3 months of amenorrhea and lower-abdominal pain as her worrisome symptom. Urine pregnancy test for Beta hCG is positive. TV-USG scan shows an empty uterus, a complex adnexal mass, and free pelvic fluid. O/E, BP is 90/60 mmHg, pulse is 110 bpm, cervical motion tenderness is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ruptured ectopic pregnancy

A woman of reproductive age presenting with amenorrhea, abdominal pain, positive pregnancy test, adnexal mass, free pelvic fluid, hypotension, and tachycardia should be presumed to have a ruptured ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise. Classic features of ruptured ectopic pregnancy:

• Amenorrhea
• Lower abdominal/pelvic pain
• Vaginal bleeding may or may not be present
• Positive β-hCG
• Empty uterus on transvaginal ultrasound
• Adnexal mass
• Free fluid in pelvis/hemoperitoneum
• Signs of shock: hypotension, tachycardia

Cervical motion tenderness suggests pelvic irritation due to intraperitoneal bleeding. Most ectopic pregnancies occur in the fallopian tube (ampulla most common site).

Management:

• Hemodynamically unstable patient → urgent surgical management (laparotomy/laparoscopy)
• Stable, unruptured cases may be treated with methotrexate.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2, at 38 weeks’ gestation comes to the hospital due to contractions. She had a cesarean delivery for breech presentation at 39 weeks’ gestation in her second pregnancy. Her blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg, pulse is 100/min, and respirations are 22/min. Fetal heart rate tracing shows moderate variability, multiple accelerations, and no decelerations. Uterine contractions are regular and occur every 4 minutes. The cervix is 6 cm dilated and 60% effaced, and the fetal vertex is at 0 station. After 2 hours, the patient suddenly becomes restless and develops intense lower abdominal pain. Fetal heart rate monitoring now shows recurrent late decelerations. On pelvic examination, there is moderate vaginal bleeding, the cervix remains 6 cm dilated and 60% effaced, and the fetal vertex is now at −3 station. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Uterine rupture

Uterine rupture should be suspected in a laboring woman with a previous cesarean scar who suddenly develops:

• Severe abdominal pain
• Fetal distress (eg, recurrent late decelerations on fetal heart rate tracing)
• Loss of fetal station (fetal head moves from 0 station to −3 station)
• Vaginal bleeding
• Arrest of labor progress

In this patient, the prior cesarean delivery is the key risk factor. During labor, the uterine scar can rupture, causing the fetus to move back into the abdominal cavity, which explains the sudden loss of fetal station and fetal distress. This is an obstetric emergency requiring immediate emergency laparotomy and cesarean delivery.

Why other options are incorrect:

• A. Fetal nuchal cord: Causes variable decelerations, not sudden loss of station.
• B. Normal labor: Cervical dilation and fetal descent should progress.
• D. Vasa previa: Painless bleeding after membrane rupture with fetal bradycardia, but no loss of fetal station or severe maternal pain.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman, gravida 4 para 2 living 0, presents to the antenatal clinic at 10 weeks gestation confirmed by last menstrual period and transvaginal ultrasound. Her obstetric history is significant for two prior second-trimester pregnancy losses at 18 and 20 weeks gestation respectively, both preceded by painless cervical dilation without contractions. She underwent a large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ/LEEP) procedure 14 months ago for CIN III; her subsequent PAP smears and HPV testing have shown no evidence of recurrence. She is otherwise healthy with no medical comorbidities. Vital signs are normal. Speculum examination shows a well-healed cervix with a shallow ectocervical defect. Transvaginal ultrasound at this visit shows a live intrauterine pregnancy with crown-rump length consistent with 10 weeks. Cervical length measures 24 mm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?
options: Reassure and schedule routine antenatal follow-up with serial cervical length
Advise complete bed rest and pelvic rest for the duration of pregnancy
Perform transabdominal cerclage given prior failed transvaginal procedures
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perform transvaginal cervical cerclage (McDonald/Shirodkar) now

This patient has cervical insufficiency, evidenced by:

• Two previous painless second-trimester losses (18 and 20 weeks)
• Prior LEEP/LLETZ procedure (acquired cervical trauma)
• Current cervical length of 24 mm at 10 weeks gestation

Indication for Cerclage

She meets criteria for a history-indicated cerclage because of recurrent painless mid-trimester pregnancy losses suggestive of cervical insufficiency.

Preferred Management: Transvaginal cervical cerclage (McDonald or Shirodkar) at 12–14 weeks gestation

• McDonald cerclage is most commonly performed.
• Shirodkar cerclage may be considered in selected cases with a shortened or scarred cervix.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

• Reassure and schedule routine antenatal follow-up with serial cervical length: Inadequate given her strong history of cervical insufficiency.
• Advise complete bed rest and pelvic rest for the duration of pregnancy: Not proven to prevent preterm birth or pregnancy loss.
• Perform transabdominal cerclage given prior failed transvaginal procedures: Reserved for failed prior transvaginal cerclage or severely damaged/absent cervix.
• Progesterone alone: Useful for short cervix, but this patient has a clear indication for cerclage based on history.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman, gravida 4 para 4, comes to the OPD for a routine check-up 6 weeks after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery of a healthy baby. She has no current complaints and wishes to discuss contraception options. She has a history of heavy menstrual bleeding and was previously found to be mildly anemic. She is breastfeeding exclusively. Pelvic examination reveals a small, mobile uterus with no abnormalities. Which of the following is the preferred method of contraception for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Levonorgestrel-containing intrauterine device

In breastfeeding women with heavy menstrual bleeding, the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device (LNG-IUD) is the preferred contraceptive method because it provides highly effective long-acting reversible contraception (LARC) and reduces menstrual blood loss, thereby improving iron-deficiency anemia.

LNG-IUD (e.g., Mirena):

• Decreases endometrial proliferation
• Causes marked reduction in menstrual bleeding
• Safe during breastfeeding

Why not other options:

• Combined OCPs: Avoid early postpartum and during breastfeeding due to estrogen reducing milk production and VTE risk.
• Copper IUD: May increase menstrual bleeding, worsening anemia.
• Medroxyprogesterone injection: Safe in lactation but may cause irregular bleeding and does not treat heavy menstrual bleeding as effectively.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 33-year-old woman with confirmed endometriosis presents with severe, debilitating dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain unresponsive to OCPs and NSAIDs. She does not desire fertility currently. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment for her severity of disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Continuous GnRH analogues / GnRH antagonists

• Endometriosis is an estrogen-dependent chronic inflammatory condition characterized by ectopic endometrial tissue causing pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility.
• In women with Severe pain, Failure of NSAIDs and combined OCPs and No current desire for fertility: Continuous GnRH analogues (e.g., leuprolide) or GnRH antagonists (e.g., elagolix, relugolix) are considered the most effective next-line medical therapy.

GnRH agonists/antagonists cause:

• Suppression of pituitary gonadotropins
• Marked reduction in ovarian estrogen production
• Atrophy of endometriotic implants
• Significant improvement in pain symptoms

Due to hypoestrogenism:

• Hot flashes
• Vaginal dryness
• Decreased bone mineral density

Therefore, add-back therapy (low-dose estrogen/progestin) is often prescribed for prolonged treatment.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

• Letrozole: Aromatase inhibitor used in refractory cases, not first-line.
• Danazol: Effective but rarely used now due to androgenic side effects (weight gain, acne, hirsutism).
• Mifepristone: Not standard first-line therapy.
• Total abdominal hysterectomy: Reserved for severe refractory disease in women who have completed childbearing and failed medical therapy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 34-weeks G2P1L1 pregnant woman presents with bleeding per vagina and abdominal pain for the past 4 hours. Her Hb 6 g/Dl, pulse rate 120/ min, BP 80/60 mmHg. On abdominal examination, fetal heart sounds are absent and the uterus is tonically contracted. On per vaginal examination, the cervix is 2 cm dilated, 70% effaced, and the vertex is at -2 station. The patient appears distressed. What is the best management option?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Emergency LSCS

Placental abruption with maternal hemodynamic instability is an obstetric emergency requiring immediate delivery, regardless of fetal viability.

Key clues in the question:

• Painful vaginal bleeding
• Tonically contracted uterus
• Shock (BP 80/60, pulse 120, Hb 6 g/dL)
• Absent fetal heart sounds

These findings indicate severe placental abruption with maternal compromise.

Management principle:

• If the mother is unstable, immediate delivery (usually emergency LSCS) is required to control hemorrhage and stabilize the mother.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 34-year-old nulliparous woman in active labor has been pushing for the past 2 hours without progress and feels extremely fatigued. CTG is normal. On examination, the fetal head is 1 cm above the ischial spines (station −1) in the occipitoanterior position. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Emergency cesarean section

Operative vaginal delivery (forceps/vacuum) requires the fetal head to be engaged (station ≥0). If the head is high (above ischial spines, station −1) and there is failure of descent in the second stage, the appropriate management is cesarean section.

1. Station of fetal head

• 0 station: At the level of ischial spines (engaged)
• Negative station (−1, −2, etc.): Head not engaged
• Positive station (+1, +2 etc.): Head descending toward outlet

2. Requirements for operative vaginal delivery

Before attempting forceps or vacuum, the following must be present:

• Fully dilated cervix
• Ruptured membranes
• Engaged fetal head (≥0 station)
• Known fetal position
• Adequate pelvis
• No suspicion of cephalopelvic disproportion

Why cesarean section here:

• Patient has no progress after 2 hours of pushing
• Station −1 → head not engaged
• Attempting forceps with a high head is contraindicated

Why other options are incorrect:

• Observe: Already prolonged second stage with maternal exhaustion.
• Forceps: Contraindicated when head is above ischial spines.
• Fetal blood sampling: Used for abnormal CTG, but CTG here is normal.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 34-year-old nulliparous woman in active labor has been pushing for the past two hours without progress and feels extremely fatigued. The CTG remains normal. On examination, the fetal head is 1 cm above the ischial spines and in the occipitoanterior position. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Emergency cesarean section

Operative vaginal delivery (forceps/vacuum) can be performed only when the fetal head is engaged and low enough in the pelvis. Key obstetric landmark:

• Ischial spines = station 0
• Head 1 cm above spines = station –1 → unengaged head

In this patient:

• Prolonged second stage with maternal exhaustion
• Fetal head at –1 station
• Occipitoanterior position
• No descent despite pushing

Because the head is not engaged, forceps delivery is contraindicated, and the appropriate management is Emergency cesarean section

Prerequisites for operative vaginal delivery:

• Fully dilated cervix
• Ruptured membranes
• Engaged head
• Known fetal position
• Adequate pelvis
• No cephalopelvic disproportion

Attempting forceps with an unengaged head increases risk of:

• Maternal trauma
• Fetal injury
• Failed operative delivery.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 34-year-old P2L2 is taking “Chhaya” for contraception. She has been taking it for 9 months. She reports to you that she has missed taking the pill for the last 2 weeks as she had been traveling and forgot to carry the pill with her. How many tablets has she missed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2

Chhaya (Centchroman/Ormeloxifene) is a non-hormonal weekly oral contraceptive used in the Indian national family planning program.

Dosing schedule:

• First 3 months: 1 tablet twice weekly
• After 3 months: 1 tablet once weekly

In this case:

• She has been using it for 9 months → maintenance phase (once weekly).
• Missing pills for 2 weeks means she has missed 2 tablets.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman develops atonic postpartum hemorrhage after vaginal delivery. Blood pressure is 170/110 mm Hg with headache and hyperreflexia. She is a known bronchial asthma patient using inhaled steroids. Uterine atony persists after uterine massage and oxytocin infusion. The best next uterotonic choice is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Misoprostol

Mifepristone acts as a uterotonic by blocking progesterone receptors, leading to decidual breakdown and increased uterine contractility. It sensitizes the uterus to prostaglandins and is used for medical abortion, cervical ripening, and induction of labor in obstetrics.

Other options:

A.) Methylergometrine → contraindicated in hypertension

B.) Carboprost (PGF₂α) → contraindicated in asthma

C.) Misoprostol (PGE₁) is safe in both hypertension and asthma and effective for uterine atony

D.) Dinoprostone is not used routinely for PPH control

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman presents with chronic pelvic pain and dysmenorrhea. Laparoscopy reveals chocolate cysts in the ovary, confirming endometriosis. She also reports abnormal uterine bleeding. According to the PALM-COEIN classification of AUB, endometriosis falls under which category?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Not yet classified (N)

The PALM-COEIN classification is the FIGO system used to categorize causes of abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) in reproductive-age women.

• PALM = structural causes

• Polyp
• Adenomyosis
• Leiomyoma
• Malignancy & hyperplasia

• COEIN = nonstructural causes

• Coagulopathy
• Ovulatory dysfunction
• Endometrial
• Iatrogenic
• Not yet classified

Endometriosis is classified under “N – Not yet classified” because it is associated with AUB but is not included among the standard structural or nonstructural etiologies in the PALM-COEIN system.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 26 weeks’ gestation presents to the emergency department with intermittent leakage of fluid for the past 6 hours. She has no vaginal bleeding or contractions. Her previous pregnancy was complicated by preterm prelabor rupture of membranes (PPM) at 29 weeks’ gestation, and she delivered at 34 weeks after inpatient management with corticosteroids and latency antibiotics. On examination, her temperature is 39.4°C (103°F), blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg, and pulse is 114/min. The fetal heart rate is 170/min. The cervix is 2 cm dilated. In addition to antibiotics and corticosteroids, which of the following is the best next step in management?
options: Fetal fibronectin testing and fetal lung maturity assessment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immediate induction of labor

This patient has preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) complicated by chorioamnionitis.

• High fever (39.4°C)
• Maternal tachycardia (114/min)
• Fetal tachycardia (170/min)
• Leakage of amniotic fluid
• Cervical dilation

These findings indicate intra-amniotic infection (chorioamnionitis).

Management principle:

• Chorioamnionitis is an indication for immediate delivery regardless of gestational age.
• Management includes:

• Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
• Prompt induction of labor

Why other options are incorrect:

• A. Fetal fibronectin and lung maturity testing: Unnecessary once infection is present.
• C. Tocolysis: Contraindicated in infection.
• D. Expectant management (serial fetal ultrasounds and amnioinfusion): Dangerous because infection can worsen maternal and fetal outcomes.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old HIV-positive woman who smokes 15 cigarettes per day presents with multifocal raised pigmented lesions on the vulva. Biopsy shows full-thickness epithelial atypia with koilocytic changes and no stromal invasion. Which of the following best describes her condition and its most likely etiology?
options: Differentiated VIN – associated with lichen sclerosus
Paget's disease – associated with apocrine gland dysfunction
Melanoma in situ – associated with UV exposure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Usual VIN (uVIN) – associated with HPV 16

Vulvar Intraepithelial Neoplasia (VIN) is a premalignant lesion of the vulvar epithelium characterized by dysplastic changes without stromal invasion.

• HPV 16 infection (most common)
• HIV infection and immunosuppression
• Smoking
• Multiple sexual partners

Histological Features:

• Full-thickness epithelial atypia
• Loss of maturation
• Increased mitotic activity
• Koilocytosis (hallmark of HPV infection)
• No stromal invasion

Clinical Features:

• Multifocal lesions
• Pigmented, raised, or warty appearance
• Common in younger women
• May be asymptomatic or present with pruritus

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

• Differentiated VIN – associated with lichen sclerosus: Usually HPV-negative, occurs in older women, and is associated with lichen sclerosus.
• Paget's disease – associated with apocrine gland dysfunction: Presents as a red, eczematous plaque and arises from intraepithelial adenocarcinoma.
• Melanoma in situ – associated with UV exposure: Unrelated to HPV and not associated with koilocytic changes.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old nulliparous woman is diagnosed with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3. The patient has been sexually active for 15 years and has had 3 lifetime partners. She has been monogamous with her current partner for several months and has a progestin-releasing intrauterine device for contraception. The patient has never used condoms. Menarche occurred at age 9, and menses recur every 28 days and last 3 days. The patient had a plantar wart a few years ago which resolved on its own, but otherwise has no chronic medical conditions. Her mother was diagnosed with endometrial cancer at age 42. Which of the following factors most significantly contributed to the development of this patient’s cervical intraepithelial neoplasia?
options: Family history of endometrial cancer History of plantar warts
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lack of barrier contraception use

The most important risk factor for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), especially HPV types 16 and 18.

Role of barrier contraception:

• Condoms reduce transmission of HPV during sexual contact.
• Lack of barrier contraception increases the risk of persistent HPV infection, which can lead to CIN and cervical cancer.

Why other options are less relevant:

• Early menarche: not a major risk factor for CIN.
• Family history of endometrial cancer: unrelated to cervical dysplasia.
• Plantar warts: caused by low-risk HPV types that infect skin, not associated with cervical cancer.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old primigravida presents to the labor and delivery unit at 36 weeks’ gestation with abdominal pain and blood-tinged vaginal discharge. She was diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus ( GDM ) at 27 weeks but has been noncompliant with diet and insulin therapy. On cervical examination, the cervix is 6 cm dilation and 100% effaced. Her blood glucose level on admission is 290 mg/dL, and insulin therapy is initiated. The patient subsequently has a spontaneous vaginal delivery of a male infant. Which of the following examination findings is most likely to be present in this neonate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Respiratory distress

In gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), maternal hyperglycemia leads to fetal hyperglycemia, which stimulates fetal pancreatic β-cells to produce excess insulin (hyperinsulinemia).

Effect on fetal lungs:

• High fetal insulin levels inhibit surfactant production by type II pneumocytes.
• This delays lung maturation.

Neonatal consequence: Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) shortly after birth due to surfactant deficiency.

Other typical findings in infants of diabetic mothers:

• Macrosomia
• Neonatal hypoglycemia
• Polycythemia
• Hyperbilirubinemia
• Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Why other options are less likely:

• Heart murmur (congenital heart disease) is more associated with pregestational diabetes.
• Limb defects occur with early teratogenic exposure, also linked to pregestational diabetes.
• Small for gestational age is uncommon; infants are usually large for gestational age (macrosomic).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old primigravida with severe preeclampsia at 36 weeks undergoes a biophysical profile (BPP). Findings are as follows: • Reactive NST present • One episode of fetal breathing movement lasting 35 seconds • Two gross body movements in 30 minutes • One episode of extension with return to flexion • Single deepest vertical pocket of amniotic fluid = 1.5 cm What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Immediate delivery

The Biophysical Profile (BPP) is a fetal surveillance test that assesses fetal well-being using five parameters, each scored as 0 or 2 points.

Total BPP Score = 6/10

Interpretation

• 8–10/10: Normal
• 6/10: Equivocal/suspicious
• ≤4/10: Abnormal, suggests fetal compromise

However, oligohydramnios (SDP <2 cm) is an independent indication for delivery, especially in a high-risk pregnancy.

This patient has:

• Severe preeclampsia
• Gestational age 36 weeks
• Oligohydramnios
• Equivocal BPP (6/10)

These findings indicate increased risk of fetal compromise, making immediate delivery the safest option.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, at 40 weeks gestation has a protracted labor course for which a cesarean delivery is performed under epidural anesthesia. Shortly after delivery, the patient has chest pain and difficulty breathing. She becomes hypotensive, bradycardic, hypoxic, and unresponsive, and undergoes emergency intubation. The surgical incisions begin to bleed profusely and the patient goes into cardiorespiratory arrest. She is declared dead after 30 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation. The family agrees to an autopsy. Which of the following is the most likely finding during histologic evaluation of her lungs?
options: Alveolar ducts lined with hyaline membranes
Giant cell foreign body response in the lower lobe of the right lung
Pulmonary artery branch with swirls of fetal squamous cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pulmonary artery branch with swirls of fetal squamous cells

This presentation is classic for amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) — a rare but catastrophic obstetric emergency.

• Sudden respiratory distress
• Hypotension and cardiovascular collapse
• Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) with severe bleeding
• Occurs during labor, cesarean delivery, or shortly after delivery

Pathophysiology:

• Amniotic fluid enters the maternal circulation
• Causes pulmonary vascular obstruction and an anaphylactoid inflammatory response
• Leads to acute respiratory failure and DIC

Histologic finding:

• Fetal squamous cells, lanugo hair, and mucin within maternal pulmonary arteries

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, comes to the OPD for an initial prenatal visit. The patient has had no vaginal bleeding or abdominal pain and has not yet felt fetal movement. The patient’s estimated gestational age based on her last menstrual period is 16 weeks. She has type 1 diabetes mellitus that is controlled with insulin. She smokes a pack of cigarettes daily. As part of her prenatal laboratory screening, a second-trimester maternal serum quadruple screen is performed and reveals an elevated alpha-fetoprotein level. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of this patient's abnormal screening result?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dating error

Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is measured during the second-trimester quadruple screen (15–20 weeks) to screen for fetal abnormalities.

Causes of elevated maternal AFP:

• Incorrect gestational dating (most common cause)
• Open neural tube defects (e.g., spina bifida, anencephaly)
• Abdominal wall defects (e.g., omphalocele, gastroschisis)
• Multiple pregnancy
• Fetal demise

Reason for dating error:

• AFP levels increase with advancing gestational age.
• If the pregnancy is further along than estimated, AFP appears artificially elevated.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 16 weeks’ gestation presents for a prenatal visit. She reports increased urinary frequency but otherwise feels well. Urinalysis reveals mild glucosuria. Laboratory studies show a non-fasting serum glucose concentration of 100 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient’s glucosuria?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased glomerular filtration rate

During normal pregnancy, there is a physiologic increase in renal plasma flow and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) by approximately 40–50%.

Because of this increased GFR, a larger amount of glucose is filtered at the glomerulus.

The renal tubules may not completely reabsorb this increased glucose load, resulting in mild physiologic glucosuria, even when serum glucose levels are normal.

Key features of physiologic glucosuria in pregnancy:

• Occurs due to increased GFR

• Normal blood glucose levels

• Common finding in pregnancy

• Not diagnostic of gestational diabetes

Why other options are incorrect:

• Decreased SGLT2 expression → not the physiologic change in pregnancy

• Increased glomerular filtration barrier permeability → would cause proteinuria, not glucosuria

• Splay phenomenon → refers to variability in nephron glucose reabsorption but is not the primary mechanism here

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 36-year-old woman, G4P3 presents at 34 weeks gestation for an antenatal visit. She has a history of previous cesarean deliveries. During her routine ultrasound examination, the radiologist reports findings suggestive of placenta accreta. The patient has no symptoms at present. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option for this patient?
options: Expectant management with close monitoring and regular ultrasounds
Initiation of antenatal corticosteroids and scheduled cesarean section at 37 weeks gestation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Preoperative planning for cesarean hysterectomy

Placenta accreta spectrum occurs when the placenta abnormally adheres to or invades the myometrium due to defective decidua basalis. It commonly occurs in women with previous cesarean deliveries. Major Risk Factors:

• Previous cesarean section (most important)
• Placenta previa
• Multiparity
• Previous uterine surgery or curettage

Normally the placenta separates after delivery.

In placenta accreta, the placenta is firmly attached to the myometrium, so attempted placental removal can cause massive postpartum hemorrhage.

When placenta accreta is diagnosed antenatally, the recommended management is Planned cesarean hysterectomy with placenta left in situ.

Usually planned at 34–36 weeks before onset of labor.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

• Immediate cesarean section: unnecessary if the patient is stable and asymptomatic.
• Expectant management alone: dangerous due to risk of sudden hemorrhage.
• Cesarean at 37 weeks: may allow labor or bleeding to occur, increasing maternal risk.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 36-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2, at 35 weeks’ gestation comes to the emergency department with leakage of fluid and painless vaginal bleeding. She experienced rupture of membranes 30 minutes ago; the fluid was initially clear but became bloody a few minutes later. The patient has not received prenatal care during this pregnancy, and her two previous pregnancies resulted in term cesarean deliveries. She has a history of hypertension but stopped taking her medication when she became pregnant. Speculum examination confirms rupture of membranes; the cervical os is 1 cm dilated with minimal vaginal bleeding. Doppler ultrasound is unable to detect fetal heart tones. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vasa previa

Vasa previa is a condition in which fetal blood vessels run through the fetal membranes across or near the cervical os without protection from the placenta or umbilical cord.

When the membranes rupture, these exposed fetal vessels can tear, leading to rapid fetal hemorrhage and fetal death.

• Rupture of membranes followed by painless vaginal bleeding
• Bleeding occurs immediately after ROM
• Rapid fetal distress or absent fetal heart tones
• Maternal vital signs usually remain stable because the bleeding is fetal blood

Unprotected fetal vessels (often due to velamentous cord insertion) lie over the cervical os.

When membranes rupture → fetal vessels rupture → fetal hemorrhage → rapid fetal demise.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

• Abruptio placentae: painful bleeding with uterine tenderness and fetal distress.
• Intraamniotic infection: fever, uterine tenderness, foul-smelling discharge.
• Placenta previa: painless bleeding but not triggered by rupture of membranes and fetal heart tones are usually present initially.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 8 weeks’ gestation comes to the office for a follow-up visit. Earlier in the pregnancy, she experienced nausea and breast tenderness which resolved several days ago. At her initial prenatal visit one week ago, ultrasound revealed an intrauterine gestational sac with a yolk sac but no fetal pole. Pelvic examination reveals a closed cervix with no vaginal discharge or bleeding. A repeat transvaginal ultrasound shows findings unchanged from the prior visit. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Missed abortion

A missed abortion refers to intrauterine fetal demise before 20 weeks gestation with retention of the products of conception in the uterus, without expulsion.

• Loss of early pregnancy symptoms (e.g., nausea, breast tenderness)
• Closed cervix
• No vaginal bleeding
• Ultrasound showing nonviable pregnancy (e.g., gestational sac ± yolk sac but no fetal pole or cardiac activity) with no interval growth on repeat scan

In this case:

• Initial ultrasound: gestational sac + yolk sac but no fetal pole
• Repeat ultrasound after 1 week: no change
• Symptoms of pregnancy have resolved
• Closed cervix with no bleeding

These findings indicate a nonviable intrauterine pregnancy retained in the uterus → missed abortion.

| Abortion Classification | Characteristics | Cervical Os | Passage of Fetal Tissue

| ----------------------- | --------------- | ----------- | -----------------------

| Threatened | Abdominal pain or bleeding in the first 20 weeks of gestation | Closed | None

| Inevitable | Abdominal pain or bleeding in the first 20 weeks of gestation | Open | None

| Incomplete | Abdominal pain or bleeding in the first 20 weeks of gestation | Open | Yes (some products of conception still remain in uterus)

| Complete | Abdominal pain or bleeding in the first 20 weeks of gestation | Closed

• Complete passage of fetal parts and placenta
• Uterus contracted

| Septic | Infection of uterus during miscarriage, fever and chills. Usually due to Staph. aureus

• Open with purulent cervical discharge
• Uterine tenderness

| None or may be incomplete

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 8 weeks’ gestation comes to the office for a follow-up visit. Earlier in the pregnancy, the patient had nausea and breast tenderness that resolved several days ago. At her initial prenatal visit 1 week ago, ultrasonography revealed an intrauterine gestational sac with a yolk sac but no fetal pole. The β-hCG level at that visit was 27,325 IU/L. She is taking a prenatal vitamin and does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Her current blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, pulse is 68/min, and BMI is 23 kg/m². Pelvic examination reveals a closed cervix and no vaginal discharge or bleeding. Bimanual examination reveals a normal-sized, retroverted uterus with no cervical motion or adnexal tenderness. A repeat transvaginal ultrasound is unchanged from the prior visit. The β-hCG level is now 25,659 IU/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Missed abortion

Missed abortion is a form of early pregnancy loss in which the embryo or fetus has died but is retained in the uterus without expulsion.

• Loss of pregnancy symptoms (e.g., nausea, breast tenderness)
• No fetal pole or cardiac activity on repeat ultrasound
• β-hCG levels plateau or decrease
• Closed cervical os with no bleeding

Ultrasound criteria for early pregnancy failure:

• Gestational sac with yolk sac but no fetal pole on repeat scan
• Lack of interval growth or development.

Why not the other options:

A) Ectopic pregnancy: Ultrasound shows an intrauterine gestational sac with yolk sac, which essentially rules out ectopic pregnancy.

B) Hydatidiform mole: Typically shows very high β-hCG levels and “snowstorm” appearance on ultrasound with no normal gestational sac or yolk sac.

D) Threatened abortion: Characterized by vaginal bleeding with a closed cervix and a viable fetus with cardiac activity. This patient has no fetal pole and falling β-hCG, indicating nonviability.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 38-year-old woman presents for counseling about her future risk of ovarian cancer. She has no personal history of malignancy and tested negative for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations. Her mother was diagnosed with epithelial ovarian cancer at age 62. The patient has had two full-term pregnancies and is considering a long-term strategy to reduce her ovarian cancer risk. Which of the following interventions has been shown to most effectively reduce the risk of epithelial ovarian cancer in women like this patient?
options: Long-term use of combined oral contraceptive pills
Routine measurement of serum CA-125 levels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Long-term use of combined oral contraceptive pills

Long-term use of combined oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) significantly reduces the risk of epithelial ovarian cancer by suppressing ovulation.

• Repeated ovulation causes recurrent disruption and repair of the ovarian surface epithelium
• Ovulation suppression decreases epithelial injury and malignant transformation risk

Protective factors for ovarian cancer:

• OCP use
• Multiparity
• Breastfeeding
• Late menarche/early menopause

Risk factors:

• BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations
• Nulliparity
• Infertility
• Early menarche and late menopause

Why other options are incorrect:

• Transvaginal ultrasound and CA-125 are not effective screening tools for average-risk women
• Prophylactic bilateral oophorectomy is reserved mainly for high-risk women (eg, BRCA mutation carriers)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 39-week primigravida is planned for induction of labor. Vaginal examination reveals: • Cervical dilatation: 2 cm • Effacement: 60% • Station: –1 • Cervix soft and anterior Which of the following best describes the cervix?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Favorable cervix for induction

| Parameter | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3

| --------- | --- | --- | --- | ---

| Cervical dilatation (cm) | Closed | 1–2 cm | 3–4 cm | ≥5 cm

| Cervical effacement (%) | 0–30% | 40–50% | 60–70% | ≥80%

| Station of presenting part | –3 | –2 | –1 / 0 | +1 / +2

| Cervical consistency | Firm | Medium | Soft | —

| Cervical position | Posterior | Mid-position | Anterior | —

Total Bishop Score = 8

| Bishop Score | Interpretation | Induction Outcome

| ------------ | -------------- | -----------------

| ≤4 | Unfavorable cervix | Low chance of successful induction

| 5–8 | Moderately favorable | May require cervical ripening

| ≥9 | Favorable cervix | High likelihood of successful vaginal delivery

A favorable cervix:

• Responds well to oxytocin induction
• Has a higher chance of vaginal delivery
• Usually does not require cervical ripening before induction

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

• Unfavorable Bishop score: Score is 8, indicating a favorable cervix.
• Cervical incompetence: Refers to painless cervical dilatation in pregnancy, unrelated to labor induction assessment.
• Failed induction: Can only be diagnosed after an adequate attempt at induction.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 39-year-old nulliparous woman presents to the OPD with pelvic pressure and constipation that have progressively worsened over the past year. She frequently experiences a sensation of incomplete evacuation after defecation. Her menstrual cycles are regular ( every 28 days ) without heavy bleeding or severe pain. She has no dyspareunia and uses of condoms for contraception. Examination reveals an irregularly enlarged uterus and normal rectal tone. What is the most likely etiology of this patient’s constipation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior subserosal uterine leiomyoma

A posterior subserosal uterine leiomyoma (fibroid) can cause pressure symptoms by compressing adjacent pelvic organs, particularly the rectum, leading to constipation and a sensation of incomplete evacuation.

• Subserosal fibroids grow outward from the uterine surface.
• When located posteriorly, they may compress the rectum.
• This results in pelvic pressure, constipation, and tenesmus-like symptoms.
• Menstrual cycles may remain normal because subserosal fibroids usually do not distort the endometrial cavity.

Constipation with pelvic pressure and an irregularly enlarged uterus in a reproductive-age woman suggests a posterior subserosal leiomyoma causing rectal compression.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 39-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 38 weeks gestation, comes to the office for a routine prenatal visit. The patient feels well and reports normal fetal activity. Last week, she had nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea for 24 hours, but she has been able to eat and drink normally for the past several days. For the past 2 days, the patient has had increased clear vaginal discharge with irregular, painful contractions but no vaginal bleeding. Temperature is 99.6 °F (37.6 °C), blood pressure is 132/86 mm Hg, and pulse is 96/ min. The uterus is nontender and the fundal height is 34 cm. Fetal heart tones are 135/ min. Fetal ultrasound shows a cephalic fetus, measuring at the 50th percentile for gestational age, and an amniotic fluid index of 2 cm (normal: >5 cm). Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's amniotic fluid level?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rupture of membranes

Oligohydramnios is defined as amniotic fluid index (AFI) ≤5 cm.

In late pregnancy, the most common cause of sudden oligohydramnios is rupture of membranes (ROM). When the amniotic sac ruptures, amniotic fluid leaks through the cervix and vagina, resulting in:

• Decreased amniotic fluid
• Oligohydramnios on ultrasound

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

• Fetal congenital infection: usually causes fetal anomalies, growth restriction, or hydrops, not isolated oligohydramnios.
• Maternal dehydration: may cause mild reduction in fluid but not severe AFI of 2 cm.
• Normal gestational age variant: AFI <5 cm is abnormal at any gestational age.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 40-year-old nulligravida woman comes to the office with a 2-month history of worsening right pelvic pain. She experiences the pain daily, and its intensity does not vary during her menstrual cycle. In addition, the patient's waist size has increased despite a decreased appetite. Pelvic examination shows an irregularly shaped, fixed adnexal mass. One week later, she undergoes surgery to remove a large ovarian neoplasm. Within the true pelvis, the surgeon can most likely palpate the right ureter immediately anterior to which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Internal iliac artery

In the true pelvis, the ureter runs anterior to the internal iliac artery after crossing the pelvic brim.

Important Ureteric Relationships:

• At the pelvic brim → ureter crosses anterior to the bifurcation of the common iliac artery.
• In the true pelvis → ureter passes anterior to the internal iliac artery.
• Near the cervix → “water under the bridge” (ureter passes under the uterine artery).

Knowledge of these relationships is important during pelvic surgeries (e.g., hysterectomy, ovarian tumor surgery) to prevent ureteric injury.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman comes with a history of postcoital bleeding and a visible mass seen in cervix per speculum. The next step to be done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Targeted biopsy

Postcoital bleeding with a visible cervical growth should be considered cervical carcinoma until proven otherwise. The diagnosis of cervical cancer requires histopathological confirmation.

Appropriate Next Step

• Targeted biopsy from the cervical lesion is the investigation of choice.
• It provides definitive tissue diagnosis and guides further staging and management.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect?

• Conisation: Used for selected preinvasive lesions or when biopsy/colposcopy findings are inconclusive, not as the initial step for an obvious cervical mass.
• Cryotherapy: A treatment modality used only after appropriate diagnosis; should not be performed before biopsy.
• Pap smear: A screening test, not a diagnostic test for a visible suspicious cervical lesion.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman, gravida 5 para 0 aborta 4, at 35 weeks’ gestation presents to labor and delivery triage because she has not felt fetal movements for the past 24 hours. She has had poor oral intake due to nausea. A nonstress test shows a baseline fetal heart rate in the 130s with moderate variability, no decelerations, and no accelerations despite vibroacoustic stimulation. Tocometry shows no uterine contractions. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Biophysical profile

A nonstress test (NST) evaluates fetal well-being by assessing fetal heart rate accelerations with fetal movement.

Interpretation:

• Reactive NST: ≥2 accelerations in 20 minutes → reassuring
• Nonreactive NST: No accelerations despite stimulation → requires further evaluation

When an NST is nonreactive but baseline rate and variability are normal, the next step is a Biophysical Profile (BPP).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 41-year-old woman has stress urinary incontinence confirmed on urodynamics. She has intrinsic sphincter deficiency, no significant prolapse, and wants the most evidence-supported minimally invasive option. What is the best surgery in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mid-urethral sling procedure

Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) is the involuntary leakage of urine during activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure, such as coughing, sneezing, or exercise.

In Intrinsic Sphincter Deficiency (ISD)

• The urethral sphincter fails to maintain adequate closure pressure.
• Leakage occurs even with minimal increases in abdominal pressure.

Mid-urethral sling (MUS) procedure is the current gold-standard surgical treatment for SUI. Common types:

• Tension-free vaginal tape (TVT)
• Transobturator tape (TOT)

Advantages

• Minimally invasive
• High long-term cure rates
• Effective in both urethral hypermobility and intrinsic sphincter deficiency
• Short recovery period

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

• Anterior colporrhaphy: Primarily repairs cystocele; inferior success rates for SUI.
• Le Fort colpocleisis: Obliterative procedure for advanced prolapse in elderly women who no longer desire vaginal intercourse.
• Posterior colpoperineorrhaphy: Used for rectocele and perineal defects, not stress incontinence.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman presents to a district hospital in India with 6 months of heavy menstrual bleeding and fatigue. BMI is 33 kg/m². She has no intermenstrual bleeding. Urine pregnancy test is negative. The exam is normal. A bimanual exam suggests a normal-sized uterus. What is the most appropriate next step to evaluate the cause of bleeding?
options: Start tranexamic acid and review in 3 months
Transvaginal ultrasound as the first-line investigation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Transvaginal ultrasound as the first-line investigation

In women with abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), the first-line investigation is transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) to evaluate uterine and endometrial pathology.

• Assess endometrial thickness
• Detect fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis
• Evaluate ovaries and adnexa

If TVS shows endometrial thickening or suspicious lesions, then endometrial biopsy or hysteroscopy is performed.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman, gravida 4 para 4, presents with heavy and painful menstrual bleeding for the past 3 months. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. Menarche occurred at age 10, and her cycles last 3–5 days every 30 days. She is sexually active and denies dyspareunia. She underwent bilateral tubal ligation 3 years ago. On bimanual exam, the uterus is uniformly enlarged and tender. Urine hCG is negative. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
options: Benign myometrial smooth muscle cell proliferation
Blastocyst implantation in the fallopian tube
Endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium
Localized overgrowth of endometrium into the uterine cavity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium

Adenomyosis is characterized by the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, leading to uterine enlargement and dysmenorrhea.

• Heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia)

• Painful menses (dysmenorrhea)

• Uniformly enlarged, tender “boggy” uterus

• Common in multiparous women aged 35–50 years

Endometrial tissue invades the myometrium, causing:

• Hypertrophy and hyperplasia of surrounding myometrium

• Diffuse enlargement of the uterus

• Cyclic bleeding within the myometrium → pain and heavy bleeding

Why other options are incorrect:

• Benign myometrial smooth muscle proliferation: Refers to uterine fibroids (leiomyoma), which typically cause irregular, firm uterine enlargement rather than diffuse tenderness.

• Blastocyst implantation in the fallopian tube: Ectopic pregnancy, usually presents with amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and positive hCG.

• Localized overgrowth of endometrium: Suggests endometrial polyp, which does not cause diffuse uterine enlargement.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman comes to the OPD due to unintentional weight loss of 6.8 kg over the past 6 months. She has also reported epigastric pain but denies dysphagia, regurgitation, vomiting, or diarrhea. Pelvic ultrasonography shows bilateral complex ovarian masses with solid and cystic components. Chest x-ray is normal. CT scan reveals gastric wall thickening in addition to the ovarian masses. Which of the following is most likely to be seen on histologic evaluation of the ovaries?
options: Nests of epithelial cells with abundant clear cytoplasm
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mucin-secreting signet ring cells

Krukenberg tumor refers to metastatic ovarian tumors, most commonly originating from gastric adenocarcinoma.

• Bilateral ovarian masses
• Solid and cystic components
• Associated primary gastric carcinoma
• Histology shows mucin-producing signet ring cells

Gastric cancer spreads to the ovaries via lymphatic or hematogenous routes. Mucin accumulation displaces the nucleus to the periphery, creating the characteristic signet ring appearance. Usually bilateral ovarian involvement

Why not the other options:

• A) Bilobed nuclei and inclusion-like nucleoli → Seen in papillary thyroid carcinoma, not ovarian metastasis from gastric cancer.
• B) Intercellular bridges and keratin pearls → Characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma.
• D) Nests of epithelial cells with abundant clear cytoplasm → Seen in clear cell carcinoma of the ovary or kidney, not metastatic gastric cancer.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 48-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 6 mm. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. EA/ECC

Postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) must always be evaluated to exclude endometrial malignancy.

Role of Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVS):

• Endometrial thickness ≤4 mm → Low risk of malignancy → Usually observation.
• Endometrial thickness >4 mm → Endometrial sampling is required to rule out pathology such as Endometrial cancer or Endometrial hyperplasia.

In this case:

• Postmenopausal bleeding + endometrial thickness 6 mm (>4 mm)

→ Next step: Endometrial aspiration / Endometrial curettage (EA/ECC) for histopathological diagnosis.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Tamoxifen therapy: Not a treatment here; it can actually increase the risk of endometrial pathology.
• Hysterectomy: Definitive treatment but not done before histologic confirmation.
• Saline infusion sonohysterography: Useful for evaluating focal intrauterine lesions (polyps, submucous fibroids) but biopsy is required first in PMB with thickened endometrium.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 48-year-old woman presents with postcoital bleeding and foul-smelling vaginal discharge. On examination, the cervix is indurated and irregular. CT scan shows hydroureter with hydronephrosis. Cystoscopy demonstrates bullous edema of the bladder. What is the FIGO stage of carcinoma cervix?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stage IIIB

In carcinoma cervix, ureteric involvement/hydroureter with hydronephrosis corresponds to Stage IIIB disease. Bullous edema on cystoscopy alone does not qualify as bladder involvement. Stage IVA requires true bladder mucosal involvement. Parametrial involvement corresponds to Stage IIB. Thus, hydroureter with bullous edema but no bladder mucosal infiltration is staged as Stage IIIB.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 49-year-old multiparous woman with chronic PID presents with persistent lower abdominal pain. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy

In chronic pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) with persistent pain and completed family, the definitive treatment is total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAH + BSO).

• Removes chronically infected uterus, tubes, and ovaries
• Prevents recurrent infection and chronic pelvic pain
• Preferred in multiparous or perimenopausal women

Why not other options:

A) Supracervical hysterectomy + bilateral salpingectomy: Cervix and ovaries remain, infection may persist.

B) Radical hysterectomy: Done for cervical cancer, not PID.

D) Supracervical hysterectomy + tuboplasty: Tuboplasty is fertility surgery; not useful in chronic PID with completed family.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 49-year-old woman, gravida 5 para 5, presents to the OPD with involuntary, intermittent leakage of urine for the past 5 months. She leaks a small amount of urine when asked to cough. She has no dysuria, urgency, or hematuria and she usually awakens once at night to void. Her postvoid residual urine volume is 40 mL. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Urethral hypermobility

Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) is characterized by involuntary leakage of urine during activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure, such as coughing, sneezing, or laughing, without urgency.

Most common mechanism:

• Urethral hypermobility due to weakening of pelvic floor support (pubourethral ligaments and endopelvic fascia).
• Common in multiparous women because repeated childbirth stretches pelvic support structures.

Supporting features in this case:

• Leakage only on coughing
• No urgency or dysuria
• Normal postvoid residual (40 mL)
• History of multiple vaginal deliveries

Why other options are incorrect:

• Detrusor overactivity: causes urgency and urge incontinence.
• Bladder outlet obstruction: usually causes high postvoid residual urine.
• Vesicovaginal fistula: causes continuous leakage, not intermittent.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with abdominal distension and vague pelvic discomfort. Imaging reveals a unilateral ovarian mass. She undergoes staging laparotomy. The tumor is found to be limited to the ovary, with no capsular breach or surface involvement. However, peritoneal washings show malignant cells on cytology. What is the most appropriate FIGO stage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stage IC3

According to the FIGO staging system for ovarian carcinoma, Stage I tumors are confined to the ovaries or fallopian tubes.

Stage IC includes tumors limited to the ovary but with additional high-risk features:

• IC1 → surgical spill
• IC2 → capsule rupture before surgery or tumor on ovarian surface
• IC3 → malignant cells present in ascites or peritoneal washings

In this patient:

• Tumor confined to ovary
• No capsular breach or surface involvement
• Positive peritoneal washings

Therefore, the correct stage is: FIGO Stage IC3

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with vasomotor symptoms and is started on hormone therapy. The clinician considers a drug that provides symptomatic relief without increasing the risk of endometrial hyperplasia. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tibolone

Tibolone is a synthetic steroid with estrogenic, progestogenic, and androgenic activity used in postmenopausal women for the treatment of:

• Vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes, night sweats)
• Prevention of osteoporosis
• Improvement in libido and sexual well-being

Unlike unopposed estrogen therapy, tibolone:

• Provides relief of menopausal symptoms
• Has a progestogenic effect on the endometrium
• Does not stimulate endometrial proliferation significantly
• Therefore, does not increase the risk of endometrial hyperplasia when used appropriately

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

• Tamoxifen: Estrogen agonist effect on the endometrium → increases risk of endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma.
• Raloxifene: Does not stimulate the endometrium but does not relieve hot flushes (may worsen them).
• Estradiol alone: Effective for vasomotor symptoms but causes endometrial hyperplasia in women with an intact uterus unless combined with a progestogen.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 54-year-old postmenopausal woman presents to the OPD with increasing vaginal pressure for the past 3 months. She reports no vaginal bleeding or abnormal discharge. Her BMI is 18 kg/m², and vital signs are normal. On speculum examination, the anterior vaginal wall bulges with the Valsalva maneuver. On bimanual examination, the uterus is small and mobile. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pudendal nerve injury

This patient has anterior vaginal wall prolapse (cystocele) --> suggested by bulging of the anterior vaginal wall during the Valsalva maneuver and a sensation of vaginal pressure.

Pelvic organ prolapse occurs due to weakness of the pelvic floor muscles and connective tissue support.

One important mechanism is injury to the Pudendal nerve, which innervates the levator ani muscles and external sphincters.

Damage to this nerve leads to:

• Loss of pelvic floor muscle tone ; Weak support of pelvic organs

• Descent of the bladder into the vagina (cystocele)

Common causes of pudendal nerve injury:

• Vaginal childbirth (most common)

• Chronic increased intra-abdominal pressure

• Aging and postmenopausal estrogen deficiency

• Pelvic floor trauma

Why other options are incorrect:

• Chronic endometriosis → causes pelvic pain and infertility, not prolapse.

• Prior uterine artery ligation → affects uterine blood supply but not pelvic support.

• Uterine leiomyomas → cause menorrhagia and enlarged uterus, not anterior vaginal wall prolapse.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman presents with complaints of continuous urinary dribbling from the vagina. A Methylene blue three-swab test is performed, and the middle swab is stained blue. Which of the following is the least likely cause of the underlying condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pelvic inflammatory disease ( PID )

The methylene blue three-swab test is used to identify the type of urogenital fistula causing continuous urinary leakage per vagina.

How it's performed

1. Methylene blue dye is instilled into the bladder via catheter
2. Three cotton swabs are placed in the vagina:

• Upper swab — near the vault/cervix
• Middle swab — mid-vagina
• Lower swab — near the introitus

3. The patient ambulates or performs a Valsalva manoeuvre
4. Swabs are examined for blue staining

| Swab Position | Stains Blue | Implication

| ------------- | ----------- | -----------

| Upper | Yes | High VVF

| Middle | Yes | Mid-vaginal fistula

| Lower | Yes | Low/urethrovaginal fistula

Common causes of vesicovaginal fistula:

• Neglected/obstructed labor (most common in developing countries)
• Gynecologic surgery, especially hysterectomy
• Direct tumor invasion, e.g., carcinoma of cervix or bladder

Least likely cause:

• Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) rarely leads to vesicovaginal fistula, making it the least likely cause.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with irregular vaginal bleeding for the past 4 months. On transvaginal ultrasound, the overall endometrial thickness is 2 mm, but a focal area measures 6 mm. What is the next best step to diagnose the cause of bleeding in this patient?
options: Fractional curettage of the endometrium and endocervix
Dilatation and curettage of the endometrium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hysteroscopic inspection with selective biopsy

In postmenopausal bleeding, transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) is the initial investigation. An endometrial thickness ≤4 mm generally suggests a low risk of endometrial carcinoma. However, the presence of a focal thickened area (as in this case) raises suspicion for localized pathology such as an endometrial polyp or focal carcinoma.

Best diagnostic approach:

• Hysteroscopy with directed (selective) biopsy allows direct visualization of the uterine cavity and targeted sampling of the abnormal area.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Fractional curettage or blind D&C: may miss focal lesions because sampling is not targeted.
• Hysterectomy: not performed without establishing a diagnosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 6-year-old girl develops precocious puberty. Image shows café-au-lait pigmentation and fibrous dysplasia. Which finding is not associated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High LH

The child has McCune–Albright syndrome (MAS), characterized by the triad of precocious puberty, café-au-lait macules with irregular "coast of Maine" borders, and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia. MAS is caused by an activating mutation of the GNAS gene, leading to autonomous endocrine hyperfunction. The precocious puberty is gonadotropin-independent (peripheral precocious puberty); therefore, LH and FSH are suppressed due to negative feedback from excess sex steroids. MAS may also be associated with growth hormone excess, hyperthyroidism (low TSH due to elevated thyroid hormones), Cushing syndrome, and phosphate wasting. Hence, high LH is not a feature of McCune–Albright syndrome.

| Feature | McCune–Albright Syndrome

| ------- | ------------------------

| Gene | GNAS mutation

| Precocious puberty | Peripheral (GnRH-independent)

| LH & FSH | Low/Suppressed

| Café-au-lait spots | Coast of Maine (irregular borders)

| Bone lesion | Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia

| Other endocrinopathies | GH excess, hyperthyroidism (↓TSH), Cushing syndrome

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 62-year-old female achieved menopause with smooth transition. She is on hormone replacement therapy. She developed abdominal pain. On examination, a right adnexal mass was palpable and non-tender. On ultrasound, a 3 X 3 cm cyst in her ovary was noted. What is the next best step?
options: Reassure and advice regular follow up once in 6 months
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CA-125 levels

An ovarian cyst in a postmenopausal woman should always be evaluated carefully because the risk of ovarian malignancy increases after menopause.

Next Best Step: Serum CA-125 level

In a postmenopausal woman with:

• Palpable adnexal mass
• Ovarian cyst on ultrasound

CA-125 is the initial investigation used to assess the risk of malignancy and calculate the Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI).

Management Approach

• Simple unilateral cyst <5 cm + normal CA-125 → Conservative follow-up with repeat ultrasound.
• Elevated CA-125 or suspicious ultrasound features → Further evaluation with CT imaging and surgical assessment.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

• Reassure and advice regular follow up once in 6 months: Not appropriate before excluding malignancy.
• CECT scan: Performed after risk stratification, not as the first step.
• Exploratory laparoscopy: Not indicated without prior evaluation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 62-year-old multiparous woman presents to the gynecology clinic with a sensation of vaginal fullness and difficulty completely emptying her bladder. Her symptoms worsen at the end of the day and improve when she lies down. She has a history of four vaginal deliveries and chronic constipation. Pelvic examination reveals a bulge of the anterior vaginal wall that becomes more pronounced when the patient performs a Valsalva maneuver. The cervix remains well supported, and no posterior vaginal wall defect is noted. Weakening of which of the following anatomic structures is the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pubocervical fascia

This patient has a cystocele (anterior vaginal wall prolapse) caused by weakening of the pubocervical fascia, which supports the bladder and anterior vaginal wall.

Risk factors:

• Multiparity
• Vaginal deliveries
• Chronic increased intra-abdominal pressure (eg, constipation)
• Aging and menopause

Clinical features:

• Vaginal fullness or bulge
• Urinary hesitancy/incomplete emptying
• Symptoms worsen with standing or straining

Anatomic correlations:

• Pubocervical fascia defect → cystocele
• Rectovaginal septum weakness → rectocele
• Cardinal and uterosacral ligament weakness → uterine prolapse/apical prolapse

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 63-year-old woman is found to have a right-sided ovarian mass incidentally on transvaginal ultrasound. Surgery is planned to remove the right ovary along with the mass. To avoid excessive bleeding during the oophorectomy, which of the following structures should the surgeon ligate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Suspensory ligament of the ovary

During oophorectomy, the major vascular supply to the ovary comes through the suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament).

• The suspensory ligament of the ovary connects the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall.
• It contains the ovarian artery, ovarian vein, lymphatics, and nerves.
• These vessels arise from the abdominal aorta (ovarian artery).

Surgical importance:

• During removal of the ovary, the infundibulopelvic ligament must be ligated to control the ovarian vessels and prevent significant bleeding.

Other options:

• A. Mesosalpinx: part of the broad ligament supporting the fallopian tube.
• B. Ovarian ligament: connects ovary to the uterus but contains no major vessels.
• C. Round ligament of uterus: maintains uterine anteversion and passes to the labia majora.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 65-year-old man with advanced prostate cancer and bone metastases has been treated with a GnRH agonist for the last 4 months, which has reduced his bone pain. He now reports discomfort in the anterior chest wall. Physical examination reveals bilateral, mildly tender gynaecomastia (enlargement of breast tissue behind the nipple-areolar complex). Which medication would be most appropriate to start early to prevent these breast symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tamoxifen

Gynecomastia in men receiving androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) occurs due to hormonal imbalance between estrogen and androgens.

GnRH agonists suppress testosterone production, leading to relative estrogen predominance --> stimulates proliferation of breast glandular tissue.

Tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM), is the most appropriate drug to prevent or treat gynecomastia and breast pain in these patients.

• Tamoxifen blocks estrogen receptors in breast tissue
• Prevents estrogen-mediated breast glandular proliferation ; Reduces breast enlargement and tenderness

Why other options are incorrect:

• Danazol: Synthetic androgen used in endometriosis and fibrocystic breast disease; not standard for ADT-induced gynecomastia.
• Finasteride: 5-alpha reductase inhibitor; can cause gynecomastia.
• Spironolactone: Antiandrogenic effect and commonly causes gynecomastia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 65-year-old obese woman with diabetes and hypertension presents with post-menopausal bleeding. Endometrial biopsy shows adenocarcinoma grade 1. What is the 'gatekeeper' gene for endometrial cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. PTEN

The patient has Type I (endometrioid) endometrial carcinoma, the commonest subtype of endometrial cancer. It typically occurs in postmenopausal women with unopposed estrogen exposure and is strongly associated with obesity, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, nulliparity, and chronic anovulation. The PTEN tumor suppressor gene is the gatekeeper gene for Type I endometrial carcinoma and is the earliest and most common genetic alteration, promoting uncontrolled endometrial proliferation. In contrast, Type II (serous) endometrial carcinoma is estrogen-independent, occurs in an atrophic endometrium, and is characterized by p53 mutations with a poorer prognosis.

High-Yield

• Gatekeeper gene: PTEN
• Type I endometrial carcinoma: Endometrioid, estrogen-dependent, good prognosis
• Type II endometrial carcinoma: Serous, p53 mutation, estrogen-independent, aggressive
• Lynch syndrome (HNPCC): Associated with MMR gene mutations (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) and increased risk of endometrial carcinoma.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman is diagnosed with Stage IA vulval cancer (size <2 cm, depth <1 mm). What is the appropriate lymph node management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. No lymph node dissection

The patient has FIGO Stage IA vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, defined as a lesion ≤2 cm with stromal invasion ≤1 mm. The risk of inguinofemoral lymph node metastasis is <1%, making lymph node assessment unnecessary. Therefore, the recommended treatment is wide local excision (radical local excision/simple partial vulvectomy with adequate margins) without inguinofemoral lymph node dissection. Lymph node surgery is reserved for Stage IB or higher (stromal invasion >1 mm), where the risk of nodal metastasis increases significantly. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is considered only in selected Stage IB unifocal tumors, not Stage IA.

• Stage IA: ≤2 cm, stromal invasion ≤1 mm → No lymph node dissection
• Stage IB: Stromal invasion >1 mm → Sentinel lymph node biopsy (selected patients) or inguinofemoral lymph node assessment
• Most important prognostic factor in vulvar cancer: Inguinofemoral lymph node status

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 67-year-old woman diagnosed with uterine prolapse now presents with dyspareunia and fecal incontinence. After manually reducing the prolapse, a peristaltic bulge is seen in the posterior vaginal wall. What is the preferred method of management in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Moschcowitz repair

The clinical scenario describes:

• Uterine prolapse + fecal incontinence + posterior vaginal wall bulge after reduction
• = Enterocele (peristaltic bulge = loops of intestine in pouch of Douglas herniation)

Moschcowitz repair = purse-string sutures closing the pouch of Douglas → prevents enterocele → also addresses the fecal incontinence component via posterior compartment repair.

| Option | Procedure | Used For | Why Wrong

| ------ | --------- | -------- | ---------

| A. Moschcowitz | Purse-string sutures at pouch of Douglas | Enterocele repair ✅ | Correct

| B. Purandare's | Uterus fixed to anterior abdominal wall (ventrosuspension) | Retroverted uterus | Not for prolapse with enterocele

| C. McCall culdoplasty | Posterior cul-de-sac obliteration at time of vaginal hysterectomy | Vault prolapse prevention
Enterocele repair | Can be used for enterocele repair-But not in presence of Fecal incontinence

| D. Le Fort's | Partial colpocleisis (anterior + posterior vaginal wall stitched together) | Uterine prolapse in elderly, sexually inactive | She has dyspareunia → still sexually active → Le Fort's would make intercourse impossible

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 69-year-old man presents with progressive lower urinary tract symptoms, including weak urinary stream, hesitancy, and nocturia. Over the past 2 months, he has also developed diffuse low back and hip pain that worsens at night. Digital rectal examination reveals a hard, irregular prostate. Serum PSA is markedly elevated. A bone scan demonstrates multiple osteoblastic lesions in the vertebrae and pelvis. He is started on a medication administered as a monthly depot injection. Ten days later, he reports acute worsening of bone pain and increased difficulty urinating. One month after initiation of therapy, his symptoms significantly improve. Which of the following best explains the initial worsening of symptoms after starting this medication?
options: Competitive inhibition of androgen receptors in prostate tissue
Continuous stimulation of pituitary gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptors
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Continuous stimulation of pituitary gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptors

• Continuous GnRH receptor stimulation initially increases:

• LH and FSH release
• Testosterone production

• This temporary androgen surge worsens symptoms:

• Bone pain
• Urinary obstruction
• Possible spinal cord compression

After continued administration:

• Pituitary GnRH receptors become desensitized/downregulated
• LH and testosterone levels fall
• Symptoms improve

GnRH agonists cause an initial testosterone “flare”. GnRH antagonists (eg, degarelix) suppress testosterone immediately without flare

Prevention of flare: Antiandrogens (eg, bicalutamide, flutamide) are often given initially with GnRH agonists to block transient androgen effects.

Common prostate cancer bone metastases Osteoblastic/sclerotic lesions involving spine, pelvis, and ribs.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 76-year-old woman presented with a non-healing ulcer on the labia majora midline for the past 6 months, measuring 2 cm x 3 cm. No inguinal lymph nodes are palpable. A biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Radical vulvectomy with unilateral lymph node dissection
Radical vulvectomy with bilateral lymph node dissection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Radical vulvectomy with bilateral lymph node dissection

In squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva involving the midline (e.g., labia majora, clitoris, posterior fourchette), lymphatic drainage occurs bilaterally to the inguinal lymph nodes. Therefore, the standard surgical management is radical vulvectomy with bilateral inguinal lymph node dissection, even if lymph nodes are not clinically palpable.

• Midline vulvar lesions → bilateral lymphatic drainage → bilateral inguinal node dissection required.
• Lateral lesions (>1 cm from midline) may be managed with unilateral node dissection.
• Early-stage disease is primarily treated with surgery, while chemoradiation is reserved for advanced or unresectable disease.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A consultant is examining a post-hysterectomy patient for vault prolapse. POP-Q is performed. Which of the following is incorrect regarding this examination?
options: Point C now represents the vaginal cuff (apex)
Point D is not measured in post-hysterectomy patients
TVL is measured with the prolapse reduced to its normal anatomical position
gh is measured from the posterior fourchette to the mid-anal opening
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. gh is measured from the posterior fourchette to the mid-anal opening

The Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) system is the standardized method for assessing and describing pelvic organ prolapse using specific vaginal reference points measured relative to the hymen.

POP-Q in Post-Hysterectomy Patients

• Point C represents the vaginal cuff (vaginal apex) after hysterectomy.
• Point D represents the posterior fornix and is not measured after hysterectomy, as the cervix has been removed.
• Total Vaginal Length (TVL) is measured with the prolapse reduced to its normal anatomical position.

gh (genital hiatus) is not measured from the posterior fourchette to the mid-anal opening. Genital hiatus (gh) is measured from:

• The middle of the external urethral meatus
• To the posterior hymenal ring (posterior fourchette)

The measurement from the posterior fourchette to the mid-anal opening is called the Perineal body (pb)

Key POP-Q Measurements

• gh: External urethral meatus → posterior hymen
• pb: Posterior hymen → mid-anal opening
• TVL: Total vaginal length with prolapse reduced
• C: Cervix or vaginal cuff apex
• D: Posterior fornix (only if cervix is present)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A fetus is diagnosed with an open neural tube defect during antenatal evaluation. The parents seek counseling regarding management. According to the management approach outlined for neural tube defects, the most appropriate recommendation is:
options: Continue pregnancy and start folic acid 4 mg/day immediately
Continue pregnancy and monitor AFP serially every 4 weeks
Medical termination of pregnancy should be offered during the antenatal period
Delay decision until postnatal neurological assessment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medical termination of pregnancy should be offered during the antenatal period

| Scenario | Management

| -------- | ----------

| Previous affected child (preconception) | Folic acid 4 mg/day

| General prevention | Folic acid 400 mcg/day

| NTD detected antenatally | Termination of pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A fetus with early-onset fetal growth restriction is being closely monitored with Doppler studies. The clinician wants to identify the most reliable single Doppler parameter for predicting fetal acidemia and impending decompensation. Which of the following Doppler findings is the strongest predictor of fetal acidemia?
options: Decreased pulsatility index in middle cerebral artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Abnormal ductus venosus waveform

In early-onset fetal growth restriction (FGR), Doppler studies are used to assess the progression of placental insufficiency and identify fetuses at risk of hypoxemia, acidemia, and intrauterine death.

Sequence of Doppler Deterioration
