• Routine induction after ECV does not improve outcomes and may increase interventions.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Regarding genital tuberculosis, all of the following statements are correct except:
options: Genital TB is the most common cause of PID in virgin females
The most common presentation of genital TB is infertility
HSG is done to document tubal disease, then ATT is started for treatment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HSG is done to document tubal disease, then ATT is started for treatment

Genital TB is the most common cause of PID in virgin females. The most common presentation is infertility, followed by pain; menstrual irregularity is the third most common presentation. For investigation, HSG should be done after starting ATT, not before, because active genital TB is a contraindication for HSG. Diagnosis is confirmed by endometrial biopsy with HPE/AFB, and in virgin females, day-1 menstrual blood PCR can be used. Management is ATT for 6 months; if tubes are distorted, IVF is advised.

• Beaded tube appearance — multiple constrictions along the tube.
• Tobacco pouch appearance — terminal hydrosalpinx with fimbrial narrowing.
• Pipestem / lead-pipe tube — rigid straight tube due to fibrosis.
• Bilateral cornual block — can be physiological due to spasm, but pathological cause includes genital TB.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Regarding human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), all of the following statements are true except:
options: hCG reaches peak levels at around 10 weeks of gestation
hCG disappears from maternal blood immediately after delivery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. hCG disappears from maternal blood immediately after delivery

Important facts about hCG

| Feature | Key Point

| ------- | ---------

| Source | Syncytiotrophoblast

| Nature | Glycoprotein hormone

| α-subunit | Similar to LH, FSH, TSH

| β-subunit | Specific

| Function | Maintains corpus luteum

| Doubling time | 48 hours

| Peak level | 10 weeks

| Plateau | Around 16 weeks

| Disappearance after delivery | \~2 weeks

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Regarding instrumental delivery, all of the following statements are correct except:
options: Vacuum is applied at the flexion point
Vacuum can be used for mentoanterior face presentation
Forceps are preferred in fetal distress
Forceps cause more maternal injury than vacuum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vacuum can be used for mentoanterior face presentation

Vacuum is contraindicated in:

• Mentoanterior face presentation
• Prematurity
• After-coming head of breech

High-yield comparison

| Vacuum | Forceps

| ------ | -------

| More fetal injury | More maternal injury

| Can rotate fetal head | Better for rapid delivery

| Can be applied at ≥6 cm dilatation | Requires full dilatation

| Contraindicated in prematurity | Preferred in preterm

Forceps preferred in:

• Fetal distress
• Maternal heart disease
• Delivery of head in breech
• Preterm baby

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Regarding prenatal diagnosis of neural tube defects, all of the following statements are true except:
options: Ultrasound is the investigation of choice for antenatal detection of NTDs
Routine anomaly scan for NTD detection is commonly performed around 16 weeks gestation
Anencephaly may be identified earlier than most other NTDs
Maternal serum AFP is superior to amniotic fluid acetylcholinesterase for confirming the diagnosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Maternal serum AFP is superior to amniotic fluid acetylcholinesterase for confirming the diagnosis

High-Yield Facts

| Fact | Value

| ---- | -----

| IOC | Ultrasound

| Routine detection | \~16 weeks

| Earliest identifiable NTD | Anencephaly (10–12 weeks)

| Screening marker | AFP

| Best marker | Acetylcholinesterase

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Regarding the actions of Estrogen in pregnancy, all of the following are true except:
options: Stimulates myometrial hypertrophy and increases uterine blood flow
Promotes ductal proliferation and stromal growth in the breast
Increases hepatic production of binding proteins (TBG, CBG, SHBG)
Decreases renal sodium retention by upregulating aldosterone receptors
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decreases renal sodium retention by upregulating aldosterone receptors

Estrogen plays a major role in maintaining pregnancy and preparing the mother for labor and lactation.

Stimulates myometrial hypertrophy and hyperplasia

• Causes enlargement of the uterus
• Increases uterine blood flow

Promotes breast growth

• Stimulates ductal proliferation
• Increases stromal development
• Prepares the breast for lactation

Increases hepatic synthesis of binding proteins

• Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG)
• Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG)
• Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG)

Estrogen does not decrease renal sodium retention. In pregnancy:

• Estrogen enhances the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
• Leads to increased sodium and water retention
• Contributes to expansion of maternal plasma volume

Therefore, the statement that estrogen decreases sodium retention by upregulating aldosterone receptors is false.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Regarding the actions of Progesterone in pregnancy, all of the following are true except:
options: Maintains uterine quiescence by hyperpolarising myometrial smooth muscle (progesterone block)
Acts as an aldosterone antagonist at renal tubules, promoting natriuresis
Increases minute ventilation by sensitising the respiratory centre to CO₂
Causes urinary retention by increasing detrusor muscle tone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Causes urinary retention by increasing detrusor muscle tone

Progesterone is the key hormone responsible for maintaining pregnancy and preparing the maternal body for fetal growth.

1. Maintains uterine quiescence (Progesterone Block)

• Hyperpolarizes myometrial smooth muscle
• Reduces uterine contractility
• Prevents premature labor

2. Acts as an aldosterone antagonist

• Competes with aldosterone at renal tubules
• Promotes mild natriuresis
• Helps counterbalance pregnancy-associated sodium retention

3. Increases minute ventilation

• Sensitizes the respiratory center to CO₂
• Causes mild hyperventilation
• Leads to physiological respiratory alkalosis of pregnancy

Progesterone does not increase detrusor muscle tone. Instead, progesterone:

• Relaxes smooth muscle throughout the body
• Decreases ureteric and bladder tone
• Contributes to urinary stasis and increased urinary frequency
• Predisposes to urinary tract infections and hydronephrosis of pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Regarding the human placenta, all of the following statements are true except:
options: Placental weight at term is approximately 500 g
Ratio of placental weight to fetal weight at term is 1:6
Placental thickness greater than 3 cm at term is termed placentomegaly
Maternal part of the placenta is formed by decidua basalis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Placental thickness greater than 3 cm at term is termed placentomegaly

The placenta is a temporary fetomaternal organ responsible for nutrient exchange, gas transfer, waste removal, and endocrine support of pregnancy.

Normal Placental Characteristics at Term

• Weight: \~500 g
• Diameter: 15–20 cm
• Thickness: 2–3 cm (maximum about 4 cm)
• Placental weight: fetal weight ratio: approximately 1:6

Formation of Placenta

• Maternal part: Decidua basalis
• Fetal part: Chorion frondosum

Placentomegaly refers to an abnormally enlarged placenta and is generally diagnosed when:

• Placental thickness is >4 cm in the second trimester, or
• >6 cm at term

Therefore, placental thickness >4 cm alone is not the definition of placentomegaly at term, making this statement incorrect.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Regarding the pathophysiology of pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH)/preeclampsia, all of the following are increased vasoconstrictor markers except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Placental growth factor (PlGF)

Increased vasoconstrictors in PIH

• sFlt-1
• Endoglin
• TNF-α
• Thromboxane A2
• Increased vascular sensitivity to angiotensin II

Decreased vasodilators in PIH

• VEGF
• Placental growth factor (PlGF)
• Prostacyclin (PGI2)
• Nitric oxide
• Angiotensinase activity

A hallmark of preeclampsia is an anti-angiogenic state, with:

• ↑ sFlt-1
• ↓ VEGF and PlGF

leading to endothelial dysfunction and vasoconstriction.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Rh negative mother, ICT negative was given Anti D during 28 weeks of pregnancy. Which of the following is the ideal one?
options: No need additional dose since she is ICT negative
Give another dose of Anti-D 72 hour postpartum irrespective of baby blood group
Give another dose of Anti-D 72 hour postpartum depending on the baby blood group
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Give another dose of Anti-D 72 hour postpartum depending on the baby blood group

In Rh-negative women with an Rh-positive partner, Anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis is administered to prevent Rh sensitization. If the mother is ICT (Indirect Coombs Test) negative, an initial dose of Anti-D (300 mcg IM) is given at 28 weeks of gestation. Following delivery, an additional dose of Anti-D should be administered within 72 hours if the newborn is Rh-positive. This prevents the mother from forming antibodies against Rh-positive fetal red blood cells that might have entered her circulation during delivery.

• Anti-D (300 mcg IM) at 28 weeks: Given if ICT is negative.
• Postpartum dose within 72 hours: Required if the baby is Rh-positive. This dose is essential to neutralize any fetal Rh-positive red cells that might have entered the mother's bloodstream during delivery.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The diagnostic criteria for catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS) include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Involvement of three or more organs
Development of clinical manifestations in less than one week
Histological evidence of hydropic degeneration of villi
Presence of antiphospholipid antibodies on two occasions of least six weeks apart
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Histological evidence of hydropic degeneration of villi

Catastrophic Antiphospholipid Syndrome (CAPS) is a severe variant of antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) characterized by rapid, widespread small-vessel thrombosis leading to multiorgan failure.

Diagnostic criteria for CAPS include:

• Involvement of three or more organs, systems, or tissues
• Rapid development of manifestations (within ≤1 week)
• Histologic evidence of small-vessel thrombosis
• Presence of antiphospholipid antibodies (e.g., lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2 glycoprotein I) on repeated testing

Incorrect statement:

• Histological evidence of hydropic degeneration of villi is not a criterion for CAPS; it is typically associated with molar pregnancy, not thrombotic APS.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The following maternal infections or conditions are associated with certain characteristic fetal effects. Which of the following pair is not correctly matched?
options: Zika virus — microcephaly and cerebral malformations
Varicella infection — skin scarring and limb hypoplasia
Maternal SLE — congenital complete heart block
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. HIV infection — non-immune hydrops fetalis

• A. Zika virus → Microcephaly and cerebral malformations ✔️

Congenital Zika syndrome is characterized by severe microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, ventriculomegaly, and other CNS abnormalities.
• B. Varicella infection → Skin scarring and limb hypoplasia ✔️

Congenital varicella syndrome can cause cicatricial skin lesions, limb hypoplasia, ocular defects, and neurological abnormalities.
• C. Maternal SLE → Congenital complete heart block ✔️

Maternal anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) antibodies can cross the placenta and cause neonatal lupus, particularly congenital complete heart block.
• D. HIV infection → Non-immune hydrops fetalis ❌

HIV is not a recognized cause of non-immune hydrops fetalis. Common causes include:

• Parvovirus B19 infection
• Fetal anemia
• Cardiac anomalies
• Chromosomal abnormalities
• Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The patency of fallopian tubes can be clinically tested by which of the following methods? 1. Sonosalpingogram 2. Hysterosalpingogram 3. CT scan 4. Laparoscopic chromotubation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 4

Assessment of fallopian tube patency is an important part of infertility evaluation.

Common methods include:

1. Sonosalpingography (SSG)

• Ultrasound-based technique using saline/contrast
•

Demonstrates spill through fallopian tubes

2. Hysterosalpingography (HSG)

•

Contrast dye injected through cervix with fluoroscopic imaging

•

Evaluates uterine cavity and tubal patency

3. Laparoscopic chromotubation

•

Gold standard test

• Methylene blue dye is injected through cervix and visualized laparoscopically exiting the fimbrial ends

CT scan is not routinely used for assessing tubal patency

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The results of semen analysis of a young male have been given below. What is the appropriate diagnosis? - Sperm concentration: 5 million/mL - Progressive motility: 50% - Normal morphology: 8%
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oligospermia

Oligospermia is defined as a reduced sperm concentration (<15 million sperm/mL) on semen analysis (according to WHO criteria)

Interpretation of the given semen analysis:

• Sperm concentration: 5 million/mL → Low (oligospermia)
• Progressive motility: 50% → Normal
• Normal morphology: 8% → Normal (≥4% normal forms by strict criteria)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Asthenozoospermia: decreased motility (<32% progressive).
• Teratozoospermia: abnormal morphology (<4% normal forms).
• Oligoasthenoteratozoospermia : reduction in count, motility, and morphology simultaneously.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Ultrasound examination shows an anterior placenta covering the cervical os and oligohydramnios, with an amniotic fluid index of 1.5 cm and a single deepest vertical pocket measuring 1.5 × 1 cm. Over a 45-minute observation period, there are 4 episodes of fetal movement, 3 flexion–extension movements, and no fetal breathing movements. The fetus is in breech presentation. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these biophysical profile findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Placental insufficiency

The biophysical profile (BPP) evaluates fetal well-being using five parameters:

1. Nonstress test (NST)
2. Fetal breathing movements
3. Gross body movements
4. Fetal tone
5. Amniotic fluid volume

Interpretation in this case:

• Movements present → reassuring
• Fetal tone present → reassuring
• No breathing movements → abnormal
• Severe oligohydramnios (AFI 1.5 cm) → abnormal

Reduced amniotic fluid and decreased fetal activity suggest chronic fetal hypoxia due to placental insufficiency.

Pathophysiology:

• Placental dysfunction → reduced uteroplacental blood flow
• Decreased fetal renal perfusion → reduced fetal urine production
• Leads to oligohydramnios

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Under the Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) initiative, mild to moderate anemia in pregnant women at less than 34 weeks of gestation is treated with:
options: 60 mg elemental iron and 500 mcg folic acid daily
45mg elemental iron and 400 mcg folic acid twice daily
60 mg elemental iron and 500 mcg folic acid twice daily
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 60 mg elemental iron and 500 mcg folic acid twice daily

Under the Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategy, management of mild to moderate anemia in pregnant women (<34 weeks gestation) is done with therapeutic oral iron–folic acid supplementation.

Recommended regimen:

• 60 mg elemental iron + 500 µg folic acid
• Twice daily

Key points of AMB protocol:

• Prophylaxis: 60 mg iron + 500 µg folic acid once daily
• Treatment (mild–moderate anemia): same dose twice daily
• Severe anemia or intolerance to oral therapy: parenteral iron (e.g., IV iron sucrose) may be used

| Population | Prophylactic | Treatment of Mild and Moderate Anemia

| ---------- | ------------ | -------------------------------------

| Children 6–59 months | 20 mg iron + 100 mcg folic acid two times in a week | 3 mg/kg body weight/day

| 5–9 years | 45 mg iron + 400 mcg folic acid/week | 3 mg/kg body weight/day • Body weight up to 18.5 kg: 45 mg iron + 400 mcg folic acid/day • Body weight >18.5 kg: 60 mg iron + 500 mcg folic acid/day

| 10–19 years (girls) and boys | 60 mg iron + 500 mcg folic acid/week | 120 mg iron + 1 mg folic acid

| Pregnant women | 60 mg iron + 500 mcg folic acid/day | 120 mg iron + 1 mg folic acid

| Non-pregnant non-lactating women and lactating women | 60 mg iron + 500 mcg folic acid | 120 mg iron + 1 mg folic acid

| Men | Not applicable | 120 mg iron + 1 mg folic acid

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which cardiovascular change is more likely to be found in a 23-week Period of gestation (POG) woman?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lateral displacement of apical impulse

During mid-pregnancy (around 20–24 weeks gestation), several physiological cardiovascular changes occur due to increased blood volume and cardiac output.

• Increased plasma volume and cardiac output
• Increased heart rate
• Mild cardiac enlargement due to diaphragm elevation by the gravid uterus
• Lateral and slightly upward displacement of the apical impulse

Because the diaphragm is pushed upward by the enlarging uterus, the heart shifts leftward, causing the apical impulse to be displaced laterally.

Other Options:

• A. Mid-diastolic murmur and B. Pansystolic murmur are pathological findings.
• C. Bradycardia is not typical; pregnancy usually causes mild tachycardia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which finding would not suggest TB salpingitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Wedge-shaped defect at uterine isthmus

Wedge-shaped defect at uterine isthmus = Cesarean scar defect (Isthmocele)

• Pouch/niche at the site of previous LSCS scar
• Seen on HSG as a wedge/triangular filling defect at the isthmus
• Associated with: postmenstrual spotting, secondary infertility, scar ectopic

SIN — Correct HSG Features

| Feature | Description

| ------- | -----------

| Diverticular outpouchings | Small contrast-filled pouches off the isthmic lumen

| Nodular/beaded isthmus | Multiple small diverticula giving nodular appearance

| Bilateral | Usually both tubes affected

| Associated with | Ectopic pregnancy, infertility

SIN ≠ wedge defect — SIN shows diverticular pockets, not a single wedge-shaped niche

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which is not a mechanism of contraceptive action of Implanon?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Impaired sperm motility

Implanon (etonogestrel implant) is a long-acting reversible contraceptive (LARC) that provides effective contraception for up to 3 years through continuous release of a progestin.

Mechanisms of Contraceptive Action:

• Inhibition of ovulation (primary mechanism)
• Thickening of cervical mucus, preventing sperm penetration
• Endometrial atrophy, making the endometrium unsuitable for implantation

Implanon does not directly impair sperm motility.

Its contraceptive effect is achieved by:

• Preventing ovulation
• Blocking sperm entry through thick cervical mucus
• Altering the endometrium

It does not exert a direct spermicidal effect or impair sperm motility within the reproductive tract.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are indications for lower segment cesarean section ( LSCS )? 1. Brow presentation 2. Mentoposterior position 3. Breech presentation 4. Occipitoposterior position 5. Mentoanterior position
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2

Certain malpresentations and malpositions during labor can make vaginal delivery difficult or impossible, requiring lower segment cesarean section (LSCS).

• Brow presentation → Indication for LSCS

o    The presenting diameter (mentovertical \~13.5 cm) is too large to pass through the pelvis.

• Mentoposterior position (face presentation) → Indication for LSCS

o    In mentoposterior, the chin cannot rotate anteriorly, making vaginal delivery impossible.

• Breech presentation → Not an absolute indication

o    Vaginal delivery may be possible depending on case selection.

• Occipitoposterior position → Usually rotates spontaneously; vaginal delivery often possible.
• Mentoanterior position → Vaginal delivery possible because the chin rotates anteriorly.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following instruments are used in the cesarean section? 1. Bard-Parker blade 2. Doyen's retractor 3. Cusco's speculum 4. Allis forceps 5. Shirodkar's uterine clamp 6. Green Armytage forceps
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 4, 6

A cesarean section (LSCS) requires instruments for incision, tissue retraction, hemostasis, and handling tissues during abdominal and uterine surgery.

Instruments commonly used in cesarean section:

• Bard-Parker blade → Used to make the skin and uterine incision.

• Doyen’s retractor → Used to retract the abdominal wall and bladder, improving surgical exposure.

• Allis forceps → Used to grasp fascia, peritoneum, or tissue edges during dissection and closure.

• Green-Armytage forceps → Used to clamp bleeding edges of the uterine incision for hemostasis.

Instruments not used in cesarean section:

• Cusco’s speculum → Used for vaginal examination or procedures, not abdominal surgery.

• Shirodkar’s uterine clamp → Used in cervical cerclage procedures, not LSCS.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is a criterion for classifying a vesicovaginal fistula as complication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Size is 4 cm

• Large vesicovaginal fistulas are classified as complicated because they are technically difficult to repair and have a higher recurrence rate.
•

Size, location, prior radiation, and scarring influence management and prognosis.

•

A vesicovaginal fistula is classified as complicated if it has features such as large size (≥3 cm), involvement of the trigone/urethra, prior radiation, malignancy, recurrent fistula, or associated vaginal scarring.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is a false statement regarding uterine artery embolization (UAE) for fibroids?
options: PVA particles and glue are used as embolising agents
Ovarian failure is one possible complication
It can be done in nulliparous women
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It can be done in nulliparous women

Uterine artery embolization (UAE) is a minimally invasive radiological procedure used to treat symptomatic uterine fibroids by blocking their blood supply.

• Performed under fluoroscopic/radiological guidance.
• Embolizing agents such as polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) particles or glue are used.
• A possible complication is ovarian failure due to reduced ovarian blood supply.

UAE is not preferred in women desiring future fertility (e.g., nulliparous women) because it may affect uterine and ovarian function.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a long-acting reversible contraceptive ( LARC ) method?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Laparoscopic tubal ligation

Long-acting reversible contraception (LARC) refers to contraceptive methods that provide prolonged contraception without requiring user action and are reversible upon removal or discontinuation.

Examples of LARC:

• Copper IUCD (Copper T)
• Levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS)
• Subdermal implants (e.g., Implanon)
• Injectable contraceptives (e.g., DMPA)

Why the other option is incorrect:

• Laparoscopic tubal ligation is a permanent sterilization method, not reversible contraception.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not considered an advantage of using norgestimate-containing oral contraceptives?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reduces venous thrombosis

Norgestimate-containing combined oral contraceptives (COCs) use a third-generation progestin with low androgenic activity.

Advantages:

• Improves acne and hirsutism due to antiandrogenic effect
• Fewer metabolic side effects (less impact on lipids and glucose)
• Lower cardiovascular risk compared with older progestins

Like all estrogen-containing contraceptives, they increase the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) rather than reduce it.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of the first drug used in the regimen for medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) in first trimester?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Progesterone antagonist

The first drug used in first-trimester medical termination of pregnancy is mifepristone, a progesterone receptor antagonist.

Mechanism:

• Blocks progesterone receptors in the endometrium and decidua
• Causes decidual breakdown and detachment of the gestational sac
• Softens and dilates the cervix
• Increases uterine sensitivity to prostaglandins

Regimen:

1. Mifepristone (progesterone antagonist)
2. Followed by misoprostol (prostaglandin analogue) → induces uterine contractions and expulsion

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the primary mechanism of action of ulipristal 30mg when used for emergency contraception?
options: Inhibition of maintenance of corpus luteum
Inhibition of ovulation by suppressing or delaying the LH surge
Thickening of the endometrium to prevent implantation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inhibition of ovulation by suppressing or delaying the LH surge

Ulipristal acetate (30 mg) is used as an emergency contraceptive and acts as a selective progesterone receptor modulator (SPRM).

Primary mechanism:

• Delays or inhibits ovulation by suppressing or postponing the LH surge from the pituitary.

Because ovulation is prevented, fertilization cannot occur, making it effective even when taken close to the time of ovulation.

• Can be used up to 120 hours (5 days) after unprotected intercourse.
• More effective than levonorgestrel when taken near ovulation.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Maintenance of corpus luteum inhibition: not the primary mechanism.
• Interference with sperm penetration: mechanism of barrier methods.
• Endometrial thickening: does not occur; emergency contraceptives mainly prevent ovulation, not implantation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following prostaglandins analogue is NOT correctly paired with its clinical use?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alprostadil -Closure of Ductus Arteriosus

| Prostaglandin analogue  | Type  | Clinical use

| ----------------------- | ----- | -------------

| Dinoprostone (PGE₂)  | Prostaglandin E₂  | Cervical ripening and induction of labor

| Dinoprost (PGF₂α)  | Prostaglandin F₂α  | Management of postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony

| Misoprostol (PGE₁ analogue)  | Prostaglandin E₁  | Medical termination of pregnancy, cervical ripening, PPH management

Incorrect Pairing:

•

Alprostadil (PGE₁) is used to maintain patency of the ductus arteriosus in neonates with congenital heart disease.

•

It does not cause closure of the ductus arteriosus.

Closure of the ductus arteriosus is achieved with prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors such as indomethacin or ibuprofen.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) is approved for the treatment of senile vaginitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ospemifene

Ospemifene is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) approved for the treatment of senile (atrophic) vaginitis.

Ospemifene acts as an estrogen agonist on vaginal epithelium, leading to:

• Thickening of the vaginal mucosa

• Improved lubrication

• Reduced vaginal dryness and dyspareunia

Clinical use: Treatment of dyspareunia and vaginal atrophy in postmenopausal women

Why other options are incorrect:

• Clomiphene→ used for ovulation induction in infertility (PCOS).

• Tamoxifen→ used in estrogen receptor–positive breast cancer.

• Raloxifene→ used for osteoporosis prevention and breast cancer risk reduction.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following should be administered to a newborn delivered to a mother who is HBsAg positive?
options: Immunoglobulin, followed by vaccine at 6 weeks
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hepatitis B vaccine + Immunoglobulin

Newborns born to HBsAg-positive mothers require immediate post-exposure prophylaxis to prevent perinatal transmission of hepatitis B virus (HBV).

Recommended management:

• Hepatitis B vaccine + Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG)
• Both should be given within 12 hours of birth at different injection sites.

Rationale:

• HBIG provides passive immunity.
• Hepatitis B vaccine stimulates active immunity.
• Combined prophylaxis reduces perinatal transmission by >90%.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statement is not true regarding lupus nephritis in pregnancy?
options: Immunosuppression can be continued during pregnancy
Pregnancy to be planned once the disease has been quiescent for at least 6 months and there is no evidence of renal dysfunction
High-dose corticosteroids used for lupus flare during pregnancy are safe
Ecospirin, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, corticosteroids, and azathioprine are safe in pregnancy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ecospirin, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, corticosteroids, and azathioprine are safe in pregnancy

Management of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with lupus nephritis in pregnancy requires careful selection of immunosuppressive drugs, as some medications are teratogenic.

Safe/relatively safe drugs in pregnancy:

• Low-dose aspirin (Ecospirin) – used to reduce risk of preeclampsia and thrombosis
• Corticosteroids – used to treat lupus flares
• Azathioprine – considered safe immunosuppressant in pregnancy
• Hydroxychloroquine – recommended to continue during pregnancy

Contraindicated drugs:

• Methotrexate → strongly teratogenic
• Cyclophosphamide → teratogenic and fetotoxic, avoided especially in early pregnancy
• Mycophenolate mofetil → also contraindicated

Other important principles:

• Pregnancy should be planned when SLE has been quiescent for ≥6 months with stable renal function.
• Immunosuppressive therapy may be continued, but only pregnancy-safe drugs should be used.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect about non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT)?
options: It uses cell-free circulating fetal DNA in the maternal serum.
It is used for the confirmation of trisomy 13, 18 and 21
It can be performed after 10 weeks of gestation.
It is done after the routine first trimester ultrasound assessment.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is used for the confirmation of trisomy 13, 18 and 21

Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) is a screening test, not a diagnostic test, used to assess the risk of common fetal aneuploidies by analyzing cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA) circulating in maternal blood.

Key Features of NIPT:

• Uses cell-free fetal DNA derived from placental trophoblasts present in maternal serum.
• Can be performed from 10 weeks of gestation onwards.
• Commonly screens (not confirms) for trisomies associated with conditions like Down syndrome Trisomy 21), Edwards syndrome (Trisomy 18), and Patau syndrome Trisomy 13).
• Usually performed after routine first-trimester ultrasound (which includes nuchal translucency assessment).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect about non-invasive prenatal testing?
options: It uses cell-free circulating fetal DNA in the maternal serum
It is used for the confirmation of trisomy 13, 18 and 21.
It can be performed after 10 weeks of gestation
It is done after the routine first trimester ultrasound assessment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is used for the confirmation of trisomy 13, 18 and 21.

Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) analyzes cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA) present in maternal blood to screen for common fetal chromosomal abnormalities, especially:

• Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
• Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome)
• Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome)

Key points:

• Can be performed from 10 weeks of gestation onward
• Usually offered after routine first-trimester ultrasound screening
• Has very high sensitivity and specificity for common aneuploidies

However, NIPT is a screening test, not a diagnostic/confirmatory test. Positive results require confirmation with invasive diagnostic procedures such as:

• Chorionic villus sampling (CVS)
• Amniocentesis with karyotyping or chromosomal analysis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding Type I endometrial carcinoma?
options: It is associated with obesity and diabetes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Smoking is a high-risk factor

Type I endometrial carcinoma is the estrogen-dependent form of endometrial cancer and usually arises from endometrial hyperplasia.

• Associated with unopposed estrogen exposure
• Common risk factors: obesity, diabetes, PCOS, nulliparity
• Histology: Endometrioid adenocarcinoma
• Common genetic mutation: PTEN

Smoking is not a risk factor for Type I endometrial carcinoma; it may actually reduce estrogen levels and slightly lower risk.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding hematological changes in pregnancy is false?
options: Protein C, protein S, and antithrombin decrease
Clotting time and bleeding time are unaffected
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. The viscosity of blood increases

Pregnancy produces a hypercoagulable state to protect against hemorrhage during delivery.

Hematological changes in pregnancy:

• Decrease in natural anticoagulants: particularly Protein S (Protein C usually normal/slightly reduced; antithrombin mostly unchanged).
• Increase in clotting factors: fibrinogen, factors VII, VIII, IX, X.
• Bleeding time and clotting time: generally unchanged.
• Serum albumin: decreases due to hemodilution from increased plasma volume.
• Blood viscosity: decreases, not increases, because plasma volume rises more than RBC mass.

Why option D is false: Blood viscosity falls in pregnancy due to physiological anemia and hemodilution.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which statement is false regarding the active phase of labor?
options: Prolonged latent phase in a multipara is when it is over 12hrs.
Arrest of descent means no descent for over 1 hour
Minimum cervical dilation rate in nullipara is 1.2 cm/hr
Arrest of active phase means no dilation of 4hrs with adequate uterine contractions
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prolonged latent phase in a multipara is when it is over 12hrs.

The active phase of labor begins when cervical dilation reaches \~6 cm and is characterized by rapid cervical dilation and fetal descent.

• Minimum cervical dilation rate:

• Nullipara: \~1.2 cm/hour

• Arrest of active phase:

• No cervical dilation for ≥4 hours with adequate uterine contractions

• Arrest of descent:

• No fetal descent for ≥1 hour in second stage

The prolonged latent phase occurs before the active phase and in multipara it is >14hrs (>20hrs for primigravida)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: You are an intern conducting the delivery of a 24-year-old G2P1 woman. After delivery of the head, restitution and external rotation occur. On attempting to deliver the anterior shoulder, you notice two tight loops of umbilical cord around the neck. What is the next best step?
options: Attempt to slip the cords over the fetal head
Clamp the cord, cut it and unwind it from around the fetal neck
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Clamp the cord, cut it and unwind it from around the fetal neck

A nuchal cord occurs when the umbilical cord is wrapped around the fetal neck. It is a common finding during delivery.

Management depends on whether the cord is loose or tight:

1. Loose nuchal cord

• Slip the cord over the fetal head before delivery of the shoulders.

2. Tight nuchal cord (cannot be slipped over the head)

• Clamp the cord in two places and cut it
• Then unwind the cord from around the neck
• Proceed with delivery of the shoulders

A tight nuchal cord may compress the cord, impairing fetal blood flow and preventing further descent if not released.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: You are attending a patient in labor. The biparietal diameter of the fetal head is seen stretching the vulval outlet. After the contraction subsides, the fetal head does not recede. What is the next event expected to occur?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Extension

When the fetal head becomes visible at the vulval outlet and does not recede after a contraction, it is called crowning. Crowning indicates that the biparietal diameter has passed through the vulval ring, and the next step in the mechanism of labor is extension of the fetal head.

Sequence of cardinal movements of labor:

1. Engagement
2. Descent
3. Flexion
4. Internal rotation
5. Extension (delivery of head at the vulva)
6. Restitution
7. External rotation
8. Expulsion

Why extension occurs next:

• As the fetal head reaches the pelvic outlet, it extends around the pubic symphysis.
• This allows sequential delivery of the occiput → vertex → brow → face → chin.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 14-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea. On examination, a bluish hue is seen in vagina. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Imperforate Hymen

Imperforate Hymen is the most common obstructive cause of primary amenorrhea.

Pathophysiology

The hymenal membrane fails to perforate during fetal development, blocking menstrual outflow.

When menstruation begins:

• Blood accumulates in the vagina (hematocolpos)
• May extend to uterus (hematometra)

This causes the classic bluish bulging hymen.

Accumulation of menstrual blood behind the obstruction leads to:

• Hematocolpos → blood in vagina
• Hematometra → blood in uterus

Symptoms include:

• Pelvic pain
• Urinary retention
• Constipation (due to pelvic pressure)

Treatment:-

Cruciate incision of hymen (hymenotomy) to allow drainage of retained blood.

Small incision made in hymen --> Evacuation of retained menstrual blood --> Hymenal edges sutured

B) Transverse Vaginal Septum

• Congenital obstruction within the vagina, not at hymen.
• Usually no bluish bulging hymen.

C) Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser (MRKH) Syndrome

Features:

• Primary amenorrhea
• Absent uterus and upper vagina
• Normal secondary sexual characters

There is no bluish bulge.

D) OHVIRA Syndrome

Features:

• Uterus didelphys
• Obstructed hemivagina
• Ipsilateral renal agenesis

Usually presents with pelvic pain and mass, not the typical bluish hymenal bulge.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 15-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea and breast development corresponding to Tanner stage IV. She has sparse pubic and axillary hair. On genital examination, a blind vaginal pouch is noted. Ultrasound reveals absence of the uterus and ovaries, and testosterone levels are within the normal male range. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Complete AIS

Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS) should be suspected in an adolescent with primary amenorrhea, normal breast development, sparse or absent pubic/axillary hair, a blind-ending vagina, absent uterus, and serum testosterone in the normal male range. It results from an X-linked mutation of the androgen receptor, causing complete resistance to androgens in a 46,XY individual.

Despite normal testicular production of testosterone and anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH):

• AMH causes regression of the Müllerian ducts, resulting in absence of the uterus, cervix, and fallopian tubes.
• Because tissues cannot respond to androgens, male internal genitalia (Wolffian derivatives) fail to develop, and female external genitalia are present.
• Peripheral aromatization of testosterone to estrogen leads to normal breast development, while pubic and axillary hair are sparse or absent because hair growth is androgen-dependent.

Why not the other options?

• B. Gonadal dysgenesis: Streak gonads cause poor breast development and a present uterus due to absent AMH.
• C. MRKH syndrome: 46,XX females with normal ovaries, normal pubic/axillary hair, and female-range testosterone.
• D. Turner syndrome: 45,X with short stature, streak ovaries, poor breast development, and a present uterus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl is seen for primary amenorrhea. She has not development of breasts or hair in the pubic or axillary region. Her height is 155cm and her weight is 48 kg. She has bilateral inguinal masses. On USG examination, rudimentary uterus with fallopian tubes is present. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism

The most likely diagnosis is: Pure gonadal dysgenesis (46,XY Swyer syndrome), which presents as hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.

Why?

This patient has:

• Primary amenorrhea
• Absent breast development → estrogen deficiency
• Absent pubic and axillary hair (can occur with severe hypogonadism)
• Rudimentary uterus and fallopian tubes → Müllerian structures are present because there is no functional Sertoli cell secretion of AMH
• Bilateral inguinal masses → likely dysgenetic gonads (streak gonads) located in the inguinal canal

Diagnosis

• Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism due to gonadal dysgenesis (46,XY Swyer syndrome).

Expected hormonal profile

• ↑ FSH
• ↑ LH
• ↓ Estradiol
• Low testosterone

Why not Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (AIS)?

AIS would have:

• Absent uterus and fallopian tubes (AMH from testes causes Müllerian regression)
• Normal breast development
• Sparse/absent pubic hair
• Testes in the inguinal canal or labia

The presence of a rudimentary uterus and fallopian tubes rules out AIS.

| Feature | Swyer syndrome (46,XY gonadal dysgenesis) | Complete AIS

| ------- | ----------------------------------------- | ------------

| Karyotype | 46,XY | 46,XY

| Uterus | Present | Absent

| Breasts | Absent/poorly developed | Well developed

| Pubic hair | Reduced or absent | Sparse/absent

| Gonads | Dysgenetic streak gonads | Testes (inguinal/labial)

| Gonadotropins | ↑ FSH, ↑ LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) | Normal or mildly ↑ LH

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl presents in OPD with complaints of cyclical pain in abdomen. On examination, a suprapubic bulge can be seen in the pelvic area. PR examination reveals a swelling in the anterior aspect. On genital examination (if performed), a bluish bulging hymenal membrane is seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Transverse vaginal septum above the vagina
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Imperforate hymen

Cyclical pain with outflow obstruction and suprapubic bulge plus PR swelling along the anterior wall indicate hematocolpos due to imperforate hymen (cryptomenorrhea). Transverse septum and vaginal atresia present differently and do not show a tense bulging hymen. It is the most common obstructive anomaly of the female genital tract. Normally the hymen perforates before birth.

In imperforate hymen:

Hymenal membrane fails to perforate

↓

Menstrual blood cannot exit

↓

Blood accumulates in vagina

↓

Hematocolpos

| Feature | Reason

| ------- | ------

| Primary amenorrhea | Menstrual blood cannot exit

| Cyclical abdominal pain | Uterine contractions during menses

| Suprapubic mass | Accumulated blood

| Bluish bulging hymen | Blood behind hymen

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea. On examination, breast development is present but pubic and axillary hair are absent. Ultrasound shows an absent uterus. Karyotype is 46,XY. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Androgen insensitivity syndrome

In primary amenorrhea with breast development present and absent uterus: 46XY karyotype indicates Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome, while 46XX karyotype indicates Mullerian agenesis (MRKH syndrome).

The absent pubic/axillary hair in AIS results from androgen receptor defects despite normal testosterone production.

Pathophysiology

46 XY fetus

↓

Testes develop (SRY gene)

↓

Testosterone produced

↓

Androgen receptor defect

↓

Body cannot respond to testosterone

↓

Female external genitalia

Meanwhile: Müllerian hormone (AMH) from testes → Müllerian duct regression. Hence uterus is absent.

| Feature | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Primary amenorrhea | No uterus

| Normal breast development | Estrogen from aromatization of testosterone

| Absent pubic/axillary hair | Androgen action absent

| 46,XY karyotype | Genetic male

| Feature | AIS | MRKH

| ------- | --- | ----

| Karyotype | 46 XY | 46 XX

| Breast development | Present | Present

| Pubic hair | Absent | Present

| Uterus | Absent | Absent

Mullerian agenesis : Features:

• 46XX karyotype
• Normal pubic hair
• Uterus absent

46XY gonadal dysgenesis (Swyer Syndrome) - Features:

• No breast development
• Uterus present

Turner syndrome - Features:

• Short stature
• Streak ovaries
• Primary amenorrhea
• Poor breast development

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl with primary amenorrhoea presents to the gynaecology OPD for evaluation. She has normal secondary sexual characters. Her karyotype is 46,XX and ultrasonography reveals normal ovaries and tubes but absent uterus. What is her clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome

• The patient has the classical features:

• Primary amenorrhea
• Normal breast development and secondary sexual characteristics
• 46,XX karyotype
• Normal ovaries and fallopian tubes
• Absent uterus on ultrasonography
• agenesis or hypoplasia of the uterus and upper two-thirds of the vagina

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS):

• Karyotype: 46,XY
• Testes present, absent uterus, sparse/absent pubic and axillary hair.

• B. Turner syndrome:

• Karyotype: 45,X
• Streak ovaries, absent secondary sexual characteristics, uterus present but infantile.

• D. Primary ovarian failure: Characterized by elevated FSH, absent ovarian function, and poor secondary sexual development if occurring before puberty. The uterus is present.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman with 46XY karyotype presents with primary amenorrhoea, female external genitalia, absent uterus, short blind vagina, and absent pubic and axillary hair. Gonads are palpable in the inguinal canal. Most likely diagnosis:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Androgen insensitivity syndrome

Classic AIS features:

• 46 XY
• Testes present
• AMH causes absent uterus
• Testosterone aromatized → breasts develop
• Androgen resistance → sparse pubic hair

Differentiation:

| Disorder | Uterus | Breast | Pubic hair

| -------- | ------ | ------ | ----------

| AIS | Absent | Present | Sparse

| MRKH | Absent | Present | Normal

| Swyer | Present | Poor | Sparse

| Turner | Present | Poor | Sparse

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old athlete woman with secondary amenorrhea. Biochemical evaluation reveals LH=0.3, FSH=2, BMI 17.5. She likely suffers from which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism

linical clues from the question

• 24-year-old athlete
• Secondary amenorrhea
• Low LH (0.3)
• Low FSH (2)
• Low BMI (17.5)

These findings indicate suppression of the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian (HPO) axis.

This presentation is classic for Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhea, a form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

It occurs commonly in:

• Athletes
• Women with low body weight
• Excess physical exercise
• Stress or eating disorders

This condition is commonly part of the Female Athlete Triad.

The triad includes:

| Component | Explanation

| --------- | -----------

| Low energy availability | Excess exercise / inadequate calories

| Amenorrhea | Hypothalamic suppression

| Osteoporosis | Low estrogen levels

| Type | LH | FSH | Example

| ---- | --- | --- | -------

| Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism | ↓ | ↓ | Hypothalamic amenorrhea

| Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism | ↑ | ↑ | Ovarian failure

| Normogonadotropic | Normal | Normal | PCOS

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old female comes to the gynaecology OPD for evaluation of secondary amenorrhoea. She gives history of previous dilatation and curettage, and her FSH levels are 8 IU/L. The probable cause of amenorrhoea is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Asherman syndrome

• Asherman syndrome is characterized by intrauterine adhesions (synechiae) resulting from damage to the basal layer of the endometrium, most commonly following dilatation and curettage (D&C), especially after pregnancy-related procedures. It has Normal FSH level (8 IU/L) indicating preserved ovarian function. It is a classic cause of secondary amenorrhea with normal ovarian function.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Sheehan syndrome:

• Results from postpartum pituitary necrosis following severe postpartum hemorrhage.
• FSH, LH, and other pituitary hormones are low, and there is often failure of lactation.

• C. Premature ovarian failure: Characterized by elevated FSH (>25–40 IU/L) due to ovarian insufficiency before the age of 40.
• D. Incomplete abortion: Presents with persistent vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain, and retained products of conception, not chronic secondary amenorrhea.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman with secondary amenorrhea shows high FSH/LH and AMH 0.05. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Premature ovarian failure

Primary Ovarian Insufficiency is defined as: Loss of ovarian function before 40 years of age

It results in amenorrhea, estrogen deficiency, and elevated gonadotropins.

| Hormone | Level

| ------- | -----

| FSH | ↑ High

| LH | ↑ High

| Estrogen | ↓ Low

| AMH | ↓ Very low

AMH reflects ovarian reserve. Very low AMH suggests depleted follicles.

Clinical Features

| Feature | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Secondary amenorrhea | Loss of ovulation

| Infertility | No follicular development

| Hot flashes | Estrogen deficiency

| Vaginal dryness | Hypoestrogenism

Causes of Premature Ovarian Failure

| Cause | Example

| ----- | -------

| Genetic | Turner syndrome

| Autoimmune | Autoimmune oophoritis

| Iatrogenic | Chemotherapy / radiotherapy

| Idiopathic | Most common

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman presenting with hot flushes and vaginal dryness. Laboratory evaluation is performed to assess her hormonal status. Which of the following patterns of hormone levels is most consistent with this patient’s condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. FSH ↑, LH ↑, Estrogen ↓, Progesterone ↓

Menopause is characterized by ovarian follicular depletion, resulting in a marked decline in estrogen and progesterone production. Loss of negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis causes a rise in both FSH and LH, with FSH increasing more than LH because inhibin B levels also decline.

Why not the other options?

• A. FSH ↑, LH ↑, Estrogen ↓, Progesterone ↑: Progesterone is decreased, not increased, due to cessation of ovulation.
• B. FSH ↓, LH ↓, Estrogen ↑, Progesterone ↑: This is the opposite of the hormonal changes seen in menopause.
• D. FSH ↑, LH ↓, Estrogen ↓, Progesterone ↑: LH also increases, though less than FSH, and progesterone is low.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient develops secondary amenorrhea for 9 months following a dilatation and curettage (D&C). Both the progesterone challenge test and the estrogen + progesterone challenge test are negative. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Asherman syndrome

Asherman Syndrome occurs due to scar formation inside the uterine cavity, most commonly after D&C procedures. These adhesions obliterate the endometrial cavity, preventing menstruation.

Progesterone Challenge Test

Purpose: Detect estrogenized endometrium.

| Result | Meaning

| ------ | -------

| Withdrawal bleeding present | Estrogen present

| No bleeding | Either low estrogen OR outflow tract problem

Estrogen + Progesterone Test

This test differentiates ovarian failure from uterine causes.

| Result | Interpretation

| ------ | --------------

| Bleeding occurs | Estrogen deficiency

| No bleeding | Endometrial damage or outflow obstruction

Since both tests are negative, it indicates:Endometrial damage → Asherman syndrome.

| Cause | Example

| ----- | -------

| Post D&C | Most common cause

| Postpartum curettage | Retained products

| Uterine infection | Tuberculosis

| Endometrial surgery | Myomectomy

Best investigation: Hysteroscopy

It directly visualizes intrauterine adhesions.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient with 17α-hydroxylase deficiency is expected to have which hormonal profile?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ↑ Mineralocorticoids, ↓ Androgens, ↓ Pregnenolone

17α-hydroxylase is required for synthesis of:

• Cortisol
• Sex steroids

Deficiency causes:

• ↓ Cortisol
• ↓ Androgens
• Steroid precursors diverted toward mineralocorticoids

Clinical features:

• Hypertension
• Hypokalemia
• Sexual infantilism
• Undervirilization in XY

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A tall thin adolescent boy is found to have gynecomastia and small testes. His blood testosterone level is undetectable, and serum FSH and LH levels are elevated. Which one of the following is the likely karyotype pattern?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 47 XXY

Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is the most common cause of primary (hypergonadotropic) hypogonadism in males. It presents with tall stature, small firm testes, gynecomastia, infertility, low testosterone, and elevated LH and FSH due to testicular failure.

Why not the other options?

• A. 46 XY: Normal male karyotype.
• B. 45 XO: Turner syndrome, seen in females.
• D. Trisomy 21: Down syndrome; not associated with the classic features of primary hypogonadism described here.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: An 18-year-old girl with primary amenorrhea presents to the OPD. She has Tanner stage IV secondary sexual characters. Her karyotype is 46XX. FSH is 5 and LH is 13. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mullerian agenesis

Clinical clues

• 18-year-old girl
• Primary amenorrhea
• Tanner stage IV secondary sexual characters
• Karyotype: 46XX
• FSH = 5, LH = 13 (near normal)

These findings indicate normal ovarian function but absence of uterus, which is typical of Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser Syndrome.

MRKH syndrome occurs due to failure of Müllerian duct development.

Structures derived from Müllerian ducts include:

• Uterus
• Fallopian tubes
• Upper 2/3 of vagina

In MRKH:

• Uterus absent
• Upper vagina absent or shortened
• Ovaries normal

| Hormone | Level

| ------- | -----

| FSH | Normal

| LH | Normal

| Estrogen | Normal

This indicates normal hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis.

MRKH syndrome may be associated with:

| System | Abnormality

| ------ | -----------

| Renal | Renal agenesis

| Skeletal | Vertebral anomalies

| Cardiac | Rare congenital defects

Causes of Primary Amenorrhea with Normal Secondary Sexual Characters

| Cause | Key Feature

| ----- | -----------

| Mullerian agenesis (MRKH) | Absent uterus

| Androgen insensitivity | 46XY karyotype

| Imperforate hymen | Outflow obstruction

| Transverse vaginal septum | Vaginal obstruction

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: GnRH deficiency with hyposmia is typically seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kallmann syndrome

Kallmann syndrome is a congenital form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism caused by failure of migration of GnRH-producing neurons and olfactory neurons during embryogenesis. It is characterized by GnRH deficiency with hyposmia/anosmia, resulting in delayed puberty, infertility, and low LH, FSH, and sex steroid levels.

Why not the other options?

• B. Bardet-Biedl syndrome: Characterized by obesity, retinal dystrophy, polydactyly, renal abnormalities, and hypogonadism, but hyposmia is not a typical feature.
• C. Prader-Willi syndrome: Presents with hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity, intellectual disability, and hypogonadism, not hyposmia.
• D. Wallenberg syndrome: A lateral medullary stroke causing dysphagia, hoarseness, ataxia, and sensory deficits; not associated with GnRH deficiency.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are causes of GnRH dependent precocious puberty? 1. Constitutional 2. Tubercular encephalitis 3. McCune-Albright syndrome 4. Primary hypothyroidism Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

GnRH-dependent (central) precocious puberty (CPP) results from premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Constitutional (idiopathic): Correct. This is the most common cause, especially in girls.
• 2. Tubercular encephalitis/CNS infection: Correct. CNS infections can damage hypothalamic pathways and trigger central precocious puberty.
• 3. McCune–Albright syndrome: Incorrect. It is GnRH-independent (peripheral) due to autonomous estrogen production.
• 4. Primary hypothyroidism: Although classically categorized as GnRH-independent, severe longstanding hypothyroidism can present with precocious puberty (Van Wyk–Grumbach syndrome).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are correct regarding androgen insensitivity syndrome? 1. Inherited as X-linked recessive disorder 2. Karyotype is 46 XXY 3. It is also called testicular feminization 4. Confirmation of diagnosis by gonadal biopsy Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

• 1. Inherited as X-linked recessive disorder. ✓

• AIS is caused by mutations in the androgen receptor gene on the X chromosome and follows X-linked recessive inheritance.

• 2. Karyotype is 46 XXY. ✗

• The karyotype is 46,XY, not 47,XXY (which is Klinefelter syndrome).

• 3. It is also called testicular feminization. ✓

• Complete AIS is classically referred to as testicular feminization syndrome.

• 4. Confirmation of diagnosis by gonadal biopsy. ✓

• Histopathological examination of the gonads (showing testes) confirms gonadal tissue. In current practice, diagnosis is primarily established by 46,XY karyotype, hormonal profile, and genetic testing for androgen receptor mutations, but gonadal biopsy has traditionally been used for confirmation in examination contexts.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following investigations are useful for diagnosis of unresponsive endometrium as a cause of primary amenorrhoea? 1. Karyotype 2. Progesterone challenge test 3. Hormonal studies 4. Hysterosalpingography Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Primary amenorrhea due to an unresponsive endometrium occurs when the endometrium fails to respond to normal hormonal stimulation, most commonly because of outflow tract abnormalities (e.g., Asherman syndrome, genital tuberculosis) or endometrial destruction.

• 1. Karyotype ✗

• Karyotyping is useful for chromosomal abnormalities (e.g., Turner syndrome, androgen insensitivity syndrome), not for diagnosing an unresponsive endometrium.

• 2. Progesterone challenge test ✓

• Assesses whether the endometrium has been adequately primed by estrogen.
• No withdrawal bleeding suggests either:

• Hypoestrogenism, or
• Endometrial/outflow tract abnormality.

• 3. Hormonal studies ✓

• Serum FSH, LH, estradiol, prolactin, and TSH help determine whether the cause is ovarian, pituitary, hypothalamic, or uterine.

• 4. Hysterosalpingography (HSG) ✓

• Evaluates the uterine cavity and helps diagnose intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome) or congenital uterine abnormalities causing an unresponsive endometrium.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which one of the following is an example of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kallmann’s syndrome

Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism results from deficient secretion of GnRH or gonadotropins (LH/FSH), leading to low LH/FSH and low sex steroid levels. Kallmann syndrome is a congenital form caused by failure of GnRH neuron migration, classically associated with anosmia or hyposmia.

Why not the other options?

• B. Klinefelter syndrome: Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism due to primary testicular failure (↑ LH, ↑ FSH, ↓ testosterone).
• C. Turner syndrome: Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism due to gonadal dysgenesis (streak ovaries).
• D. Cryptorchidism: Undescended testes; may impair fertility if untreated but is not a classic cause of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old P2L2 woman presents with cervical elongation. Her family is complete. What is the preferred surgery advised?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fothergill repair

For cervical elongation in women with completed family, the preferred procedure is Fothergill (Manchester repair). Sling procedures are fertility-preserving; Le Fort is for very elderly non-sexually active women.

Cervical amputation

↓

Shortening of elongated cervix

↓

Reattachment of cardinal (Mackenrodt) ligaments

↓

Restoration of uterine support

Fothergill repair is the operation of choice for cervical elongation.

B) McCall Culdoplasty is a surgical technique used during vaginal or laparoscopic hysterectomy to prevent or treat vault prolapse or enterocele.

C) Le Fort procedure: Done for elderly women who do not desire intercourse.

D) Shirodkar sling: Used mainly for uterine prolapse, not isolated cervical elongation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old multiparous woman presents with a vaginal bulge that protrudes beyond the introitus, urinary leakage while coughing, and is able to void urine normally. She undergoes anterior colporrhaphy with mesh repair (colpopexy). Which condition is this surgery primarily performed to correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cystocele

A cystocele is the herniation of the urinary bladder through the weakened anterior vaginal wall due to defects in the pubocervical fascia. It commonly occurs in multiparous women as a result of pelvic floor weakness and presents with:

• Vaginal bulge or mass
• Stress urinary incontinence
• Pelvic pressure or heaviness
• Urinary frequency or incomplete bladder emptying

Anterior colporrhaphy is the standard surgical repair for cystocele. Mesh augmentation (colpopexy) may be used in selected patients with recurrent or severe pelvic organ prolapse to reinforce the anterior vaginal wall.

Why not the other options?

• A. Rectocele: Herniation of the rectum through the posterior vaginal wall, presenting with constipation, difficult defecation, or the need for digital pressure during defecation; treated with posterior colporrhaphy.
• C. Enterocele: Herniation of the pouch of Douglas containing small bowel through the vaginal apex, usually following hysterectomy.
• D. Vesicovaginal fistula: Presents with continuous leakage of urine through the vagina, not a vaginal bulge, and requires fistula repair.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 48-year-old female underwent total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. The surgical specimen revealed solid ovarian tumour and histology revealed thecoma-fibroma. Which one of the following is the most appropriate statement regarding this condition?
options: It is always associated with gross ascites
It is derived from germ cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endometrial hyperplasia is often associated

Thecoma-fibroma tumors are sex cord-stromal tumors of the ovary. Thecomas are estrogen-producing tumors, whereas fibromas are usually hormonally inactive. The estrogen secretion by thecoma can stimulate the endometrium, leading to endometrial hyperplasia, Abnormal uterine bleeding and, occasionally, endometrial carcinoma.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  20% of such tumours are bilateral: Fibromas and thecomas are usually unilateral (>90%). Bilaterality is uncommon.
• C. It is always associated with gross ascites:

• Ascites is not always present.
• Ovarian fibroma + ascites + pleural effusion = Meigs syndrome, which occurs only in a minority of patients.

• D. It is derived from germ cells: Thecoma-fibroma tumors arise from the sex cord-stromal cells, not germ cells.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following regarding the steps in Fothergill repair surgery for uterine prolapse: 1. Plication of Mackenrodt’s ligament in front of the cervix 2. Shortening of uterosacral ligaments 3. Plication of Mackenrodt’s ligament behind the cervix 4. Amputation of the cervix Which of the above steps form a part of steps in Fothergill repair surgery for uterine prolapse?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 4

Fothergill repair (Manchester operation) is a uterus-preserving surgical procedure for uterine prolapse, particularly in women who wish to retain the uterus.

Important steps include:

1. Plication of Mackenrodt’s (cardinal) ligaments in front of the cervix: Correct.

• The cardinal ligaments are shortened and plicated anteriorly to provide apical support.

2. Shortening of uterosacral ligaments: Incorrect.

• Shortening of the uterosacral ligaments is not a defining step of the classical Fothergill repair.

3. Plication of Mackenrodt’s ligament behind the cervix: Incorrect.

• The characteristic plication is performed anteriorly.

4. Amputation of the cervix: Correct.

• Cervical amputation is a characteristic component of the Manchester/Fothergill operation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In POPQ classification for uterovaginal prolapse, the only measurement done after reducing the prolapse is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Total vaginal length

The Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) system is the standardized and internationally accepted method for assessing pelvic organ prolapse. It uses nine specific measurements relative to the hymenal ring. Among these, Total Vaginal Length (TVL) is the only measurement recorded after completely reducing the prolapse.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Genital hiatus (GH): Measured with the prolapse present, from the external urethral meatus to the posterior hymen.
• B. Point C: Represents the leading edge of the cervix (or vaginal cuff after hysterectomy) and is measured during maximal straining, not after reduction.
• C. Point D: Represents the posterior fornix (only if the uterus is present) and is also measured with the prolapse present.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Opening of Bartholin’s duct is in the:
options: Vestibule outside the hymen at the junction of the anterior 2/3rd and posterior 1/3rd in the groove between the hymen and labium minus
Groove between labia majora and labia minora
Superficial perineal pouch at the junction of anterior 1/3rd and posterior 1/3rd
Periurethral region in anterior 1/3rd of labia minora
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vestibule outside the hymen at the junction of the anterior 2/3rd and posterior 1/3rd in the groove between the hymen and labium minus

The Bartholin’s glands (greater vestibular glands) are paired mucus-secreting glands located in the superficial perineal pouch, posterolateral to the vaginal opening. The Bartholin’s duct opens into the vestibule, outside the hymenal ring, at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third in the groove between the hymen and the labium minus. Clinically, this corresponds approximately to the 4 o’clock and 8 o’clock positions of the vaginal introitus.

Why not the other options?

• B. Groove between labia majora and labia minora: This is not the site of the duct opening.
• C. Superficial perineal pouch at the junction of anterior 1/3rd and posterior 1/3rd: The gland lies in the superficial perineal pouch, but the duct opens into the vestibule, not the pouch.
• D. Periurethral region in anterior 1/3rd of labia minora: This describes the location of the Skene’s (paraurethral) glands, not the Bartholin’s glands.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Procidentia as a degree of uterovaginal prolapse is characterised by descent of:
options: Uterine cervix outside vagina but uterine body inside vagina
Uterine body with fundus outside vagina with eversion of entire vagina
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Uterine body with fundus outside vagina with eversion of entire vagina

Procidentia is complete (third-degree) uterovaginal prolapse, in which the entire uterus, including the fundus, protrudes outside the vaginal introitus, accompanied by complete eversion of the vagina.

Why not the other options?

• A. Uterus into vagina: Describes first-degree prolapse.
• B. Uterine cervix outside vagina but uterine body inside vagina: Describes second-degree prolapse.
• C. Uterine cervix below ischial spine: Not the definition of procidentia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The Gartner’s duct cyst is usually located in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anterolateral wall of vagina

A Gartner’s duct cyst is a remnant of the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct. It is typically located in the anterolateral wall of the upper third of the vagina and is usually asymptomatic unless it becomes large.

Why not the other options?

• B. Posterolateral wall of vagina: Not the typical location.
• C. Posterior wall of vagina: Not characteristic.
• D. Labia minora: Gartner’s duct cyst does not occur here; Bartholin cyst occurs at the posterolateral vestibule (4 and 8 o’clock positions).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The ligament that maintains anteversion of the uterus during pregnancy is: (NEET PG 2018)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Round ligament

The round ligament of the uterus helps maintain the uterus in an anteverted position during pregnancy.

• Extends from the uterine cornua
• Passes through the inguinal canal
• Ends in the labia majora

Functions:

• Maintains anteversion and anteflexion of the uterus
• Supports the enlarging uterus during pregnancy

Stretching of the round ligament during pregnancy can cause round ligament pain, typically felt in the lower abdomen or groin

Other supporting ligaments:

• Cardinal ligament → main support of cervix and uterus
• Uterosacral ligament → maintains uterine position posteriorly
• Pubocervical ligament → supports bladder and cervix

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The remnants of Wolffian ducts in females are located in: (NEET PG 2020)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leaves of broad ligament

In females, remnants of the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts persist within the leaves of the broad ligament. Important Wolffian duct remnants:

• Epoophoron
• Paroophoron
• Gartner duct cysts

Locations:

• Epoophoron and paroophoron → broad ligament near ovary and fallopian tube
• Gartner duct cyst → lateral wall of vagina

Embryologic concept:

• In females, absence of testosterone causes regression of the Wolffian ducts
• Müllerian ducts develop into:

• Fallopian tubes
• Uterus
• Upper vagina

• Wolffian duct remnants can form cysts, especially Gartner duct cysts

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The vaginal pH in childbearing age normally ranges between:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 4–5.5

The normal vaginal pH in women of childbearing (reproductive) age is acidic, approximately 3.8–4.5 (many exam texts accept 4–5.5). This acidity is maintained by Lactobacilli (Döderlein bacilli), which convert glycogen into lactic acid under the influence of estrogen.

Why not the other options?

• A. 2.5–3.5: Too acidic.
• B. 1–2: Extremely acidic; not physiological.
• D. 7–8: Alkaline; seen in infections or postmenopausal women due to reduced estrogen.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most common indication for performing a Posterior Colpotomy? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Drainage of Pelvic Abscess

Posterior colpotomy is a surgical incision made through the posterior vaginal fornix into the pouch of Douglas (rectouterine pouch). The most common indication is Drainage of pelvic abscess, especially tubo-ovarian or pelvic cul-de-sac abscesses

Advantages:

• Provides direct access to the pouch of Douglas
• Avoids abdominal incision
• Allows dependent drainage of pus or fluid collections

Other occasional uses:

• Culdocentesis
• Vaginal sterilization procedures
• Access during certain gynecologic surgeries

The posterior fornix lies closest to the rectouterine pouch, making it the safest vaginal route to access the peritoneal cavity.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are correct regarding pelvic cellular tissue? 1. It supports the pelvic organs. 2. It forms protective sheath for blood vessels and terminal part of ureter. 3. It prevents infection to be spread out of pelvis. 4. Marked hypertrophy of pelvic cellular tissue occurs in pregnancy. Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Pelvic cellular tissue (endopelvic connective tissue) is a loose fibro-fatty connective tissue located between the pelvic fascia.

• 1. It supports the pelvic organs. ✓

• Pelvic cellular tissue helps support the uterus, cervix, vagina, bladder, and rectum, maintaining normal pelvic anatomy.

• 2. It forms a protective sheath for blood vessels and the terminal part of the ureter. ✓

• It encloses the uterine vessels, pelvic vessels, lymphatics, nerves, and terminal ureter, providing support and protection.

• 3. It prevents infection from spreading out of the pelvis. ✗

• Incorrect. Pelvic cellular tissue actually contains potential spaces through which infection (pelvic cellulitis/parametritis), hemorrhage, and malignant cells can spread.

• 4. Marked hypertrophy of pelvic cellular tissue occurs in pregnancy. ✓

• Under the influence of estrogen and progesterone, pelvic connective tissue becomes hypertrophied, edematous, and more vascular, facilitating uterine enlargement and childbirth.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are criteria for opting Le Fort’s operation for surgical correction of pelvic organ prolapse? I. Procidentia in old age II. Unfit for long duration surgery III. Associated uterine pathology IV. Coital function no longer required Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I, II and IV

Le Fort’s operation (Le Fort’s partial colpocleisis) is an obliterative surgery performed for advanced pelvic organ prolapse (procidentia) in elderly women who no longer desire vaginal intercourse and are poor candidates for prolonged reconstructive surgery. The procedure closes most of the vaginal canal while leaving lateral channels for drainage of cervical and uterine secretions if the uterus is retained. The following are indications for Le Fort’s operation:

• I. Procidentia in old age: It is commonly performed in elderly women with complete uterovaginal prolapse (procidentia).
• II. Unfit for long-duration surgery: It is a short, relatively simple operation with minimal blood loss, making it suitable for women with significant medical comorbidities.
• IV. Coital function no longer required: Since the vagina is obliterated, future vaginal intercourse is not possible. Therefore, it is performed only in women who no longer desire sexual activity.

Why is III incorrect?

• III. Associated uterine pathology: Le Fort’s operation is contraindicated if there is suspected or confirmed uterine, cervical, or endometrial pathology, because the uterus becomes inaccessible for future evaluation. Such patients generally require hysterectomy or another appropriate procedure.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are essential steps of Fothergill’s operation? 1. Laparoscopic or vaginal ligation 2. Amputation of cervix 3. Plication of Mackenrodt’s ligaments in front of cervix 4. Anterior colporrhaphy Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Fothergill’s operation (Manchester operation) is a uterus-preserving surgery performed for uterine prolapse associated with cervical elongation in women who wish to retain the uterus but have completed childbearing. The operation corrects uterine descent by shortening and repositioning the cardinal (Mackenrodt’s) ligaments and removing the elongated cervix.

• 1. Laparoscopic or vaginal ligation ✗

• This is not a step of Fothergill’s operation.

• 2. Amputation of cervix ✓

• Amputation of the elongated cervix is the hallmark of the procedure.

• 3. Plication of Mackenrodt’s (cardinal) ligaments in front of the cervix ✓

• The cardinal ligaments are shortened and sutured anterior to the cervix to provide uterine support.

• 4. Anterior colporrhaphy ✓

• Anterior colporrhaphy is routinely performed to repair the associated cystocele.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is measured without any straining while examination under POP-Q system?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. TVL
