questions.text: Revised In a primigravida what is a satisfactory dilation rate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1.2 cm/ hr

In a primigravida, the satisfactory rate of dilation is 1.2cm/hr.

Cervical effacement and dilatation occur in the first stage of labor. It is divided into 2 phases

Latent phase

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Revised Which of the following is not an indication for cesarean section?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Previous history of macrosomia

Previous history of macrosomia is not an indication of a cesarean section(CS).

Cesarean is needed even with a dead fetus when vaginal delivery is not possible.
The following are the absolute indication:

* Central placenta previa (Option C)

* Contracted pelvis or cephalopelvic disproportion (absolute)(Option A)

* Pelvic mass causing an obstruction (cervical or broad ligament fibroid)

* Advanced carcinoma cervix (Option D)

* Vaginal atresia or stenosis

Relative indications for cesarean section are those where vaginal delivery may be possible but risks to the mother and/or baby are high. They are as follows:

* Nonreassuring FHR

* Dystocia- It may be due to a relatively large fetus (passenger), small pelvis (passage), or inefficient uterine contractions (power)

* Antepartum hemorrhage: Placenta previa and abruptio placenta

* Malpresentation: Breech, shoulder (transverse lie), brow

* Previous cesarean delivery-a) When primary CS was due to recurrent indication (contracted pelvis), (b) Previous two CS,(c) Features of scar dehiscence, (d) Previous classical CS

* Cephalopelvic disproportion (relative)

* Failure to progress in labor

* Hypertensive disorders: Severe pre-eclampsia, eclampsia— uncontrolled fits even with antiseizure therapy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the cause of LH surge? FSH: Follicle-stimulating Hormone LH: Luteinizing hormone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Estradiol

Estradiol causes LH surge. Estradiol concentrations of 200 pg/mL for 50 hours are necessary to initiate this LH surge.

Phases of the menstrual cycle :

Follicular phase (days 0–14)

* A higher FSH level at the beginning of this phase is responsible for the recruitment of the follicle cohort that contains the follicle destined for ovulation. A primordial follicle develops to the Graafian stage, with atresia of neighboring follicles.

* LH receptors are up-regulated in theca and granulosa cells. During the mid-follicular phase, follicles produce greater amounts of estrogen and inhibin.

* Estradiol levels increase and cause proliferation of the uterus.

* FSH are suppressed by the negative feedback effect of estradiol and inhibin on the anterior pituitary.

Ovulation (day 14)

* A burst of estradiol synthesis at the end of the follicular phase has a positive feedback effect on the secretion of LH (LH surge). There is a small preovulatory rise in progesterone concentrations generates an FSH level surge, which occurs with the LH surge.

* Ovulation occurs as a result of the estrogen-induced LH surge.

Luteal phase (days 14–28)

* Ovulation is assumed to have occurred if the progesterone level exceeds 3 nglmL on cycle day 21. Progesterone levels are high in this phase.

* The corpus luteum begins to develop, and it synthesizes estrogen and progesterone. Vascularity and secretory activity of the endometrium increase to prepare for the receipt of a fertilized egg.

* If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum regresses at the end of the luteal phase. As a result, estradiol and progesterone levels decrease abruptly.

Menses (days 0–4)

* The endometrium is sloughed because of the abrupt withdrawal of estradiol and progesterone.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the definition of a post-term neonate?
options: Neonate born after 37 weeks of gestation
Neonate born between 37- 40 weeks of gestation
Neonate born after 40 weeks of gestation
Neonate born after 42 weeks of gestation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Neonate born after 42 weeks of gestation

Post-term infants are those born after 42 completed weeks of gestation, as calculated from the mother’s last menstrual period, regardless of weight at birth.

A term neonate is a neonate born any time after 37 completed weeks gestation and up until 42 completed weeks gestation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the level of the uterus immediately after delivery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Below the umblicus

The level of the uterus immediately after delivery is below the umbilicus.

The rate of involution of the uterus can be assessed clinically by noting the height of the fundus of the uterus in relation to the symphysis pubis.

* The uterus is to be centralized and the fundal height is measured above the symphysis pubis with a measuring tape. Following delivery, the fundus lies about 13.5 cm above the symphysis pubis(which is best referred to as below the umbilicus).

* During the first 24 hours, the level remains constant. Thereafter, there is a steady decrease in height by 1.25 cm in 24 hours. By the end of 2nd week, the uterus becomes a pelvic organ.

* The rate of involution thereafter slows down until by 6 weeks when the uterus becomes almost normal in size.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following finding is shown in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Linea nigra

The given image shows Linea nigra.

Linea nigra is a brownish-black pigmented area that stretches from the xiphisternum to the symphysis pubis in the midline. The pigmentary changes may be due to melanocyte-stimulating hormone from the anterior pituitary. The pigmentation disappears after delivery. Similar changes are observed in women taking oral contraceptives may be due to estrogen and progesterone may be related to it as.

Other options:

Option A: Striae gravidarum is slightly depressed linear marks with varying length and breadth found in pregnancy. They are predominantly found in the abdominal wall below the umbilicus. They appear pinkish in color. They can sometimes be found over the thighs and breasts. These stretch marks represent the scar tissues in the deeper layer of the cutis.

Option B: Chloasma gravidarum also called pregnancy mask is an extreme form of pigmentation around the cheek, forehead, and around eyes. It may be patchy or diffuse. It disappears spontaneously after delivery.

Option C: Initially, striae gravidarum are pinkish but after the delivery, the scar tissues contract and obliterate the capillaries and appear glistening white. They are called the linea alba.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the best parameter for estimation of fetal age by ultrasound in 1st trimester?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Crown rump length

Crown-rump length (CRL) is the most accurate parameter used for the sonographic estimation of gestational age in the first trimester. It has an accuracy range of ± 5 days.

Parameters for the estimation of fetal age

Trimester

Parameter

First

Crown-rump length (CRL)

Second

• Biparietal diameter (BPD)
• Abdominal Circumference (AC)
• Head Circumference (HC)
• Femur Length. (FL)

Third

Femur length

Pearl PF1960: Fetal Monitoring using Ultrasound

* The first definitive USG finding to suggest pregnancy is the visualization of the gestational sac.

* The first sign of intrauterine pregnancy is the presence of a yolk sac within the gestational sac.

* Best time to assess the gestational age by USG is 9-12 weeks(by CRL)

* CRL(mm)+42 = Days of pregnancy

* CRL(cm)+6.5 = Gestational age in weeks.

* The best indicator of fetal growth is the abdominal circumference. Abdominal circumference is the transverse measurement at the level of the stomach with the confluence of the umbilical vein and right portal vein.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct sequence of vaginal discharge during puerperium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lochia rubra>Lochia serosa>Lochia alba

The correct sequence of vaginal discharge during puerperium- Lochia rubra>Lochia serosa>Lochia alba.

Lochia is the vaginal discharge for the first fortnight during puerperium that originates from the uterine body, cervix, and vagina.

Depending upon the variation of the color of the discharge, it is named:

(1) Lochia rubra- Seen in 1–4 days after delivery. The color of the discharge is red. It consists of blood, shreds of fetal membranes and decidua, vernix caseosa, lanugo, and meconium.

(2) Lochia serosa- Seen during 5-9 days. The color is yellowish or pink or pale brownish. It consists mainly of leukocytes, wound exudate, mucus from the cervix, and micro-organisms (anaerobic streptococci and staphylococci). The presence of bacteria is not pathognomonic unless associated with clinical signs of sepsis.

(3) Lochia alba- Seen during 10–15 days. The color of the discharge is pale white. Lochia alba contains plenty of decidual cells, leukocytes, mucus, cholesterin crystals, fatty and granular epithelial cells, and microorganisms.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common location of implantation in ectopic pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A

The most common location of implantation in ectopic pregnancy is the tubal ampulla, which is labelled as A in the image.

In the given image-

B-Isthmus

C- Fimbrae

D- Infundibulum

Almost 95% of ectopic pregnancies implant within the fallopian tube. Within the fallopian tube, the ampulla is the most commonly affected location in 70% of the cases. The remaining implant is in the isthmus (12%), fimbria (11%), and interstitial tube (2%).

The other implantation sites are the ovary, peritoneal cavity, cervix, or prior cesarean scar.

Patients usually present with rupture of ectopic pregnancy with the triad of the delayed menstrual cycle, abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding.

The examination may reveal abdominal tenderness, pain in cervical motion, a bulging posterior vaginal fornix, boggy mass next to the uterus. Vaginal bleeding or spotting may be present. Ruptured ectopic will lead to intraabdominal hemorrhage leading to reciprocal changes in vital signs.

Investigations used to diagnose ectopic pregnancy include a positive beta-human chorionic gonadotropin to diagnose a pregnancy. Transvaginal ultrasound can be used to identify the gestational sac or determine if the case is a pregnancy of an unknown location. In an ectopic pregnancy, the endometrial stripe will appear as a trilaminar pattern and anechoic fluid collections may be present.

Medical management of ectopic pregnancy involves the use of methotrexate. Surgical management depends on whether the patient is hemodynamically stable, and whether she desires future fertility (salpingectomy versus salpingostomy). For a ruptured ectopic, only salpingectomy can be done.

* Hemodynamically stable - laparoscopically done

* Hemodynamically unstable - laparotomy is done

Pearl PF1615: Fallopian tube

Gross anatomy:

The fallopian tube is divided into the following parts:

* Intramural/Interstitial portion:

* Intrauterine

* The narrowest and shortest part

* Isthmus:

* The most common site for tubectomy

* Ampulla:

* The longest part

* The most common site for - fertilization and ectopic pregnancy

* Infundibulum:

* The widest part

Histology:

The ampulla, isthmus and infundibulum are extrauterine. They're covered by three layers:

* Mesosalpinx - It is the peritoneal layer. Also called serosa.

* Myosalpinx - It contains smooth muscle and has 2 layers:

* Inner circular

* Outer longitudinal

* Endosalpinx - It is the mucosal layer. It has the following features:

* Numerous branching folds, filling the entire lumen

* Basement membrane

* Ciliated, columnar epithelium

* Peg cells - non-ciliated epithelium. They help in the capacitation of sperms.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the process of breaking the clavicle during delivery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cleidotomy

Cleidotomy is the process of fracturing the clavicle using an instrument to free the anterior shoulder. It is usually done for a dead fetus (shown below).

It is a method of management of labor in the case of shoulder dystocia. Shoulder dystocia occurs when either the anterior or the posterior (rare) fetal shoulder impacts on the maternal symphysis or on the sacral promontory respectively.

Management of labor in case of shoulder dystocia is as follows:

* First line:

* McRoberts maneuver (flexion and abduction of the thigh)

* Second line:

* Woods corkscrew maneuver (Rotate the posterior shoulder to 180o in a corkscrew fashion)

* Third line:

* Zavanelli maneuver: It involves the replacement of the fetal head into the pelvis followed by cesarean delivery. (Option C)

* Cleidotomy

* Symphysiotomy: The intervening symphyseal cartilage and ligamentous supports are cut to widen the symphysis pubis. (Option B)

Option A: Craniotomy is not used in the management of shoulder dystocia. It is an operation in which a small hole is made in the skull or a piece of bone from the skull is removed to show part of the brain.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following procedures is done with the instrument shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Endometrial sampling

Pipelle aspirator (a) and Vabra (b) aspirator are shown in the image above which are used to obtain endometrial sampling.

Endometrial sampling using Pipelle aspirator - aspiration of the uterine cavity and sending the sample for histopathological examination. It is used as a screening test in menopausal women on HRT or tamoxifen.

Postmenopausal bleeding is defined as bleeding from the genital tract, more than 12 months after the last menstrual period in a woman not on hormone replacement. All postmenopausal women with unexpected uterine bleeding should be evaluated for endometrial malignancy since age is a significant risk factor for this.

Transvaginal ultrasound(TVS) is the first-line investigation.

Endometrial sampling is indicated if:

* Transvaginal ultrasound is unable to provide a distinct image of the endometrium.

* Endometrium thickness is >4mm

* Areas of heterogeneous echogenic pattern are present

* Ongoing bleeding in a woman may indicate endometrial cancer, regardless of endometrial thickness.

The image below gives a summary of the evaluation of postmenopausal bleeding, as per the FOGSI guidelines.

Leech-Wilkinson cannula is used to inject dye in hysterosalpingography. The image below is that of a Leech-Wilkinson cannula.

The instrument shown below is a Sim's uterine curette, used for endometrial curettage.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which type of hysterectomy is done in a case of carcinoma cervix stage I B?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type 3 hysterectomy

Type 3 hysterectomy/Radical hysterectomy is the treatment of choice in carcinoma cervix stage 1 B.

Stage IB lesions are defined as those with the deepest invasion ≥ 5mm yet still confined to the cervix. The stage is subcategorized either as IB1 if tumors measure <2cm or as IB2 if they measure 2cm to <4cm or as IB3 if the invasion is ≥4cm in greatest dimension.

Radical hysterectomy and pelvic lymphadenectomy for stage IB are usually chosen for premenopausal women who wish to preserve ovarian function. Oophorectomy is avoided in younger women who wish to preserve fertility.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman presents with acute onset abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She has a low-grade fever, with a pulse rate of 90 bpm and blood pressure of 126/84 mm Hg. She has regular menstrual cycles of 28 days. Pelvic examination shows a tender right adnexal mass. Ovarian torsion is suspected. What is the investigation of choice in this condition? Urine pregnancy testing- negative Serum β-HCG level- 1 mIU/L
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Doppler Ultrasound

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of ovarian torsion. The investigation of choice for an ovarian torsion is a doppler sonography.

Torsion of the ovaries is a gynecological emergency and is most commonly seen in women of the reproductive age group. Ovarian cysts including mucous cystadenomas and dermoid cysts have the highest risks of undergoing torsion. Adnexal masses measuring >6 cm in diameter have the highest rates of torsion.

A patient with torsion presents with sharp lower abdominal pain, usually localized to the involved side with radiation to the flank, groin, or thigh. Nausea and vomiting are commonly associated. Adnexal necrosis may cause a low-grade fever.

During torsion, the low-pressure veins are initially compressed by the twisting pedicle. This leads to continuous inflow with decreased outflow causing stromal edema and congestion. The increasing stromal swelling later compresses the arteries causing ischemia and necrosis.

On a doppler USG, the ovary appears enlarged, globular, and has a heterogenous appearance compared to the contralateral ovary due to edema, engorgement, and hemorrhage. Twisting of the vascular pedicle may give rise to a 'whirlpool sign', a round hyperechoic structure with concentric hypoechoic stripes. MRI or CT imaging can be used in patients with normal Doppler but with characteristic signs and symptoms of torsion, to confirm or rule out the diagnosis.

Management involves urgent laparotomy or laparoscopic evaluation. Salvage of the involved adnexa with the removal of any associated cyst/tumor and possible oophoropexy are the goals. However, necrosis of the adnexa necessitates the removal of the adnexal structures.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old primigravida with a low-risk pregnancy presents at 39 weeks for a normal health check. Her vitals are stable. On PV, her cervix is 4 cm dilated. A repeat PV after 4 hours shows that her cervix is 6 cm dilated. The fetal head is at +2 station and membranes are absent. Liquor is clear and uterine contractions are good. Fetal heart rate is 150 BPM and reassuring. What is the appropriate course of management?
options: Rupture of membranes and confirm cord prolapse
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Wait and watch

The appropriate course of management for this 28-year-old primigravida with the given clinical scenario is to wait and watch.

The patient is low-risk, stable, and in active labor with progressive cervical dilation from 4 cm to 6 cm in 4 hours. This indicates that labor is progressing adequately.

The fetal head is at +2 station, indicating descent into the birth canal, which is a positive sign of labor progression. The absence of membranes suggests that the patient has experienced spontaneous rupture of membranes (SROM), which is a normal occurrence during labor. Clear liquor and reassuring fetal heart rate (150 BPM) indicate fetal well-being.

If there are any signs of labor dystocia or fetal distress during monitoring, appropriate interventions can be considered at that time.

Other options:

* Oxytocin augmentation or rupture of membranes without clear indications may lead to unnecessary interventions and potential complications.

* Emergency Caesarean section is not warranted in the absence of fetal distress or other complications.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female patient is diagnosed with recurrent genital infections. In which of the conditions does her male partner need to be treated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Trichomoniasis

The male partner should be treated with a single dose of oral metronidazole in cases of recurrent Trichomonas infection.

Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan parasite Trichomonas vaginalis. It can cause symptoms such as vaginal discharge, itching, and irritation in females, and urethritis or prostatitis in males.

Since trichomoniasis is transmitted through sexual contact, both partners should be treated simultaneously to prevent reinfection.

The treatment options in case of Trochomoniasis include:

* An oral dose of metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days or single oral dose of metronidazole 2 g

* Vinegar douche to lower the vaginal PH

* Trichofuran suppositories

* Betadine gel

Other Options:

* Bacterial vaginosis is an imbalance of bacteria in the vagina and is not typically considered a sexually transmitted infection. Treatment of male partners is not routinely recommended.

* Candida albicans is the fungus responsible for most cases of vaginal yeast infections (vulvovaginal candidiasis). It is not considered a sexually transmitted infection, and treatment of male partners is generally not necessary unless they have symptoms of a yeast infection.

* Herpes is a viral infection caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV). While it can be sexually transmitted, the treatment of male partners may not be routinely necessary unless they are also infected or experiencing symptoms of genital herpes.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A G2P1, 38 weeks of gestation age, presented for delivery. Her last pregnancy was uncomplicated, and she underwent a cesarean section. Now, she wants to have a vaginal birth. The clinician decided to perform a TOLAC (trial of labor after cesarean). Which of the following has the least risk for this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Low segment transverse incision

In the context of attempting a trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC), the risk associated with a low segment transverse incision is relatively lower compared to other options.

A low segment transverse incision (also known as a low transverse or Pfannenstiel incision) during the previous cesarean delivery is typically associated with a lower risk of uterine rupture during a subsequent TOLAC compared to other types of uterine incisions, such as a classical or vertical incision.

Other options:

Breech presentation during labor after previous cesarean delivery may increase the risk of uterine rupture and is generally considered a contraindication for TOLAC.

Preeclampsia is a pregnancy complication characterized by high blood pressure and signs of organ damage, typically occurring after 20 weeks of gestation. While preeclampsia can pose risks during pregnancy and delivery, it is not specifically related to the risk associated with a previous LSCS and TOLAC.

A classical cesarean section involves a vertical incision on the upper portion of the uterus. This type of incision carries a higher risk of uterine rupture during a subsequent TOLAC compared to a low segment transverse incision, making it a less favorable option for attempting TOLAC.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A mother complains of cramps in her breasts while breastfeeding her child. Which hormone is responsible for this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Oxytocin

Oxytocin helps in the ejection of milk by myoepithelial contraction. This may result in cramps in the breast tissue.

Functions of oxytocin are:

* Milk ejection (Myoepithelial contraction)

* ADH like action in high doses (reduces urine output)

* Uterine contraction

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient comes to you with a history of unprotected sex 96 hours ago. Which of the following emergency contraceptives can be used in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intra uterine contraceptive device (IUCD)

Since the patient had unprotected sex 96 hours ago, an intrauterine contraceptive device(IUCD) can be used for emergency contraception in this case. It can be inserted within 5 days of coitus as a method of emergency contraception. All other methods of emergency contraception mentioned above need to be administered within 72 hours.

The administration of postcoital contraceptive agents that interfere with postovulatory events that can lead to pregnancy is known as the emergency contraception method. They are used to prevent pregnancy after unprotected intercourse.

IUCD (Intrauterine contraceptive device) prevents the implantation of a fertilized ovum. It does so by acting as a foreign body within the uterine cavity. This leads to increased contractility, tubal peristalsis, and promotes leukocytic infiltration in the endometrium so that the fertilized egg is unable to implant.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pre-menopausal woman is diagnosed with lymph node-positive, early invasive breast cancer. IHC reveals ER +, PR +, and HER-2-neu 1+. Which of the following drug will you provide for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tamoxifen

The given clinical scenario suggests early invasive breast cancer in a pre-menopausal woman, which is lymph node-positive, hormone receptor-positive (ER/PR +), and Her-2/neu negative (Her-2/neu IHC score of 1+ is considered negative). Hence Tamoxifen is the drug of choice.

Treatment of early-stage breast cancer (T1-2 N0-1 M0) includes:

Breast conservation surgery (BCS) + ALND or SLNB + Radiotherapy

• BCS is followed by radiotherapy
• Mastectomy is done if BCS is contraindicated.
• Clinical N0 status-sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) at the time of surgery.
• Clinical N1 status-ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA): axillary lymph node dissection (ALND) if positive and sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) if negative.

Endocrine therapy: for hormone receptor (ER/PR) positive

• For Premenopausal women-tamoxifen (selective estrogen receptor modulator, SERM)
• For post-menopausal women (usually >50 years)-anastrozole (Aromatase inhibitor)
• Tamoxifen has an agonistic action on the endometrium, leading to an increased risk of endometrial cancers Hence, it is not used in post-menopausal women.

Anti-Her-2 therapy: for Her-2/neu positive breast cancer

• Trastuzumab is given
• Her-2/neu IHC interpretation:

•   0 or 1+ = Negative
•   2+ = Equivocal cases ->        confirmed with Fluorescence    in situ hybridization (FISH)      analysis
•   3+ = Positive

Chemotherapy

Indicated for:

• Lymph nodes positive
• Lymph nodes negative but tumor size of >1 cm
• Lymph nodes negative and tumor size of >0.5 cm with

• Blood vessel/Lymph vessel invasion
• ER/PR –ve
• Her-2/neu overexpression
• High grade

• Triple-negative breast carcinoma
• High recurrence score after Oncotype Dx

The table below shows the summary of the adjuvant treatment approach:

Tumor hormone receptor status (ER, PR)

Tumor HER status
Positive
Negative

Positive
Endocrine therapy + chemotherapy + trastuzumab
Chemotherapy + trastuzumab

Negative
Endocrine therapy ± chemotherapy
Chemotherapy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman is suspected to have endometriosis. Which of the following is the investigation of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Laparoscopy

For endometriosis, the investigation of choice which can help with both the diagnosis and treatment is laparoscopy. It is used to locate the sites, take a biopsy and surgically remove the deposits.

Endometriosis is the presence of endometrium at a site outside the uterine cavity. It can be found in ectopic sites such as the ovary, pouch of Douglas, uterosacral ligaments, appendix, pelvic lymph nodes, lower segment cesarean section (LSCS) scar endometriosis, umbilicus, and lung.

Dysmenorrhea is the most common presenting symptom, associated with abdominal and pelvic pain, menorrhagia, dyspareunia and infertility. Laparoscopy is the gold standard modality for the diagnosis and treatment of endometriosis. Typical characteristics include 'powder-burn' - puckered black spots, red vascular, bluish, blackish cysts, chocolate cysts, and dense adhesions in the pelvis.

For minimal disease, medical management with NSAIDs and oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are given if associated menstrual complaints are present. OCPs inhibit gonadotropin release and decrease the menstrual flow. For moderate to severe diseases oral progestogens, GnRH agonists or danazol that antagonize estrogenic effects on the endometrium, causing endometrial atrophy are used.

Surgery is preferred in patients with infertility. Endometrial deposits are destroyed by electrocautery/laser, and resection of endometrioma can be done. Total hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy is a definitive and most effective therapy for women with endometriosis who do not wish to retain fertility.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Amsel's criteria is used in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bacterial vaginosis

Amsel's criteria is used in bacterial vaginosis.

According to Amsel's criteria, the discharge has the following characteristics.

* White milky non-viscous discharge, adherent to the vaginal wall

* The pH of the discharge is more than 4.5

* Fishy odor when mixed with 10% KOH. This is called the Whiff test.

* Presence of clue cells-the epithelial cells have a fuzzy border due to the adherence of bacteria.

* Decrease in the number of lactobacilli and increase in the number of Gardnerella and other bacteria.

It is treated with 500 mg of metronidazole twice daily for 7 days.

Shown below is the Gram-stained smear of vaginal discharge of a patient diagnosed with bacterial vaginosis. It reveals vaginal epithelial cells that have a fuzzy border due to the adherence of bacteria. These are called clue cells.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Arrange the sequence of lactation in the right order * Mammogenesis * Lactogenesis * Galactokinesis * Galactopoiesis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 - 2 - 3 - 4

The correct order of lactation is: Mammogenesis – lactogenesis – galactokinesis – galactopoiesis

Function
Definition
Hormone

Mammogenesis
Breast growth and development

Estrogen (ductal growth)

Progesterone (alveolar growth)

Lactogenesis
Initiation of milk secretion
Prolactin

Galactokinesis
Ejection of milk
Oxytocin

Galactopoiesis
Maintainence of lactation
Prolactin

Mammogenesis: This refers to the development and growth of the mammary glands. It occurs during puberty and pregnancy under the influence of hormones like estrogen and progesterone.

Lactogenesis: This is the process of milk production. There are two phases:

* a. Lactogenesis I: Also known as colostrum secretion, it begins during late pregnancy and continues after birth for a few days. The mammary glands produce colostrum, a thick, yellowish fluid rich in antibodies and nutrients.

* b. Lactogenesis II: Also known as transitional milk secretion, it begins around 2-5 days after birth. The mammary glands switch to producing mature milk.

Galactokinesis: This involves the movement of milk through the mammary ducts towards the nipple. It is facilitated by the contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the alveoli in response to oxytocin release.

Galactopoiesis: This refers to the maintenance and regulation of milk production. It involves hormonal regulation, primarily prolactin, which stimulates milk synthesis and secretion. Additionally, factors like frequent breastfeeding or milk removal help maintain milk production.

So, the correct sequence is Mammogenesis (development of mammary glands) – Lactogenesis (milk production) – Galactokinesis (movement of milk) – Galactopoiesis (maintenance of milk production.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Revised A 24-year-old primigravidae at 38 weeks gestation presents to the antenatal clinic with complaints of faintness on lying down for the past one week. She feels better when she turns to a side and while in sitting position. What is the reason for her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IVC compression

This is a case of IVC compression known as supine hypotension syndrome (postural hypotension).

* During late pregnancy, the gravid uterus produces a compression effect on the IVC when the patient is in supine position. In majority of pregnants, to compensate/avoid this effect there will be opening up of collaterals of paravertebral/Azygous veins.

* When there is failure of opening up of collaterals, venous return of the heart is curtailed leading to hypotension, tachycardia and syncope.

* The normal BP is quickly restored by turning the patient to lateral position.Hence pregnant females are adviced to lie in lateral positions (left lateral is better).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The maternal component of placenta would be
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decidua Basalis

The decidua basalis, also known as the basal plate, is the portion of the endometrium (uterine lining) that lies beneath the conceptus (embryo/fetus) and contributes to the formation of the maternal component of the placenta. It forms the maternal part of the placenta by coming into direct contact with the chorionic villi, allowing for the exchange of nutrients, gases, and waste products between the maternal and fetal circulations.

The definitive placenta (see image) consists of the chorionic plate on the fetal aspect and a basal plate on the maternal aspect with the intervillous space between them. The structures in each of these parts are as follows:

Fetal side: Chorionic plate

* Amnion

* Primary (extraembryonic) mesoderm with fetal blood vessels

* Cytotrophoblast (Langhan's layer)

* Syncytiotrophoblast

Maternal side: Basal plate

* Stratum spongiosum of decidua basalis containing maternal blood vessels

* Outer layer of syncytiotrophoblast (Nitabuch’s layer)

* Outer shell of cytotrophoblast

* Inner layer of syncytiotrophoblast (Rohr’s fibrinoid stria)

Between basal plate and chorionic plate

* Intervillous space

* Maternal blood flowing in the intervillous space

* Stem villi

* Fetal blood flowing within the fetal villi

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the standard glucose load given for identifying diabetes in pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 75 g

For IADPSG criteria, an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is done in the fasting state using 75 g of glucose, and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is diagnosed if any one of the following cut-offs is met i.e.

* Fasting: >92 mg/dl

* 1 hour: >180 mg/dl

* 2 hour: >153 mg/dl

Earlier, a two-step approach was being used to diagnose GDM. In this, the first step (screening) is a 50-gram one-hour glucose challenge test (GCT). The patients having a positive result of >140mg/dl, are candidates for the OGTT. A 100-gram, three-hour oral glucose tolerance test (GTT), is the diagnostic test for gestational diabetes mellitus. GDM is diagnosed if two or more values are positive.

Diabetes in Pregnancy Societies of India(DIPSI) recommends a 1-step procedure with 75 g oral glucose without regard to the time of the last meal. A venous plasma glucose value at 2 hours >140 mg/dL is diagnosed as GDM.

Some complications of GDM include:

* Maternal

* Hypertension, preeclampsia

* Hydramnios

* Increased operative interventions

* Future development of diabetes mellitus

* Fetal and neonatal

* Fetal macrosomia

* Congenital anomalies

* Metabolic abnormalities such as hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and neonatal hypoglycemia.

* Respiratory distress syndrome

* Subsequent childhood and adolescent obesity

Screening is usually done at 24-28 weeks of gestation. Early diagnosis and treatment are important to prevent complications.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of these steps is followed first for the management of shoulder dystocia after McRoberts maneuver?
options: Flex the legs over the abdomen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Apply gentle supra pubic pressure

Applying a gentle suprapubic pressure is the first step in the management of shoulder dystocia after the McRoberts maneuver.

Shoulder dystocia drill to better organize emergency management:

* Call for help. Initially, a gentle attempt at traction is made. Drain the bladder if it is distended.

* Episiotomy

* McRoberts maneuver: involves flexing the legs on the abdomen with concurrent suprapubic pressure. This causes straightening of the sacrum relative to the lumbar vertebrae, rotation of the symphysis pubis toward the maternal head, and a decrease in the angle of pelvic inclination. This tends to free the impacted anterior shoulder. It is shown in the image below.

These maneuvers will resolve most cases of shoulder dystocia. If not -

* Delivery of the posterior arm is attempted.

* Woods screw maneuver is applied.

* Rubin maneuver is attempted.

Other techniques generally should be reserved for cases in which all other maneuvers have failed. These include intentional fracture of the anterior clavicle and the Zavanelli maneuver.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman presents with irregular periods, acne & excessive hair growth. What is the first line management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lifestyle modification

The first line of treatment for this woman with signs and symptoms of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) such as irregular periods, acne & excessive hair growth (hirsutism) is lifestyle modification.

PCOS is an endocrinopathy seen in women of reproductive age, affecting multiple systems. A weight loss of 10% through lifestyle modifications such as diet and exercise are considered first-line.

The Rotterdam criteria are used to diagnose PCOS. The presence of any two of the three components of this criteria establishes the diagnosis of PCOS:

* Clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne)

* Menstrual abnormalities (oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea), anovulation, infertility

* Polycystic ovaries on ultrasonography.

Sonographic criteria for polycystic ovaries include ≥ 12 small cysts or an increased ovarian volume (> 10 mL) or both.

Management:

* Weight reduction and lifestyle changes are considered the first-line treatment for infertility in obese women with PCOS.

* Letrozole is considered the first-line therapy for anovulatory infertility in PCOS patients. Unlike clomiphene citrate, which has anti-estrogenic effects, letrozole does not exert adverse peripheral effects on the endometrium or cervical mucus.

* Patients with PCOD are more prone to developing insulin resistance, which can be controlled with metformin (Option C)

* Oral contraceptive pills (OCP), preferably fourth-generation are used to treat menstrual abnormalities. It also reduces acne and further hirsutism (Option D).

* Anti-androgens are useful in treating hirsutism. OCP with cyproterone acetate is prescribed for PCOS patients with hirsutism.

Surgical options include laparoscopic ovarian drilling or puncture of not more than four cysts in each ovary. It restores endocrine levels and improves fertility. Surgery is indicated only in the case of

* Failure of medical therapy

* Hyperstimulation

* Infertile women

* Previous pregnancy losses

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 34 year old woman presents with irregular bleeding. Endometrial biopsy revealed endometrial hyperplasia without atypia. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment modality in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MIRENA IUD

Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (MIRENA) is the preferred treatment for endometrial hyperplasia without atypia in this patient..

Endometrial hyperplasia is defined as endometrial thickening with the proliferation of irregularly sized and shaped glands and an increased gland-to-stroma ratio. It is a pre-malignant lesion for endometrial carcinoma.

2014 Revised WHO Classification of endometrial hyperplasia:

* Hyperplasia without atypia

* Atypical hyperplasia

Architectural complexity is no longer included in the classification. In the new WHO system, a diagnosis of endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia (EIN) is considered equivalent to atypical hyperplasia."

Transvaginal ultrasonography (TVS) is the first-line investigation that checks for endometrial thickness. An endometrial thickness of >4mm calls for further investigation by endometrial sampling. Endometrial sampling can be done using:

* OPD procedures such as an Endometrial Aspiration Cytology (EAC) and methods like Pipelle aspirator/Vibra aspirator are used for aspiration of the uterine cavity. The obtained sample is then sent for histopathological examination.

* In-patient procedures for endometrial sampling like Fractional curettage (dilatation and curettage) with Hysteroscopy.

Hysteroscopic inspection & fractional curettage is the gold standard procedure to diagnose focal endometrial lesions. On biopsy, depending on whether endometrial hyperplasia is without or with atypia, we decide on giving continuous progesterone therapy or doing a hysterectomy for the patient, respectively.

The flowchart below gives a summary of the evaluation of postmenopausal bleeding:

Management of endometrial hyperplasia:

1) Hyperplasia without atypia:

Progesterone, administered either orally or via the intrauterine route (using a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system [LNG-IUS], such as Mirena), is effective in achieving regression of endometrial hyperplasia without atypia.

The LNG-IUS is recommended as the first-line medical treatment, as it offers a higher regression rate, a more favourable bleeding pattern, and fewer adverse effects compared to oral progestogens.

For women who decline the LNG-IUS, continuous oral progestogen therapy (medroxyprogesterone 10–20 mg/day or norethisterone 10–15 mg/day) is advised. Treatment with either oral progestogens or the LNG-IUS should continue for at least six months to achieve histological regression of endometrial hyperplasia without atypia.

2) Atypical hyperplasia:

Atypical hyperplasia is associated with a considerable risk of progressing to endometrial carcinoma, estimated to be between 8% and 29%. As a result, total hysterectomy is typically recommended to reduce this risk. However, in young women who wish to preserve fertility, treatment with high-dose progesterone can be considered, with close follow-up through frequent endometrial biopsies to monitor for any signs of cancer progression."

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female presents with hirsutism, delayed periods & obesity. USG findings are given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome

The given clinical scenario and the ultrasound image given below showing an enlarged ovary with multiple follicles in the periphery(a string of pearls) is indicative of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS).

PCOS is an endocrinopathy seen in women of reproductive age, affecting multiple systems. The Rotterdam criteria are used to diagnose PCOS. The presence of any two of the three components of this criteria establishes the diagnosis of PCOS:

* Clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne)

* Menstrual abnormalities (oligo/amenorrhoea), anovulation, infertility

* Polycystic ovaries on ultrasonography.

Sonographic criteria for polycystic ovaries include ≥ 12 small cysts, an increased ovarian volume (> 10 mL) or both.

Management:

* Weight reduction alone is beneficial in mild hirsutism and lifestyle changes (like smoking cessation) are advised in the management of PCOS.

* Oral contraceptive pills (OCP), preferably fourth-generation pills with 30 mcg E2 and 2-3 mg drospirenone are used to treat menstrual abnormalities. It also reduces acne and further hirsutism.

* Anti-androgens are useful in treating hirsutism. OCP with cyproterone acetate is prescribed for PCOS patients with hirsutism.

* Patients with PCOD are more prone to developing insulin resistance which can be controlled with metformin. Acarbose can be used if metformin is contraindicated

* Patients presenting with infertility are treated by inducing ovulation using clomiphene as a first-line drug, along with dexamethasone and letrozole.

Surgical options include laparoscopic ovarian drilling or puncture of not more than four cysts in each ovary. This is done either by laser or by unipolar electrocautery. It restores the endocrine levels and improves fertility.

Surgery is indicated only if,

* Medical therapy fails

* Hyperstimulation occurs

* Infertile women

* Previous pregnancy losses

Other Options:

Option B: Molar Pregnancy will produce a characteristic Snowstorm appearance on ultrasound.

Option C: Enlarged ovaries meeting in the midline having large cysts are suggestive of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

Option D: The image below depicts multiple theca lutein cysts.

Pearl PF1877: Endocrinological changes of PCOD

* Elevated Estrone/E1 levels.

* LH level is raised over 10 IU/mL. FSH level remains normal to low, but FSH/LH ratio falls.

* Testosterone and epi-androstenedione levels rise.

* Testosterone elevated but < 200 ng/dL (normal range 20 - 70 ng/dL)

* Testosterone > 200 ng/dL suggests androgen-secreting ovarian tumor

* DHEA-S values may be normal or slightly elevated

* DHEA >700 ng/mL suggests adrenal tumour

* Serum SHBG is reduced.

* Triglyceride level >150 mg/dL-hyperlipidaemia HDL <50 mg/dL.

* Fasting blood glucose/fasting insulin <4.5 suggests insulin resistance

* Prolactin is mildly raised in 15% cases

* Fasting insulin is more than 10 mIU/L in PCOS in 50–70%cases

* Thyroid function tests may be abnormal (hypothyroidism)

* 17-a-hydroxyprogesterone in the follicular phase >300 ng/dL suggests adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

* Urinary cortisol <50 μg/24 h.

Pearl PF1729: Management of PCOD

Complaint
Management

Irregular periods
OCPs

Obesity
Lifestyle modification

Insulin resistance
Metformin

Hirsutism /acne
OCPs with cyproterone acetate

Infertility
Clomiphene

Note: Letrozole is as effective as Clomiphene in treating infertility in PCOD with fewer side effects. However, it's pending FDA approval and is used off-label.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A man underwent vasectomy recently. The surgeon advises the patient to abstain from sexual activity for a certain period after the procedure before confirming the success of the vasectomy. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding the duration of abstinence post-vasectomy?
options: 3 months and after semen analysis is done
1 month and after semen analysis is done
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 3 months and after semen analysis is done

A patient who has undergone a vasectomy should abstain from sexual activity for 3 months and undergo a semen analysis afterwards.

Vasectomy is a permanent sterilization procedure done in males, where a segment of the vas deferens is resected and ligated bilaterally.

This procedure is done under local anesthesia. A small incision is made in the scrotum. The vas deferens are divided on both sides, disrupting the passage of sperms. The no-scalpel technique has been now adopted. One single incision is made with special forceps and a skin stitch is not required. Clips and plugs can be applied over the vas instead of cutting. The failure rate of vasectomy is 0.15%.

It is a relatively simple procedure with low rates of complications. A patient who had a vasectomy is not sterile immediately after the procedure as semen is stored in distal channels of the vas deferens for varying periods.

Hence, for this reason, it is estimated that at least 20 ejaculations or 3 months are required to empty the stored semen. During this time, additional contraceptive measures should be used.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient underwent a forceps delivery a few hours ago and subsequently developed severe pain at the episiotomy site. Examination reveals vulvar swelling with bluish discoloration, along with hypotension (80/60 mmHg) and tachycardia. Which of the following should not be done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Remove the suture in ward

To remove the suture in the ward would be unadvisable since symptoms of hypotension and bluish discoloration of the vulva are indicative of a vulvar hematoma.

The vulva is the most common site for pelvic hematoma and the pudendal artery is the most common artery involved in vulval hematoma

Hematomas <5 cm can be managed conservatively with cold compress. Larger hematomas need to be explored surgically. And as the patient is already hypotensive , it suggests that hematoma is quite large in size. Hence trying to manage it in ward by removing the sutures can lead the hematoma to bleed profusely can cause further detoriation of patient's condition and should be avoided. The next best step to manage it to resuscitate the patient in OT until she can be managed surgically.

Types of pelvic hematomas:

Feature
Infralevator hematoma
Supralevator hematoma

Incidence
Common
Rare

Location
Below the levator ani
Above the levator ani

Causes
Improper hemostasis during repair of vaginal/ perineal tears or episiotomy wound
Extension of cervical laceration, lower uterine segment rupture

Presentation
Severe pain with rectal tenesmus
Unexplained shock with features of internal haemorrhage

Treatment
Small hematomas can be conservatively managed with cold compress
Laparotomy

Other Options:

Option B, C and D are warranted actions in the management of the hematoma.

Option B: Blood transfusion should be one of the steps of management as vulvar hematoma are known to cause heavy bleeding and blood transfusion has to be done as patient is already hypotensive.

Option C: Resuscitation in the OT is also a better approach as if there was failure to control the bleeding , patient can be managed surgically as soon as possible.

Option D: Any individual should inform senior staff in cases like the one given above. Vulvar Hematoma causing hypotension warrants an emergency and senior staff should be informed to take necessary action as soon as possible if needed.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient with a history of obstructed labor and cesarean section presents with continuous dribbling of urine through vagina on day 7. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vesicovaginal fistula

The clinical scenario is suggestive of vesicovaginal fistula.

Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF) is a type of genital fistula, which is an abnormal communication between the genital tract and the urinary tract.

Vesicovaginal fistulae occur mostly due to obstetric injuries such as prolonged labor, and instrumental or manipulative deliveries. Patients present with true incontinence characterized by constant dribbling of urine. The presence of urine in the undergarments is uncomfortable and leads to pruritus and excoriation of the genital area

In obstructed labour, ischemia necrosis occurs as a result of prolonged compression effect on the bladder base between the head and symphysis pubis leading to infection → sloughing → fistula. Thus, it takes around 3–5 days following delivery to produce a fistula.

Clinical assessment by the introduction of a speculum helps to determine the size, number, and location of the fistulae. A methylene blue test helps confirm the diagnosis and determine the type of repair operation.

Small fistulas due to difficult childbirth can heal spontaneously. Most established fistulas need to be repaired vaginally usually after 3 months to allow the inflammation to subside.

The repair operation includes the Latzko procedure. The procedure involves denuding the vaginal epithelium around fistulous edges and approximating the raw surfaces. Another is the Chassar-Moir technique of widely separating the bladder and vagina and suturing them separately in two layers.

Post-operatively, continuous bladder drainage for 14 days along with antibiotics is recommended. Vaginal or speculum examination and intercourse are not advised for 3 months. Avoiding pregnancy for a year is also recommended. A cesarean section is usually done for future pregnancies.

Other options:

Option A: Vesicouterine fistula occurs during cesarean section or uterine rupture or placenta accreta. Patients complain of cyclical hematuria due to the trickling of menstrual blood into the bladder through this anomalous condition. But the urinary continence of the patient remains normal. This is also known as Youssef syndrome.

Option B: In urethrovaginal fistulae, the patient is continent and dry, but may dribble urine during micturition. This usually follows surgery for a paravaginal cyst or urethral diverticulum, or after a penetrating injury from a fall or criminal abortion. The fistulous opening is visible on speculum examination.

Option C: Ureterovaginal fistulae result from direct injury to the ureter during gynecologic surgery (Eg: Wertheim's procedure for Ca cervix). Urine dribbles from both vagina and urethra post-surgery. The three-swab test will not stain with methylene blue, but with urine.

Pearl PF1921: Methylene blue - 3 swab test

Procedure:

A catheter is introduced into the bladder through the urethra. The vaginal cavity is packed with three (or four) sterile cotton swabs.

50–100 mL of dilute methylene blue dye is injected into the bladder using a catheter.

Results:

* Upper swabs get wet and not stained - the leak is from the ureter: Ureterovaginal fistula

* Upper swabs get stained - the leak is from the bladder: Vesicovaginal fistula

* Lower swabs get stained - the leak is from the urethra: Urethrovaginal fistula.

Pearl PF2104: Difference between bladder fistula & ureteric fistula

Bladder fistula
Ureteric fistula

Etiology

Obstetric causes:

• Prolonged obstructed labor
• Instrumental deliveries
• Iatrogenic injury during caesarean section or sling operations

Surgical injury during:

• Abdominal hysterectomy
• Vaginal hysterectomy
• Wertheim's hysterectomy
• Laparoscopic surgeries
• Caesarean section

Clinical features

Dribbling of urine present from the vagina

The patient is unable to micturate

Dribbling of urine present from the vagina

The patient is able to micturate

Methylene blue 3-swab test
Middle swab stains with methylene blue
Uppermost swab stains with urine, but not with methylene blue

Intravenous pyelography
Normal
Hydronephrosis and hydroureter present on the affected side

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Following denotes which sign of pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chadwick's sign

The sign seen, giving a dusky bluish discoloration of the anterior vaginal wall is known as Jacquemier’s or Chadwick’s sign. The discoloration is due to local vascular congestion.

Some other signs seen in pregnancy are given in the image below:

Pearl PF1683: Uterine Signs in Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the area marked in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rectovesical pouch

The arrow in the image points to the rectovesical pouch.

The peritoneum covering the anterior surface of the rectum is reflected anteriorly to cover the posterosuperior surface of the bladder in males, forming a rectovesical pouch. This is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in males and an important site for pelvic fluid collection.

Other options:

Option B: Rectouterine pouch- The peritoneum which covers the anterior surface of the rectum is reflected anteriorly to cover the posterior surface of the posterior fornix of the vagina and the uterus, forming a rectouterine pouch.

Option C: Vesicouterine pouch- The peritoneum covering the fundus and body of the uterus, is reflected anteriorly to cover the posterosuperior surface of the bladder forming a vesico uterine pouch

Option D: Pouch of Morrison (hepatorenal recess) - The peritoneum covering the posterior surface of the right lobe of the liver is reflected posteriorly to cover the anterior surface of the right kidney and right suprarenal gland, forming a deep, vertical groove. This is the deepest peritoneal recess in the supine position and an important site for fluid collection.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the condition depicted in the laparoscopic image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Genital tuberculosis

The laproscopic image above depicts multiple miliary nodules on the uterine and peritoneal surfaces. This guides us towards the diagnosis of female genital tuberculosis (FGTB).

Genital Tuberculosis is caused by M. tuberculosis and almost always occurs secondary to primary infection elsewhere in the extragenital states. Most common route of spread is hematogenous and the most common site is bilateral fallopian tubes (the most common part affected is ampulla and most common pathology encountered is endosalpingitis). 20-30 years age group is affected the most. Infertility is the most common symptom.

Site of genital TB
% involved

Fallopian tubes
90-100

Uterus
50-60

Ovaries
20-30

Vagina/vulva
1-2

Other signs of genital tuberculosis include:

* Tobacco-pouch appearance: Tubes appear dilated with fimbrial end open and pouting

* External surface: Greyish with tubercles

* On cut section: Lumen has yellowish-grey caseous matter or serosanguinous fluid (Tuberculous hematosalpinx) and pyosalpinx.

Other Options:

Option A: Hydrosalpinx is depicted in the image below.

Option D: A chocolate cyst is depicted below.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the CTG pattern shown in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Early deceleration

The given CTG shows early decelerations. It is seen in fetal head compression.

In early decelerations, the onset, nadir, and recovery of deceleration coincide with the beginning, peak, and ending of uterine contraction respectively.

This finding in CTG is suggestive of fetal head compression causing vagal nerve activation.

Other options:

Option A: The CTG given below shows late decelerations, Here the fetal heart rate begins to drop after the end of uterine contraction. It is mostly associated with uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxia.

Other causes of late decelerations include:

* Placental pathologies like- postmaturity, hypertension, diabetes, placental abruption

* Excessive uterine contractions

* Excessive use of oxytocin

* Epidural anesthesia

Option B: The CTG given below shows variable decelerations as seen in umbilical cord compression.

Option D: The CTG given below shows a sinusoidal pattern. It resembles a sine wave. It is often associated with fetal anemia, fetomaternal hemorrhage, and fetal acidosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the procedure being done.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intrauterine balloon tamponade

The given image shows an intrauterine balloon tamponade.

A Bakri postpartum balloon may be inserted and inflated to tamponade the endometrial cavity and stop bleeding. It is used to manage refractory uterine atony.

The insertion process requires two or three team members. First-person to perform abdominal sonography during the procedure. Another to place the deflated balloon into the uterus and stabilize it. The third person instills normal saline to inflate the balloon, rapid infusion of at least 150 mL followed by further instillation over a few minutes for a total of 300 to 500 mL to arrest hemorrhage. Once the bleeding subsides, the catheter is generally removed after 12 to 24 hours.

Segstaken Blakemore, Rusch, and ebb balloons, Foley's catheter, and condom catheters can also be used instead.

In the technique where Foley's catheter is utilized, a 24F-30F size of the catheter with 30ml balloon is used, the tip is guided into the uterine cavity and filled with 60-80ml of saline. In some cases, if the balloon ruptures, a 34F with 60ml balloon can be used. Once the bleeding subsides, the catheter can be removed after 12 -24 hours.

Types of PPH:

Primary/early PPH: Hemorrhage occurring within 24 hours of childbirth. Causes include:

* Atony: Primi, grand multipara, over distended uterus, hydramnios, precipitate labor, prolonged labor, uterine malformations, fibroid uterus

* Trauma: Instrumental deliveries, episiotomy, precipitate labor, macrosomia

* Retained tissues: retained placenta, blood clots

* Bleeding disorders: Sepsis, Intrauterine death, HELLP syndrome.

Secondary/ late PPH: Hemorrhage occurring after 24 hours and up to 12 weeks postpartum. Causes include:

* Placental polyp: Retained products undergo necrosis with fibrin deposition and eventually form a placental polyp, which on detachment from the myometrium causes brisk hemorrhage.

* Abnormal involution of the placental site.

* Retention of placental cotyledon or products of conception.

* Uterine artery pseudoaneurysm.

* Endometritis

* Coagulopathy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the structure in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Blastocyst

The arrow is pointing at Blastocyst.

Around the 4th/5th day of development, the morula becomes the blastocyst. Fluid passes into the morula from the uterine cavity and converts it to a blastocyst with a fluid-filled cavity called blastocoele. This fluid partially separates the cells of the inner cell mass from the outer cell mass.

Cell masses in the blastocyst:

* The outer cell mass is called the trophoblast and forms a major part of the placenta

* The inner cell mass is called the embryoblast and forms the embryo proper

The blastocyst normally implants in the functional layer of the uterine endometrium.

Timeline of implantation:

* 3-4 days after fertilization: The morula (12-16 cells) enters the uterus.

* 4th day after fertilization: The advanced morula reaches the uterine lumen.

* 4-5 days after fertilization: The early blastocyst stage is seen.

* 6-7 days after fertilization: The blastocyst implants in the uterus. Implantation corresponds to 20-22 days of the menstrual cycle.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify this sign in pregnancy.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hegar's sign

The image dipicts Hegar's sign.

Hegar's sign: the examiner performs a bimanual examination. Two fingers of one hand are placed in the anterior fornix of the vagina and the fingers of the other hand are placed, over the abdomen and behind the uterus. The abdominal fingers and the vaginal fingers appear to oppose each other below the body of the uterus. This can be elicited between 6-10 weeks.

This sign is based on the fact that the lower part of the body of the uterus is empty and extremely soft, and the upper part is enlarged by the growing fetus.

Other options :

Option A- Palmer's sign is regular rhythmic uterine contraction during the bimanual examination, which is seen as early as 4-8 weeks.

Option C- Osiander's sign is increased pulsation felt through lateral fornix by 8 weeks.

Option D- Goodell's sign is softening of the cervix by the 6th week.

Pearl PF1633: Clinical Signs in Obstetrics

*

Chadwick’s Sign: Bluish hue to the vestibule and anterior vaginal wall. Seen in the first trimester of pregnancy. The cause is increased blood flow to the pelvic organs. Also known as Jacquemier’s Sign. /

*

Cullen Sign: Bluish discoloration of the skin around the umbilicus. Occurs due to intraperitoneal hemorrhage. Seen in ruptured ectopic pregnancy

*

Goodell Sign: Marked softening of the cervix in contrast to a non-pregnant state. Also due to increased blood flow

* Hegar Sign: An indication of Pregnancy. The softening of the lower parts of the uterus enables the approximation of vaginal and abdominal fingers on bimanual pelvic examination.

*

Kustner’s Sign: Sign of placental separation. On pushing the uterus upwards does not move the cord with it due to the separation.

*

Ladin’s Sign: Softening in the midline of the uterus anteriorly at the junction of the uterus and cervix. It occurs at about 6 weeks gestation

* Osiander’s Sign: Pulsations in the lateral fornix due to the increased vascularity.

* Palmer’s Sign: Regular rhythmic contractions of uterus felt as early as 6-8 weeks. It is a sign of pregnancy

*

Piskacek’s Sign: Asymmetric growth occurs to the uterus in the initial stages of pregnancy due to the lateral implantation of the blastocyst. The area of implantation feels soft compared to the other parts.

*

Schroeder’s Sign: A sign of placental separation. Uterus rises up when the separated placenta is passed downwards

*

Stallworthy’s Sign: Slowing of fetal heart rate on pressing the head down into the pelvis and prompt recovery on the release of pressure is termed Stallworthy’s sign. This sign is suggestive of posterior placenta praevia.

*

Turtle Sign: This is when the fetal head suddenly retracts back against the mother's perineum after it has emerged from the vagina. This retraction of the fetal head is caused by the baby's anterior shoulder being caught on the back of the maternal pubic bone, preventing delivery of the remainder of the baby.

*

Von Braun-Fernwald's Sign: Irregular softening and enlargement of the uterine fundus during early pregnancy. It occurs at 5-8 weeks gestation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In developed countries, which kind of screening saved the most lives ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cervical cancer screening

Cervical cancer screening has been the most successful cancer screening program in medical history for developed countries.

According to WHO, widespread use of screening in high-income countries has resulted in a dramatic decline in cervical cancer mortality over the last three decades. Moreover, IARC concludes that there is sufficient evidence that cervical cancer screening can reduce cervical cancer mortality by 80% or more among screened women.

The introduction of the Pap smear by Dr. George Papanicolaou led to a dramatic reduction in cervical cancer mortality, with death rates declining by more than 70% since its implementation in the 1950s. This success is due to the test's ability to detect precancerous changes (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia) before they become invasive cancer, allowing for early intervention and prevention. WHO suggests that, in high resource settings, cytology (pap smear) is the most widely used screening test. A

The key distinction is that Pap smear screening not only detects early cancer but can prevent it entirely by identifying precancerous changes, making it uniquely effective among cancer screening programs.

Other options:

Option B: Breast cancer screening, while important, has shown more modest mortality reduction (around 20-30%) and has generated controversy regarding overdiagnosis and false positives;

Option C: Oral cancer screening has not demonstrated significant population-level mortality benefits in developed countries, partly due to its lower incidence and the lack of a standardized screening program;

Option D: Prostate cancer screening with PSA testing has been particularly controversial due to concerns about overdiagnosis, overtreatment, and unclear mortality benefit, with some studies showing minimal impact on overall survival.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which of the following scenarios is this instrument contraindicated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Obstructed labour

The image shows Piper's forceps, identified by its distinct perineal curve. It is contraindicated in obstructed labour.

Piper forceps is a specialized forceps, used to assist the delivery of the after-coming head of the breech (Option A). It can also be used in cases of occipito-posterior position and caesarian delivery (Options B and C). It has a cephalic curve, reverse pelvic curve, and long parallel shanks that permit the baby’s body to rest against it during head delivery.

Pearl PF1918: Obstetrics forceps

Commonly used forceps:

1) Simpson forceps

* The most commonly used types of forceps in outlet delivery.

* Has elongated cephalic curve.

* These are used when there is substantial molding of the fetal head.

2) Elliot forceps

* Has an adjustable pin for regulating the lateral pressure on the handles.

* They are used most often when there is minimal molding.

* More suitable for outlet delivery.

3) Kielland forceps

* Has small pelvic curve and a sliding lock.

* Suitable for head with little molding.

* The most common forceps used for rotational delivery.

* Helps correct asynclitism.

4) Piper forceps

* Distinct perineal curve.

* Allows for application to the after-coming head in breech delivery.

5) Tucker-McLane forceps

* Suitable for fetal head with little molding.

* Used in rotational delivery.

6) Barton forceps and traction handle

* Used in rotational delivery.

* Most importantly used for delivery of occipitotransverse positions in a platypelloid pelvis.

* It is an obsolete procedure.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Revised How much time delay should there be between the delivery of the head and delivery of the shoulder in the case of shoulder dystocia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 60 seconds

Shoulder dystocia is defined as head to shoulder delivery time more than 60 seconds.

Risk factors

Prelabour (Mnemonic: DOPE)
Intrapartum

D: Diabetes Mellitus

Prolonged 1st and 2nd stage of labour

O: Obesity
Instrumental delivery

P: Postdatism and prior history

Augmentation of labour with oxytocin

E: Excessive weight gain during pregnancy

Management of labour in case of shoulder dystocia includes the following.

* Gentle downward traction of the fetal head with suprapubic pressure (not fundal).

* Mc. Roberts manoeuvre involves the flexing of the legs against the abdomen with concurrent suprapubic pressure. Below is a diagram depicting the Mc. Roberts manoeuvre.

Woods corkscrew manoeuvre involves the progressive rotation of the posterior shoulder by 180 degrees in a corkscrew fashion to release the impacted anterior shoulder. Below is a diagram depicting the Woods corkscrew manoeuvre.

Zavanelli manoeuvre: It involves the replacement of the fetal head into the pelvis followed by cesarean delivery.
Other manoeuvres include Rubin's maneuver (rocking fetal shoulders side to side) Gaskin maneuver (All fours maneuver), Symphysiotomy (cutting the symphyseal cartilage and ligamentous supports) and cleidotomy (fracture of the clavicle using an instrument). Below is a diagram depicting the cleiodotomy procedure.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The earliest sign seen in pregnancy on ultrasound is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gestational sac

The earliest sonographic sign of pregnancy is the visualization of the gestational sac which is seen as the double decidual sign.

The double decidual sac sign (DDSS) is a useful feature on early pregnancy ultrasound to confirm an early intrauterine pregnancy when the yolk sac or embryo is still not visualised. It consists of the decidua parietalis (lining the uterine cavity) and decidua capsularis (lining the gestational sac) and is seen as two concentric rings surrounding an anechoic gestational sac.

The double decidual sac sign differentiates normal pregnancy from the pseudo-gestational sac of an ectopic pregnancy. Pseudosac is irregular, usually centrally located in the uterus, has no double decidua sign, and the sac remains empty. The illustration below shows the difference:

Other options:

Option C: Roberts sign shows the presence of gas shadow within the chambers of the heart and in large vessels of the fetus. It is the earliest sign of intrauterine death, seen within 12 hours of death.

Option D: In a normal intrauterine pregnancy a gestational sac will be visible on TVS by 5 weeks of LMP and the embryonic poles can be visualized by 5.5 weeks. The fetal cardiac activity can be first visualized on TVS around 5.5-6 weeks, when the crown-rump length (CRL) is around 5mm.

Pearl PF1942: Radiological Signs in Obstetrics

Bagel Sign (USG)

It is seen in unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy. It is also known as the tubal ring sign or the blob sign. It refers to the appearance of an anechoic gestational sac in the adnexa surrounded by a hyperechoic ring.

Twin Peak Sign/ Lambda Sign (USG)

Chorionicity of the placenta is best diagnosed by ultrasound at 10–13 weeks of gestation. In dichorionic twins, there is a thick triangular projection of placental tissue between the two gestational sacs. This is known as the lambda sign or twin peak sign.

T Sign (USG)

The T sign which is seen in monochorionic diamniotic gestation is thin and T-shaped because there is no extension of placental tissue or chorion in between the amniotic membranes.

Double Decidual Sac Sign (USG)

It is seen in early intrauterine pregnancy as two concentric echogenic rings surrounding the gestational sac.

Lemon Sign (USG)

At the level of the lateral ventricles, there is inward bowing or scalloping of frontal bones (indicated by the arrow in the image below) giving rise to the lemon sign. It is suggestive of spina bifida. It is also characteristically associated with Chiari II Malformation.

Banana Sign (USG)

Anterior curvature of the cerebellum with effacement of the cisterna magna in the posterior fossa is seen as banana sign.

Spalding sign (USG)

It usually appears 7 days after intrauterine death and is caused by liquefaction of the brain matter and softening of the ligamentous structures supporting the vault, leading to irregular overlapping of the cranial bones on one another.

Frog Eye Sign (USG)

It is seen in anencephaly. Due to the absence of calvaria, the orbits appear more prominent. This is known as the "frog-eye sign".

Omphalocele (USG)

It is a congenital midline abdominal wall defect at the base of the umbilical cord insertion, with herniation of the solid abdominal viscera and/or bowel out of the fetal abdomen  (indicated with an asterisk). The extruded abdominal contents are covered in a sac.

Double Bubble Sign (USG)

Dilatation of stomach and first part of duodenum due to duodenal atresia.

Bunch of grapes sign or Snowstorm appearance (USG)

The appearance of multiple cystic spaces or lesions in a complete mole.

Ball sign (X-ray)

It is due to the crumpled up spine of the fetus seen in case of intrauterine death.

Robert’s sign (X-ray)

The presence of gas in the fetal great vessels in case of intrauterine fetal demise is known as Robert's sign.

Stuck twin sign (USG)

Smaller twin is held in a fixed position along the uterine wall due to the severe oligohydramnios. It is seen in twin-twin transfusion syndrome.

Butterfly sign (USG)

Normal appearance of the choroid plexuses on axial imaging of the fetal brain. An absence of this sign suggests holoprosencephaly.

Cloverleaf skull (USG)

Seen in craniosynostosis

Empty amnion sign (USG)

Visualization of an amniotic sac without concomitant visualization of an embryo. It is an indicator of pregnancy failure.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The presence of edematous villi, a 46 XX karyotype, and negative p57Kip2 suggests a diagnosis of ___________________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Complete mole

Edematous villi with 46 XX chromosome and a negative p57Kip2 immunostaining is suggestive of Complete Mole.

Hydatidiform moles may be either partial or complete:

Complete moles:

* They occur due to the fertilization of an egg that has lost its female chromosomes.

* In about 90% of the cases, the genetic material of one sperm is duplicated, resulting in a diploid 46, XX karyotype.

* In the remaining 10% of the cases, the empty egg is fertilized by two sperms, resulting in a diploid karyotype, which is either 46, XX, or 46, XY.

* In complete moles, the embryo usually dies early in the development, and hence, cannot be identified.

* p57Kip2 immunostaining is negative.

Partial moles (Option C):

* They occur due to the fertilization of an egg with two sperms.

* The karyotype is usually triploid (69, XXY) or occasionally tetraploid (92, XXXY).

* Fetal tissues are typically present.

* They are associated with an increased risk of persistent molar disease but are not associated with choriocarcinoma.

* p57Kip2 immunostaining is positive.

Option A: Ectopic pregnancy is one in which the fertilized ovum is implanted and develops outside the normal endometrial cavity. The majority of ectopic pregnancies occur in the fallopian tube, the ampulla being the most common site.

Option B: Choriocarcinoma is the neoplasm of trophoblastic cells. It secretes large quantities of hCG hormone, which is used as a tumor marker in the diagnosis and management of the tumor.

1–5%

Often present
