questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The risk of cancer that can be reduced with OCP use are all, except? OCP- Oral contraceptive pills
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Breast Cancer

Oral contraceptive pills (OCP) are not protective against breast cancer.

OCPs have no effect on the incidence of Breast Cancer.

OCPs protect against ovarian cancer (Option A). Oral contraceptives cause prolonged suppression of gonadotropin stimulation of ovary on long term use. This may account for lower incidence of ovarian malignancy noted in contraceptive users.

Other benefits of oral contraceptive pills:

* Lesser incidence of endometrial carcinoma due to progestin component in OCP (Option D).

* Regularisation of menstrual cycles results in relief of dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia.

* Reduced incidence and relief of fibrocystic breast disease and ovarian cysts.

* Endometriosis and pelvic inflammatory disease are improved.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the characteristic feature seen in ectopic pregnancy? hCG- Human chorionic gonadotropin
options: Ovarian mass with thin layer of endometrium
Empty uterus with adnexal mass and fluid in pelvis
Empty uterus and adnexal mass with ground glass appearance
Trilayer endometrium without an adnexal mass
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Empty uterus with adnexal mass and fluid in pelvis

An empty uterus with an adnexal mass and fluid in pelvis is the sign most suggestive of an ectopic pregnancy.

A pregnancy is considered ectopic if implantation occurs at a site outside the uterine cavity. The majority of ectopic pregnancies occur in the fallopian tube, the ampulla being the most common site.

The most appropriate management for an unruptured ectopic pregnancy is single-dose methotrexate.

Management of ectopic pregnancy:

Expectant management: Ectopic pregnancies measuring <3 cm and with declining beta hCG levels initially <1500 mIU/mL may resolve without intervention and can be managed expectantly.

Medical management with single or multiple-dose methotrexate is preferred if:

* Hemodynamic stability

* Serum beta-hCG ≥1500 mIU/ml and ≤5000 mIU/mL

* Mean sac diameter <3.5cm with no fetal cardiac activity detected on transvaginal ultrasound.

* Patients are willing and able to comply with post-treatment follow-up and have access to emergency medical services within a reasonable time frame in case of a deterioration in the clinical status.

Methotrexate(MTX) can be given as a single IM dose of 50 mg/m2 or as a multiple-dose regimen of 1mg/kg on days 1, 3, 5, and 7.

Surgical management with salpingectomy or salpingostomy is done when:

* Criteria for expectant and medical management are not met

* Gestational sac >3.5 cm

* Fetal cardiac activity present

* Beta hCG > 5000 mIU/mL

* Significant pain and hemoperitoneum

* Failure of expectant or medical management

* Clinical status of patient warrants urgent intervention

* Doubtful compliance with medical management

Milking of the tube through the fimbriae carries a high risk of bleeding, damage to the tube, the persistence of trophoblastic tissue, and recurrence of ectopic pregnancy.

Other Options:

Option A: Ovarian mass with thin layer of endometrium  is suggestive of an ovarian cyst.

Option C: Empty uterus and adnexal mass with ground glass appearance is suggestive of a chocolate cyst/ ovarian endometrioma.

Option D: Trilayer endometrium without an adnexal mass is the physiological state of the uterus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which hormone plays a major role in home based pregnancy tests?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Beta-HCG

Beta Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is the basis of home-based pregnancy tests.

hCG is produced by the syncitiotrophoblasts of the placenta. It is a glycoprotein hormone with two subunits. The alpha-subunit is similar to LH, FSH and TSH. The beta-subunit is specific and is measured by pregnancy tests.

hCG can be detected in maternal blood 8 days after fertilisation. Thus, it can help in diagnosis of pregnancy even before the period is missed. Its levels nearly doubles every 48 hours in early pregnancy reaching a maximum of 50000 - 100000 IU/L by 60-70 days of gestation. Then the level starts falling reaching a minimum at 16 weeks, which continues throughout pregnancy.

The various placental hormones and their functions are given below.

Placental hormones
Functions

Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)

Structurally similar to - LH, FSH, TSH

• Maintains corpus luteum function
• Regulates testosterone secretion from fetal testes
• Stimulates maternal thyroid

Placental lactogen (PL)

Structurally similar to - GH, Prolactin

• Helps the mother adapt to fetal energy requirements

Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH)

• Vascular and myometrial smooth muscle relaxation
• Initiation of parturition
• Stimulates placental ACTH production

Placental adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)

Stimulates fetal and maternal adrenal glucocorticoid production

Other placental hormones include:

* GnRH, TRH, GHRH, Growth hormone variant (hGH-V)

* Parathyroid hormone-releasing protein (PTH-rP)

* Inhibin

* Activin

* Relaxin

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following hormone is responsible for the following natural process?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Oxytocin

Oxytocin helps in the ejection of milk by myoepithelial contraction which can be felt as cramps.

Functions of oxytocin are:

* Milk ejection (Myoepithelial contraction)

* ADH like action in high doses (reduces urine output)

* Uterine contraction

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the best non-invasive tool for assessing fetal anaemia?
options: Middle cerebral artery doppler peak systolic velocity (MCA PSV)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Middle cerebral artery doppler peak systolic velocity (MCA PSV)

Middle Cerebral Artery Doppler peak systolic velocity (MCA PSV) is the best non-invasive way of monitoring fetal anemia.

MCA PSV is used for the monitoring of fetuses of Rh-negative sensitized mothers, and if it exceeds 1.5 MoM and the gestational age less than 34 or 35 weeks, fetal blood sampling followed by transfusion is considered.

Serial measurements of the peak systolic velocity of the fetal MCA is reliable, noninvasive, and the recommended test to detect fetal anemia. Blood gets shunted to the brain to maintain adequate oxygenation. A rise in cardiac output and a fall in blood viscosity enhance the peak systolic velocity in the MCA.

The threshold value to identify fetuses with anemia is 1.5 multiples of the median (MoM) for gestational age and is 100% sensitive.

For an MCA PSV between 1.0 and 1.5 MoM, weekly Doppler monitoring to be done. If MCA PSV exceeds 1.5 MoM and the gestational age is lesser than 34 or 35 weeks, fetal blood sampling followed by fetal transfusion to be done if needed.

Beyond 34 weeks, the false-positive rate of MCA peak systolic velocity increases due to the normal increase in cardiac output that develops at this gestational age.

Middle cerebral artery velocimetry is more accurate than and has replaced amnionic fluid spectral analysis and is not associated with the risks of increased alloimmunization and amniocentesis. It is also applied clinically to evaluate fetal growth restriction.

Other Options:

Option A: Biophysical profile, aka Modified Manning score, is a screening test for uteroplacental insufficiency. The fetal CNS is highly sensitive to diminished oxygenation and helps plan the next course of action.

Option B: If the MCA peak systolic velocity > 1.5 MoM and the gestational age is <34 or 35 weeks, fetal blood sampling should be considered and followed by fetal transfusion if needed. But it will fall under invasive method.

Option C: Amniocentesis is the most common prenatal diagnostic procedure. It is performed using an aseptic technique, under direct sonographic guidance, using a 20–22 gauge spinal needle.Approximately 20 to 30 mL of fluid is collected for fetal karyotyping or chromosomal microarray analysis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the pathological heart sound seen during pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diastolic Murmur

Diastolic murmur is considered to be a pathological change in pregnancy.

It is the ejection systolic murmur which is a physiological change.

CVS physiological changes in pregnancy:

* Pulse rate: Increases

* Diastolic BP: Decreases

* S1: Loud and split

* S2:Normal

* S3:prominent (occasional)

* Jugular venous distension and venous hum

* Murmurs

* Ejection systolic murmur at left sternal border.

* Continous murmur at 2nd-4th intercostal space (known as mammary souffle)

* Heart is displaced upwards and to the left

* ECG changes

* Left axis deviation (due to elevation of diaphragm)

* T wave inversion, Biatrial enlargement.

* Mild ST changes in the inferior leads.

* Premature atrial and ventricular contractions are relatively frequent.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the safest hysterectomy surgery to minimise the risk of ureteric injury on the OT table?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vaginal Hysterectomy

Vaginal hysterectomy is the safest surgical approach to minimize the risk of ureteric injury on the OT table.

This is because the vaginal approach allows surgeons to follow natural anatomical planes and typically requires less dissection and manipulation of the uterus.

In a retrospective review of study involving 3114 hysterectomies, the following rates of ureteric injury were noted :

Procedure
Incidence of Ureteric injury

Abdominal hysterectomy
(5/940) 0.53%

Vaginal hysterectomy
(1/304) 0.33%

Robotic hysterectomy
(7/1088) 0.64%

Laparoscopic hysterectomy
(4/782) 0.51%

Injuries to the urinary tract occur during major gynecologic surgeries. These injuries usually happen when dissection is carried out near the ureter or the bladder. When a hysterectomy is performed through the vaginal route, the likelihood of ureteric injury is lower. In comparison, the open and laparoscopic approaches show higher rates of such complications.

Patients with ureteric injuries have a complicated post-operative period. They can present with the following features:

* Fever

* Flank pain

* Abdominal distension

* Prolonged paralytic ileus - bowel sounds are absent

* High drain outputs, in case abdominal drains are placed.

CT urogram and retrograde pyelography are the investigations of choice. They reveal urinary extravasation from the ureter. Ureteric injuries are prevented by careful division of tissue planes during pelvic or genitourinary surgeries. The condition is managed by prompt surgical repair by ureteroureterostomy or percutaneous ureterostomy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following platinum based drugs are used in cervical cancer along with radiotherapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cisplatin

Cisplatin is the drug of choice for chemotherapy for cervical cancer.

The primary management for cervical cancer is chemoradiation therapy. This involves the combination of external beam radiation therapy, brachytherapy, and chemotherapy (usually with cisplatin). This approach has been shown to improve overall survival and reduce the risk of local and distant recurrence compared to radiation therapy alone.

Following chemoradiation, patients should be closely monitored for treatment response and potential side effects or complications. This includes regular physical examinations, Pap tests, and imaging studies as needed. The prognosis for stage IIB cervical cancer depends on various factors, such as the size of the tumor, lymph node involvement, and the patient's overall health. With appropriate treatment, the 5-year survival rate for stage IIB cervical cancer is around 58-63%.

Other Options:

Option A: Chemotherapy with doxorubicin is used in case of very aggressive recurrent tumors and residual tumors.

Option B: Trastuzumab is indicated for adjuvant therapy in early and metastatic HER2 positive breast cancer.

Option D: Bleomycin is an anticancer antibiotic used for the treatment of squamous cell cancer and Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which part of the placenta is shown in this picture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fetal side

Fetal side of the placenta is depicted in the picture.

Placenta has two components - basal plate (the one on the maternal side) and chorionic plate (the one towards the fetal side which gives rise to the chorionic villi).

Usually, in a normal placenta, both basal and chorionic plates end simultaneously at the margin of the placenta.

The fetal surface, known as the chorionic plate, creates the roof of the intervillous space and is covered by the amnion, a thin avascular membrane. This plate contains chorionic vessels that branch from the umbilical vessels and is composed of distinct layers including the amniotic epithelium, connective tissue layer, primary stem villi containing fetal vessels, and both cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast layers. This complex arrangement facilitates the crucial transfer of nutrients and gases between mother and fetus.

The placental structure, from the maternal aspect, begins with the basal plate which forms the maternal floor of the intervillous space (Option B). This critical interface contains multiple components arranged in layers, including the decidual layer (composed of decidual cells from the endometrium) (Option A), the fibrinoid or Nitabuch's layer (containing fibrin deposits marking the boundary between maternal and fetal tissues), and the cytotrophoblastic shell. The basal plate is characterized by grooves that create cotyledons and houses the spiral arteries and veins from maternal circulation, making it essential for maternal-fetal exchange  (Option D).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female patient with post partum hemorrhage has been given ergometrine and oxytocin. The bleeding still continues. Which prostaglandin derivative can be given in this situation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carboprost

Carboprost, 15-methyl PGF2α can be used in a setting where both ergometrine and oxytocin have not been able to control the bleeding.

Oxytocin is used as the first-line agent in preventing postpartum hemorrhage. When oxytocin fails or is not available, ergot derivatives can be used for second-line treatment.

Carboprost, 15-methyl PGF2α is the drug of choice for PPH and can be used for uterine atony in a dose of 0.25 mg IM. This dose can be repeated if necessary at 15-90 min intervals, up to a maximum of eight doses.

Misoprostol: PGE1

* In settings where injectable uterotonics are not feasible or recommended, PGE1 is a useful option.

* Misoprostol-induced fever can be distressing and may result in unnecessary sepsis workups and antibiotic use.

* No evidence shows that misoprostol is better than other uterotonics for treating PPH.

Postpartum hemorrhage:

It is defined as a loss of more than 500 ml of blood after completion of the third stage of labor (in vaginal delivery).

PPH is blood loss of more than 1000 mL from the genital tract following cesarean section.

Depending upon the amount of blood loss, PPH can be, minor (<1L) or major (>1L). Major is further subdivided into moderate (1L-2L) and severe (>2L).

Types of PPH:

Primary/early PPH: Hemorrhage occurring within 24 hours of childbirth. Causes include

* Atony: Primi, grand multipara, over-distended uterus, hydramnios, precipitate labor, prolonged labor, uterine malformations, fibroid uterus

* Trauma: Instrumental deliveries, episiotomy, precipitate labor, macrosomia

* Retained tissues: retained placenta, blood clots

* Bleeding disorders: Sepsis, Intrauterine death, HELLP syndrome.

Secondary/ late PPH: Hemorrhage after 24 hours - 12 weeks postpartum. Causes include

* Placental polyp forms when retained placental tissue undergoes necrosis and fibrin deposition; detachment from the myometrium can then result in sudden, heavy bleeding

* Abnormal involution of the placental site.

* Retention of placental cotyledon or products of conception.

* Uterine artery pseudoaneurysm.

* Endometritis

* Coagulopathy

Resuscitative measures include

* Airway, breathing, circulation assessment

* A high concentration of oxygen (10–15 l/min) via a facemask

* Blood transfusion if clinically required

* Fluid resuscitation with warmed fluids up to 3.5 liters, starting with up to 2 liters of crystalloids such as normal saline and ringer's lactate. Colloids can be used when there is a need for packed RBCs transfusion, until blood is arranged.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female undergoes a methylene blue 3 swab test and the middle swab is stained with blue. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vesicovaginal fistula

The given clinical scenario with methylene blue swab test showing staining of middle swab is suggestive of vesicovaginal fistula.

Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF) is a type of genital fistula, which is an abnormal communication between the genital tract and the urinary tract. It can be classified as simple or complicated. Their features are given in the table below.

Simple VVF
Complicated VVF

Size ≤ 3 cm
Size > 3 cm

Located near the cuff or supra-trigonal
Located away from the cuff / there is the involvement of trigone

No prior malignancy
Pelvic malignancy present

No prior radiation
Prior radiation therapy

The vaginal length remains normal
Vaginal length shortened

Vesicovaginal fistulae occur mostly due to obstetric injuries such as prolonged labor, and instrumental or manipulative deliveries. Patients present with true incontinence characterized by constant dribbling of urine. The presence of urine in the undergarments is uncomfortable and leads to pruritus and excoriation of the genital area.

Investigations to be performed include

* Urine culture and treatment of infection if required

* Ultrasound of the kidney, ureter, and bladder

* Intravenous pyelography

* Methylene blue - 3 swab test if the fistula is small. Here, methylene blue is injected into the bladder via the catheter, and three sterile swabs are placed into the vaginal cavity.

* The uppermost swab gets wet and not stained - the leak is from the ureter, seen in the ureterovaginal fistula

* The middle swab gets stained - the leak is from the bladder, seen in vesicovaginal fistula

* The lowermost swab gets stained- the leak is from the urethra, seen in the urethrovaginal fistula

* Cystourethroscopy helps in fistula localization, determination of its proximity to the ureteral orifices, inspection for multiple fistula sites, etc.

Vesicovaginal fistula is treated surgically. It can be attempted after 3 months to allow the inflammation to subside and clear the infection. After this, the Latzko procedure can be performed. Here, the vaginal epithelium around the fistula is removed and the edges are approximated. The Chassar Moir technique can also be attempted. Here, the vagina and bladder are separated and sutured into two layers taking care to avoid tension and overlapping suture lines.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A girl presented with complaints of irregular periods, acne, and increased facial hair growth.USG revealed multiple ovarian follicles. Which of the following would be increased in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serum testosterone

In the given clinical scenario history of irregular periods, acne, increased facial hair growth, and USG showing multiple ovarian follicles is suggestive of polycystic ovarian disease(PCOD). In PCOD, serum testosterone would be elevated.

Insulin induces LH to cause theca-cell hyperplasia and secrete androgens, testosterone, and epiandrostenedione which are converted to estrogen in the granulosa cells. Epi-androstenedione is converted in the peripheral fat to oestrone. This leads to rise in estrogen and inhibin levels. These in turn cause high LH surge. While the oestrone level increases, the oestradiol level remains normal which raises the Oestrone: Oestradiol ratio.

Endocrinological changes of PCOD:

* Elevated Estrone/E1 levels.

* LH level is raised over 10 IU/mL. FSH level remains normal to low, but FSH/LH ratio falls.

* Testosterone and epi-androstenedione levels rise.

* Testosterone elevated but < 200 ng/dL (normal range 20 - 70 ng/dL)

* Testosterone > 200 ng/dL suggests androgen-secreting ovarian tumor

* DHEA-S values may be normal or slightly elevated

* DHEA >700 ng/mL suggests adrenal tumour

* Serum SHBG is reduced.

* Triglyceride level >150 mg/dL-hyperlipidaemia HDL <50 mg/dL.

* Fasting blood glucose/fasting insulin <4.5 suggests insulin resistance

* Prolactin is mildly raised in 15% cases

* Fasting insulin is more than 10 mIU/L in PCOS in 50–70%cases

* Thyroid function tests may be abnormal (hypothyroidism)

* 17-a-hydroxyprogesterone in the follicular phase >300 ng/dL suggests adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

* Urinary cortisol <50 μg/24 h.

Polycystic ovarian syndrome

Important clinical features of PCOS are Menstrual abnormalities (70%) - oligomenorrhea, amenorrhea, obesity, hirsutism, acne, and alopecia due to hyperandrogenism, acanthosis nigricans due to insulin resistance, and infertility.

Rotterdam criterion is used to diagnose PCOS. The presence of any two of the three components of this criteria establishes the diagnosis of PCOS.

* Oligo/ amenorrhoea, anovulation, infertility

* Hirsutism/ acne

* Ultrasound findings-

Investigations

* Enlarged ovaries with ovarian volume will be more than 10 mm3

* 12 or more small follicles each 2-9 mm in size placed peripherally.

Hormonal studies

* USG is diagnostic of PCOS - it shows enlarged ovaries with multiple follicles in the periphery. It also rules out other pathologies like ovarian tumors, endometrial hyperplasia.

* Laparoscopy (therapeutic). It reveals bilateral enlarged ovarian cysts.

The ultrasound image below shows an enlarged ovary with multiple follicles in the periphery.

Management of PCOD is individualized. Weight reduction and lifestyle changes are the first-line therapy for PCOD. Oral contraceptive pills (OCP), preferably fourth-generation pills with 30 mcg E2 and 2-3 mg drospirenone are used to treat menstrual abnormalities. Hirsutism and acne are managed with OCP with cyproterone acetate and topical agents such as eflornithine, clindamycin lotion 1%, erythromycin gel 2%, and isotretinoin.

Patients with PCOD are more prone to developing insulin resistance which can be controlled with metformin and acarbose. Patients presenting with infertility are treated by inducing ovulation using clomiphene as a first-line drug, along with dexamethasone and letrozole.

Surgical management includes laparoscopic ovarian drilling or puncture of not more than four cysts in each ovary.

Note:

PCOS in association with diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and cardiovascular disease presenting in reproductive age group is known as "X syndrome".

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A male was referred to the urology OPD for evaluation of infertility. Karyotyping analysis revealed an XXY karyotype. Which of the following statements is not true about the condition?
options: Levels of follicle-stimulating hormone are reduced
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Levels of follicle-stimulating hormone are reduced

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Klinefelter's syndrome. In this condition, the follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels are elevated.

The clinical features include:

* Eunuchoid body habitus - elongated body and long legs (increased length between the soles and the pubic bone)

* Absence of secondary sexual characteristics - lack of body and facial hair, deep voice

* Small atrophic testes

* Micropenis

* Gynecomastia

* Lower IQ, but no mental retardation

The following hormonal variations are seen in these patients:

* Elevated FSH

* Elevated estradiol

* Low testosterone

* Insulin resistance - increased incidence of type 2 diabetes

Patients with Klinefelter syndrome are at a higher risk for:

* Male breast cancer (20x more common than in normal males)

* Extragonadal germ cell tumors

* Autoimmune diseases - systemic lupus erythematosus

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman at 32 weeks of gestation, presented with severe abdominal pain, bleeding per vagina, and loss of fetal movements. On examination, her uterus is tender. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Abruptio placenta

The given clinical picture with abdominal pain, bleeding per vagina, tender uterus and loss of fetal movements in a pregnant woman points to the diagnosis of placental abruption.

Abruptio placenta is the partial/total separation of a normally implanted placenta before delivery.

The bleeding may be either

* Revealed - Blood dissects downwards between membranes and uterine wall to escape through the cervix. Or,

* Concealed -Blood accumulates between the detached placenta and uterus. Or,

* Mixed

Risk factors for abruption placenta include prior abruption history, preterm premature rupture of membranes, and pregnancy-associated hypertension. The haemorrhage into decidua basalis causes separation and compression of the placenta. This compromises fetal circulation leading to fetal distress.

Depending upon the degree of placental abruption and its clinical effects, the cases are graded as follows:

Grade 1
Grade 2
Grade 3

Vaginal bleeding is slight
Vaginal bleeding mild to moderate
Bleeding is moderate to severe or concealed.

Uterus irritable, minimal tenderness

Uterine tenderness is always present
Uterine tenderness is marked.

Maternal BP and fibrinogen unaffected
Maternal pulse increased, BP maintained
Shock is pronounced

FHS good
Fetal distress present
Fetal death is the rule

Maternal shock absent
Maternal shock absent
Associated coagulation defect or anuria may complicate

Placenta previa occurs when the placenta is implanted in the lower uterine segment over or very close to the cervical os. Vaginal bleeding is usually painless in this condition. Fetal condition is generally good until bleeding is severe which occurs in later stages. High-risk factors include multiparty, previous cesarean, or myomectomy scar in the uterus.

In preterm labour, fetal movements are not compromised. Polyhydramnios does not present with bleeding PV.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman presented with complaints of passing grape-like vesicles vaginally. A USG scan was done and is shown below. Which of the following hormonal levels need to be checked in this patient? hCG - Human Chorionic Gonadotropin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. hCG

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of molar pregnancy and beta hCG levels need to be measured.

Molar pregnancy may present with bleeding per vaginum or an acute discharge of vesicular mass per vaginum. On examination, the uterine size is more than the corresponding period of amenorrhea. It shows a characteristic snowstorm appearance on USG.

Suction and evacuation is the treatment of choice. The patient is followed up every week till the hCG levels normalize, after which follow-up is done monthly for 6 months.

Post-evacuation recommendations:

* Anti-D immune globulin if Rh D-negative

* Initiate effective contraception (IUD contraindicated)

* Review pathology report

* Serum hCG levels: within 48 h of evacuation, weekly until undetectable, then monthly for 6 months.

Pregnancy is allowed after 6 months following a negative hCG titer. However, it is advised to avoid pregnancy for 1 year, preferably 2 years, as a fresh pregnancy will interfere with the hCG titers.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida woman gives birth to a baby with the following defect. Identify the anomaly.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Craniorachischisis

The above image showing anencephaly and a contiguous bony defect of the spine, is suggestive of craniorachischisis. It occurs due to failure of complete closure of the neural tube.

Rachischisis is the most severe type of neural tube defect, where the entire neural tube fails to close. Rachischisis can occur in the spinal cord or brain regions of the neural tube. The exposed neural tissues often become necrotic.

The image given below shows craniorachischisis.

Spina bifida is a general term used for neural tube defects affecting the spinal region and associated with splitting of the vertebral arches. It is characterized by gaps in the vertebral arches and may or may not involve the underlying neural tissue.

The illustration shown below shows spina bifida.

The 3 main types of spina bifida:

* Spina bifida occulta - This is the mildest form of spina bifida. The defect in the vertebral arches is covered by the skin. The splits in the vertebrae are so small that the spinal cord does not protrude. The skin at the site of the lesion may be normal, or it may have some hair growing from it.

* Meningocele - The defect in the vertebra allows the meninges to protrude through the defect.

* Myelomeningocele (meningomyelocele) - Defect in the vertebral column allows the spinal cord with the meningeal coverings to protrude.

The image given below shows the different types of spina bifida.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman requests for medical termination of pregnancy (MTP). The doctor decides to perform a suction evacuation. Till when can this be performed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 12 weeks of gestation

Suction and Evacuation (S&E) is best carried out between 7-12 weeks.

The various methods of termination of pregnancy are:

Timing
Medical methods
Surgical methods

1st trimester

(up to 12 weeks)

• Mifepristone
• Mifepristone and misoprostol
• Methotrexate and misoprostol
• Tamoxifen and misoprostol

• Menstrual regulation
• Vacuum aspiration (MVA/EVA)
• Suction evacuation and/or curettage
• Dilatation and evacuation -

• Rapid method
• Slow method

2nd trimester

(13 - 20 weeks)

• Misoprostol
• Mifepristone and misoprostol
• Dinoprostone

• Oxytocin infusion

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman, who is 5 days postpartum, presented with tearfulness, mood swings, and occasional insomnia. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Postpartum blues

Postpartum blues is the most likely diagnosis in a postpartum woman with tearfulness, mood swings, and insomnia from day 4.

Postpartum blues, also known as baby blues, is a transient mood disorder characterized by sadness, tearfulness, confusion, and dysphoria. There are no suicidal thoughts or thoughts of harming the baby. These symptoms typically develop 3-5 days after delivery. They are thought to be due to hormonal changes, the stress of giving birth, and the responsibilities of motherhood. They resolve spontaneously within 10-14 days.

Management involves reassurance, education, and support. The patient must be followed-up and assessed if symptoms persist for >2 weeks to evaluate postpartum depression.

Other options:

Option A: Postpartum depression is when the symptoms of depressed mood, anxiety, insomnia, and weight changes persist for >4 weeks as per DSM 5 or >6 weeks as per ICD 11. The onset is within 4-6 weeks post-delivery. The patient may have occasional thoughts of harming the baby and suicidal thoughts. It can persist for months to years when untreated.

Option C: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency that usually occurs within 4 weeks after delivery (DSM 5) or 6 weeks after delivery (ICD 11). The predominant symptoms are hallucinations, delusions, suicidal thoughts, and thoughts of harming the baby. Psychotic symptoms such as insomnia, restlessness, labile mood, and agitation are seen. Lithium, antipsychotics, and an antidepressant is the treatment of choice.

Option D: Postpartum anxiety is not defined by DSM-5. However, some platforms might describe postpartum anxiety as excessive or severe worry after childbirth.

Pearl PF1851: Postpartum mood disorders

Disorders and features
Incidence and timeline
Harmful thoughts
Treatment

Postpartum blues:

Depressed affect, tearfulness and fatigue

30-75%

Starts 2-3 days after delivery. Resolves within 10 days.

No thoughts of harming the baby
Support and follow up

Postpartum depression:

Depressed affect, anxiety and poor concentration

10-15%

Starts within 12 weeks from delivery and persists for ≥ 2 weeks.

Thoughts of harming the baby often present
CBT and SSRIs

Postpartum psychosis:

Mood-congruent delusions, hallucinations

0.1-0.2%
Thoughts of harming the baby or self
Hospitalization, atypical antipsychotics and ECT for refractory cases

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young primigravida at 32 weeks of gestation was admitted since her BP was 150/90 mmHg and urine dipstick was 2+ on antenatal checkup. On examination, she has pedal edema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Preeclampsia

The given case scenario suggests a likely diagnosis of pre-eclampsia.

Pre-eclampsia occurs due to the failure of the invasion of extravillous trophoblasts into the spiral artery. It is characterized by blood pressure of >140/90 mmHg on two occasions 4 hours apart with proteinuria or signs of end-organ damage.

Criteria to diagnose pre-eclampsia:

* Proteinuria of ≥ 300 mg (0.3 g) in 24 hours or urine protein:creatinine ratio of ≥0.3

* Platelet count of <1 lakh/cu.mm

* Serum creatinine level of >1.1 mg/dL

* Serum transaminase levels twice the normal concentration

* Headache, visual disturbances, or epigastric pain

* Pulmonary edema

Clinical types of pre-eclampsia:

* Nonsevere pre-eclampsia: Blood pressure >140/90 mmHg but <160/110 mmHg without significant proteinuria

* Severe pre-eclampsia: Persistent increase of systolic blood pressure above 160 mmHg or diastolic above 110 mmHg with any of the following, proteinuria, oliguria (<400 mL in 24 hours), platelet count <1 lakh/cu.mm, serum creatinine level of >1.1 mg/dL, persistent severe epigastric pain, marked elevation of liver enzyme levels, cerebral (convulsions) or visual disturbances, intrauterine growth restriction of the fetus, and pulmonary edema.

Complications of pre-eclampsia:

* Eclampsia

* HELLP syndrome

* Acute respiratory distress syndrome

* Cerebral hemorrhage

* Preterm labor

* Postpartum hemorrhage

* Shock

* Sepsis

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the maneuver shown in the image below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ritgen’s manoeuvre

The above image depicts Ritgen’s manoeuvre, a technique used during the second stage of labor to assist in the controlled delivery of the fetal head, reducing the risk of perineal tears and trauma.

Steps in Ritgen’s Maneuver:

* The right hand is draped with a sterile towel.

* The fingers of the right hand pressing posterior to the rectum exerts upward pressure to the chin and extends the head. The extension of the head prevents the head from slipping back in between the contractions.

* The left hand placed over the occiput exerts a downward counterpressure to prevent the rapid extension of the head

* The ritgen’s manoeuvre thus helps in the controlled delivery of the head of the fetus.

Other options:

Option B: Pinard’s manoeuvre is used to facilitate the delivery of legs in case of frank breech presentation.

Option C: Lovset’s manoeuvre is used to facilitate the delivery of arms in breech presentation.

Option D: In Zavanelli maneuver is an obstetric procedure used as a last-resort technique during shoulder dystocia when other manoeuvres fail to deliver the baby vaginally. The fetal head is rotated to the pre-restitution position and pushed back into the pelvis to perform an emergency cesarean section.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which trimester is the quadruple test performed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2nd trimester

Quadruple screening is a second-trimester multiple marker screening test for the detection of chromosomal anomalies like trisomy 21-Down syndrome.

Pregnancies with Down syndrome are characterized by elevated β-hCG, Inhibin and lower estriol, AFP levels.  It is performed from 15 to 21 weeks of gestation.

The triple test findings in pregnancies with fetal Down’s syndrome are characterized by:

* Low MSAFP (maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein) levels, approximately 0.7 MoM (multiples of median).

* Low unconjugated estriol levels, approximately 0.8 MoM.

* High hCG levels, approximately 2.0 MoM.

The triple test is done between 15-18 weeks for the diagnosis of Down's syndrome.

Various antenatal screening tests for aneuploidy are as follows:

Dual test (1st trimester)
Triple test (2nd trimester)
Quadruple test (2nd trimester)

Beta HCG
Beta HCG
Beta HCG

PAPPA
Unconjugated estriol
Unconjugated estriol

This can be combined with nuchal translucency by USG
MSAFP
MSAFP

Serum inhibin A

First-trimester screening with biochemical analytes (↓) PAPP-A and (↑) hCG and USG measurement of NT (↑) can improve the detection rate (87%) of Down’s syndrome. For confirmation, a prenatal genetic study (CVS, amniocentesis or cordocentesis) has to be performed.

Second-trimester screening (quad screening) at 15–18 weeks: (↓) MSAFP, (↓) uE3, (↑) inhibin A and (↑) hCG can detect trisomy 21 in 85% of cases with a false-positive rate of 0.9%. When it is combined with first-trimester screening, the detection rate is increased to 95%.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: McCall culdoplasty is done in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Enterocele repair

McCall's culdoplasty is used in enterocele repair.

An enterocele is herniation of the pouch of Douglas and small bowel loops into the rectovaginal septum. Enteroceles are most commonly associated with uterine prolapse. Patients present with the following clinical features:

* Fecal incontinence

* Sexual dysfunction

* Constipation/diarrhea

* Mass descending PV

* Pelvic pain or pelvic discomfort

* A bulge in the posterior vaginal wall:

* Upper 1/3rd - enterocele

* Lower 2/3rd - rectocele

* Peristalsis may be observed in the bulge

Enterocele repair is done via the following methods:

* Vaginal approach - it is usually preferred over an abdominal approach. In McCall's culdoplasty, the uterosacral ligaments are used to suspend the vaginal vault. The posterior peritoneum and uterosacral ligaments are approximated.

* Abdominal approach - it is preferred in cases where there is associated fecal incontinence. It includes:

* Moschcowitz repair - the pouch of Douglas is obliterated by several purse-string sutures.

* Halban's procedure - the peritoneal sac is obliterated using vertical sutures. This can also be done transvaginally.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The screening method for GDM recommended in India is done between:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 24-28 weeks of gestation

Universal screening for GDM is done for all pregnant women. The first testing should be done during the first antenatal contact as early as possible in pregnancy. The second testing should be done during 24-28 weeks of pregnancy if the first test is negative.

The screening method for GDM recommended in India is a 75 gram oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) irrespective of the last meal timing. A value of ≥140 mg/dL after 2 hours is considered a positive test, indicating GDM.

Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) refers to any degree of glucose intolerance having its onset or first recognition during pregnancy.

For IADPSG criteria, an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is done in the fasting state using 75 g of glucose, and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is diagnosed if any one of the following cut-offs is met i.e.

* Fasting: >92 mg/dl

* 1 hour: >180 mg/dl

* 2 hour: >153 mg/dl

Earlier, a two-step approach was being used to diagnose GDM. In this, the first step (screening) is a 50-gram one-hour glucose challenge test (GCT). The patients having a positive result of >140mg/dl, are candidates for the OGTT. A 100-gram, three-hour oral glucose tolerance test (GTT), is the diagnostic test for gestational diabetes mellitus. GDM is diagnosed if two or more values are positive.

Diabetes in Pregnancy Societies of India(DIPSI) recommends a 1-step procedure with 75 g oral glucose without regard to the time of the last meal. A venous plasma glucose value at 2 hours >140 mg/dL is diagnosed as GDM.

Some complications of GDM include:

* Maternal

* Hypertension, preeclampsia

* Hydramnios

* Increased operative interventions

* Future development of diabetes mellitus

* Fetal and neonatal

* Fetal macrosomia

* Congenital anomalies

* Metabolic abnormalities such as hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and neonatal hypoglycemia.

* Respiratory distress syndrome

* Subsequent childhood and adolescent obesity

Screening is usually done at 24-28 weeks of gestation. Early diagnosis and treatment are important to prevent complications.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the other name for an outlet forceps?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wrigley's forceps

Wrigley's forceps is an outlet forceps. It is used to provide traction force and can also be used in cesarean sections.

It is shown in the image below.

Pearl PF1918: Obstetrics forceps

Commonly used forceps:

1) Simpson forceps

* The most commonly used types of forceps in outlet delivery.

* Has elongated cephalic curve.

* These are used when there is substantial molding of the fetal head.

2) Elliot forceps

* Has an adjustable pin for regulating the lateral pressure on the handles.

* They are used most often when there is minimal molding.

* More suitable for outlet delivery.

3) Kielland forceps

* Has small pelvic curve and a sliding lock.

* Suitable for head with little molding.

* The most common forceps used for rotational delivery.

* Helps correct asynclitism.

4) Piper forceps

* Distinct perineal curve.

* Allows for application to the after-coming head in breech delivery.

5) Tucker-McLane forceps

* Suitable for fetal head with little molding.

* Used in rotational delivery.

6) Barton forceps and traction handle

* Used in rotational delivery.

* Most importantly used for delivery of occipitotransverse positions in a platypelloid pelvis.

* It is an obsolete procedure.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following can not be used for emergency contraception?
options: Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg single dose in 72 hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg single dose in 72 hours

Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg single dose in 72 hours would not be enough for emergency contraception. Levonorgestrel (LNG) 1.5 mg, i.e., 2 tablets of LNG 0.75 mg, can be used as a single-dose emergency contraceptive. This should be taken within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse. Alternatively, one tablet of LNG 0.75 mg can be followed by another tablet 12 hours later.

Advantages of LNG:

* It does not contain estrogen and therefore precludes the associated side effects.

* It can be used in hypertensive, cardiac, and diabetic patients.

* It is suitable for lactating women.

* It can be given up to 120 hours after unprotected intercourse.

* It can be given as a single-dose therapy.

Combined oral pills consisting of both estrogen and progesterone act on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis to inhibit the release of GnRH (and thus subsequently LH and FSH) and thus inhibit ovulation.

Emergency contraception refers to backup methods for contraceptive emergencies that women can use within the first few days after unprotected intercourse to prevent an unwanted pregnancy. Administration of postcoital contraceptive agents that interfere with postovulatory events that can lead to pregnancy.

The various emergency contraceptive methods, along with their mechanism of action, have been described below:

* Ethinyl estradiol 50 μg + norgestrel 0.25 mg is administered as two tablets within 72 hours of coitus, followed by the 2 tablets after 12 hours. The hormone may delay ovulation if taken soon after intercourse.

* Ulipristal is given as a 30 mg tablet and should be taken within 5 days. It is a synthetic progesterone hormone receptor modulator. The drug attaches to the progesterone receptor, delays ovulation, and suppresses the endometrium, thereby preventing implantation.

* IUCD (intrauterine contraceptive device) prevents the implantation of a fertilized ovum. It does so by acting as a foreign body within the uterine cavity. This leads to increased contractility, tubal peristalsis, and leukocytic infiltration in the endometrium.

* Centchroman is administered as two tablets of 60 mg, taken twice over a duration of 24 hours and within 24 hours of intercourse. It acts by preventing the implantation of the blastocyst in the endometrium.

Pearl PF1657: Hormonal contraceptives

Oral pills:

* Combined oral contraceptive pills (COC)

* Mala D - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate

* Mala N - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate (Govt. supply, free of cost)

* Progesterone only pills (POP) - suitable for lactating women

* Norethisterone 350 μg

* Norgestrel 75 μg

* Levonorgestrel (LNG) 30 μg

* Once a month or long-acting pills - highly disappointing results

* Quinestrol (long-acting estrogen) + short-acting progesterone

* Gossypol - male pill : Cottonseed derivative and causes azoospermia and severe oligospermia

* Post-coital pills or interceptive

* Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg, 2 doses, 12 hours apart

* Mifepristone 10-600 mg

* Ulipristal 30 mg, within 5 days of intercourse

* Centchroman 60 mg, 2 tablets, within 24 hrs of intercourse

* GnRH agonists

* CuT IUCD, inserted within 5 days

Injectable contraceptives

* Progesterone only injectables

* DMPA 150 mg IM every 3 months

* NET-EN 200 mg IM every 2 months

* Combined injectables

* Cyclofem - DMPA 25 mg + Estradiol cypionate 5 mg

* Mesigyna - NET-EN 50 mg  + Estradiol valerate 5 mg

Subdermal implants

* Norplant I - Levonorgestrel 35 mg

* Norplant II or Jadelle - 2 rods with levonorgestrel 70 mg in each and released at a rate of 50 μg/day

Others

* Hormonal IUCD - Mirena which contains LNG 52 mg with release rate of 20 μg/day

* Orthoevra patch - Norelgestomin + Ethinyl estradiol weekly for 3 weeks, then patch free for 1 week

* Vaginal ring or Nuvaring - Etonogestrel + ethinyl estradiol daily release, use for 3 weeks with withdrawal for 1 week

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is a direct cause of maternal death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Eclampsia

Eclampsia is a direct cause of maternal death, whereas the other options given are indirect causes of maternal death.

The ICD(International Classification of Diseases) has recommended dividing maternal deaths into two groups :

* Direct obstetric deaths are maternal deaths resulting from obstetric complications of the pregnant state like pregnancy, labor and puerperium or from interventions like incorrect treatment or a chain of events resulting from any of the above.

* Indirect obstetric deaths are maternal deaths resulting from previous existing diseases or diseases that developed during pregnancy and which were not due to direct obstetric causes, but which were aggravated by physiological effects of pregnancy.

The main global causes of maternal deaths are:

* Severe bleeding

* Indirect causes (anemia, malaria, heart diseases)

* Direct causes (infections, unsafe abortions, eclampsia, obstructed labor, ectopic pregnancy, anesthesia-related complications, etc.).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a hyper-estrogenic condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Low BMI

Low body mass index (BMI) is not a hyper-estrogenic condition. In fact, low BMI can lead to decreased estrogen levels, as body fat plays a role in estrogen production.

Hyper-estrogenic conditions refer to conditions where there is an excessive level of estrogen in the body.

Estrogen is a hormone that plays a key role in the development of female sexual characteristics and the regulation of the menstrual cycle.

Other options:

* Some specific subtypes of ovarian tumors, such as Granulosa Cell Tumors and Sertoli-Leydig Cell Tumors, can produce excess estrogen, leading to hyper-estrogenic effects. However, the majority of ovarian cancers are not typically associated with hyper-estrogenic conditions.

* Tamoxifen is a medication often used in the treatment of estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer. It acts as a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM), blocking estrogen receptors. It acts as an estrogen antagonist in the breast and an estrogen agonist in the endometrium.

* Endometriosis involves the growth of tissue similar to the lining of the uterus (endometrium) outside the uterus. It's often associated with estrogen, as estrogen can stimulate the growth of endometrial tissue.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not an indication of inducing labor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Placenta previa

Placenta previa is an indication for cesarean delivery, not to induce labor.

Induction of labor is the process of stimulating uterine contractions for vaginal delivery by medical or surgical methods. It is indicated when the benefit to the mother or fetus outweighs the benefit of continuing the pregnancy.

Indications of induction of labor:

*

Gestational hypertension

*

Chronic hypertension

* Pre-eclampsia

*

Post-term pregnancy

*

Abruption placentae

*

IUGR(intra-uterine growth restriction)

*

IUD(Intra-uterine death)

*

Oligohydramnios

Contraindications of induction of labor:

* Contracted pelvis & CPD

* Cord prolapse

* Abnormally implanted placentae

* Previous classical cesarean/ hysterotomy

* Active genital herpes

* Appreciable macrosomia

* Severe hydrocephalus

* Malpresentation

* Pelvic tumor & Ca cervix

* Overdistention or complete transection of the uterus

* Two or more previous low transverse cesarean sections

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old nulligravid patient came to the clinic complaining of irregular bleeding for the past month. What is the next best investigation you would perform?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Perform a urine pregnancy test

The next best investigation for a nulligravid patient presenting with irregular bleeding is a urine pregnancy test.

The first investigation to be done in a case of abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) in the reproductive age group (15-49 years) is urine β-hCG estimation. This is done to rule out pregnancy.

A urine pregnancy test detects pregnancy by identifying the presence of the hormone human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which is produced by the developing placenta shortly after a fertilized egg implants in the uterine wall. The test contains antibodies that specifically bind to hCG, typically providing a visible result when the hormone is detected. hCG levels rise rapidly in early pregnancy, allowing the test to indicate pregnancy as early as one to two weeks after conception. This sensitivity makes urine hCG tests a reliable early indicator of pregnancy.

In the reproductive age group, anovulatory uterine bleeding is encountered less often. Therefore, pregnancy must be excluded. Pregnancy complications such as miscarriage, ectopic pregnancies, and molar pregnancies may present with AUB, hence, these need to be ruled out by urine β-hCG levels. This is done for all women in the reproductive age group.

The urine pregnancy test is non-invasive, cost-effective, and provides rapid results, making it an essential initial step in the diagnostic workup.

Other investigations to be done for AUB are:

* Pap smear: to rule out cervical cancer and preinvasive lesions (CIN). Cervical cancer screening should start at age 21. Women aged 21–29 should have a Pap smear every 3 years, while women aged 30-65 should have both HPV and Pap co-test every 5 years.

* Transabdominal ultrasound: to visualise the pelvic organs and lesions such as endometrial hyperplasia, polyps, fibroids, etc.

* Transvaginal ultrasound: to visualise the pelvic organs. It is done after evaluating β-hCG. This is more comfortable for a patient than a transabdominal ultrasound, as it doesn't require a full bladder.  is the first-line investigation in a patient with post-menopausal bleeding. All postmenopausal women with abnormal uterine bleeding should be evaluated for endometrial malignancy since age is a significant risk factor for this.

questions.text: A 28-year-old G2P1 patient at 17 weeks of gestation comes for a routine antenatal visit. Her blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg. A repeat blood pressure after 6 hours measures 148/92 mm Hg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chronic hypertension

In this scenario of hypertension in a patient with a gestational age <20 weeks, the diagnosis is chronic hypertension.

Chronic hypertension is diagnosed when the patient is a known hypertensive (or) BP > 140/90 mmHg before 20 weeks of gestation.

Chronic hypertension with superimposed pre-eclampsia or eclampsia is diagnosed with the following presentation: aggravation of hypertension, new onset of proteinuria after 20 weeks, development of headache, scotoma, epigastric pain, and HELLP syndrome. (Option A)

Gestational hypertension: BP≥ 140/90 mm of hg for the first time in pregnancy after 20 weeks of gestation in a previously normotensive woman without proteinuria. (Option D)

Pre-eclampsia (Option C): Gestational hypertension along with any of the following features:

* Proteinuria

* Thrombocytopenia

* Renal insufficiency

* Liver involvement

* Cerebral symptoms

* Pulmonary edema

* Eclampsia: Pre-eclampsia + seizures and or coma

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman is in labour, and during delivery, the baby's head is delivered, but the shoulders get stuck. The baby's head is at the introitus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Shoulder dystocia

This clinical vignette of a 28-year-old woman in labour with the baby's head at the introitus and the shoulders being stuck is suggestive of shoulder dystocia.

Shoulder dystocia, defined as a head-to-body delivery time >60 seconds, occurs when either the anterior or the posterior (rare) fetal shoulder impacts on the maternal symphysis or the sacral promontory respectively.  A positive turtle sign may be seen which refers to a definite recoil of the head back against the perineum.

Risk factors for the development of shoulder dystocia include maternal diabetes mellitus, obesity, post-dated pregnancy, excessive weight gain during pregnancy, etc.  Wood's corkscrew maneuver is used to deliver the impacted shoulder in this condition.

Woods corkscrew maneuver: Progressive rotation of the posterior shoulder 180 degrees in a corkscrew fashion releases the impacted anterior shoulder.

Other options:

Option A: Face Presentation - In a face presentation, the baby presents with the face as the presenting part instead of the vertex. The baby’s head is typically fully extended, leading to complications during delivery. However, once the head is delivered, the body usually follows without significant issues. The scenario described involves difficulty after the head is delivered, specifically with the shoulders, which is not characteristic of face presentation.

Option B: Occipito-sacral arrest- This refers to the baby being in a persistent occiput posterior position (with the baby facing up towards the mother’s abdomen rather than down). Labor may progress more slowly or stop when the baby’s head fails to rotate and descend properly. However, like with CPD, occipito-sacral arrest typically results in difficulty before the head is delivered, not after. If the head has been delivered but the shoulders are stuck, it indicates a different issue.

Option C: Cephalopelvic disproportion(CPD) - CPD occurs when the baby's head or body is too large to fit through the mother's pelvis. This can lead to labor not progressing or being arrested before the baby’s head is fully delivered. In CPD, labor arrest or failure to descend is seen, and the baby’s head may not pass through the pelvis at all. Since in the scenario described above, the head is already delivered and the shoulders are the issue, CPD is less likely to be the cause.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A nulligravida woman presents to the outpatient department with uterine prolapse. There is no evidence of associated cystocele or rectocele on examination. Which surgical procedure is most appropriate in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Abdominal sling surgery

For a nulligravid woman with uterine prolapse and no cystocele or rectocele, we will perform an abdominal sling surgery.

Abdominal sling operations are designed for women with type II or III degree prolapse and who are desirous of retaining childbearing function and menstrual function.

The descent of one or more of the genital organs below their normal anatomical position is called pelvic organ prolapse (POP). It occurs when the muscles and tissues that support the pelvic organs become weakened or damaged, leading to one or more organs bulging into the vaginal canal.

Clinical types are:

1. Vaginal prolapse

a) Anterior vaginal wall

*

*

* Upper two-thirds – Cystocele

* Lower one-third – Urethrocele

b) Posterior vaginal wall

*

*

* Upper one-third – Enterocele

* Lower two-thirds – Rectocele

2. Uterine descent

Treatment options may include pessary, pelvic floor exercises or surgery depending on the severity of prolapse.

Abdominal sling surgeries: Young women desirous of retaining menstrual and reproductive functions are ideal candidates. These surgeries use tapes as slings to prevent organ descent. These include:

* Abdominal wall cervicopexy (modified by Purandare and Mathre): sling attached to cervix posteriorly near uterosacral ligaments.

* Shirodkar's sling surgery: the sling fixes the cervix to the lumbosacral fascia.

* Khanna's sling surgery: - sling fixed to the anterior superior iliac spine, strengthening the Mackenrodt's ligament.

Other options :

Option A: Le fort's repair - is done in patients who satisfy the following criteria:

* Very elderly menopausal patient with an advanced prolapse

* Do not wish to retain sexual function

* Medically unfit for major surgeries

Option B: Fothergill surgery - Also known as Manchester's operation is suitable for women under 40 years who are desirous of retaining their menstrual and reproductive functions. It involves anterior colporrhaphy with amputation of the cervix. The mackenrodt ligaments are sutured in the front of the cervix and colpoperineorrhaphy is done. It increases the risk of cervical incompetence leading to recurrent abortions and preterm deliveries. Shirodkar's modification of Fothergill's repair avoids cervical amputation, hence subsequent pregnancy complications are avoided.

Option D: Shirodkar sling surgery - the sling fixes the cervix to the lumbosacral fascia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents to the outpatient department with spotting following IUD insertion. No pain or fever was reported. What is the next best step in this scenario? IUD - Intrauterine device
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Give iron tablets and observe

In this scenario of a woman presenting to the outpatient department with spotting following an IUD insertion with no complaints of fever or pain, the next best step would be to give iron tablets and observe.

Spotting is a common side effect after IUD insertion and often resolves on its own without intervention. Since no other complications are present in this patient, there is no need to remove the IUD or prescribe any medications. The patient just needs to be under observation.

It's important to monitor the woman for any signs of heavy bleeding, severe pain, fever, or other unusual symptoms that could indicate complications such as infection or perforation.

Complications following an IUD insertion :

* Pain accounts for 15–40% of IUD removal, hence, it is the most common cause of IUD removal.

* However, bleeding is the most common side-effect reported after IUD insertion.

* Disturbances in menstrual bleeding are very commonly reported in the form of increased blood loss or irregular bleeding.

* Studies have shown that larger non-medicated IUDs cause greater incidences of bleeding than copper devices and hormone-releasing devices.

* Other side effects and complications are pain, pelvic infection, uterine perforation, and ectopic pregnancies.

Contraindications for IUD usage include:

Absolute contraindications
Relative contraindications

• Suspected pregnancy
• PID
• Vaginal bleeding of unknown etiology
• Carcinoma cervix/uterus/adnexa /other pelvic tumours

• Anemia
• Menorrhagia
• History of PID since the last pregnancy
• Purulent cervical discharge
• Distortions of the uterine cavity due to fibroids
• Uterine malformations
• An unmotivated person

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with a non-recurring indication of a previous lower segment cesarean section now presents with an occipitoposterior fetal position. What is the best next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Attempt a normal vaginal delivery

In a woman with a non-recurring indication of lower segment cesarean sections who now presents with an occipitoposterior fetal position, the next step of management would be to try to attempt a vaginal delivery.

Occipitoposterior position is an abnormal position of the vertex and can undergo normal labor in favorable circumstances.

In a majority of cases, the occiput rotates through 3/8th of the circle, and the baby is born in the occipitoanterior position. Hence, when the diagnosis of occipitoposterior position is made, labor is allowed to proceed normally when there are good uterine contractions and a favorable pelvis.

The occipitoposterior (OP) position of the fetus is when the occiput is situated posteriorly over the sacroiliac joint or directly over the sacrum. It is the most common fetal malposition. It is an abnormal position seen in the vertex presentation, not an abnormal presentation.

* Occipitoposterior position is commonly seen in the android pelvis/deflexed head.

* The engaging diameter of this position is sub-occipitofrontal.

* The most common type in the occipitoposterior position is right OP.

* A persistent occipitoposterior position results from a failure of internal rotation prior to birth.

Examination findings of OP position:

* Inspection: The abdomen appears flattened below the umbilicus (infra-umbilical flattening).

* Pelvic grips:

* The head is not engaged.

* The sinciput (cephalic prominence) is not prominently felt.

* Auscultation: Fetal heart sounds are heard maximally over the flanks. However, in direct OP position, they are heard in the midline.

Features of occipitoposterior position include infra-umbilical flattening and fetal heart sounds localized to the flank. The fetal parts are more prominently felt near the midline.

Other options

Option A: Indications of cesarean section in occipitoposterior position:

* Arrest of labor

* Inadequate uterine contraction

* Fetal distress

* Other obstetrical indications

Option C: External cephalic version (ECV) is done in non-cephalic presentations like breech and transverse lie, to bring the favorable cephalic pole to the lower pole of the uterus. The ideal time to do the external cephalic version is 37 weeks.

Option D: Vaccum-assisted delivery is used to help with prolonged labor, fetal distress, maternal exhaustion, or ineffective pushing and fetal malposition.

Pearl PF1974: Fetal Skull Dimensions

Note:

Longest diameter of fetal skull: Mentovertical 14 cm > Submentovertical / occipitofrontal - 11.5cm

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young woman came to the clinic requesting a post-coital pill. Which of the following would you prescribe?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Levonorgestrel

Levonorgestrel can be prescribed to a young woman requesting a post-coital pill.

Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg single dose within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse, can be used for emergency contraception. Alternatively, it can also be administered in two doses of 0.75 mg. The first dose is taken within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse, and the 2nd dose is taken 12 hours apart. The tablets can be offered up to 120 hours but the efficacy decreases with the longer coital-drug interval.

Advantages of LNG tablets:

* It has no estrogen and its associated side effects.

* It can be offered to hypertensive, cardiac and diabetic women.

* It can be offered to a lactating woman.

* It can be given as late as 120 hours after unprotected intercourse (but efficacy decreases).

* Single-dose therapy is an advantage.

Combined oral pills consisting of both estrogen and progesterone act on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis to inhibit the release of GnRH (and thus subsequently LH and FSH) and thus inhibit ovulation.

Emergency contraception refers to backup methods for contraceptive emergencies that women can use within the first few days after unprotected intercourse to prevent an unwanted pregnancy. Administration of postcoital contraceptive agents that interfere with postovulatory events that can lead to pregnancy.

The various emergency contraceptive methods, along with their mechanism of action have been described below:

* Ethinyl estradiol 50 μg + norgestrel 0.25 mg is administered as two tablets within 72 hours of coitus, followed by the 2 tablets after 12 hours. The hormone may delay ovulation if taken soon after intercourse.

* Ulipristal is given as a 30 mg tablet and should be taken within 5 days. It is a synthetic progesterone hormone receptor modulator. The drug attaches to the progesterone receptor, delays ovulation, and suppresses endometrium, thereby preventing implantation.

* IUCD (intrauterine contraceptive device) prevents the implantation of a fertilized ovum. It does so by acting as a foreign body within the uterine cavity. This leads to increased contractility, tubal peristalsis, and leukocytic infiltration in the endometrium.

* Centchroman is administered as two tablets of 60 mg, taken twice over a duration of 24 hours and within 24 hours of intercourse. It acts by preventing the implantation of the blastocyst in the endometrium.

Pearl PF1657: Hormonal contraceptives

Oral pills:

* Mala D - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Banana and lemon signs are seen in which of the following fetal anomalies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neural tube defect

Banana and lemon signs are seen in case of neural tube defects.

Signs of neural tube defect on targeted sonography:

* Small biparietal diameter

* Ventriculomegaly

* Frontal bone scalloping or the lemon sign

* Anterior curvature of the cerebellum with effacement of the cisterna magna known as banana sign.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Early cord clamping is done in which of the following cases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Non-vigorous baby

Early cord clamping will be done in the case of a non-vigorous baby.

Early cord clamping is performed within the first 60 seconds after birth, typically when the newborn requires urgent resuscitation. A non-vigorous baby, characterised by poor respiratory effort, low muscle tone, or a heart rate below 100 beats per minute, necessitates immediate intervention, making ECC necessary.

Indications for early cord clamping include:

* Babies needing immediate resuscitation: In emergencies, rapid neonatal stabilisation takes precedence, and delayed cord clamping (DCC) may not be possible.

* Fetal hydrops

* Maternal or placental complications: Situations such as placental abruption or postpartum hemorrhage may require early clamping to ensure maternal safety.

Delayed cord clamping involves waiting for a minimum of 1-3 minutes after birth before clamping the umbilical cord. It is recommended for both term and preterm babies as part of standard delivery care.

Benefits of DCC:

* In term infants, delayed umbilical cord clamping leads to higher haemoglobin levels at birth, improved iron stores during the first few months of life, and a reduced risk of neonatal anaemia.

* In preterm infants, delayed cord clamping is associated with lower rates of intraventricular haemorrhage and necrotising enterocolitis, as well as a decreased need for blood transfusions.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the contraceptive device given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lippe

The contraceptive device shown in the image above is a Lippe's loop.

Lippes Loop is a 1st generation IUD that comes in four sizes – A, B, C and D. It is an S-shaped device, usually made of polyethene. The tail, which is usually made of fine nylon, projects into the vagina after insertion. The larger loops, used in multiparous women, have higher rates of removal due to side effects but have greater anti-fertility effects.

The Lippes Loop has a minimal amount of barium sulphate in it to allow for X-ray observation.

IUD - Intrauterine devices are contraceptive devices inserted into the uterine cavity. The different generations of IUDs include:

* First-generation IUDs : Inert or non-medicated devices like Lippes loop.

* Second-generation IUDs : Medicated with metallic elements like copper eg: Cu-T-220 C, Nova T, Multi-load Cu-250, Multi-load Cu-375.

* Third-generation IUDs: Hormone-containing IUDs like Progestasert, Mirena (LNG-20).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which of the following scenarios can outlet forceps be used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Head at perineum

Outlet forceps can be used when the head of the fetus is at the perineum.

Outlet forceps/ Wrigley's forceps is light, about a third of the weight of ordinary long-curved forceps. The instrument is short which is due to a reduction in the length of the shanks and handles. It has a marked cephalic curve with a slight pelvic curve.

Criteria for outlet forceps delivery:

* Scalp at introitus without separating labia

* Skull at the pelvic floor

* Sagittal suture in anterioposterior diameter, right or left occiput anterior, occiput anterior

* Fetal head on the perineum

* Rotation less than 45 degrees

The image below shows Wrigley's forceps/outlet forceps:

Pearl PF1918: Obstetrics forceps

Commonly used forceps:

1) Simpson forceps

* The most commonly used types of forceps in outlet delivery.

* Has elongated cephalic curve.

* These are used when there is substantial molding of the fetal head.

2) Elliot forceps

* Has an adjustable pin for regulating the lateral pressure on the handles.

* They are used most often when there is minimal molding.

* More suitable for outlet delivery.

3) Kielland forceps

* Has small pelvic curve and a sliding lock.

* Suitable for head with little molding.

* The most common forceps used for rotational delivery.

* Helps correct asynclitism.

4) Piper forceps

* Distinct perineal curve.

* Allows for application to the after-coming head in breech delivery.

5) Tucker-McLane forceps

* Suitable for fetal head with little molding.

* Used in rotational delivery.

6) Barton forceps and traction handle

* Used in rotational delivery.

* Most importantly used for delivery of occipitotransverse positions in a platypelloid pelvis.

* It is an obsolete procedure.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Puerperal pyrexia can be diagnosed if a woman has :
options: A temperature of >100.4 F, 12 hours after delivery
A temperature of >100.4 F, 6 hours after delivery
A temperature of >100.4 F, 24 hours after delivery
A temperature of >100.4 F, 3 hours after delivery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A temperature of >100.4 F, 24 hours after delivery

Puerperal fever is defined as a temperature of >100.4 °F (38 °C or higher) on 2 separate occasions at 24 hours apart (excluding the first 24 hours) within the first 10 days following delivery.

In the first 24 hours, a slight rise in temperature is not uncommon. Hence the first 24 hours are excluded to define puerperal pyrexia.

Note: Generally, fever in an adult is defined as an oral temperature of >37.5 °C.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Until when can a postpartum intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) be inserted?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 48 hours

Postpartum IUCD should be inserted within 48 hours.

An intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) prevents the implantation of a fertilized ovum. It does so by acting as a foreign body within the uterine cavity. This leads to increased contractility, tubal peristalsis, and promotes leukocytic infiltration in the endometrium so that the fertilized egg is unable to implant.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the ideal number of recommended ANC visits during pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 12-14

The recommended ideal number of antenatal visits is 12–14 during pregnancy.

The generally recommended ideal number of antenatal visits is 12-14:

* Monthly visits up to 28 weeks

* Two weekly visits between 28-36 weeks

* Weekly visits from 36 weeks onward.

* This means a total of 12–14 visits.

According to the 2016 WHO ANC model, the antenatal visits should be a minimum of 8 visits:

* Contact 1: Upto 12 weeks

* Contact 2: 20 weeks

* Contact 3: 26 weeks

* Contact 4: 30 weeks

* Contact 5: 34 weeks

* Contact 6: 36 weeks

* Contact 7: 38 weeks

* Contact 8: 40 weeks

* Return for delivery at 41 weeks if not delivered yet.

The older Focused Antenatal Care (FANC) guidelines by the WHO recommended a minimum of 4 visits, as given below

* 1st visit: Within 12 weeks, preferably as soon as pregnancy is suspected, for the registration of pregnancy and 1st antenatal check-up.

* 2nd visit: Between 24-26 weeks

* 3rd visit: At 32 weeks

* 4th visit: Between 36-38 weeks

* Return for delivery at 41 weeks if not delivered yet.

A booked case is one that has at least 3 antenatal visits, with two visits in the third trimester.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the location of the Bartholin cyst?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior ⅓ of the vulva

Bartholin cysts are located in the posterior 1/3 of the vulva.

The Bartholin glands are known as the greater vestibular glands in females. These glands are located in the posterior part of the vestibule and open through a duct into the vaginal orifice at approximately 5 and 7 o’clock positions. They secrete mucus during sexual arousal for lubrication. They are the homologs of the male bulbourethral or Cowper glands.

Bartholin cyst is caused by obstruction of the duct due to infection, trauma, mucus changes, and congenitally narrowed ducts. If the cyst gets infected, it leads to the formation of a Bartholin abscess. Escherichia coli is the most common causative agent, however, other gram-positive and gram-negative organisms can also cause the same.

Clinical features:

* If the size is big, it might cause abdominal and vaginal discomfort with dyspareunia.

* A vulval cleft of 'S' shape is usually noted on inspection.

* It is fluctuant swelling and transillumination can be positive as the fluid collected is generally clear.

Treatment:

* Analgesics for pain

* Antibiotic for combating infections.

* Specific treatment:

* Drainage under anesthesia: Generally conservative method, chances of re-infection and formation of granulation tissue can happen.

* Marsupialization Complete excision of sac and cyst along with drainage of the substance. The edges are also clearly approximated. This is the ideal management.  The advantages of marsupialization over other methods include:

* Simple procedure

* Can be done even under local anesthesia.

* Shorter hospital stay (24 hours).

* The postoperative complication is almost nil.

* Gland function (moisture) remains intact.

* Incision and drainage with word catheter placement: A deflated word catheter is used to tuck the vagina here and prevent it from damage that can happen during movement of the perineum and thus avert re-infection and granulation tissue formation. Alternatively, a 14 F foley catheter can also be used.

* Bartholinectomy: This is a very invasive surgery and carries a greater morbidity profile. This is also associated with loss of lubricant function.

Notes:

In any woman above the age of forty with recurrent Bartholin cyst, a suspicion of Bartholin gland cancer should arise and the cyst wall should be sent for biopsy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most common cause of thrombocytopenia in pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Gestational thrombocytopenia

The most common cause of thrombocytopenia in pregnancy is gestational thrombocytopenia. This may be due to hemodilution and increased platelet consumption in pregnancy.

Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state. Hematological changes in pregnancy include:

* All clotting factors are increased (except factor 11,13) and fibrinogen levels are also increased.

* Clotting time and bleeding time are unaffected.

* The viscosity of blood doesn’t increase since plasma volume increases more in comparison to red cell volume, it merely decreases whole blood viscosity.

* Anticoagulants Protein C, Protein S and antithrombin decrease during pregnancy.

* Fibrinolytic activity remains depressed till about 15 minutes after pregnancy
