| Risk factor | Reason

| ----------- | ------

| Gestational diabetes | Fetal macrosomia

| Macrosomia | Large shoulders

| Obesity | Difficult delivery

| Post-term pregnancy | Larger fetus

Mnemonic for Shoulder Dystocia

| Letter | Step

| ------ | ----

| H | Help

| E | Episiotomy

| L | Legs (McRoberts)
Hyperflex maternal hips toward abdomen
Effect:

• Straightens lumbosacral angle
• Widens pelvic outlet

| P | Pressure (suprapubic)

| E | Enter maneuvers (Rubin/Woods)
Pressure applied to posterior aspect of anterior shoulder.
Effect:

• Rotates shoulders
• Reduces shoulder diameter.

| R | Remove posterior arm

| R | Roll patient (Gaskin) Mother placed in all-fours (hands and knees) position.
Effect:

• Changes pelvic dimensions
• Helps release shoulder.

Zavanelli Maneuver (Last Resort)- Fetal head pushed back into vagina

Then: Emergency cesarean section performed.

Used only when all other maneuvers fail.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: According to the WHO Intrapartum Care Guidelines, 2018, the active phase of labour starts from what dilatation of cervix?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5 cm

According to the WHO Intrapartum Care Guidelines (2018), the active phase of the first stage of labour begins at 5 cm cervical dilatation, rather than the previously accepted 3–4 cm. This change was made because cervical dilatation before 5 cm is highly variable among women, and diagnosing active labour too early may lead to unnecessary obstetric interventions.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  3 cm: This was part of older definitions and is no longer accepted by WHO.
• B. 4 cm: Previously used in some labour management protocols but replaced by the 5 cm threshold in the WHO 2018 guidelines.
• D. 6 cm: Although some organizations (e.g., ACOG/SMFM) consider 6 cm as the onset of active labour, WHO 2018 uses 5 cm.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: According to WHO Intrapartum Care Guideline, which of the following are correct about birthing position? I. For a woman without epidural analgesia, adoption of birthing position is individual woman’s choice. II. For a woman without epidural analgesia, upright birthing position may be adopted. III. For a woman with epidural analgesia, lithotomy and supine position only are recommended. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I and II only

The WHO Intrapartum Care Guidelines (2018) recommend a woman-centered approach to childbirth. Women should be encouraged to choose the birthing position that is most comfortable for them, provided there are no obstetric contraindications. Routine use of the supine or lithotomy position is not recommended, as upright positions are associated with several maternal benefits. The following statements are correct:

• I. For a woman without epidural analgesia, adoption of birthing position is individual woman’s choice: WHO recommends that women should be encouraged to adopt the position of their choice during labor and birth.
• II. For a woman without epidural analgesia, upright birthing position may be adopted: Upright positions (standing, sitting, squatting, kneeling, or all-fours) are recommended because they may:

• Shorten the second stage of labor
• Reduce assisted vaginal delivery
• Improve maternal comfort
• Utilize gravity to aid fetal descent

Why is III incorrect?

• III. For a woman with epidural analgesia, lithotomy and supine position only are recommended: WHO does not recommend restricting women with epidural analgesia to lithotomy or supine positions only. Position should be individualized, and women should be encouraged to adopt any position that is safe and comfortable.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: According to WHO Intrapartum Care Guidelines, which one of the following is correct about duration of first stage labour?
options: Duration of latent phase of primigravida has not been established
Duration of active stage of multigravida should not exceed 6 hours
Duration of active stage of primigravida should not exceed 8 hours
Duration of active stage of primigravida should not exceed 18 hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Duration of latent phase of primigravida has not been established

The WHO Intrapartum Care Guidelines (2018) emphasize that normal labor progression varies considerably among women, and rigid time limits should not be used to diagnose abnormal labor, particularly during the latent phase. Therefore, the normal duration of the latent phase has not been clearly established, especially in primigravidae. Women should be managed based on maternal and fetal well-being, rather than arbitrary time limits.

Why not the other options?

• B. Duration of active stage of multigravida should not exceed 6 hours: WHO does not specify a maximum permissible duration for the active phase.
• C. Duration of active stage of primigravida should not exceed 8 hours: WHO recognizes wide variation in labor progress and does not recommend a strict upper limit.
• D. Duration of active stage of primigravida should not exceed 18 hours: No such recommendation exists in the WHO 2018 guidelines.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: All of the following are core components of Active Management of the Third Stage of Labor (AMTSL) except:
options: Administration of 10 IU oxytocin IM/IV immediately after birth of the baby
Controlled cord traction (CCT) during uterine contraction with counter-traction
Assessment of uterine tone and uterine massage if the uterus is found to be atonic after placental delivery
Immediate clamping and cutting of the umbilical cord within 30 seconds of birth
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Immediate clamping and cutting of the umbilical cord within 30 seconds of birth

Active Management of the Third Stage of Labor (AMTSL) is performed to prevent postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) by promoting uterine contraction and placental separation.

Core Components of AMTSL

• Administration of a uterotonic: Oxytocin 10 IU IM/IV within 1 minute after birth (preferred uterotonic).
• Controlled cord traction (CCT): Performed by a trained provider with uterine counter-traction after signs of placental separation.
• Assessment of uterine tone: Following placental delivery, the uterus is palpated and uterine massage is performed if the uterus is atonic.

Why Option D is Incorrect

• Immediate cord clamping (<30 seconds) is no longer recommended in routine deliveries.
• Delayed cord clamping (at least 1 minute, or until cord pulsations cease if feasible) is recommended for both term and preterm newborns as it:

• Improves neonatal iron stores.
• Reduces infant anemia.
• Does not increase the risk of postpartum hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Antepartum haemorrhage is defined as bleeding from genital tract:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. After 28 weeks of pregnancy

Antepartum hemorrhage (APH) is defined as bleeding from or into the genital tract after 28 weeks of gestation and before the birth of the baby (classical definition used in many MBBS/NEET PG texts).

Why not the other options?

• A. Before 20 weeks of pregnancy: This is considered abortion/early pregnancy bleeding.
• B. Before 24 weeks of pregnancy: Not the definition of APH.
• D. After 34 weeks of pregnancy: Too late; APH begins after 28 weeks.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: As per the WHO recommendations, all of the following may be given for active management of third stage of labour, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inj. Carboprost

Active management of the third stage of labour aims primarily to prevent postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) by promoting effective uterine contraction.

• A. Inj. Oxytocin: Correct. The uterotonic of choice for routine prophylaxis of PPH.
• B. Inj. Methergine: Correct. A potent uterotonic that can be used for prevention of PPH, but should be avoided in women with hypertension/pre-eclampsia.
• C. Inj. Misoprostol: Correct. A prostaglandin analogue that can be used for PPH prevention, particularly when oxytocin is unavailable.
• D. Inj. Carboprost: Incorrect. Carboprost is primarily used for treatment of established atonic PPH, rather than routine prophylaxis during AMTSL.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Collapse in a patient during labor/ delivery followed by bleeding and DIC in the absence of coexisting conditions is most likely due to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Amniotic fluid embolism

Amniotic Fluid Embolism is a rare but catastrophic complication of pregnancy.

It occurs when amniotic fluid, fetal cells, or debris enter the maternal bloodstream, triggering a massive inflammatory and coagulation response.

Amniotic fluid enters maternal circulation

↓

Pulmonary vasospasm

↓

Acute respiratory failure

↓

Massive inflammatory reaction

↓

DIC and severe bleeding

AFE = sudden collapse + respiratory distress + DIC during labor.

Management is supportive and emergency-based.

Steps include:

• Immediate resuscitation
• Oxygen and ventilation
• Blood products for DIC
• Intensive care support

| Feature | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Sudden cardiovascular collapse | Hypotension, shock

| Respiratory distress | Acute hypoxia

| DIC | Severe bleeding

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding the cause for onset of labour: Statement 1: Alteration in estrogen-progesterone ratio results in prostaglandin synthesis and onset of labour. Statement 2: Decreased fetal production of dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S) and cortisol inhibits the conversion of fetal pregnenolone to progesterone. Which one of the following is correct with respect to the above statements?
options: Both Statements 1 and 2 are true and Statement 2 is the correct explanation of Statement 1
Both Statements 1 and 2 are true but Statement 2 is not the correct explanation of Statement 1
Statement 1 is true but Statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false but Statement 2 is true
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Statement 1 is true but Statement 2 is false

Statement 1: True

• Near term, there is a functional increase in the estrogen-to-progesterone ratio.
• Estrogen promotes:

• Prostaglandin synthesis
• Increased oxytocin receptors
• Formation of gap junctions between myometrial cells
• Increased myometrial contractility

• These changes contribute to the onset of labour.

Statement 2: False

• It is increased fetal cortisol and DHEA-S, not decreased production, that contributes to the hormonal changes preceding labour.
• Fetal adrenal DHEA-S is converted by the placenta into estrogens, while fetal cortisol promotes placental estrogen production.
• Thus, decreased fetal DHEA-S and cortisol would not explain the onset of labour.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding the WHO Labour Care Guide for labour monitoring: 1. Active phase starts from 5 cm of cervical dilatation. 2. There is fixed rate for dilatation for every hour of labour in active phase. 3. There are no alert or action lines on the partograph. 4. There is a separate section for intensive monitoring for second stage of labour as well. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3 and 4

1. Active phase starts from 5 cm — Correct

• The WHO Labour Care Guide considers 5 cm cervical dilatation as the beginning of the active phase of labour.

2. Fixed rate of cervical dilatation for every hour — Incorrect

• The Labour Care Guide rejects the traditional 1 cm/hour rule. Cervical dilatation does not follow a fixed hourly rate, and slower progress alone should not automatically trigger intervention.

3. No traditional alert/action lines — Correct

• Unlike the conventional partograph, the Labour Care Guide does not use fixed alert and action lines. Instead, it uses evidence-based time thresholds/alert values for cervical dilatation and second-stage progress.

4. Separate monitoring of the second stage — Correct

• The Labour Care Guide extends monitoring through the second stage of labour, including a specific threshold for prolonged second stage and assessment of pushing, descent, fetal status, and maternal condition.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following surgical methods: 1. Haultain’s method 2. Gilliam’s operation 3. Spinelli’s operation 4. Cutting anterior cervical ring Which of the methods given above may be used for surgical management of chronic uterine inversion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Chronic uterine inversion is managed surgically when manual reduction is unsuccessful or the inversion has become longstanding.

The relevant surgical methods include:

1. Haultain’s method — Correct

• An abdominal approach.
• Involves making a posterior incision in the constricting cervical ring to facilitate repositioning of the uterus.

2. Gilliam’s operation — Incorrect

• Gilliam operation is a uterine suspension procedure and is not a standard method for correcting chronic uterine inversion.

3. Spinelli’s operation — Correct

• A vaginal approach to correction of chronic uterine inversion.
• Involves incision of the constricting ring to facilitate repositioning.

4. Cutting the anterior cervical ring — Correct

• This is associated with the Spinelli procedure, where the anterior cervical ring is incised.

Therefore:

Haultain + Spinelli + cutting anterior cervical ring → C.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Following the delivery of a macrosomic baby, the shoulders become impacted. What is the first maneuver that should be attempted to release the shoulders?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. McRoberts maneuver

McRoberts Maneuver involves hyperflexion of the maternal hips toward the abdomen.

Mechanism

Hyperflex maternal hips

↓

Straightens lumbosacral angle

↓

Increases pelvic outlet diameter

↓

Releases impacted shoulder

| Risk factor | Reason

| ----------- | ------

| Fetal macrosomia | Large shoulders

| Diabetes in pregnancy | Macrosomia

| Prolonged second stage | Difficult delivery

| Operative vaginal delivery | Instrumental delivery

Stepwise Management of Shoulder Dystocia

1. McRoberts maneuver

2. Suprapubic pressure

3. Rubin maneuver

4. Woods corkscrew maneuver

5. Gaskin maneuver

6. Zavanelli maneuver

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In the mechanism of normal labour, the engaging transverse diameter is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Biparietal diameter (9.5 cm)

Engagement is said to occur when the biparietal diameter (BPD) of the fetal head (the largest transverse diameter) passes through the pelvic inlet.

Why not the other options?

• A. Suboccipitobregmatic diameter (9.5 cm): This is the engaging anteroposterior diameter of a well-flexed fetal head, not the transverse diameter.
• C. Bimastoid diameter (7.5 cm): Smaller transverse diameter; not the engaging diameter.
• D. Suboccipitofrontal diameter (10 cm): An anteroposterior diameter seen with incomplete flexion.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Mrs. A, who is 9 months pregnant, presents to the labour room with complaints of severe pain in abdomen and vaginal bleeding for 30 minutes. She is 2nd gravida (producing second child) and delivered her first child 2 years back by caesarean delivery. On examination, she has scar tenderness, vaginal bleeding and haematuria. On CTG, she has an abnormal FHR tracing. What is her likely clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Scar rupture/dehiscence during labour

• The patient has multiple classical features of uterine rupture:

• Previous cesarean section (most important risk factor)
• Severe abdominal pain
• Scar tenderness
• Vaginal bleeding
• Hematuria (suggesting bladder involvement)
• Abnormal fetal heart rate (FHR) on CTG, often the earliest sign of uterine rupture

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Urinary tract infection: UTI may cause dysuria and hematuria but does not cause scar tenderness, vaginal bleeding, severe abdominal pain, or fetal distress.
• C. Labour pain: Normal labour pain is associated with regular uterine contractions and does not produce scar tenderness, hematuria, or abnormal CTG.
• D. Rupture of urinary bladder: Although hematuria may occur, bladder rupture alone does not explain vaginal bleeding, scar tenderness, and fetal distress. Bladder injury is often secondary to uterine rupture.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Onset of labour is initiated by which of the following? 1. Uterine distension 2. Increased CRH and ACTH from foetal hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis 3. Increased level of progesterone immediately before labour 4. Increased synthesis of myometrial receptors for oxytocin due to effect of oestrogen Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

The onset of labour is a complex process involving maternal, fetal, placental, and hormonal factors.

• 1. Uterine distension ✓

• Uterine stretching due to fetal growth contributes to labour by increasing myometrial excitability and promoting the expression of contraction-associated proteins.

• 2. Increased CRH and ACTH from fetal hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis ✓

• Activation of the fetal HPA axis increases fetal ACTH and cortisol production. The placenta also secretes increasing amounts of CRH, which stimulates prostaglandin production and enhances uterine contractions.

• 3. Increased level of progesterone immediately before labour ✗

• There is no significant rise in progesterone before labour in humans. Instead, there is a functional progesterone withdrawal, with estrogen effects becoming dominant.

• 4. Increased synthesis of myometrial receptors for oxytocin due to effect of oestrogen ✓

• Rising estrogen levels increase oxytocin receptor expression and gap junction formation in the myometrium, making the uterus highly responsive to oxytocin during labour.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The diameter of engagement of foetal skull in marked deflexion is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Occipitofrontal diameter

The diameter of the fetal skull that engages depends on the degree of flexion of the fetal head. As flexion decreases (deflexion increases), progressively larger diameters present at the pelvic inlet, making labour more difficult.

In marked deflexion (military attitude), the presenting anteroposterior diameter is the occipitofrontal diameter, which measures approximately 11.5 cm.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Suboccipitofrontal diameter: Seen with incomplete flexion, measuring approximately 10 cm.
• C. Mentovertical diameter: Seen in brow presentation (partial extension) and is the largest AP diameter (13.5 cm), making vaginal delivery usually impossible.
• D. Suboccipitobregmatic diameter: Seen in complete flexion (vertex presentation) and is the smallest engaging diameter (9.5 cm), allowing the easiest vaginal delivery.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The incidence of scar rupture in a previous lower segment cesarean section (LSCS) is approximately: (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1-2%

Women with a previous lower segment cesarean section (LSCS) have a small risk of uterine scar rupture during labor, especially during trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC).

The approximate incidence of scar rupture after prior LSCS is 1–2%. Risk is lowest with Previous low transverse uterine incision.

Risk factors increasing scar rupture:

• Classical cesarean scar
• Induction with prostaglandins
• Multiple previous cesarean sections
• Obstructed labor
• Excessive oxytocin use

Clinical features of uterine rupture:

• Sudden abdominal pain
• Fetal distress
• Vaginal bleeding
• Loss of fetal station
• Maternal shock

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The Matthews Duncan process has been described for:
options: Marginal separation of placenta in normal labour
Central separation of placenta in normal labour
Controlled contraction in active management of third stage of labour
Reposition of acute inversion of uterus following vaginal delivery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Marginal separation of placenta in normal labour

Matthews Duncan mechanism describes the marginal separation of the placenta during the third stage of labor. Separation begins at the placental margin, causing blood to escape early, resulting in visible vaginal bleeding before placental expulsion. The placenta is delivered sideways with the maternal surface appearing first.

Why not the other options?

• B. Central separation of placenta in normal labour: This describes the Schultze mechanism, not Matthews Duncan.
• C. Controlled contraction in active management of third stage of labour: Active management involves controlled cord traction, uterotonics, and uterine massage, not the Matthews Duncan process.
• D. Reposition of acute inversion of uterus following vaginal delivery: Acute uterine inversion is managed by Johnson’s maneuver, not Matthews Duncan.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The maximum dose of PGF2 alpha in postpartum hemorrhage is? (NEET PG 2019)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 mg

Prostaglandin F2 alpha (PGF2α), also known as carboprost, is used for the treatment of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) due to uterine atony. The therapeutic regimen and maximum dosage are crucial for effective management and patient safety.

• Dose and Administration: The approved dose for treating uterine atony with PGF2α is 0.25 mg administered intramuscularly (IM).
• Maximum Dose: The maximum cumulative dose is 2 mg. This is achieved by administering a total of 8 doses of 0.25 mg each.
• Dosing Interval: These doses can be repeated at intervals of 15 to 90 minutes, depending on the clinical response and the patient's condition.

Contraindications

• Bronchial Asthma: PGF2α can cause bronchoconstriction, which makes it contraindicated in patients with bronchial asthma.
• Suspected Amniotic Fluid Embolism: Due to its potential to cause pulmonary airway and vascular constriction, it is also contraindicated in cases of suspected amniotic fluid embolism.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The most common cause of maternal mortality in India is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Obstetric haemorrhage

Obstetric haemorrhage is the leading direct cause of maternal mortality in India.

• Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) – most common
• Antepartum hemorrhage (placenta previa, abruptio placentae)
• Ruptured ectopic pregnancy

Rapid blood loss can lead to hypovolemic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and death if not managed promptly.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Obstructed labour: An important cause of maternal morbidity and mortality but less common than hemorrhage.
• C. Unsafe abortion: A significant preventable cause but contributes fewer maternal deaths than hemorrhage.
• D. Toxaemia of pregnancy (Hypertensive disorders): Includes preeclampsia and eclampsia; the second leading direct cause of maternal mortality in India.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The normal rate of dilatation of the cervix in a primigravida in the active phase of labor is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1 cm/hour

During the active phase of labor, the expected rate of cervical dilatation in a primigravida is approximately 1 cm/hour. This is an important parameter used to assess the progress of labor.

Why not the other options?

• A. 0.25 cm/hour: Too slow; suggests abnormal labor.
• B. 0.5 cm/hour: Below the expected rate for normal active labor.
• C. 0.75 cm/hour: Less than the accepted normal rate.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is restitution in the events of labour?
options: Head rotated by 1/8th of a circle
Head rotating due to untwisting of the neck
The shoulder undergoing rotation by 1/8th of circle
The movement by which the head is born
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Head rotating due to untwisting of the neck

During a normal vaginal delivery, the fetal head undergoes a series of movements called the cardinal movements of labour.

The sequence is:

1. Engagement
2. Descent
3. Flexion
4. Internal rotation
5. Extension
6. Restitution
7. External rotation

| Feature | Restitution | External Rotation

| ------- | ----------- | -----------------

| Cause | Untwisting of neck | Shoulder rotation

| Degree of rotation | \~45° (1/8 circle) | Further rotation

| Occurs when | Immediately after head delivery | After restitution

| Purpose | Align head with shoulders | Align shoulders with pelvis

A) Head rotated by 1/8th of a circle

Although restitution involves 1/8th rotation, the definition emphasizes that it occurs due to untwisting of the neck.

C) Shoulder undergoing rotation by 1/8th circle

This describes internal rotation of the shoulders, not restitution.

D) Movement by which the head is born

This refers to extension, not restitution.

“ReSTitution = Straightening of the neck.”

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the optimal peak negative pressure to be achieved during vacuum-assisted delivery? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 0.8 kg/cm²

Vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery requires gradual creation of negative pressure between the vacuum cup and the fetal scalp to ensure secure attachment and minimize cup detachment.

The optimal peak negative pressure is 0.8 kg/cm2 (approximately 600 mm Hg)

Purpose of negative pressure:

• Creates a firm chignon on the fetal scalp
• Allows effective traction during contractions
• Reduces cup slippage (“pop-offs”)

Important principles of vacuum delivery:

• Pressure should be increased gradually
• Traction should be synchronized with uterine contractions
• Excessive pressure increases risk of scalp injury and cephalohematoma

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Where will be the level of the uterus on the second-day post-delivery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Two finger breadths below umbilicus

Uterus is at the umbilicus after delivery and involutes \~1 fingerbreadth per day. Therefore, on day 2 it lies 2 fingerbreadths below.

| Postpartum Day | Fundal Position

| -------------- | ---------------

| Immediately after delivery | At the level of the umbilicus

| Day 1 | 1 finger breadth below umbilicus

| Day 2 | 2 finger breadths below umbilicus

| Each subsequent day | Descends \~1 cm/day

| 10–14 days | Not palpable abdominally

The controversy:

• The dispute is entirely about the day-counting convention, not the physiology. Both camps agree on \~1 FB/day. They disagree on when the clock starts.

The two models

| | Model A | Model B

| --- | ------- | -------

| Reckoning | Day of delivery = Day 0, fundus at umbilicus | Fundus static for first 24 h; descent begins on day 2

| Day 1 | 1 FB below | at umbilicus

| Day 2 | 2 FB below ✅ | 1 FB below

| Day 7 | 7 FB below | 6 FB below

| Day 12–14 | \~12–13 FB below = pelvic organ ✅ | 13 FB below — overshoots

Why Model A wins on internal consistency

• Immediately postpartum, fundus ≈ 13.5 cm above symphysis (DC Dutta) — i.e., roughly umbilical level.
• Involution rate = 1.25 cm (½ inch)/day ≈ 1 fingerbreadth/day.
• Umbilicus → symphysis ≈ 12–13 cm.
• 13.5 cm ÷ 1.25 cm/day ≈ day 11–12 → uterus reaches the pelvis.
• This lands squarely on the universally-agreed endpoint: "pelvic organ by the end of the 2nd week."

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which drug is contraindicated in a patient with atonic PPH with a history of hypertension?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ergotamine

Postpartum Hemorrhage is defined as:

• ≥500 mL blood loss after vaginal delivery
• ≥1000 mL after cesarean section

The most common cause (\~70–80%) is uterine atony.

Uterotonic Drugs Used in Atonic PPH

| Drug | Class | Important Note

| ---- | ----- | --------------

| Oxytocin | First-line uterotonic | Safe in hypertension

| Misoprostol | PGE₁ analogue | Safe

| Carboprost (PGF₂α) | Prostaglandin | Avoid in asthma

| Ergometrine / Ergotamine | Ergot alkaloid | ❌ Avoid in hypertension

Why Ergotamine is Contraindicated-

Ergot derivatives (ergometrine/ergotamine):

• Cause powerful uterine contraction
• Also cause systemic vasoconstriction

This can lead to:

• Severe hypertension
• Stroke
• Coronary vasospasm

Therefore they are contraindicated in hypertensive patients and preeclampsia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which is not an indication of instrumental vaginal delivery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CPD

Instrumental vaginal delivery uses tools like forceps or vacuum (ventouse) to assist delivery of the fetus during the second stage of labour.

Common instruments:

• Forceps Delivery
• Vacuum Extraction

These procedures are used when expedited vaginal delivery is required but vaginal delivery is still possible.

Forceps and Vacuum Instruments-

Both instruments help:

• Apply traction to fetal head
• Shorten the second stage of labour
• Assist delivery when maternal effort is inadequate.

Indications for Instrumental Delivery

| Indication | Reason

| ---------- | ------

| Fetal distress | Rapid delivery needed

| Maternal exhaustion | Mother unable to push effectively

| Prolonged second stage of labour | Failure of descent

| Maternal medical illness | Avoid excessive pushing

In CPD:

• The fetal head is too large for the maternal pelvis
• Vaginal delivery is mechanically impossible

Using forceps or vacuum would not overcome this obstruction and may cause:

• Uterine rupture
• Fetal injury
• Maternal trauma

Therefore the correct management is: Cesarean section

Before using forceps or vacuum, certain conditions must be met.

| Requirement | Explanation

| ----------- | -----------

| Fully dilated cervix | 10 cm dilation

| Ruptured membranes | Required

| Head engaged | Station ≥ 0

| Known fetal position | For correct instrument placement

| No CPD | Pelvis adequate

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are contraindications to External Cephalic Version (ECV) in breech? I. Pregnancy less than 36 weeks II. Multiple pregnancy III. Previous cesarean delivery IV. Rhesus isoimmunization Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. II, III and IV

External Cephalic Version (ECV) is a procedure in which the fetus is manually rotated from breech or transverse lie to cephalic presentation by external manipulation through the maternal abdomen. It is usually attempted at 36–37 weeks of gestation in uncomplicated singleton breech pregnancies to reduce the need for cesarean delivery. The following are contraindications to ECV:

• II. Multiple pregnancy: Correct. ECV is contraindicated in multiple gestations because of the increased risk of fetal complications and technical difficulty.
• III. Previous cesarean delivery: Correct (as per this examination). Previous cesarean section is considered a contraindication in many traditional examination settings, although current guidelines consider one previous lower-segment cesarean section a relative rather than absolute contraindication.
• IV. Rhesus isoimmunization: Correct. Rh isoimmunization is considered a contraindication because fetal manipulation may increase fetomaternal hemorrhage and worsen alloimmunization.

Why is I incorrect?

• I. Pregnancy less than 36 weeks: Incorrect. ECV is not recommended before 36 weeks because many breech fetuses will spontaneously turn to cephalic presentation. Therefore, gestation less than 36 weeks is not considered a contraindication but rather not the appropriate timing for routine ECV.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are contraindications to external cephalic version in antenatal management of breech presentation? 1. Antepartum haemorrhage 2. Multiple pregnancy 3. Reactive non-stress test 4. Severe oligohydramnios Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

External cephalic version (ECV) is performed at 36–37 weeks to convert a breech fetus into a cephalic presentation and reduce the need for cesarean delivery. It should not be attempted when there are contraindications to vaginal delivery or conditions that make the procedure unsafe.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Antepartum haemorrhage: Correct. Contraindication due to the risk of worsening bleeding (e.g., placenta previa or placental abruption).
• 2. Multiple pregnancy: Correct. ECV is generally contraindicated in multiple gestation (except selected situations after delivery of the first twin).
• 3. Reactive non-stress test: Incorrect. A reactive NST is a prerequisite for performing ECV, indicating fetal well-being.
• 4. Severe oligohydramnios: Correct. Reduced liquor decreases the chance of success and increases the risk of fetal injury.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are indications of vaginal examinations during labour? 1. To stretch the vagina intermittently 2. At the onset of labour 3. To monitor progress of labour 4. Following rupture of membranes Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Vaginal examination (VE) during labor is performed only when clinically indicated. It should be performed under strict aseptic precautions and kept to the minimum necessary to reduce the risk of infection.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. To stretch the vagina intermittently: Incorrect. Vaginal examination is not performed to stretch the vagina.
• 2. At the onset of labour: Correct. To confirm labor, assess cervical dilatation, effacement, presentation, position, station, and membrane status.
• 3. To monitor progress of labour: Correct. Usually repeated every 4 hours in normal labor or earlier if indicated.
• 4. Following rupture of membranes: Correct. Performed if clinically indicated to assess labor progress or exclude complications (e.g., cord prolapse), although unnecessary repeated examinations should be avoided after membrane rupture.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are positive indicators for breech vaginal delivery?
options: Fetal weight less than 1.5 kg, flexed fetal head, frank breech
Frank breech, fetal weight more than 3.5 kg, gestational age more than 34 weeks
Frank breech, fetal weight 1.5 kg to 3.5 kg, gestational age more than 34 weeks
Flexed breech, fetal weight 1.5 kg to 3.5 kg, gestational age more than 34 weeks
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Frank breech, fetal weight 1.5 kg to 3.5 kg, gestational age more than 34 weeks

Vaginal breech delivery may be considered when the fetus has favorable characteristics:

• Frank breech presentation → hips flexed and knees extended; generally favorable.
• Estimated fetal weight 1.5–3.5 kg → avoids the increased risks associated with very small or macrosomic fetuses.
• Gestational age >34 weeks → better developed fetus with a lower risk of complications related to prematurity.

Why not the other options?

• A. Fetal weight less than 1.5 kg, flexed fetal head, frank breech → Very low birth weight/prematurity is unfavorable for planned vaginal breech delivery.
• B. Frank breech, fetal weight more than 3.5 kg, gestational age more than 34 weeks → Suspected macrosomia increases the risk of difficult delivery and head entrapment.
• D. Flexed breech, fetal weight 1.5 kg to 3.5 kg, gestational age more than 34 weeks → Not the classic favorable breech type; frank breech is preferred.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are the prerequisites of outlet forceps delivery? 1. Bladder should be empty. 2. Membranes should be intact. 3. Cervix should be fully dilated. 4. Fetal skull has reached level of pelvic floor. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Outlet forceps delivery is performed when the fetal head has descended to the pelvic floor and delivery can be safely expedited. Certain prerequisites must be fulfilled before applying forceps.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Bladder should be empty. Correct. Reduces the risk of bladder injury and facilitates descent.
• 2. Membranes should be intact. Incorrect. Membranes must be ruptured before forceps application.
• 3. Cervix should be fully dilated. Correct. An incompletely dilated cervix is an absolute contraindication.
• 4. Fetal skull has reached the level of the pelvic floor. Correct. This is a defining feature of outlet forceps.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following factors are associated with cord prolapse during labour? I. Malpresentations II. Contracted pelvis III. Stabilizing induction IV. Prematurity Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II, III and IV

Umbilical cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency in which the umbilical cord descends below or alongside the presenting part after rupture of membranes, leading to cord compression, acute fetal hypoxia, and fetal death if not managed promptly.

Cord prolapse is more likely whenever the presenting part is not well applied to the cervix, allowing the cord to slip past it. All the listed factors increase the risk of cord prolapse:

• I. Malpresentations: Breech, transverse lie, compound presentation, and unstable lie prevent proper engagement of the presenting part, increasing the risk of cord prolapse.
• II. Contracted pelvis: A contracted pelvis prevents engagement of the fetal head, leaving space for the umbilical cord to prolapse.
• III. Stabilizing induction: During stabilizing induction (artificial rupture of membranes after external cephalic version or procedures to stabilize the presenting part), if the presenting part is not well engaged, the risk of cord prolapse increases.
• IV. Prematurity: Premature fetuses have smaller presenting parts, which are less likely to engage, predisposing to cord prolapse.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following factors favour posterior position of the vertex? I. Anthropoid pelvis II. Low inclination pelvis III. Attachment of placenta on the anterior wall IV. Primary brachycephaly Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, III and IV

The occipitoposterior (OP) position is the most common malposition of the fetal head during labor. In this position, the occiput is directed towards the maternal sacrum rather than the symphysis pubis. The following factors favor a posterior position of the vertex:

• I. Anthropoid pelvis: The anthropoid pelvis has a long anteroposterior diameter, which predisposes the fetal occiput to enter the pelvis in the occipitoposterior position.
• III. Attachment of placenta on the anterior wall: An anterior placenta occupies the anterior uterine wall, encouraging the fetal back to lie posteriorly and thereby increasing the likelihood of an occipitoposterior position.
• IV. Primary brachycephaly: A brachycephalic fetal head has a broad biparietal diameter and is associated with persistence of the occipitoposterior position.

Why is II incorrect?

• II. Low inclination pelvis: A high pelvic inclination, not low inclination, favors persistence of the occipitoposterior position.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following features are correct regarding onset of true labour? 1. Regular uterine contractions 2. Progressive cervical dilatation and effacement 3. Presence of show 4. Labour and delivery are synonymous Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

• 1. Regular uterine contractions ✓

• True labour is marked by regular, rhythmic contractions that increase in frequency, duration, and intensity.

• 2. Progressive cervical dilatation and effacement ✓

• The defining feature of true labour is progressive cervical effacement and dilatation resulting from effective uterine contractions.

• 3. Presence of show ✓

• Show is the passage of blood-stained mucus due to expulsion of the cervical mucus plug as the cervix begins to dilate. It is a common sign of the onset of labour.

• 4. Labour and delivery are synonymous ✗

• Labour is the physiological process leading to birth, whereas delivery is the expulsion of the fetus and placenta. They are related but not synonymous.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to TOLAC? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prior classical hysterotomy

Trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC) is contraindicated in women with a prior classical cesarean section because the vertical incision in the upper uterine segment carries a high risk of uterine rupture during labor.

Types of uterine incisions:

• Classical hysterotomy: Vertical upper-segment incision → absolute contraindication to TOLAC
• Kerr hysterotomy: Low transverse incision → safest and commonly eligible for VBAC
• Kronig hysterotomy: Low vertical incision → relative risk depends on extent

Why classical incision is dangerous:

• Upper uterine segment contracts strongly during labor
• Scar has poor tensile strength
• Increased risk of catastrophic uterine rupture, fetal distress, and maternal hemorrhage

Therefore, prior classical hysterotomy is an absolute contraindication to TOLAC/VBAC.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a contraindication for the induction of labor? (NEET PG 2019)
options: History of lower transverse cesarean section in last two pregnancies
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Heart disease

Induction of labor is contraindicated when vaginal delivery would pose significant maternal or fetal risk.

Contraindications include:

• Pelvic tumors obstructing the birth canal
• Active genital herpes infection
• Multiple previous cesarean sections with risk of uterine rupture
• Placenta previa
• Transverse fetal lie

Heart disease is not an absolute contraindication to induction of labor. In many cardiac conditions:

• Vaginal delivery is preferred over cesarean section
• Carefully monitored induction may be performed to reduce maternal stress and hemodynamic instability

A prior low transverse cesarean scar may allow trial of labor in selected cases, but repeated scars increase rupture risk.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct order of the cardinal movements of labor? (NEET PG 2015)
options: Descent, engagement, internal rotation, flexion, external rotation
Descent, engagement, internal rotation, flexion, external rotation+
Engagement, Descent, Flexion, Internal, Rotation, Extension, External Rotation, Expulsion
Engagement, descent, external rotation, internal rotation, flexion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Engagement, Descent, Flexion, Internal, Rotation, Extension, External Rotation, Expulsion

The cardinal movements of normal labor describe the positional changes the fetus undergoes while passing through the birth canal.

Correct sequence:

1. Engagement
2. Descent
3. Flexion
4. Internal rotation
5. Extension
6. External rotation (restitution)
7. Expulsion

Key concepts:

• Engagement: Biparietal diameter passes pelvic inlet
• Flexion: Chin moves toward chest, presenting smaller diameter
• Internal rotation: Occiput rotates anteriorly toward symphysis pubis
• Extension: Head extends while passing under pubic symphysis
• External rotation: Head realigns with shoulders after delivery
• Expulsion: Delivery of shoulders and body

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding shoulder dystocia? I. It can be predicted during early labour. II. Anencephaly is a risk factor. III. Turtle neck sign is present. IV. Episiotomy should always be given. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. II, III and IV

Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency in which, after delivery of the fetal head, the anterior shoulder becomes impacted behind the maternal pubic symphysis (or less commonly, the posterior shoulder behind the sacral promontory), preventing delivery of the shoulders. It requires prompt recognition and a series of obstetric maneuvers to prevent fetal hypoxia and birth trauma. The following statements are true:

• II. Anencephaly is a risk factor: Anencephalic fetuses have a small head with relatively normal-sized shoulders, increasing the risk of shoulder dystocia.
• III. Turtle neck sign is present: The turtle sign is the classic clinical sign of shoulder dystocia, in which the delivered fetal head retracts against the maternal perineum after expulsion because the shoulders are impacted.
• IV. Episiotomy should always be given: Although an episiotomy does not relieve the bony obstruction, it is commonly performed to provide additional space for internal maneuvers (e.g., Rubin or Woods screw maneuver). Hence, many traditional examination questions consider it appropriate.

Why is I incorrect?

• I. It can be predicted during early labour: Shoulder dystocia is largely unpredictable. Although several risk factors are recognized, most cases occur without warning, and many women with risk factors deliver without shoulder dystocia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following uterotonic agents is contraindicated in the management of postpartum hemorrhage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dinoprostone

Postpartum hemorrhage is defined as:

•

≥500 mL blood loss after vaginal delivery

•

≥1000 mL after cesarean section

The most common cause is uterine atony, where the uterus fails to contract after delivery.

Uterotonic drugs are given to stimulate uterine contraction and reduce bleeding.

Uterotonic Drugs Used in PPH

| Drug  | Mechanism  | Use in PPH

| ----- | ---------- | -----------

| Oxytocin  | Stimulates uterine smooth muscle contraction
Class- Hormone  | ✔ First-line drug

| Misoprostol (PGE1)  | Causes uterine contraction
PGE1 analogue  | ✔ Used in PPH

| 15-methyl PGF₂α (Carboprost)  | Strong uterine contraction
PGF₂α analogue  | ✔ Used in refractory PPH

| Dinoprostone (PGE2)  | Cervical ripening  | ❌ Not used in PPH

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which one of the following correctly defines puerperal pyrexia?
options: Rise in maternal oral temperature of 100.4°F or more 24 hours apart within first 7 days of delivery
Rise in maternal oral temperature of 101.4°F or more 24 hours apart within first 10 days of delivery
Rise in maternal oral temperature of 100.4°F or more 24 hours apart within first 10 days of delivery
Rise in maternal oral temperature of 101.4°F or more 24 hours apart within first 7 days of delivery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rise in maternal oral temperature of 100.4°F or more 24 hours apart within first 10 days of delivery

Puerperal pyrexia (also called puerperal fever) is defined as:

A temperature of ≥100.4°F (38°C) occurring on any two of the first 10 days postpartum (excluding the first 24 hours), taken orally, by standard technique, at least 4 times a day.

Key points of the definition:

| Component | Detail

| --------- | ------

| Temperature threshold | ≥100.4°F (38°C)

| Duration criterion | Present on any 2 of the first 10 postpartum days

| Exclusion | First 24 hours postpartum are excluded (a mild transient rise in temperature on day 1 is common and often physiological — due to dehydration, breast engorgement, or normal postpartum catabolic changes — and is not counted)

| Measurement | Oral temperature, checked at least 4 times daily using a standardized technique

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which step is not included in active management of third stage of labor (AMTSL)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bimanual compression

AMTSL consists of three main steps-

| Step | Description

| ---- | -----------

| Administration of uterotonics | Oxytocin given immediately after delivery

| Controlled cord traction | Brandt–Andrews maneuver

| Delayed cord clamping | Usually 1–3 minutes after birth

The third stage of labour is the period from delivery of the baby to expulsion of the placenta. Proper management is crucial to prevent Postpartum Hemorrhage, the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide.

1. Administration of Oxytocic

Oxytocin (10 IU IM/IV) is given immediately after delivery.

• Stimulates uterine contraction
• Compresses uterine blood vessels
• Prevents postpartum hemorrhage

Oxytocin is the drug of choice for prevention of PPH.

2. Brandt–Andrews Maneuver (Controlled Cord Traction)

This technique helps deliver the placenta safely.

Steps:

• One hand supports the uterus suprapubically
• The other hand applies traction on the umbilical cord

This prevents uterine inversion.

3. Delayed Cord Clamping

Delayed cord clamping means clamping the cord after 1–3 minutes.

Benefits:

• Improves neonatal hemoglobin levels
• Increases iron stores
• Reduces anemia in infancy

Bimanual Compression

Bimanual compression is not part of routine AMTSL.

It is used in management of postpartum hemorrhage, particularly when:

• Uterine atony occurs
• Bleeding persists despite uterotonics

Thus it is a treatment step, not a preventive step.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: While performing a repair following delivery, what is the appropriate sequence of layer closure in a mediolateral episiotomy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mucosa → muscle → skin

Mediolateral Episiotomy is a surgical incision made in the perineum to enlarge the vaginal opening during delivery. It is commonly used when:

• Instrumental delivery is anticipated
• Shoulder dystocia
• Fetal distress requiring rapid delivery

A mediolateral episiotomy cuts through:

| Layer | Structure

| ----- | ---------

| Vaginal mucosa | Inner lining

| Perineal muscles | Bulbospongiosus, transverse perineal muscles

| Skin | Perineal skin

| Type | Description

| ---- | -----------

| Mediolateral episiotomy | Most commonly performed

| Median (midline) episiotomy | Easier repair but higher risk of anal tear

| Lateral episiotomy | Rarely used

A mediolateral episiotomy cuts through:

| Layer | Structure

| ----- | ---------

| Vaginal mucosa | Inner lining

| Perineal muscles | Bulbospongiosus, transverse perineal muscles

| Skin | Perineal skin

Typical steps:

1. Continuous suturing of vaginal mucosa
2. Interrupted sutures for perineal muscles
3. Subcuticular sutures for skin

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: You are applying a vacuum to deliver a baby in a patient with prolonged 2nd stage. The point at which the vacuum is applied is:
options: 3 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle
6 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle
4 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle
Midway between the anterior and posterior fontanelle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 3 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle

Vacuum Extraction is used in the second stage of labor to assist delivery.

Common indications:

| Indication | Explanation

| ---------- | -----------

| Prolonged second stage | Maternal exhaustion

| Fetal distress | Need for rapid delivery

| Medical conditions | Avoid maternal pushing

The optimal cup placement is the flexion point, located 3 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle. This ensures maximum flexion of the fetal head and presents the smallest diameter through the pelvis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: You are examining a multigravida in the second stage of labor for the past two hours. On examination, contractions are adequate, the cervix is fully dilated with the head at station 0 with molding 2+ and caput 2+. The sagittal suture is in the right occipito-transverse position. The fetal heart rate is 140 beats/minute. Which of the following is carried out for the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lower segment cesarean section

Several concerning findings are present:

| Finding | Significance

| ------- | ------------

| Station 0 | Head not descended sufficiently

| Occipito-transverse position | Malposition

| Molding 2+ | Suggests cephalopelvic disproportion

| Caput 2+ | Obstructed labor signs

| Prolonged second stage | Failure of descent

These features suggest possible obstructed labor / cephalopelvic disproportion, making operative vaginal delivery unsafe.

In normal labor:

Occipito-transverse

↓

Internal rotation

↓

Occipito-anterior

↓

Vaginal delivery

But when descent fails and molding/caput appear, obstruction is suspected.

| Feature | Meaning

| ------- | -------

| Molding | Overlapping of fetal skull bones

| Caput succedaneum | Scalp swelling due to pressure

Grades of molding:

| Grade | Description

| ----- | -----------

| 1+ | Sutures touching

| 2+ | Sutures overlapping but reducible

| 3+ | Fixed overlap (severe CPD)

Indications for Cesarean in Second Stage

| Indication | Example

| ---------- | -------

| Cephalopelvic disproportion | Large fetus

| Failed descent | Station not progressing

| Malposition | Persistent OP or OT

| Severe molding/caput | Obstruction

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 21-year-old primigravida presents to the antenatal OPD. Her school going nephew who lives in the same house has contracted varicella. A blood sample is taken for Antibodies against varicella. The report is negative. What does this signify? (NEET PG 2021)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Susceptible to chicken pox

A negative antibody test for varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in a pregnant woman indicates absence of immunity and susceptibility to primary varicella (chickenpox) infection.

Important implications in pregnancy:

• Primary maternal varicella can cause severe maternal pneumonia
• Fetal risks include congenital varicella syndrome, especially in early pregnancy
• Neonatal varicella may occur if maternal infection develops near delivery

Management after exposure in a susceptible pregnant woman:

• Varicella-zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) should be considered
• Close monitoring for symptoms is required

Important distinction:

• Primary infection → chickenpox
• Reactivation of latent virus → herpes zoster (shingles)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22y type 1 DM is in the post operative ward following a cesarean done for failed induction (for preeclampsia with severe features). She complains of drowsiness and altered sensorium. She is on maintenance MgSO4 infusion and on IV infusion of insulin. On examination, her PR is 70/ min. BP is 140/ 98 mmHg. RR is 10/min. Auscultation of lungs reveals bilateral normal air entry. Abdominal examination reveals a firm uterus with normal tenderness. Pfannenstiel scar is intact and there is no significant vaginal bleeding. B/l patellar reflexes are absent. A urine dipstick for protein and sugar is negative and a capillary glucose sample is 270 mg%. The suspected diagnosis is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Magnesium sulphate toxicity

Magnesium sulfate is widely used in Preeclampsia to prevent seizures.

However, excess magnesium can depress the neuromuscular and respiratory systems. Classic signs of MgSO₄ toxicity include:

| Sign  | Explanation

| ----- | ------------

| Loss of deep tendon reflexes  | Earliest sign

| Respiratory depression  | RR < 12/min

| Drowsiness / confusion  | CNS depression

| Cardiac arrest  | Severe toxicity

Loss of patellar reflex is the earliest sign of magnesium toxicity.

| Serum Mg level  | Effect

| --------------- | -------

| 4–7 mEq/L  | Therapeutic level

| >10 mEq/L  | Loss of reflexes

| >12 mEq/L  | Respiratory depression

| >15 mEq/L  | Cardiac arrest

Treatment is immediate administration of: Calcium Gluconate

Dose: 10 ml of 10% calcium gluconate IV slowly

Other steps:

•

Stop MgSO₄ infusion

•

Support respiration

•

Monitor urine output

To prevent toxicity, monitor:

| Parameter  | Safe level

| ---------- | -----------

| Respiratory rate  | >12/min

| Urine output  | >25–30 ml/hr

| Patellar reflex  | Present

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 23-year-old woman with eclampsia is on a maintenance dose of MgSO₄. When will you stop MgSO₄?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Urine output 60 ml in 4 hr

Magnesium Sulfate in Eclampsia

MgSO₄ Regimen

| Step | Dose

| ---- | ----

| Loading dose (Pritchard) | 14 g total

| Maintenance dose | 5 g IM every 4 hours

| Duration | 24 hrs after delivery or last seizure

Magnesium Sulfate is used to:

• Prevent seizures
• Control convulsions in eclampsia

Pritchard Regimen Monitoring

Patients on MgSO₄ must be monitored using three key parameters before each maintenance dose.

| Parameter | Safe Limit

| --------- | ----------

| Respiratory rate | >12/min

| Patellar reflex | Present

| Urine output | >100 ml in 4 hours

If any of these are abnormal, MgSO₄ must be withheld.

Magnesium is excreted by the kidneys.

Reduced urine output

↓

Magnesium accumulates in blood

↓

Magnesium toxicity

↓

Respiratory depression

If urine output falls below safe levels, MgSO₄ should be stopped.

Magnesium Toxicity Signs

| Serum Mg Level | Clinical Sign

| -------------- | -------------

| Loss of knee jerk | First sign

| Respiratory depression | Severe toxicity

| Cardiac arrest | Very high levels

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old primigravida comes to ANC clinic at 8 months amenorrhoea. Her BP is found to be 160/100 mm Hg. Lab findings reveal thrombocytopenia, increased SGOT/SGPT and LDH. What is her diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HELLP syndrome

HELLP syndrome is a severe variant of preeclampsia characterized by Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelet count. It is an obstetric emergency associated with significant maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality and usually occurs in the third trimester or early postpartum period.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Obstetric cholestasis: Presents with intense pruritus, elevated bile acids, and mild transaminase elevation, without thrombocytopenia or hemolysis.
• B. Hepatitis B: Causes elevated liver enzymes but is not associated with hypertension and thrombocytopenia characteristic of HELLP syndrome.
• D. Eclampsia: Eclampsia is defined as preeclampsia with generalized tonic-clonic seizures. This patient has no history of seizures.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old G2P1 at 8 weeks diagnosed to have hyperthyroidism. What is the drug of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Propylthiouracil

PTU is preferred in the 1st trimester because methimazole/carbimazole are linked to congenital anomalies (e.g., aplasia cutis). Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated. After 1st trimester, therapy is usually switched to methimazole. This switch reduces PTU-related hepatotoxicity later in pregnancy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman at 28 weeks of gestation presents for a routine checkup and is asymptomatic. On examination, a soft early to mid-systolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border, with no associated thrills, heaves, or other abnormal findings. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Physiological murmur of pregnancy

During pregnancy, increased plasma volume and cardiac output produce a physiological flow murmur, typically heard as a soft (grade I–II), early-to-mid systolic ejection murmur along the left sternal border or pulmonary area. It is not associated with thrills, heaves, or other abnormal cardiac findings and requires no treatment.

Why not the other options?

• A. Mitral stenosis: Characterized by a mid-diastolic murmur with an opening snap, not a systolic murmur.
• B. Aortic stenosis: Produces a harsh ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, often with a thrill.
• D. Ventricular septal defect: Causes a loud pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border, frequently associated with a palpable thrill.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old pregnant woman in her first trimester is found to have asymptomatic bacteriuria on routine screening, with urine culture growing E. coli. What is the most common complication associated with this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Preterm labor

A 29-year-old pregnant woman in the first trimester has asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) detected on routine screening with E. coli growth on urine culture.

Correct Answer:C) Preterm labor

Physiological changes during pregnancy predispose to infection:

• Progesterone → ureteric dilation
• Urinary stasis
• Reduced bladder tone
• Vesicoureteral reflux

These changes allow bacteria to ascend from bladder to kidneys.

Asymptomatic bacteriuria is defined as:

• ≥10⁵ colony-forming units/mL bacteria in urine culture
• No urinary symptoms

It occurs in 2–10% of pregnancies.

Most common organism: Escherichia coli (\~80–90%)

Untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria may lead to:

| Complication | Mechanism

| ------------ | ---------

| Acute pyelonephritis | Ascending infection

| Preterm labor | Infection-induced inflammatory mediators

| Low birth weight | Placental inflammation

| Preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) | Infection weakening membranes

Treatment

Common safe antibiotics in pregnancy:

| Drug | Example

| ---- | -------

| Beta-lactams | Amoxicillin

| Cephalosporins | Cephalexin

| Nitrofurantoin | Used except near term

| Fosfomycin | Single dose therapy

Drugs avoided in pregnancy:

• Fluoroquinolones
• Tetracyclines

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old G2P1 is diagnosed to have DVT at 30 weeks. The drug of choice is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. LMWH (Low Molecular Weight Heparin)

LMWH is the treatment of choice for DVT in pregnancy because it does not cross the placenta and has a predictable safety profile. Warfarin and DOACs (e.g., apixaban) cross the placenta and are unsafe. Fondaparinux is reserved for HIT.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient presents at 35 weeks with chronic HTN and 3+ proteinuria. Her BP is 170/100 mmHg and she complains of headache and blurring of vision. What is the best management option?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Labetalol + MgSO4 + Expedite delivery

Severe Preeclampsia

Preeclampsia is diagnosed when:

• BP ≥140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks
• Proteinuria ≥300 mg/day

Severe preeclampsia includes:

| Severe feature | Explanation

| -------------- | -----------

| BP ≥160/110 mmHg | Severe hypertension

| Headache | Cerebral edema

| Visual disturbances | Retinal vasospasm

| Epigastric pain | Hepatic involvement

This patient has severe hypertension + neurological symptoms.

Management of Severe Preeclampsia

Management includes three immediate steps.

| Step | Purpose

| ---- | -------

| Labetalol | Control severe hypertension

| Magnesium sulfate | Prevent seizures

| Expedite delivery | Definitive treatment

Magnesium Sulfate is used to:

• Prevent eclamptic seizures
• Stabilize neuronal membranes

Monitoring during therapy:

| Parameter | Requirement

| --------- | -----------

| Respiratory rate | >12/min

| Urine output | >25–30 mL/hr

| Patellar reflex | Present

Antidote for toxicity: Calcium gluconate

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant lady with 34 weeks of amenorrhea has the following findings: LDH - 700 IU/L, platelets - 75,000/ mm3, serum bilirubin - 1.5 mg/dL, SGOT - 200 U/L, SGPT - 150 U/L, and BP - 140/96 mm Hg. Her coagulation profile and renal function tests are normal. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HELLP syndrome

HELLP is an obstetric emergency usually occurring in the third trimester.

H → Hemolysis

EL → Elevated Liver enzymes

LP → Low Platelet count

| Parameter  | Finding

| ---------- | --------

| Hemolysis  | ↑ LDH (>600 IU/L), ↑ bilirubin

| Liver enzymes  | AST/ALT elevated

| Platelets  | <100,000/mm³

In this case:

•

LDH 700 → Hemolysis

•

Platelets 75,000 → Thrombocytopenia

•

AST/ALT elevated → Liver injury

Abnormal placentation

↓

Endothelial injury

↓

Microvascular thrombosis

↓

Hemolysis + liver damage

↓

Platelet consumption

Patients may present with:

•

Right upper quadrant pain

•

Nausea / vomiting

•

Hypertension

•

Proteinuria

Complications include:

•

DIC

•

Placental abruption

•

Liver rupture

Treatment involves:

•

Stabilization

•

Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis

•

Control blood pressure

•

Definitive treatment: delivery of fetus

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant lady with a history of recurrent abortions is now diagnosed to have antiphospholipid syndrome. What would be the best mode of treatment for her? (NEET PG 2019)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aspirin + heparin

Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is an autoimmune thrombophilic disorder associated with:

• Recurrent abortions
• Recurrent fetal loss
• Preeclampsia
• Placental insufficiency
• Arterial and venous thrombosis

Best treatment during pregnancy: Low-dose aspirin + heparin (usually low-molecular-weight heparin)

Mechanism:

• Aspirin reduces platelet aggregation
• Heparin prevents placental thrombosis and improves placental circulation

Why other options are incorrect:

• Aspirin alone is less effective
• Steroids are not routinely recommended unless another autoimmune condition (eg, active SLE) is present due to maternal and fetal side effects

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant patient at 36 weeks of gestation has a blood pressure of 150/105 mmHg and a +3 albuminuria. The presence of which of the following are signs of impending eclampsia? 1. Headache 2. Persistent pedal edema 3. Blurring of vision 4. Epigastric pain
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3, 4

Preeclampsia

A pregnancy-specific hypertensive disorder occurring after 20 weeks of gestation characterized by:

• Hypertension ≥140/90 mmHg
• Proteinuria ≥300 mg/day

Severe disease can progress to eclampsia, which involves generalized tonic-clonic seizures.

Severe hypertension with heavy proteinuria at 36 weeks raises concern for imminent eclampsia. The true warning signs are headache, visual disturbances, and epigastric/RUQ pain from hepatic capsular stretch.

1. Headache

Mechanism

•

Cerebral vasospasm

•

Increased intracranial pressure

•

Cerebral edema

Clinical clue

•

Severe frontal or occipital headache

•

Often persistent and not relieved by analgesics

2. Blurring of Vision

Cause

•

Retinal arteriolar spasm

•

Cerebral edema affecting visual cortex

Symptoms

•

Blurring of vision

•

Scotomas

•

Photophobia

•

Temporary blindness

3. Epigastric Pain

Mechanism

•

Liver ischemia

•

Stretching of Glisson’s capsule

•

Associated with HELLP syndrome

Clinical significance

•

Indicates severe preeclampsia

•

Often precedes seizures or hepatic rupture

Although pedal edema is nonspecific in pregnancy, persistent or sudden worsening edema is a worsening sign but not included in criteria for impending eclampsia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman at 36 weeks of gestation with a prosthetic valve replacement for mitral stenosis is on warfarin therapy 4mg/day. What is the appropriate next step in management? (NEET PG 2021)
options: Stop warfarin, start LMWH and aspirin.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stop warfarin and start LMWH.

Pregnant women with mechanical prosthetic heart valves require continuous anticoagulation because they are at high risk of valve thrombosis. Warfarin considerations in pregnancy:

• Warfarin crosses the placenta
• Near term, it increases the risk of:

• Fetal intracranial hemorrhage
• Maternal bleeding during labor

Therefore, at around 36 weeks gestation:

• Warfarin should be stopped
• Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) or unfractionated heparin should be started

Why LMWH is preferred:

• Does not cross the placenta
• Safer for the fetus
• Provides effective anticoagulation

Important point:

• Aspirin is not routinely added unless specifically indicated
• Continuing warfarin near delivery is unsafe

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman with no other comorbid conditions develops preeclampsia. She enquires about the cause. The doctor explains that it is due to the failure of the invasion of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Spiral artery by extravillous trophoblasts

During early pregnancy, Extravillous Trophoblast invade the maternal uterine vessels. Their role is to remodel the maternal spiral arteries.

Extravillous trophoblast invasion

↓

Remodeling of spiral arteries

↓

Low resistance vessels

↓

Adequate placental blood flow

This transformation converts narrow spiral arteries into wide, low-resistance vessels.

In Preeclampsia:

Failure of trophoblastic invasion

↓

Spiral arteries remain narrow

↓

High resistance blood flow

↓

Placental ischemia

↓

Release of antiangiogenic factors

↓

Maternal endothelial dysfunction

↓

Hypertension and proteinuria

Preeclampsia results from abnormal spiral artery remodeling.

Spiral arteries supply the placenta and intervillous space. Their remodeling is crucial for:

• Adequate uteroplacental circulation
• Proper fetal growth

Failure leads to:

• Preeclampsia
• Fetal growth restriction

A) Spiral artery by villous trophoblasts

Villous Trophoblast

• Responsible for maternal–fetal exchange, not arterial invasion.

B) Radial artery by cytotrophoblasts

• Radial arteries are not the primary vessels remodeled in pregnancy.

D) Arcuate artery by extravillous trophoblasts

• Arcuate arteries lie deeper in the uterus and do not undergo trophoblastic remodeling.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida presents at 37 weeks. She is a known case of heart disease with a prosthetic valve on warfarin. What is the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Switch to LMWH

Warfarin is unsafe near term due to fetal and maternal bleeding risk. Near delivery, warfarin increases the risk of:

| Complication | Reason

| ------------ | ------

| Fetal intracranial hemorrhage | Placental transfer

| Maternal bleeding during labor | Anticoagulation

| Neonatal bleeding | Long half-life

Therefore, warfarin is replaced by heparin near term.

At 36–37 weeks, anticoagulation is switched to LMWH, which does not cross the placenta. Delivery is planned only after stopping LMWH for an appropriate interval.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida presents to you in her early pregnancy with anemia. She is 7 weeks pregnant as seen on ultrasound. Her haemoglobin level is 9 g/dL. When should the iron supplements be started for her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 8 to 10 weeks

A primigravida at 7 weeks' gestation has Hb = 9 g/dL, which is anemia, not merely a candidate for routine prophylaxis.

• Therapeutic iron should be started as soon as iron deficiency anemia is diagnosed, even in the first trimester.
• In practice, oral iron is usually initiated around 8–10 weeks, once pregnancy is confirmed and the diagnosis is established, rather than waiting until the second trimester.
• Delaying treatment until after 14 weeks is appropriate for routine prophylactic iron in some older recommendations, not for treatment of established anemia.

Why the other options are incorrect

• A. 10–12 weeks – Delays treatment unnecessarily in a woman already diagnosed with anemia.
• C. After 14 weeks – Too late for therapeutic treatment; this timing is associated with some prophylactic regimens, not treatment.
• D. After 20 weeks – Clearly inappropriate and risks worsening maternal and fetal outcomes.

A useful distinction is:

| Situation | When to start iron

| --------- | ------------------

| Routine prophylaxis (non-anemic pregnant woman) | Varies by guideline (often 14–16 weeks in older recommendations; earlier in some national programs)

| Iron deficiency anemia diagnosed in pregnancy | Start treatment immediately/as soon as diagnosed (in MCQs, this is often represented as 8–10 weeks if the woman presents at 7 weeks)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman post-emergency LSCS for preeclampsia with fetal distress. Which is the best drug for thromboprophylaxis postpartum?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. LMWH

Pregnancy and postpartum are hypercoagulable states due to physiological changes that prepare the body to prevent bleeding.

Risk factors present in this case:

| Risk Factor | Reason

| ----------- | ------

| Cesarean section | Surgical trauma

| Preeclampsia | Endothelial injury

| Postpartum state | Hypercoagulability

This increases risk of Deep Vein Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolism.

Low Molecular Weight Heparin- Inhibits Factor Xa

Examples:

• Enoxaparin
• Dalteparin

| Advantage | Reason

| --------- | ------

| Safe in breastfeeding | Minimal secretion in milk

| Predictable pharmacokinetics | Less monitoring

| Lower bleeding risk | Compared with UFH

| Once daily dosing | Convenient

Duration of Postpartum Thromboprophylaxis

| Risk level | Duration

| ---------- | --------

| Moderate risk | 7–10 days

| High risk | Up to 6 weeks

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with diabetes on insulin therapy plans to conceive and presents for preconception counseling. Her HbA1c is 8.5%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Conceive, increase insulin dose and then start folic acid
Increase insulin dose, reduce HbA1C levels and then conceive
Plan conception and increase the insulin dose once she conceives
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increase insulin dose, reduce HbA1C levels and then conceive

Women with pre-existing diabetes should achieve optimal glycemic control before conception to reduce the risk of congenital malformations, miscarriage, and adverse maternal-fetal outcomes. Pregnancy should be deferred until HbA1c is optimized, with insulin therapy adjusted as needed.

Why not the other options?

• A. Conceive, increase insulin dose, then start folic acid: Organogenesis occurs in the first 8 weeks, so poor glycemic control at conception increases the risk of fetal anomalies. Folic acid should also be started before conception.
• C. Plan conception and increase insulin dose once she conceives: Optimizing glucose control after conception is too late to prevent many congenital malformations.
• D. Start folic acid and conceive: Although folic acid is essential, HbA1c of 8.5% indicates suboptimal glycemic control, which should be corrected before pregnancy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: All are normal physiological changes in pregnancy except? (NEET PG 2019)
options: Mild ST changes in inferior leads
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pansystolic murmur

A pansystolic murmur is not a normal finding in pregnancy. It suggests pathological regurgitation — mitral, tricuspid, or a ventricular septal defect — and warrants full cardiac evaluation.

Why the other three are normal:

A. Left axis deviation — as the uterus enlarges, the diaphragm is pushed upward, mechanically displacing the heart to the left and superiorly. This produces an average \~15° left axis shift on ECG, which is entirely physiological.

B. Mild ST changes in inferior leads — the same diaphragmatic elevation alters the heart's positional relationship to the chest wall, producing mild non-specific ST and T-wave changes in the inferior leads. These are positional, not ischaemic.

C. Atrial and ventricular premature contractions — the hyperdynamic circulation, increased sympathetic tone, and expanded plasma volume of pregnancy make ectopic beats relatively common and generally benign in structurally normal hearts.

Normal cardiovascular findings in pregnancy — quick reference:

| System | Normal finding | Mechanism

| ------ | -------------- | ---------

| Murmurs | Ejection systolic (aortic/pulmonary areas) | Increased cardiac output → flow murmur

| Murmurs | Mammary soufflé (2nd–4th ICS, continuous) | Increased breast blood flow

| Murmurs | Venous hum | Increased venous return

| Heart sounds | Loud, widely split S1 | Increased flow + hyperdynamic state

| Heart sounds | Increased P2, split S2 | Increased pulmonary flow

| Apex beat | Shifted to 4th ICS, 2.5 cm lateral to MCL | Diaphragmatic elevation displacing heart

| ECG | \~15° left axis deviation | Diaphragm elevation

| ECG | Mild inferior ST/T changes | Positional cardiac shift

| ECG | Atrial/ventricular ectopics | Hyperdynamic circulation

| ECG | T-wave inversion, bi-atrial enlargement | Volume overload physiology

| Echo | Increased LV mass, increased LA end-diastolic dimension | Volume overload

| Echo | Trivial tricuspid regurgitation | Annular dilatation from volume load

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: An 18-year-old girl presents with a history of low-grade fever, weight loss, abdominal pain and amenorrhea for six months. On examination, a pelvic mass is felt on the left side and signs of ascites are positive. What is your diagnosis? (NEET PG 2020)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tuberculosis with tubo-ovarian mass

This clinical picture is classical for genital tuberculosis complicated by a tubo-ovarian mass. The key diagnostic clues in this case are:

• Young age (18 years) — genital TB predominantly affects women of reproductive age
• Constitutional symptoms — low-grade fever and weight loss are hallmark features of tuberculosis
• Amenorrhea — resulting from endometrial involvement by TB
• Left-sided pelvic mass — consistent with a tubo-ovarian mass formed due to tuberculous inflammation
• Ascites — suggestive of peritoneal involvement, commonly seen in abdominal/pelvic TB

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

• Option B — Ovarian Malignancy: Less likely in an 18-year-old; constitutional TB symptoms are more consistent with an infective etiology
• Option C — Ectopic Pregnancy: Would not account for 6 months of amenorrhea alongside constitutional symptoms and ascites
• Option D — Submucous Fibroid: Does not explain fever, weight loss, or ascites

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: As per ICMR guidelines, which of the following are the criteria for SARS-CoV-2 exposure for a pregnant female during COVID-19 pandemic? 1.
