Travel to an affected country within previous 14 days 2. Close contact with a confirmed case within a distance of 1 metre for more than 15 minutes 3. Living in neighbourhood of a confirmed case 4. Direct contact with body fluids of a confirmed case Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

According to ICMR/WHO definitions used during the COVID-19 pandemic, SARS-CoV-2 exposure includes

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Travel to an affected country within the previous 14 days: Correct.
• 2. Close contact with a confirmed case within 1 metre for more than 15 minutes: Correct.
• 3. Living in the neighbourhood of a confirmed case: Incorrect. Neighborhood proximity alone is not considered exposure.
• 4. Direct contact with body fluids of a confirmed case: Correct (e.g., respiratory secretions).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following abnormalities in a woman with preeclampsia: 1. Platelet count less than 1 lakh/cumm 2. Serum creatinine > 1.1 mg/dL 3. Pulmonary edema 4. Proteinuria > 1 g per day Which of the above describe severe features of preeclampsia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Preeclampsia is considered to have severe features when there is evidence of significant maternal end-organ dysfunction.

1. Platelet count <1 lakh/cumm — Correct

• Thrombocytopenia below 100,000/µL is a severe feature.

2. Serum creatinine >1.1 mg/dL — Correct

• Renal impairment with serum creatinine >1.1 mg/dL or doubling of the baseline value is a severe feature.

3. Pulmonary edema — Correct

• Pulmonary edema indicates significant end-organ involvement and is a severe feature.

4. Proteinuria >1 g/day — Incorrect

• The quantity of proteinuria does not determine the severity of preeclampsia.
• Once proteinuria is ≥300 mg/24 h (or equivalent), increasing amounts do not classify the disease as severe.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Detection of magnesium toxicity in a patient receiving magnesium sulphate is noticed by which of the following? I. Loss of tendon reflexes II. Increased respiratory rate III. Chest pain, heart block IV. Cardiac arrest Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, III and IV

Magnesium sulphate (MgSO₄) is the drug of choice for prevention and treatment of seizures in severe preeclampsia and eclampsia. Because it has a narrow therapeutic index, patients receiving magnesium therapy must be closely monitored for magnesium toxicity, which primarily affects the neuromuscular, respiratory, and cardiovascular systems. The following are features of magnesium toxicity:

• I. Loss of tendon reflexes: Loss of deep tendon (patellar) reflexes is the earliest clinical sign of magnesium toxicity. ⭐
• III. Chest pain, heart block: High magnesium levels can cause cardiac conduction abnormalities, including heart block, hypotension, and cardiovascular depression.
• IV. Cardiac arrest: Severe magnesium toxicity can lead to complete heart block, cardiac arrest, and death. ⭐

Why is II incorrect?

• II. Increased respiratory rate: ❌ Magnesium toxicity causes respiratory depression with a decreased respiratory rate, not an increased respiratory rate.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Early onset pre-eclampsia is defined as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Before 34 weeks

Preeclampsia is a pregnancy-specific hypertensive disorder characterized by:

• Hypertension ≥140/90 mmHg
• Proteinuria ≥300 mg/day or evidence of end-organ dysfunction
• Occurs after 20 weeks of gestation

| Type | Definition

| ---- | ----------

| Early-onset preeclampsia | Occurs before 34 weeks

| Late-onset preeclampsia | Occurs after 34 weeks

Mechanism

Abnormal trophoblast invasion

↓

Failure of spiral artery remodeling

↓

Placental ischemia

↓

Release of antiangiogenic factors

↓

Maternal endothelial dysfunction

↓

Hypertension + proteinuria

Doppler Findings in Early-Onset Preeclampsia

Typical findings:

• Increased uterine artery resistance
• Early diastolic notch

These indicate poor placental perfusion.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In a case of MgSO₄ toxicity, all of the following parameters are monitored except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serum Mg level

Magnesium toxicity is monitored clinically by RR, urine output, and DTR. Loss of patellar reflex is the earliest sign of MgSO₄ toxicity. Routine serum Mg levels are not required unless toxicity is suspected. Magnesium is cleared through the kidneys.

Reduced urine output

↓

Magnesium accumulation

↓

Risk of toxicity

Therefore: Urine output should be >25–30 mL/hour.

Clinical monitoring is more reliable and practical in obstetric practice.

| Serum Mg Level | Effect

| -------------- | ------

| 4–7 mEq/L | Therapeutic level

| 7–10 mEq/L | Loss of DTR

| 10–12 mEq/L | Respiratory depression

| >15 mEq/L | Cardiac arrest

Serum Mg Level Is Not Monitored Routinely

Although it can be measured, routine monitoring relies on clinical parameters because they are:

• Rapid
• Bedside accessible
• Clinically reliable

Antidote for Magnesium Toxicity- Calcium Gluconate

Dose:

• 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV slowly

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Magnesium sulphate has no role in: (NEET PG 2019)
options: Prevention of seizures in severe pre-eclampsia
Prevention of recurrent seizures in eclampsia
Prevention of RDS in premature baby
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prevention of RDS in premature baby

Obstetric Indications for MgSO4

Magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) is utilized across several obstetric contexts:

1.      Eclampsia — MgSO4 serves as the drug of choice for both the prevention and treatment of seizures in eclamptic patients.

2.      Severe Pre-eclampsia — It is administered prophylactically to reduce the risk of seizure progression in women diagnosed with severe pre-eclampsia.

3.      Tocolysis in Preterm Labor — MgSO4 functions as a tocolytic agent, suppressing uterine contractions and helping to delay preterm delivery.

4.      Fetal Neuroprotection in Extreme Prematurity (<29 weeks) — Administration of MgSO4 offers neuroprotective benefits to the fetus, lowering the incidence of cerebral palsy and associated neurological complications in severely preterm neonates.

MgSO4 has no role in preventing Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS). This indication is instead managed with antenatal corticosteroids — specifically betamethasone or dexamethasone — which promote fetal lung maturation and significantly reduce the risk of RDS in preterm neonates.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What are the typical levels of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) in a patient with Turner’s syndrome? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. High FSH, high LH

Turner syndrome (45,XO) is characterized by gonadal dysgenesis leading to ovarian failure. Because the ovaries fail to produce adequate estrogen:

• Negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary is lost
• Gonadotropin levels rise

Therefore, patients typically have:

• High FSH
• High LH

This pattern represents hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. Typical clinical features of Turner syndrome:

• Primary amenorrhea
• Short stature
• Webbed neck
• Shield chest
• Streak ovaries
• Infertility

FSH is usually elevated more than LH because ovarian follicular depletion markedly reduces inhibin production.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the dose of corticosteroids for lung maturity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dexamethasone 6 mg 12 hourly 4 doses

Antenatal corticosteroids are given to pregnant women at risk of Preterm Birth to accelerate fetal lung maturation.

They significantly reduce complications like:

• Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS)
• Intraventricular hemorrhage
• Necrotizing enterocolitis
• Neonatal mortality

Corticosteroids stimulate type II pneumocytes in the fetal lungs.

Corticosteroids

↓

Type II pneumocyte stimulation

↓

↑ Surfactant production

↓

Improved lung expansion

↓

Reduced respiratory distress syndrome

Two standard regimens are used.

| Drug | Dose | Schedule

| ---- | ---- | --------

| Dexamethasone | 6 mg IM | Every 12 hours × 4 doses

| Betamethasone | 12 mg IM | Every 24 hours × 2 doses

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the total loading dose of magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄) in the Pritchard regimen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 14 g

Magnesium Sulfate is the drug of choice for prevention and treatment of seizures in Eclampsia. It stabilizes neuronal membranes and reduces neuromuscular excitability.

The Pritchard regimen is a commonly used intramuscular protocol for magnesium sulfate therapy.

Loading Dose

| Route | Dose

| ----- | ----

| IV | 4 g MgSO₄

| IM | 5 g in each buttock

Total loading dose:

4 g IV + 5 g IM (right buttock) + 5 g IM (left buttock)

= 14 g total

Maintenance Dose

| Route | Dose

| ----- | ----

| IM | 5 g every 4 hours in alternate buttocks

Maintenance is continued for:

• 24 hours after delivery

or
•

24 hours after last seizure

•

Because magnesium toxicity can occur, the following must be monitored:

| Parameter | Requirement

| --------- | -----------

| Respiratory rate | >12/min

| Urine output | >25–30 mL/hr

| Patellar reflex | Present

Antidote for Magnesium Toxicity- Calcium Gluconate

Dose: 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV slowly

| Regimen | Loading Dose

| ------- | ------------

| Pritchard regimen | 14 g total

| Zuspan regimen | 4 g IV

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following aneuploidies is most likely to be missed in prenatal neonatal screening? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Klinefelter’s Syndrome

Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is commonly missed during prenatal and neonatal screening because affected individuals often lack obvious congenital abnormalities at birth.

Typical features appear later in life and may include:

• Tall stature
• Small firm testes
• Infertility
• Gynecomastia
• Reduced facial/body hair
• Learning or behavioral difficulties

In contrast:

• Trisomy 21 and Trisomy 18 usually present with characteristic dysmorphic features and congenital anomalies detectable prenatally or neonatally.
• Turner syndrome often presents with cystic hygroma, lymphedema, or cardiac defects.

Thus, Klinefelter syndrome is more likely to remain undiagnosed until adolescence or adulthood.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are neonatal complications of maternal diabetes during pregnancy? I. Hyperbilirubinemia II. Hypercalcemia III. Cardiomyopathy IV. Hypoglycemia Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, III and IV

Maternal diabetes (pre-gestational or gestational) is associated with several neonatal metabolic, respiratory, hematological, and cardiac complications. These complications occur mainly because maternal hyperglycemia causes fetal hyperglycemia, leading to fetal hyperinsulinemia, which persists after birth. The following neonatal complications are seen in infants of diabetic mothers:

• I. Hyperbilirubinemia: Common due to polycythemia and increased red blood cell breakdown after birth. ⭐
• III. Cardiomyopathy: Fetal hyperinsulinemia causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, particularly hypertrophy of the interventricular septum, which may result in left ventricular outflow obstruction. ⭐
• IV. Hypoglycemia: After birth, the maternal glucose supply stops abruptly, but fetal hyperinsulinemia persists, causing early neonatal hypoglycemia, the most common metabolic complication. ⭐

Why is II incorrect?

• II. Hypercalcemia: Infants of diabetic mothers typically develop hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia, especially during the first 24–72 hours after birth.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following drug is most commonly associated with neural tube defects due to its teratogenic effects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sodium valproate

Sodium valproate is the antiepileptic drug most strongly associated with neural tube defects (NTDs) when taken during early pregnancy. Valproate interferes with folate metabolism, which is essential for DNA synthesis and neural tube formation.

Mechanisms include:

• Folate antagonism
• Oxidative stress
• Histone deacetylase inhibition

This results in failure of neural tube closure.

Valproate exposure in pregnancy increases risk of spina bifida by 10–20 times.

Neural tube defects occur due to failure of neural tube closure during early embryogenesis.

Timing

Neural tube closes between:

• Day 21–28 of gestation

If closure fails, defects occur such as:

| Defect | Description

| ------ | -----------

| Anencephaly | Absence of brain and skull

| Spina bifida | Defect in vertebral arch

| Meningomyelocele | Herniation of meninges and spinal cord

Prevention of Neural Tube Defects

High-dose folic acid supplementation reduces risk.

| Group | Folic acid dose

| ----- | ---------------

| Normal pregnancy | 400 µg/day

| High-risk women | 4–5 mg/day

High-risk groups include:

• Previous NTD pregnancy
• Women taking antiepileptic drugs like valproate.

Teratogenic Drugs in Pregnancy

| Drug | Congenital defect

| ---- | -----------------

| Valproate | Neural tube defects

| Isotretinoin | Craniofacial defects

| Thalidomide | Limb defects (phocomelia)

| Warfarin | Nasal hypoplasia

| ACE inhibitors | Renal dysgenesis

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following hematological findings are seen in pregnant women with thalassemia trait?
options: Low serum total iron binding capacity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Raised HbA₂ and low MCV

Thalassemia trait (thalassemia minor) is characterized by microcytic, hypochromic anemia due to reduced synthesis of globin chains. During pregnancy, it is an important differential diagnosis of microcytic anemia, as it can be mistaken for iron deficiency anemia. In β-thalassemia trait, the hallmark laboratory findings are:

• Raised HbA₂ (>3.5%)
• Low Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)

Why not the other options?

• B. Low MCHC: MCHC may be mildly reduced but is not the characteristic diagnostic finding. Low MCV with raised HbA₂ is much more specific.
• C. Low serum total iron-binding capacity (TIBC)

• TIBC is usually normal in thalassemia trait.
• Low TIBC is more suggestive of anemia of chronic disease.

• D. Low HbA₂ and raised MCV

• This is the opposite of the findings in β-thalassemia trait.
• Raised MCV is seen in vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, not thalassemia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a recognized clinical use of magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase renal perfusion

Magnesium sulfate acts primarily as a central nervous system depressant and anticonvulsant.

Mechanism of action

• Blocks NMDA receptors
• Reduces acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junction
• Stabilizes neuronal membranes

This results in seizure prevention and neuroprotection.

Recognized Clinical Uses

1. Prevention and Treatment of Eclampsia

Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for seizure prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia and treatment of eclampsia.

MgSO₄ is superior to diazepam and phenytoin for eclamptic seizures.

2  Fetal Neuroprotection

Magnesium sulfate is given in imminent preterm delivery (<32 weeks).

Purpose:

• Protects fetal brain
• Reduces risk of cerebral palsy

Exam pearl:

MgSO₄ is used for fetal neuroprotection in preterm labor.

3. Prevention of Eclamptic Seizures

In severe preeclampsia, magnesium sulfate prevents progression to eclampsia (seizures).

Indications include:

• Severe hypertension
• Visual disturbances
• Severe headache
• Epigastric pain

Because MgSO₄ can cause respiratory depression, monitoring is essential.

| Parameter | Normal value

| --------- | ------------

| Respiratory rate | >12/min

| Urine output | >25–30 mL/hr

| Patellar reflex | Present

·         Antidote for toxicity:

·         ➡ Calcium Gluconate

Magnesium sulfate does not improve renal blood flow or renal perfusion.

In fact, in severe preeclampsia:

• Renal perfusion is reduced
• MgSO₄ is given only for seizure prevention, not for renal function improvement.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements about mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV is incorrect? (NEET PG 2016)
options: Transmission most commonly occurs during early gestation
Majority of fetuses are not infected even without any intervention
The risk of mother-to-child transmission can be reduced by elective cesarean section
The risk is related to the status of infection in the mother
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Transmission most commonly occurs during early gestation

Mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV can occur:

• In utero (during pregnancy)
• Intrapartum (during labor and delivery) — most common
• Postnatally through breastfeeding

Therefore, the statement that transmission most commonly occurs during early gestation is incorrect.

Risk factors for MTCT:

• High maternal viral load
• Advanced maternal HIV disease
• Prolonged rupture of membranes
• Breastfeeding without ART

Prevention strategies:

• Maternal antiretroviral therapy (ART)
• Elective cesarean section in selected patients with high viral load
• Avoidance or modification of breastfeeding depending on guidelines

Without intervention:

• Most fetuses are still not infected
• Transmission risk is approximately 15–45%
• With proper ART, risk can be reduced to <2%

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding peripartum cardiomyopathy? 1. It is usually seen in multiparous women. 2. Echocardiography shows ejection fraction less than 45%. 3. ACE inhibitors are contraindicated. 4. History of prior heart disease is mostly present. Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 3

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy that presents with heart failure due to left ventricular systolic dysfunction in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months postpartum, in the absence of pre-existing heart disease.

• 1. It is usually seen in multiparous women. ✓

• PPCM is more common in multiparous women, especially those with advanced maternal age, multiple pregnancy, preeclampsia, or hypertension.

• 2. Echocardiography shows ejection fraction less than 45%. ✓

• Echocardiography is the key diagnostic test and typically demonstrates:

• LVEF <45%
• Left ventricular systolic dysfunction
• Dilated left ventricle (may or may not be present)

• 3. ACE inhibitors are contraindicated. ✓

• ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated during pregnancy because of fetal toxicity. They can be started after delivery (especially if the mother is not pregnant; several ACE inhibitors are compatible with breastfeeding in appropriate clinical settings).

• 4. History of prior heart disease is mostly present. ✗

• By definition, PPCM occurs in women without pre-existing structural heart disease.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following treatments are recommended for a pregnant woman suffering from sickle cell disease? I. Folic acid 1 mg daily II. Azathioprine III. Penicillin prophylaxis IV. Thromboprophylaxis with low molecular weight heparin Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, III and IV

Pregnancy in women with sickle cell disease (SCD) is considered high-risk because of increased maternal and fetal complications, including vaso-occlusive crises, acute chest syndrome, preeclampsia, fetal growth restriction, preterm birth, and venous thromboembolism. Management focuses on preventing complications and optimizing maternal and fetal outcomes. The following treatments are recommended:

• I. Folic acid 1 mg daily: Correct. Folic acid supplementation is recommended because of chronic hemolysis, which increases folate requirements for erythropoiesis. (Many guidelines recommend an even higher dose, e.g., 5 mg/day during pregnancy.)
• III. Penicillin prophylaxis: Correct. Patients with functional asplenia are at increased risk of infections with encapsulated organisms. Penicillin prophylaxis is recommended in selected patients, particularly those already receiving it.
• IV. Thromboprophylaxis with low molecular weight heparin (LMWH): Correct. Pregnancy and sickle cell disease are both prothrombotic states. LMWH thromboprophylaxis is recommended during hospitalization and in the postpartum period, and antenatally in women with additional risk factors.

Why is II incorrect?

• II. Azathioprine: Incorrect. Azathioprine is not a routine treatment for sickle cell disease. Disease-modifying therapy for SCD is hydroxyurea, which is generally avoided during pregnancy because of potential teratogenicity.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which one of the following is not a risk factor for pre-eclampsia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Placenta previa

Pre-eclampsia is associated with abnormal placentation and maternal vascular dysfunction. Several maternal factors increase the risk, but placenta previa is not a risk factor.

Why not the other options?

• A. Primigravida: Risk factor for pre-eclampsia.
• B. Obesity: Risk factor due to increased metabolic and inflammatory changes.
• C. Pre-existing vascular disease: Risk factor (e.g., chronic hypertension, diabetes with vasculopathy, chronic kidney disease).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of sudden heat sensation associated with profuse sweating and flushing over the past several months. She has irregular menstrual cycles suggestive of the menopausal transition. Which of the following is the most appropriate confirmatory investigation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serum FSH level

In women with vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes, flushing, night sweats) and irregular menstrual cycles suggestive of the menopausal transition, the most useful laboratory test—if confirmation is required—is serum FSH. Ovarian follicular depletion leads to reduced estrogen production, causing loss of negative feedback and a rise in FSH (typically >25–30 IU/L, though levels fluctuate during perimenopause).

High-Yield Points

• Most menopausal women do not require laboratory confirmation if they are >45 years with typical symptoms.
• If testing is indicated (e.g., younger women or uncertain diagnosis), FSH is the preferred investigation.
• FSH ↑, LH ↑ (less marked than FSH), Estradiol ↓.
• Progesterone is not useful for diagnosing menopause.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient is planned to undergo hysteroscopic polypectomy using bipolar electrocautery. What is the ideal agent for distention? (NEET PG 2020)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Normal saline

During hysteroscopy, the uterine cavity is distended using fluid media to allow visualization and operative procedures.

For bipolar electrocautery, the ideal distension medium is Normal saline.

• Bipolar systems can safely function in electrolyte-containing solutions
• Saline is isotonic and reduces risk of hyponatremia and fluid-related complications

Important distinctions:

• Monopolar electrosurgery requires nonconductive, electrolyte-free media such as glycine or sorbitol
• Glycine absorption can cause:

• Hyponatremia
• Cerebral edema
• Hyperammonemia

CO₂ is mainly used for diagnostic hysteroscopy and not operative procedures.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding vaginal epithelium in adult female: 1. From puberty till menopause, the vaginal epithelium is devoid of any gland. 2. The basal epithelial layer contains glycogen. 3. Intermediate and superficial cells become continuous with those covering vaginal portion of cervix. 4. Unlike skin, it does not contain hair follicle. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 3 and 4

1. From puberty till menopause, vaginal epithelium is devoid of glands: Correct.

• The vagina has no glands in its epithelium.
• Vaginal lubrication mainly comes from cervical mucus and transudation through the vaginal wall.

2. Basal epithelial layer contains glycogen: Incorrect.

• Glycogen is mainly present in the intermediate and superficial cells under estrogenic influence.
• Lactobacilli metabolize glycogen to lactic acid, maintaining the acidic vaginal pH.

3. Intermediate and superficial cells become continuous with those covering the vaginal portion of cervix: Correct.

• The vaginal epithelium is non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and is continuous with the squamous epithelium of the ectocervix.

4. Unlike skin, it does not contain hair follicles: Correct.

• Vaginal mucosa lacks hair follicles, sebaceous glands and sweat glands

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following statements with respect to endometrial cycle: 1. The basal zone is uninfluenced by any hormone. 2. Saw-toothed glandular epithelium is seen in secretory phase. 3. Stratum compactum contains mainly the glands and less stroma. 4. Pseudostratification is seen in proliferative phase of menstrual cycle. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

1. Basal zone is uninfluenced by hormones — Correct

• The stratum basale is relatively unaffected by cyclical hormonal changes and remains after menstruation.
• It serves as the source for regeneration of the functional layer.

2. Saw-toothed glandular epithelium is seen in secretory phase — Correct

• Under progesterone influence, endometrial glands become tortuous/coiled (“saw-toothed”) and begin secreting glycogen.

3. Stratum compactum contains mainly glands and less stroma — Incorrect

• The stratum compactum contains densely packed stromal cells and relatively fewer glands.
• The stratum spongiosum contains more prominent, dilated glands.

4. Pseudostratification is seen in proliferative phase — Correct

• During the estrogen-driven proliferative phase, the endometrial glands are relatively straight and show pseudostratified columnar epithelium.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which part of the fallopian tube does fertilization occur? (NEET PG 2020)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ampulla

Ampulla:

• The ampulla is the widest section of the fallopian tube and is the most common site for fertilization.
• This region provides an optimal environment for the sperm to meet the ovum and for the subsequent fertilization process to occur.
• The ampulla is also the most common site of ectopic pregnancy, where a fertilized egg implants and grows outside the main cavity of the uterus.

The fallopian tube has four main parts:

1. Infundibulum: The funnel-shaped opening near the ovary with finger-like projections called fimbriae.
2. Ampulla: The widest and longest part where fertilization typically occurs.
3. Isthmus: A narrow section adjacent to the uterus.
4. Interstitial (or intramural): The part that traverses the uterine wall and opens into the uterine cavity.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The growth and differentiation of primordial follicles is under the control of which hormone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. FSH

FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) promotes the growth and differentiation of ovarian follicles, particularly from the preantral/antral stages onward.

• A. LH: Acts mainly on theca cells and is important for androgen production and ovulation.
• B. FSH — Correct: Stimulates follicular growth and granulosa-cell proliferation, and promotes aromatization of androgens to estrogen.
• C. Growth hormone: Has supportive metabolic effects but is not the primary regulator of follicular development.
• D. Progesterone: Predominantly acts after ovulation during the luteal phase

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The most potent natural estrogen is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Estradiol

Estradiol (E₂) is the most potent natural estrogen with the highest receptor affinity. Estrone is predominant post-menopause, while estriol is weakest and rises in pregnancy.

| Estrogen Type | Source / Predominance | Potency | Key Feature

| ------------- | --------------------- | ------- | -----------

| Estradiol | Ovaries (reproductive years) | Most potent | Highest receptor affinity, main active estrogen

| Estrone | Postmenopausal women | Moderate | Main estrogen after menopause

| Estriol | Pregnancy | Weakest | Predominant during pregnancy

Estradiol is the main estrogen during reproductive years.

Source

• Granulosa cells of ovarian follicles
• Produced from androgens via aromatase enzyme

Major functions

| Function | Effect

| -------- | ------

| Endometrial proliferation | Prepares uterus for implantation

| Secondary sexual characters | Breast development

| Bone metabolism | Prevents osteoporosis

| Cervical mucus | Makes it thin and receptive

Estradiol dominates during the follicular phase of menstrual cycle.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What hormone levels are typical during days 21–25 of a 28-day cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Estrogen ↑, Progesterone ↑ ; FSH ↓, LH ↓

Days 21–25 correspond to the mid-luteal phase, when the corpus luteum is fully functional. Progesterone peaks, and estrogen remains moderately elevated. High steroid levels exert negative feedback on the pituitary, suppressing FSH and LH, matching option A.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: When does the secondary oocyte complete the second meiotic division?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Just after fertilization

The secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II at the time of ovulation.

It completes the second meiotic division only after fertilization, when sperm entry triggers completion of meiosis II and formation of the:

• Mature ovum
• Second polar body

Therefore, the correct answer is D. Just after fertilization.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are indications of endometrial sampling? I. Endometrial tuberculosis II. Endometrial polyp III. Postmenopausal bleeding IV. Abnormal uterine bleeding Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, III and IV

Endometrial sampling (endometrial biopsy) is a minimally invasive procedure used to obtain endometrial tissue for histopathological examination. It is primarily indicated to evaluate abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), exclude endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma, and diagnose specific endometrial diseases such as tuberculosis. The following are indications for endometrial sampling:

• I. Endometrial tuberculosis: Endometrial biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing genital tuberculosis, demonstrating granulomatous inflammation and allowing microbiological testing (AFB stain, culture, PCR). ⭐
• III. Postmenopausal bleeding: Any postmenopausal bleeding requires evaluation for endometrial carcinoma, and endometrial sampling is indicated, especially when endometrial thickness is >4 mm or bleeding is recurrent. ⭐
• IV. Abnormal uterine bleeding: Endometrial biopsy is recommended in:

• Women ≥45 years with AUB
• Women <45 years with persistent AUB, failed medical treatment, or risk factors for endometrial carcinoma.

Why is II incorrect?

• II. Endometrial polyp: The preferred investigations are transvaginal ultrasound, saline infusion sonography, or hysteroscopy. Although a removed polyp is sent for histopathology, endometrial sampling alone is not the investigation of choice for diagnosing an endometrial polyp.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following effects of puberty are not mediated by estrogen? (NEET PG 2020)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hair growth

• Hair growth (Pubarche): The development of axillary and pubic hair is not mediated by estrogen. It occurs due to testosterone in both sexes.
• Estrogen effects: Estrogen plays a crucial role in various aspects of puberty, including:

• Breast development (thelarche)
• Development of internal genitalia
• Menarche
• Regulation of growth spurt
• Epiphyseal closure
• Cervical mucus plug formation

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which one of the following statements explains self-priming of gonadotrophs?
options: Lower GnRH pulse frequencies favour FSH secretion and higher frequencies favour LH secretion.
Lower GnRH pulse frequencies favour LH secretion and higher frequencies favour FSH secretion.
Higher GnRH pulse frequencies favour LH as well as FSH secretion.
Lower GnRH pulse frequencies favour LH as well as FSH secretion.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lower GnRH pulse frequencies favour FSH secretion and higher frequencies favour LH secretion.

GnRH is released in a pulsatile manner, and the frequency of GnRH pulses determines the relative secretion of LH and FSH:

• Low-frequency GnRH pulses → preferentially stimulate FSH
• High-frequency GnRH pulses → preferentially stimulate LH

This differential response is called GnRH pulse-frequency modulation.

Self-priming of gonadotrophs refers to the phenomenon whereby repeated GnRH stimulation enhances the gonadotroph response, particularly during the preovulatory GnRH/LH surge.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• B. Lower GnRH pulse frequencies favour LH secretion and higher frequencies favour FSH secretion: Reverses the normal frequency relationship.
• C. Higher GnRH pulse frequencies favour LH as well as FSH secretion: Does not explain differential regulation by GnRH pulse frequency.
• D. Lower GnRH pulse frequencies favour LH as well as FSH secretion: Incorrect; low-frequency pulses do not preferentially stimulate both LH and FSH.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: 28-year-old taking testosterone injections for bodybuilding. Expected gonadotropin levels:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. GnRH ↓, LH ↓, FSH ↓

• Exogenous testosterone causes: Negative feedback on hypothalamus and pituitary
• Therefore: ↓ GnRH, ↓ LH, ↓ FSH

Consequence:

• Testicular atrophy
• Impaired spermatogenesis

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman with primary infertility is found to have bilateral tubal block on HSG. The next best step is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Laparoscopy with chromopertubation

HSG is a screening test for tubal patency.

• HSG findings must be confirmed --> by laparoscopy with chromopertubation.
• This allows direct visualization and dye testing for tubal patency.

IVF is considered only after confirmation, IUI and Letrozole are ineffective with bilateral block.

Methylene blue dye injected through cervix

↓

Dye passes through uterus

↓

Spillage from fimbrial end

↓

Confirms tubal patency

If no dye spill is seen, tubal obstruction is confirmed.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man undergoes semen analysis as part of an infertility evaluation. According to the WHO 2021 (6th edition) reference values, what is the lower reference limit for total sperm motility (progressive + non-progressive)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 42%

According to the WHO Laboratory Manual for the Examination and Processing of Human Semen (6th edition, 2021), the lower reference limit for total sperm motility (progressive + non-progressive) is 42%, while progressive motility alone should be ≥30%.

Why not the other options?

• A. 42%: Correct. Current WHO 2021 lower reference limit for total motility.
• B. 40%: WHO 2010 (5th edition) lower reference limit; no longer current.
• C. 30%: Refers to progressive motility, not total motility.
• D. 50%: WHO 1999 (4th edition) lower reference limit; outdated.

High-Yield WHO 2021 Semen Reference Values

| Parameter | Lower Reference Limit

| --------- | ---------------------

| Semen volume | 1.4 mL

| Sperm concentration | 16 million/mL

| Total sperm number | 39 million/ejaculate

| Total motility | 42%

| Progressive motility | 30%

| Vitality (live sperm) | 54%

| Normal morphology | 4%

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old married woman who came for the evaluation of infertility was found to have a septum in her uterine cavity. What would be the appropriate management of this case? (NEET PG 2021)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hysteroscopy and septoplasty

A uterine septum is the most common congenital Müllerian anomaly associated with:

• Infertility
• Recurrent pregnancy loss
• Preterm labor
• Malpresentation

The treatment of choice is Hysteroscopic septoplasty (hysteroscopic septal resection).

Advantages of hysteroscopic management:

• Minimally invasive
• Preserves fertility
• Short recovery time
• High success rate for improving reproductive outcomes

Why other options are incorrect:

• A. Hysterectomy is unnecessary in women desiring fertility
• D. Laparotomy/B. Laparoscopic metroplasty is mainly used for bicornuate uterus, not septate uterus

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A couple has been attempting to conceive for the past two years with unprotected intercourse yet without success. What percentage of infertile women have unexplained infertility?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 15%

Infertility is defined as:

• Failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse.

Evaluation usually includes assessment of:

• Ovulation
• Tubal patency
• Uterine cavity
• Male factor

If all tests are normal but pregnancy still does not occur, the condition is called unexplained infertility.

Unexplained infertility occurs when:

• Ovulation is normal
• Tubes are patent
• Semen analysis is normal
• No uterine pathology is detected

Yet the couple is unable to conceive.

Prevalence- Approximately 10–20% of infertile couples have unexplained infertility.

Major steps in infertility evaluation:

| Investigation | Purpose

| ------------- | -------

| Semen analysis | Male factor

| Ovulation assessment (progesterone, LH) | Ovulatory function

| Hysterosalpingography (HSG) | Tubal patency

| Ultrasound pelvis | Ovarian and uterine structure

| Laparoscopy | Endometriosis or adhesions

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A couple presented to OPD with complaint of inability to conceive for last 3 years. Husband was advised semen analysis. What is the WHO criterion for minimum sperm count per ml in normal semen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 15 million

According to the WHO semen analysis reference values (2010 and retained in WHO 2021 lower reference limits), the lower reference limit for sperm concentration is 15 million sperm/mL.

Why not the other options?

• A. 10 million/mL: Below the WHO lower reference limit.
• C. 30 million/mL: Older reference values; not the current WHO criterion.
• D. 40 million/mL: Not a WHO lower reference limit.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A teenage patient presented with a history of dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain. On ultrasonography, a transverse vaginal septum was seen. Which of the following is she likely to have? (NEET PG 2021)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endometriosis

A transverse vaginal septum can obstruct menstrual outflow, leading to cryptomenorrhea and retrograde menstruation.

Clinical features:

• Dysmenorrhea
• Chronic pelvic pain
• Hematocolpos or hematometra
• Cyclical pain after menarche

Retrograde menstruation allows endometrial tissue to reflux through the fallopian tubes into the pelvic cavity, increasing the risk of endometriosis.

Why other options are incorrect:

• B. Tubo-ovarian abscess is usually related to pelvic inflammatory disease
• C. Dermoid cyst is a benign ovarian germ cell tumor
• D. Theca lutein cysts are associated with high β-hCG states

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young female presented with complaints of lower abdominal pain, vaginal discharge, history of IUCD use for last 3–4 years. On examination, the patient had fever, adnexal/cervical motion tenderness and increased ESR and C-reactive protein. What is the probable clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Acute PID

Acute Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) is an ascending polymicrobial infection of the upper female genital tract, involving the uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, and pelvic peritoneum. The patient has the classical features:

• Lower abdominal pain
• Vaginal discharge
• Long-term IUCD use (risk factor)
• Fever
• Cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness
• Raised ESR and CRP indicating inflammation

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Ectopic pregnancy: Usually presents with amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding. Pregnancy should always be excluded with a β-hCG test, but vaginal discharge and cervical motion tenderness with inflammatory markers favor PID.
• B. Acute appendicitis: Typically causes right iliac fossa pain, anorexia, nausea, and localized peritoneal signs without vaginal discharge or cervical motion tenderness.
• C. Diverticulitis: Usually occurs in older patients, presenting with left lower quadrant pain, fever, and bowel symptoms rather than gynecological findings.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following diagnostic criteria for acute pelvic inflammatory disease (PID): 1. Lower abdominal tenderness 2. Oral temperature >38°C 3. Adnexal tenderness 4. Cervical motion tenderness Which of the above are included in the minimum criteria for diagnosis of PID?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

The minimum clinical criteria for presumptive diagnosis of acute PID are the presence of any one of the following on pelvic examination:

1. Lower abdominal tenderness
2. Adnexal tenderness
3. Cervical motion tenderness

Therefore, 1, 3 and 4 → C.

Oral temperature >38°C is a supportive/additional criterion, not one of the minimum criteria.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which of the following conditions, hysteroscopy can be done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Asherman syndrome

It is characterized by fibrous adhesions inside the uterine cavity--> Causes of Asherman Syndrome

Common causes include:

| Cause | Example

| ----- | -------

| Post-curettage trauma | After abortion

| Postpartum curettage | Retained placenta

| Uterine surgery | Myomectomy

Asherman syndrome consists of intrauterine adhesions and hysteroscopy is the investigation and treatment of choice (hysteroscopic adhesiolysis).

Hysteroscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

Direct visualization of uterine cavity

↓

Identify intrauterine adhesions

↓

Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis

Tubal ligation is laparoscopic, subserosal fibroids are extrauterine, and endocervical polyps are usually removed by simple excision.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The maternal use of which of the following hormones is most likely to cause hypospadias in a male child? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diethylstilbestrol

Diethylstilbestrol (DES) is a synthetic estrogen that was historically used during pregnancy and is associated with congenital abnormalities of the reproductive tract.

Maternal exposure to DES during pregnancy can cause:

• Hypospadias and cryptorchidism in male offspring
• Vaginal clear cell adenocarcinoma in female offspring
• Uterine and cervical malformations
• Infertility and pregnancy complications

Hypospadias occurs due to abnormal fusion of the urethral folds during male genital development, which can result from estrogenic endocrine disruption during fetal life.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Tolbutamide → sulfonylurea used in diabetes
• Clomiphene → ovulation induction agent
• Clonazepam → benzodiazepine associated mainly with CNS depression/withdrawal effects

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most appropriate initial treatment for an infertile woman diagnosed with bilateral cornual block on Hysterosalpingography? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hysteroscopic Cannulation

Cornual (proximal tubal) block on hysterosalpingography (HSG) may be due to:

• Tubal spasm
• Mucus plugs
• Debris
• True proximal tubal obstruction

The initial management is hysteroscopic or transcervical tubal cannulation, which:

• Confirms true obstruction
• Can restore tubal patency
• Is minimally invasive

Why other options are incorrect:

• IVF is reserved when tubal recanalization fails or severe tubal disease exists
• Salpingectomy is mainly indicated for hydrosalpinx or damaged tubes before IVF
• Salpingostomy is used for distal tubal obstruction, not proximal cornual block

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the underlying embryological defect responsible for bicornuate uterus?
options: Failure of fusion of the Müllerian ducts
Failure of descent of the Müllerian ducts
Failure of fusion of the Wolffian ducts
Failure of resorption of the Müllerian septum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Failure of fusion of the Müllerian ducts

A bicornuate uterus results from incomplete fusion of the two Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts, producing a uterus with two uterine horns and a deep fundal cleft (>1 cm).

| Embryological defect | Uterine anomaly

| -------------------- | ---------------

| Failure of Müllerian duct fusion | Bicornuate uterus, uterus didelphys

| Failure of resorption of Müllerian septum | Septate uterus (most common Müllerian anomaly)

| Failure of development of one Müllerian duct | Unicornuate uterus

| Complete agenesis of Müllerian ducts | Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are risk factors for developing pelvic inflammatory disease in females? 1. Use of oral contraception pills 2. Multiple sexual partners 3. Lower socioeconomic status 4. Genetic predisposition Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an ascending infection of the upper female genital tract, most commonly caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Use of oral contraceptive pills: Incorrect. OCPs are not a risk factor and may even reduce the risk of ascending infection by thickening cervical mucus.
• 2. Multiple sexual partners: Correct. Increases exposure to sexually transmitted infections.
• 3. Lower socioeconomic status: Correct. Associated with a higher prevalence of STIs and reduced access to healthcare.
• 4. Genetic predisposition: Correct. Host genetic factors influencing immune response may increase susceptibility to PID and its complications.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are risk factors for Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)? 1. Use of contraceptive pills 2. IUD use 3. Genetic predisposition 4. Sexually active teenagers Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 3 and 4

Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) is an ascending polymicrobial infection of the upper female genital tract. It is most commonly caused by Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Several behavioral and gynecological factors increase the risk of acquiring PID.

• 1. Use of contraceptive pills ✗

• Combined oral contraceptive pills are not a risk factor for PID. They may even reduce the risk of ascending infection by thickening cervical mucus.

• 2. IUD use ✓

• There is a slightly increased risk of PID during the first 3 weeks after IUCD insertion. Long-term IUCD use itself does not significantly increase the risk if no STI is present, but for examination purposes it is considered a risk factor.

• 3. Genetic predisposition ✓

• Host genetic factors affecting immune response may increase susceptibility to PID and its complications.

• 4. Sexually active teenagers ✓

• Adolescents are at increased risk because of:

• Higher prevalence of STIs
• Cervical ectopy, facilitating infection
• High-risk sexual behavior

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are symptoms of genital tuberculosis? 1. Postmenopausal bleeding 2. Infertility 3. Chronic pelvic pain 4. Oligomenorrhoea Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Female Genital Tuberculosis (FGTB) is an important cause of infertility in countries where tuberculosis is endemic. It usually results from hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis from a primary focus (commonly the lungs) and most frequently involves the fallopian tubes, followed by the endometrium.

• 1. Postmenopausal bleeding ✗

• Postmenopausal bleeding is not a typical feature of genital tuberculosis and should raise suspicion for endometrial carcinoma or other uterine pathology.

• 2. Infertility ✓

• Infertility is the most common presenting symptom of genital tuberculosis due to tubal damage and endometrial involvement.

• 3. Chronic pelvic pain ✓

• Chronic pelvic pain is common because of chronic inflammation, adhesions, and tubo-ovarian disease.

• 4. Oligomenorrhoea ✓

• Menstrual disturbances such as oligomenorrhea, hypomenorrhea, amenorrhea, or occasionally menorrhagia may occur due to endometrial involvement.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following criteria are required to be fulfilled for hospitalization in a case of pelvic inflammatory disease? 1. Coexisting pregnancy 2. Mild fever and pain responding well to antibiotics 3. Suspected tubo-ovarian abscess 4. Coexistent HIV infection Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 3 and 4

Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) is an ascending infection of the upper female genital tract, involving the uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, and pelvic peritoneum. While most cases are managed as outpatients, hospitalization is indicated in selected high-risk situations to prevent severe complications such as tubo-ovarian abscess, infertility, and sepsis.

• 1. Coexisting pregnancy ✓

• PID during pregnancy is uncommon but potentially serious and requires hospitalization for parenteral antibiotics and close maternal-fetal monitoring.

• 2. Mild fever and pain responding well to antibiotics ✗

• Patients with mild to moderate PID who respond to oral antibiotics can usually be managed as outpatients.

• 3. Suspected tubo-ovarian abscess ✓

• A tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA) requires hospitalization, intravenous antibiotics, and possible drainage or surgery if there is no clinical improvement or rupture is suspected.

• 4. Coexistent HIV infection ✓

• HIV-positive women with PID are generally hospitalized, particularly if severely ill, because of the increased risk of severe infection and complications.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following operative procedures is/are confirmatory for the diagnosis of bicornuate uterus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hysteroscopy and laparoscopy

A bicornuate uterus is a Class IV Müllerian duct anomaly resulting from partial failure of fusion of the Müllerian ducts, leading to a uterus with two uterine horns and a deep external fundal cleft (>1 cm). The definitive diagnosis requires assessment of both the uterine cavity and the external uterine contour, making combined hysteroscopy and laparoscopy the operative gold standard.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Dilatation with curettage (D&C): D&C has no role in diagnosing congenital uterine anomalies.
• B. Hysteroscopy: Hysteroscopy alone visualizes only the uterine cavity and cannot assess the external fundal contour, making it difficult to distinguish a bicornuate uterus from a septate uterus.
• D. Hysterectomy: Hysterectomy is not a diagnostic procedure and is unnecessary for confirming a bicornuate uterus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements about indications of hysterosalpingography are correct? I. Tubal patency assessment following tuboplasty operation II. Diagnosis of uterine synechiae III. Detection of IUD IV. Diagnosis of subserosal fibroid Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is a radiographic procedure in which a water-soluble contrast medium is injected through the cervix to visualize the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes under fluoroscopy. It is primarily used in the evaluation of infertility, especially to assess tubal patency and abnormalities of the uterine cavity. The following are appropriate uses of HSG:

• I. Tubal patency assessment following tuboplasty operation: HSG is used to evaluate the success of tubal reconstructive surgery (tuboplasty) by confirming tubal patency.
• II. Diagnosis of uterine synechiae: HSG can demonstrate intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome) as irregular filling defects or partial obliteration of the uterine cavity.
• III. Detection of IUD: HSG can demonstrate the presence and position of an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUD) within the uterine cavity.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Diagnosis of subserosal fibroid: Subserosal fibroids lie on the outer surface of the uterus and do not distort the uterine cavity, so they are not detected by HSG. They are better evaluated by ultrasonography or MRI.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of these is not a test for the measurement of ovarian reserve?
options: Serum FSH in the early follicular phase
Serum Estradiol in the early follicular phase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serum Estradiol in the early follicular phase

Ovarian reserve tests reflect quantity of remaining follicles. Day-2/3 FSH, AMH, and Antral Follicle Count are validated markers. Ovarian reserve refers to the quantity and functional capacity of the remaining ovarian follicles and predicts response to ovarian stimulation in infertility treatment. Estradiol (E2), though measured in the early follicular phase, is not a reliable ovarian-reserve indicator—levels fluctuate and can even appear normal despite diminished reserve by suppressing FSH. Hence option D is not a true ovarian reserve test.

1. Serum FSH (Day 2–3 of Cycle)

Measured in the early follicular phase (Day 2–3).

Principle

If ovarian reserve decreases → ovaries respond poorly → FSH increases due to reduced negative feedback.

| FSH Level | Interpretation

| --------- | --------------

| <10 IU/L | Normal ovarian reserve

| 10–15 IU/L | Reduced reserve

| >15 IU/L | Poor reserve

2. Antral Follicle Count (AFC)

Number of 2–10 mm follicles seen in ovaries on transvaginal ultrasound.

| AFC | Interpretation

| --- | --------------

| >15 | Good reserve

| 8–15 | Normal

| <5 | Poor ovarian reserve

3. Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH)

Produced by:

Granulosa cells of pre-antral and small antral follicles.

Advantages

• Most reliable ovarian reserve marker
• Cycle independent
• Declines with age

| AMH Level | Interpretation

| --------- | --------------

| >3.5 ng/mL | High reserve / PCOS

| 1–3.5 ng/mL | Normal

| <1 ng/mL | Low ovarian reserve

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which one of the following is an abnormal parameter in accordance with WHO Semen Analysis Criteria (Normal reference value)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Viscosity > 4

According to WHO semen analysis criteria, increased semen viscosity is an abnormal finding. Hyperviscous semen impairs sperm motility and may contribute to male infertility.

Why not the other options?

• A. Volume ≥2 mL: Normal (older WHO criteria; current WHO lower reference is ≥1.4–1.5 mL).
• B. Viscosity >4: Abnormal. Normal semen liquefies within 15–60 minutes and should not be excessively viscous.
• C. Progressive forward motility of sperms >50%: Normal (older WHO criteria; current WHO lower reference is ≥32% progressive motility).
• D. Normal morphology of sperms >14%: Normal (older WHO strict criteria; current WHO lower reference is ≥4% normal forms using Kruger strict criteria).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is true regarding genital tuberculosis?
options: The most common site of affection is ovary.
Abdominal ostium is closed in tobacco pouch appearance.
The most common mode of spread from primary to genital organs is haematogenous.
Genital tuberculosis occurs in 1–2% of patients who had pulmonary tuberculosis in adolescence.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The most common mode of spread from primary to genital organs is haematogenous.

• A. The most common site of affection is ovary: Incorrect. The fallopian tubes are the most commonly affected site in female genital tuberculosis, not the ovary.
• B. Abdominal ostium is closed in tobacco pouch appearance: Incorrect. In tuberculous salpingitis, the abdominal ostium may be blocked, producing a tobacco-pouch appearance due to a distended, club-shaped tube. The statement as worded is not the best description of the classic finding.
• C. The most common mode of spread from primary to genital organs is haematogenous: Correct. Genital TB usually results from hematogenous spread from a primary focus, commonly pulmonary TB.
• D. Genital tuberculosis occurs in 1–2% of patients who had pulmonary tuberculosis in adolescence: Incorrect. Genital TB is not limited to 1–2% of patients with adolescent pulmonary TB; the association is considerably more complex.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A 16-year-old girl with primary amenorrhea has the following features. What is the most probable diagnosis?

• Normal stature
• Thelarche - absent
• FSH, LH - high
• Karyotype - 46 XX
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gonadal dysgenesis

The scenario of a 16-year-old girl with absent secondary sexual characters, normal stature, with XX karyotype and high FSH and LH is suggestive of pure gonadal dysgenesis.

46 XX and 46 XY gonadal dysgenesis without the phenotype of Turner's syndrome (short stature, webbed neck) is described as pure gonadal dysgenesis. It is characterized by the presence of primary amenorrhea with or without normal secondary sexual characteristics.

Option A: Testicular feminizing syndrome occurs in karyotype XY. Secondary sexual characters are present and the uterus is absent.

Option C: Kallmann syndrome is a form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. GnRH synthesis is reduced, therefore FSH and LH are low, and secondary sexual characters are absent.

Option D: Turner syndrome is associated with short stature and karyotype X0. Secondary sexual characters and the uterus is present, but the ovaries are streaked.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old lady complains of post-coital bleeding. She has a positive pap smear. What is the next line of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Colposcopy directed biopsy

The appropriate management of a 45-year-old with a positive pap smear and post-coital bleeding is a colposcopy-directed biopsy.

A per speculum examination must be done whenever a female comes with post-coital bleeding in order to evaluate for carcinoma of the cervix. If growth is visible, a punch biopsy should be done, and else if no growth is visible, then a pap smear is done. A pap smear is a screening test for cervical cancer. The presence of abnormal cells/ a positive test requires further evaluation by colposcopy, cervical biopsy, or fractional curettage.

Cervical cancer screening should start at age 21. Women aged 21-29 should have a pap smear every 3 years, while women aged 30-65 should have both HPV and pap co-test every 5 years. Women should stop having cervical cancer screening after the age of 65 years. If a pap smear is suspicious, then screening is continued till 75 years. HIV+ve women should have annual checkups until three consecutive negative tests followed by testing every 3 years for life.

Pap testing should be done prior to vaginal examination. Lubricants should not be used and the patient should not be menstruating during the pap test. The patient should not have intercourse 24hrs prior to the test. The ideal time is around ovulation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 55-year-old lady comes with abnormal uterine bleeding. A hysterectomy was performed and the following specimen was retrieved. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Leiomyoma

The given cut section image showing multiple nodules, well-circumscribed, firm, and white-greyish with a whorled appearance is Leiomyoma (Fibroid).

Leiomyoma is the most common benign and the most common pelvic tumor in females and is more common in obese females(hyper-estrogenism). They are mostly asymptomatic and the most common symptom is menorrhagia.

Leiomyomas can also present with bleeding areas, cystic degeneration, and calcifications. The uterine cavity is compressed.

The image below different types of uterine fibroids classified according to their locations:

Sub-mucous fibroids are the most symptomatic type and intra-mural fibroids are the most common type of uterine fibroids.

Other options:

Option B: Endometrial cancer presents as a polypoid mass protruding into the uterine cavity or as a diffuse thickening of the endometrium. The cut surface may appear white to yellow and may show areas of necrosis or hemorrhage.

Option C: Endometrial polyps are usually small and may be single or multiple. Grossly, they appear as soft, red to pink, often pedunculated (attached by a stalk) masses protruding into the uterine cavity. It presents with heavy cyclic or intermenstrual bleeding, or without complaints as an incidental finding on imaging. Estrogen and progesterone have been implicated in the growth of endometrial polyps, and higher receptor levels are seen compared with the normal endometrium.

Option D: In Adenomyosis (Endometriosis interna), the uterus may appear bulky and symmetrically enlarged. On the cut section, the myometrium may appear thickened and may show tiny cystic spaces filled with old blood (chocolate cysts). The preferred treatment is hysterectomy. Localised excision or levonorgestrel IUCD is tried in younger women.

The image below shows both the gross and histologic appearances of adenomyosis:

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman presents with obstructed labor and is grossly dehydrated. Investigations reveal fetal demise. What will be the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cesarean section

The best management in the given clinical scenario is cesarean section.

Obstructive labor management involves administering intravenous fluids to correct dehydration, providing antibiotics to prevent infection, and promptly performing a cesarean section to relieve the obstruction. If the fetus is alive, an immediate cesarean section is typically performed. Management of obstructed labor never involves a wait-and-watch approach or augmenting with oxytocin.

Clinical features of obstructed labor include maternal exhaustion, dehydration, tachycardia, tachypnea, genital sepsis, postpartum hemorrhage, and shock.
On P/A examination the upper uterine segment is tender and tonically contracted. The lower uterine segment is thin and stretched. A groove/depression is felt between the upper uterine segment and the lower uterine segment. This is called a Bandls ring.

Complications of obstructed labor include rupture of the uterus and vesicovaginal fistula.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman is diagnosed to be positive for HIV in her first trimester. What is the appropriate management?
options: Start ART immediately and continue till 6 weeks after delivery
Start ART after 1st trimester and continue life-long
Start ART immediately and continue life-long
Start ART after 1st trimester and continue till 6 weeks after delivery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Start ART immediately and continue life-long

ART should be initiated immediately and continued lifelong in all pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV. This is regardless of their WHO clinical stage and CD4 cell count.

*Note: Pearl attached below has been updated according to the NACO ART guidelines 2021. Efavirenz has been replaced by Dolutegravir as per the new guidelines.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: All are true regarding peripartum cardiomyopathy except _____
options: Development of cardiac failure within 5 months of delivery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Left ventricular diastolic dysfunction

Left ventricular systolic dysfunction is a feature of peripartum cardiomyopathy (also known as postpartum cardiomyopathy) and not diastolic dysfunction.

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a type of dilated cardiomyopathy. It develops during the last month of pregnancy or within the first 5 months following delivery.

The predisposing factors include Cardiac gene mutations involving several genes like TTNC1, TTN, and STAT3, Twin pregnancy/ multifetal gestation, Smoking, and Preeclampsia. Other proposed causes include viral myocarditis, abnormal immune response to pregnancy, malnutrition, inflammation, etc.

PPCM is associated with increased secretion of prolactin by the pituitary and antiangiogenic molecule sFlt-1 (soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase) by the placenta at term gestation.

Pearson’s diagnostic criteria for PPCM:

• Development of cardiac failure in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months after delivery
• Absence of an identifiable cause for the cardiac failure
• Absence of recognizable heart disease prior to the last month of pregnancy, and
• Left ventricular systolic dysfunction demonstrated by echocardiographic criteria, such as ejection fraction <45% or fractional shortening <30% along with a dilated left ventricle.

Management involves treating the features of heart failure. Bromocriptine has been found useful in this condition. Many women recover within 6 months of delivery, while some continue to have residual effects.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Fimbriectomy is also known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Kroener's procedure

Fimbriectomy is also known as Kroener's procedure. This procedure involves ligation of the distal ampulla of the tube with two permanent sutures. Then, resection of the infundibulum of the tube is done.

Some more techniques of permanent sterilization include:

Pomeroy method - The fallopian tube is identified on each side, brought out through the incision. The middle portion is formed into a loop which is tied at the base with catgut and excised. This is the most commonly used technique.

Uchida's method - The tubal serosa is stripped off the muscular layer in the midsegment of the tube. The muscle layer is excised. The proximal end is ligated and buried in the broad ligament. This minimal excision of the tube preserves the potential for tuboplasty.

Irving's procedure - The mid-portion of the tube is ligated and the intervening portion is excised. The proximal end is buried in the myometrium and the distal end is buried in the broad ligament. It is a reliable method but irreversible and may require a laparotomy incision.

Madlener's procedure - A loop of the fallopian tube is crushed and then ligated with a nonabsorbable suture.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In superfecundation, which of the following is seen?
options: Fertilisation of 2 ova released at the same time by sperms released at single intercourse
Fertilisation of 2 ova released in the same cycle by sperms released at intercourse on 2 different occasion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fertilisation of 2 ova released in the same cycle by sperms released at intercourse on 2 different occasion

Superfecundation is the fertilization of two different ova released in the same cycle, by two separate acts of coitus within a short period of time.

Superfecundation is the fertilization of two different ova in the same menstrual cycle (as suggested by the same gestational age) by separate acts of coitus. It can occur even after artificial reproductive therapy. Hence, after embryo transfer, intercourse must be avoided. Heteropaternal superfecundation is used to refer to instances of two different males fathering fraternal twins. This leads to the possibility of twins also being half-siblings. This may give rise to the doubt of adultery and infidelity.

Superfetation is the fertilization of two ova released in different menstrual cycles. This is not seen in humans. The nidation and development of one fetus over another fetus is theoretically possible until the decidual space is obliterated by 14-16 weeks of pregnancy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which trimester does acute fatty liver manifest most commonly during pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Third trimester

Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) occurs most commonly in the third trimester or early postpartum period.

Risk factors include Pre-eclampsia/HELLP syndrome, male fetus, previous history of AFLP, and multiple gestations.

AFLP (acute yellow atrophy or acute fatty metamorphosis) is the most common cause of acute liver failure in pregnancy. It usually occurs in the later stages of pregnancy, particularly in the third trimester. It occurs due to fetal deficiency of long-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase (LCHAD) or poor placental mitochondrial function.

The patients present with persistent nausea and vomiting, progressive jaundice, and epigastric pain. Features like acute hemolysis, hypoglycemia, hypertension, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, and edema can also be present. Symptoms may progress to fulminant hepatic failure with encephalopathy, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and death.

Liver function tests such as AST, ALT, and serum bilirubin levels are raised. Hypofibrinogenemia, hypocholesterolemia, and prolonged clotting time can be seen. An elevated d-dimer is seen. Microscopy reveals a characteristic microvesicular fatty infiltration.

The condition worsens till delivery after which the hepatic dysfunction resolves. A trial of labor by induction or delivery by Cesarean is done. Intensive supportive measures including blood transfusion should be provided.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Long-standing pelvic inflammation may lead to which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pyometra

Long-standing pelvic inflammation may lead to pyometra. This refers to the collection of pus in the uterine cavity.

The initial infection involves the cervix uteri and urethra which may extend to Bartholin glands, skene glands, endometrium, and fallopian tubes. Unilateral pain and swelling over the labia may be caused by the inflammation of the Bartholin glands.

Depending on the extent of tissue involved, PID can be classified into five stages

• Stage I - Acute salpingitis without peritonitis - No adhesions
• Stage II - Acute salpingitis with peritonitis - purulent discharge
• Stage III - Acute salpingitis with superimposed tubal occlusion or tubo ovarian complex
• Stage IV - Ruptured tubo-ovarian abscess
• Stage V - Tubercular salpingitis

Long-standing pelvic inflammation may also lead to:

• Dyspareunia
• Infertility
• Ectopic pregnancy
• Formation of adhesions like hydrosalpinx, pyosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscess
• Chronic pelvic pain

Note: Chronic pelvic inflammation leads to dense adhesions between the uterus and the appendages. Thus, it becomes difficult to define the uterus from the pelvic masses. They form a hard mass which is called the frozen pelvis.

The most common cause of the spread of PID: Ascending infection along with sperms
The only PID that does not spread with the sexual route is genital TB. It has a hematogenous spread.
The most common PID in virgin females is genital TB.
Investigation of choice in PID: Abdominal USG
The surest sign of salpingitis is pus extruding from the fimbrial end of the tube.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Quadruple testing is done during:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 15-20 weeks

The quadruple screening test is ideally done in the second trimester, during 15-20 weeks of gestation. The most accurate values are seen during 16-18 weeks of gestation.

It is the measurement of maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP), unconjugated estriol, hCG, and inhibin-A.

In Down's syndrome (trisomy 21) or Edward's syndrome (trisomy 18), quadruple-marker screenings do not provide any added benefit over first-trimester screenings. It is generally used as a stand-alone test if screening is done for the first time in the second trimester or if first-trimester screening is not available.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The best time to identify the type of twin pregnancy on ultrasound is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 11-14 weeks

The best time to identify the type of twin pregnancy on ultrasound is 11-14 weeks.

Twin pregnancies should ideally be dated when the crown–rump length (CRL) measurement is between 45 and 84 mm (i.e. 11 + 0 to 13 + 6 weeks of gestation).

Chorionicity should be ideally determined between 11 + 0 and 13 + 6 weeks of gestation (the earliest time to identify chorionicity is 7 weeks). This is done using the membrane thickness at the site of insertion of the amniotic membrane into the placenta. The T‐sign (in monochorionic twins) or lambda sign (in dichorionic twins) can be seen here. As the determination of chorionicity is most accurate when the amnion and chorion have not yet been fused, the first‐trimester scan in twin pregnancy is highly important.

Markers of dichorionicity include 4 layers of membranes between the twins, membrane thickness >2mm, different sex of twins, 2 different placentas, and positive twin peak sign.

Women with an uncomplicated dichorionic twin pregnancy should have a first‐trimester scan, a detailed second‐trimester scan, and scans every 4 weeks thereafter.

Women with uncomplicated monochorionic twins should have a first‐trimester scan and then scans every 2 weeks from 16 weeks onwards. This is done in order to detect TTTS and TAPS in a timely manner.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The fate of the Mullerian duct is determined by the:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Y chromosome

The fate of the Mullerian duct is determined by the presence or absence of the Y chromosome as follows:

• In presence of the Y chromosome, the SRY gene (Sex-determining Region of the Y chromosome) produces the protein called the testis determining factor which leads to the gonads developing as the testes. The Sertoli cells of the testis will then produce a peptide hormone, the Müllerian inhibiting substance (MIS), also known as Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), and cause the Müllerian ducts to regress.
• In absence of the Y chromosome and the SRY gene consequently, the gonads will develop as ovaries and the Mullerian duct will differentiate into the fallopian tubes and the upper part of the vagina. The WNT4 gene on the 1st chromosome promotes female sex development.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The ligament that maintains anteversion of the uterus during pregnancy is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Round ligament

The round ligament helps maintain the anteversion of the uterus during pregnancy.

However, the anteversion in the non-pregnant uterus is maintained by both the uterosacral ligament and round ligament.

Anteflexion of uterus is at the level of internal os.

Angle of anteversion
Angle of anteflexion

Angle between the cervix and vagina
Angle between cervix and uterus

90o
120o

(Mnemonic - V for version, V for vagina)

The uterus normally lies in a position of anteversion and anteflexion.

In anteversion, the external os is directed downward and backward, so that on vaginal examination, the fingers find that the lowest part of the cervix is the anterior lip.

When the uterus is retroverted, the cervix is directed downward and forward, and the lowest part of the cervix is either the external os or its posterior lip.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is altered in thyroid profile throughout pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Total T3 level

Total T3 levels are altered throughout pregnancy.

Total T3 and total T4 increase due to stimulation of thyroid tissue by hCG (α-subunit of hCG is similar to TSH) during the early period of gestation. However, there is no change in free T3 and T4 due to an increase in thyroid-binding globulin (TBG).

This leads to a transient fall in TSH (but remains in the normal range) during the early weeks of gestation. The level of TSH becomes normal during the second and third trimesters.
